News.title: Benefits cheat who swindled £44k by claiming she was single exposed by her own wedding pics on Facebook
News.content:
CAUGHT OUT Benefits cheat who swindled £44k by claiming she was single exposed by her own wedding pics on Facebook







Next

A BENEFITS cheat who swindled £44,000 by claiming to be single was caught out by her own wedding pictures on Facebook.

Judith Blackmore simply “didn’t mention” she was married when filling out the form to receive Universal Credit.



The 64-year-old was handed the benefit and a reduction on her council tax on the basis she was single and had no other income.

But Blackmore was snared after investigators saw photos of her wedding reception and honeymoon on Facebook.



She has now admitted fraud between September 2018 and June 2024 but was avoided jail and was instead handed a 16-month suspended sentence.

Hull Crown Court heard Blackmore applied for Universal Credit on October 14, 2018.

She confirmed she was single, was living with a joint tenant and had no money and savings.

Blackmore also claimed she was caring for a relative, prosecutor Holly Thompson said.

She added: “She was required to notify the DWP if she was living with a partner while she was in receipt of Universal Credit.

“She signed a declaration to confirm the information she had given was complete and correct and that she would report any changes promptly.”



On July 27, 2019, Blackmore reported a change to her address and housing costs and claimed she lived with another tenant.

But an investigation of bank statements for her and the “co-tenant” showed “financial interdependency” rather than them simply being joint tenants.

Authorities found large sums of money had been transferred between their bank accounts – including £96,000 into Blackmore’s accounts and £73,000 into his.



As a result, investigators dug into the crook’s Facebook and discovered she had been in a relationship with the man since 2013.

They also discovered photos of Blackmore’s wedding reception and her luxury honeymoon.

A marriage certificate was obtained that confirmed Blackmore had got married to the so-called tenant on May 3, 2024.

Companies House records further showed he was a director of a horsebox firm owned by Blackmore.

In total, the cheat was overpaid £44,415 – £40,023 from Universal Credit and £4,392 from council tax discount.



When questioned by the authorities, Blackmore admitted she had lived with the man for many years but denied they were in a relationship the entire time.

Julia Baggs, mitigating, said her client had debt from setting up the horsebox business.

She added: “She buried her head in the sand. It is something that she has let spiral out of control and she feels a deep sense of shame.

“She has always been a hard-working lady.”

As well as a suspended jail term, Blackmore was also ordered to carry out 120 hours of unpaid work.



Sentencing, Recorder Richard Wright KC said: “This was persistent dishonesty over a long period of time and there were numerous opportunities to cease the dishonest conduct.

“You persisted in deliberately obtaining money which you knew full well you were not entitled to obtain.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“That money was not, of course, free money. It comes from hardworking taxpayers to provide a safety net. Over a persistent period of time, you were stealing something in the region of £44,000 – a significant sum of money.

“This was a case of multiple false declarations over a considerable period of time. I accept that you are ashamed and remorseful.”

News.title: Inside nine-year Putney Pusher mystery from chilling vid to royal link… & how prime suspect was found before shock death
News.content:
Next

A JOGGER charges towards a woman on a busy London bridge before appearing to knock her straight into the path of an oncoming bus.

The driver swerves with inches to spare, narrowly avoiding crushing her beneath the wheels. It was a few seconds of CCTV that sparked one of Britain’s most enduring mysteries: who was the Putney Pusher?



Police spent years chasing leads and arrested three men, but nobody was ever charged.



Then, nine years later, detectives arrested wealthy banker and former Army officer Nicholas Brandram over the notorious attack.

Now the 44-year-old has been found dead at a home in West London.

It comes days after the police confirmed that the suspect had been released under investigation.

Here, we reveal how the Putney Pusher mystery unfolded, from the innocent men caught up in the hunt to the fresh information which put detectives on the trail of Brandram.

It began on an otherwise ordinary Friday morning in May 2017.



At around 7.40am, the 33-year-old victim was walking across Putney Bridge in south-west London on her way to work when a jogger came running towards her.

CCTV showed the pair approaching each other on the pavement before the runner appeared to veer towards her and knock her into the road.

She stumbled off the curb and fell directly into the path of a number 430 double-decker bus.

Driver Olivier Salbris swerved sharply, bringing the 12-ton vehicle to a stop just inches from her.

A passenger got off to help the woman, who escaped with minor injuries.



Salbris later said: “If I hadn’t swerved, I would have smashed her head.

“It was a reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her – and for me.”

The jogger though kept running.

Around 15 minutes later, police said he came back across the bridge in the opposite direction.

The victim recognised him and tried to speak to him about what had happened, but he did not acknowledge her and carried on.



It was the last reported sighting of the man who became known as the Putney Pusher.

For three months, detectives had little to go on.

On August 8, Scotland Yard released the CCTV and appealed for help identifying the jogger.

He was described as white, in his early to mid-30s, with short brown hair, brown eyes and an athletic build.



He was wearing a light grey T-shirt, dark blue shorts and grey trainers.

The footage went around the world and names began pouring in.

One of them was American investment banker Eric Bellquist, then 41, who was arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm.



His name became public, but Bellquist’s lawyers soon produced what they described as “irrefutable proof” that he had been in the US on May 5, so he was ruled out.

Two other men were arrested during the investigation and also released without charge.

Detectives ultimately looked at more than 50 people of interest, researching and reviewing each before eliminating them.

In June 2018, the Met admitted it had run out of leads.

All reasonable lines of inquiry had been exhausted and the investigation was closed.



But the strange footage was not forgotten.

For almost eight years, there was no public sign of movement in the police investigation.

That changed this summer.

A fresh tip-off led detectives to speak to the former partner of millionaire banker Nicholas Brandram.

His arrest followed his separation from his second wife, with whom he had a young son.



The family is believed to have lived in Fulham, not far from Putney Bridge.

It is understood police were contacted by someone close to his estranged wife with information about the Putney Pusher.

Information she gave police was reported to have played a part in what followed.

On June 15, officers arrested Brandram at his £1.4million West London home on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm.

The 44-year-old was a director at a private bank and a former British Army captain who had served overseas during an eight-year military career.



He had been awarded the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal and was a descendant of Queen Victoria.

Officers searching his property also allegedly found suspected drugs.

Once in custody, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of possessing Class A and Class B drugs.

The substances were reported to be cocaine and cannabis.

He was bailed while both investigations continued.



Earlier this month, the Met confirmed his bail had been cancelled and he had been released under investigation.

Brandram had not been charged and police had not established that he was the jogger seen in the CCTV.

Days later, he was found dead.

Police and paramedics were called to an address in Chiswick, West London, at 7.12pm on Tuesday after Brandram was found unresponsive. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

His death is being treated as unexpected but is not believed to be suspicious.



The Met said: “At 19.12hrs on Tuesday, 15 September officers and the London Ambulance Service attended an address in Chiswick, Hounslow after a man was found unresponsive inside a property.

“Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed.

“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.

“A file will be prepared for the coroner in due course.”

A London Ambulance Service spokesperson added: “We were called at 7.55pm on Tuesday 15 September to reports of an incident.



“We sent resources to the scene including an ambulance crew, a paramedic in a fast response car, an advanced paramedic and a clinical team manager.

“Very sadly, a person was pronounced dead at the scene.”

News.title: Migrant arrested in Ceuta after ‘slashing 17-year-old’s face with knife’ as locals fume over lack of deportations
News.content:
Next

A MIGRANT has been arrested in Ceuta for allegedly stabbing a 17-year-old’s face with a knife.

Local outrage in the Spanish territory is continuing to spiral over the lack of deportations and plans to house up to 10,000 people in the enclave.



Two migrants were arrested this morning – with one accused of slashing a teenager with a blade.

The other was detained on suspicion of burglary.



Police said the alleged stabbing ordeal took place at 3am after receiving reports of an assault near the Trampolin settlement.

The suspect has been accused of cutting a young man’s face with a knife.



Local cops arrested him at the scene.

It comes amid reports only 307 migrants have been deported since the mass border crossing from Morocco in July.



The country’s socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez has also announced plans to house up to 10,000 migrants in the city.

Around 80,000 people swam and stormed across the border in just 24 hours at the end of July.

The city, with a population of just 84,000 itself, was completely overwhelmed.

With nothing to eat, and nowhere to sleep or defecate apart from on streets or beaches, most left voluntarily in the days after the mass border crossing.

But nearly 10,000 migrants remain, many sleeping in shacks which now cover the city’s beaches.



More than 4,000 people have already been put up in temporary accommodation by the Spanish government.

More than 4,000 people have been put up in temporary accommodation by the Spanish government.

As terrified locals cower in their homes, Sánchez said the crisis could last as long as the end of this year.

He told TV show El Intermedio on Tuesday that 6,000 migrants will be housed by the end of this week, adding: “We hope to have stabilised the situation by the end of the year.”

307 migrants have been deported, according to the head of the unified command Ángel Víctor Torres.



More than 5,000 have returned to Morocco voluntarily, he said. The rest are waiting to be processed.

Torres said around 90 per cent of those remaining in the Spanish enclave are from North Africa and will ultimately be sent home.

They must first be processed and will be housed in the government accommodation announced by Sanchez.

It comes after bombshell documents reveal Spanish spies had warned about social media calls for a mass migrant crossing from Morocco the day before tens of thousands charged into Ceuta.

Sánchez insisted that the border breach had been impossible to predict.



But opposition parties claimed the documents prove the government misled the public.

They uncovered a warning given by the country’s National Intelligence Service (CNI) to Moroccan and Ceuta authorities.

Police and central government representation in Ceuta were also warned about the messages.

The report warned that social media groups reaching some 180,000 people were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.

One such message read: “Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

At least 100 people died during the crossing.

Sánchez had told the Spanish parliament that there was “no information that conveyed the magnitude” of the “crisis we were going to suffer”.

News.title: UK weather: Brits to enjoy ‘final taste of summer’ next week with temperatures expected to reach 25C
News.content:
Next

BRITS are set to indulge in the “final taste of summer” next week as temperatures are expected to hit 25C.

Wetter, colder and cloudier conditions have marked the beginning of September after a warm and dry summer.

The Met Office has forecast “warmer-than-average” weather moving into next week, with some regions experiencing 25C highs on Monday.



A transition to drier and brighter weather is expected to begin on Sunday and Monday, with the pleasant conditions lasting until the end of the week.



According to the Met Office: “These temperatures would be notably warm for late September and could offer a final taste of summer before autumn becomes more firmly established.”

From midday today, rain is expected to begin clearing from the southeast, leaving the south with a mostly dry and sunny rest of the day, while some heavy showers and strong winds continue in the north.

By this evening, showers will mainly have faded across the central and eastern areas of the UK, with longer periods of rain continuing in the west and north.



Moving into the weekend, Scotland is forecast to be hit by the heaviest rainfall, with patchy rain expected in the south and west.

Once the changeable conditions are over, vast parts of the country will enjoy a drier and sunnier Sunday and Monday.

Peak temperatures will be recorded at the start of the week in the south of England, with London, Reading and Cambridge all forecast for 25C highs at 4pm on Monday.



Even larger swathes of the country, including Glasgow, Manchester and Plymouth will enjoy temperatures of at least 20C at that time, alongside Birmingham reaching 24C.

Warm sunshine will persist through the middle of next week, with temperatures across the country ranging from the high teens and early twenties between Tuesday and Thursday.

London is forecast to hit a high of 24C next Friday, with peak temperatures remaining in the low twenties until the beginning of October.

News.title: Psychedelic pop artist Peter Max whose work epitomised 60s ‘flower power’ movement dies aged 88 after dementia battle
News.content:
ARTIST GONE Psychedelic pop artist Peter Max whose work epitomised 60s ‘flower power’ movement dies aged 88 after dementia battle







Next

PSYCHEDELIC pop art icon Peter Max, whose work epitomised the 1960s “summer of love” movement, has died aged 88.

Close friend Michael Pagnotta, who has worked for Peter since the 80s, said he died in a Manhattan hospital after a long battle with dementia.



He said that Peter is survived by his children, Adam and Max, who “loved him very much”.

Peter’s trippy posters of flowers, butterflies, rainbows and planets sold millions, making him one of the most successful artists of his time.



The counterculture icon was famed for his brightly-coloured portraits of everyone from Bob Dylan and Princess Diana to Barack Obama and Taylor Swift.

Pagnotta said: “He had a very expansive mind. As much as the Beatles provided a soundtrack for the era and generation, Peter visualised it and just exploded onto the scene in the late 1960s.

“Whatever kind of post-war optimism existed in the country, even though it was very turbulent times, Peter was able to capture that and marry it to that spiritual eastern magical mystery thing, and it worked perfectly.

“And he believed in the mass appeal of what he was doing. He believed in making art accessible to people.”

His son Adam wrote: “We will remember his extraordinary creativity, his warmth, his curiosity, and the way he saw beauty and possibility everywhere.

“His art became part of American culture, but the man behind that art – the father we knew and loved – is the person we will miss most.”



The German-American artist began his career as a graphic designer, who captured the essence of the 1960s “summer of love”.

Peter, who has been a teetotaler since 1966, said he used yoga to expand his mind and inspire his psychedelic art.

He once said: “I see everything through rainbow eyes.”



A prolific worker, Peter served as the official artist of the Olympics, the Super Bowl, the Indianapolis 500, the World Cup, the World Series, and many other events.

He also created the logo for MTV in the 1980s, as well as marketable work that was licensed for many consumer products, from shower curtains to planes and cruise ships, and even a line of art clocks.

Born Peter Max Finkelstein in Berlin in 1937, his family left Germany during the rise of the Nazis, traveling through Asia, the Middle East and Paris, before settling in New York when he was 16.

He studied art at the city’s prestigious School for Visual Arts and the Pratt Institute, and then opened his own design studio.

Peter’s unique style became a hit and spawned a booming commercial business.



He reflected: “My work was really, I would say, almost exploited. It was on mugs, it was on bedsheets, it was on dresses, it was on silks and scarves and ties – 70 product lines.”

And that success brought its challenges later in his career.

In 1998, he was sentenced to community service teaching art in Harlem and a $30,000 (£22k) fine after prosecutors charged him with concealing $714,000 (£532k) in income from art sales between 1988 and 1991.



In his plea, Peter acknowledged bartering art for real estate and hiding income to buy real estate in Southampton, the US Virgin Islands, the city and upstate New York.

In the last decade, disputes over his treatment and ownership of his art landed in court.

The artist’s family and friends traded “lurid allegations of kidnapping, hired goons, attempted murder” and moneymaking schemes, the New York Times reported.

One major source of income and lawsuits has reportedly been in champagne-fuelled art auctions on board major cruise lines.

But those sales drew lawsuits from buyers who said the art they received didn’t meet their expectations.



Max told the outlet in 2019 that he was “wowed by the universe.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “I love colour. I love painting. I love shapes. I love composition. I love the people all around me. I’m adoring it all.

“My legacy is in the hands of other people.”

News.title: Moment thug is taken down by police dog after stabbing man twice with huge zombie knife in street attack after row
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a thug who stabbed a man twice with a huge zombie knife was dramatically taken down by a police dog.

Luke Hurdowar, 23, pulled up his car alongside the victim, who was known to him, in Ilkeston, Derbyshire, at around noon on June 26.



CCTV footage starts by showing the pair in a heated argument before the shirtless victim started throwing punches at Hurdowar on Cotmanhay Road.

But instead of backing off or engaging in a fist-fight the cowardly knifeman moved away from his car before reaching into the waistband of his trousers.



He was caught on camera pulling out a 30cm blade before he launched a brutal attack.

Disturbing footage captured the exact moment the thug lashed out with the weapon in the brazen street attack.

He stabbed the man twice, leaving him to collapse on the pavement while bleeding heavily.

Hurdowar was then seen on CCTV quickly getting into his car and driving away.



The injured man was rushed to hospital for treatment while Hurdowar fled the scene.

Cops later found Hurdowar travelling in the same car nearby but he attempted to flee on foot from an officer and police dog into a park

Body-cam captured the officer and police dog Ultor giving chase before the canine caught up and dragged the suspect to the ground.



Hurdowar, of no fixed address, was arrested, charged and remanded the following day.

He later admitted wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and possession of a bladed article.

Hurdowar was jailed for three years and nine months at Derby Crown Court on September 2.

Detective Constable Danielle Causer, of Derbyshire Police, said: “This was a brazen attack in the middle of the day on a summer afternoon.

“Although it was a targeted assault there were members of the public nearby at the time, including children.



“No-one should be made to feel that the streets they walk on with their children are unsafe and Hurdowar showed complete disregard for anyone else that day.

“Had there not been people around to come to the victim’s aid in the immediate aftermath of this incident, the outcome could have been very different.

“The effects of knife crime are felt far beyond the immediate victims, and we remain committed to tackling those who carry knives.”

News.title: Female tourist, 37, mauled by shark in horror attack during dolphin viewing trip in the Bahamas
News.content:
SHARK HORROR Female tourist, 37, mauled by shark in horror attack during dolphin viewing trip in the Bahamas







Next

A TOURIST has been mauled by a shark in a savage attack during a dolphin excursion.

The Austrian woman, 37, sustained serious injuries when the predator sank its teeth into her right leg in the waters off North Bimini, in the Bahamas.



She was rushed to hospital following the terrifying incident on Monday afternoon, where she remains for further treatment.

The Royal Bahamas Police Force are investigating the attack.



They said: “The initial report indicates that she was participating in a dolphin excursion approximately three nautical miles off the coast of North Bimini when the incident occurred.

“The woman reportedly sustained serious injuries to her right ankle.

“She was subsequently airlifted to New Providence.”

Authorities have not said what type of shark was involved in the attack.

Bimini is the closest point in the Bahamas to the mainland United States, with its waters home to a plethora of predators.

Despite the Bahamas being marketed as a paradise for beachgoers, the country has one of the highest rates of shark attacks in the world.



Roughly 40 shark species, including bull sharks, tiger sharks and hammerheads, prowl its crystal waters.

According to the International Shark Attack File, there have been seven confirmed unprovoked shark attacks in the Bahamas over the last decade.

Since records began in 1947, a total of 28 attacks have been recorded -meaning a quarter of all recorded incidents have occurred within the last 10 years.

The most common species in these incidents were bull and tiger sharks.

In August, an American tourist was left fighting for their life after being attacked by a shark while spearfishing in the Bahamas.



The 63-year-old man was mauled by the beast near Big Grand Cay.

He sustained “severe injuries”, according to the Royal Bahamas Police Force and was airlifted to hospital.

In June an American boy was rushed to hospital after he was savaged by a shark in front of his horrified family in the Bahamas.

The 12-year-old was in the popular Exuma Cays area when the attack happened, according to the Royal Bahamas Police Force.

Authorities said the boy had been swimming with his brother during a family tour when the shark struck.



His shocked family were forced to watch the horror unfold before the injured child was hurried onto a boat and transported to New Providence for medical treatment.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Worldwide, there were 65 unprovoked shark bites recorded in 2025 out of 105 shark-human interactions, according to the International Shark Attack File.

Experts advise swimmers to stay in groups, avoid areas with schools of fish and steer clear of the water at dawn or dusk, when sharks are most active.

News.title: Poland shuts two airports and suspends all flights ‘due to military operations’ after Russian strikes on Ukraine
News.content:
Next

POLAND was today forced to shut down major airports and suspend dozens of flights amid a “military operation” in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine.

Explosions were reported close to the Polish-Ukrainian border while thousands of attack threat alerts were sounded in the region.



Two airports in Lublin and Rzeszow were suspended due to “operations of military aviation”, authorities said.

The Polish Armed Forces said the operations were “in connection with strikes carried out by the Russian Federation using jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles on the western territory of Ukraine“.



They added: “Ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness.”

The actions were aimed at “securing airspace and its protection especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions”, the military said.

Both airports have since resumed operations following the temporary closure.

An urgent aerial threat alert was also sent to thousands of residents in eastern Poland during the chaos today.



Ukrainian officials said multiple explosions were also heard just kilometres from the border with Poland.

Warsaw’s latest air defence deployment is the third so far this week following intensified Russian attacks across the whole of Ukraine.

Meanwhile, tensions between Nato and Russia are continuing to boil over.



Fears of all-out war with Moscow have been brewing – particularly after a suspected targeted attack on Boris Johnson and several European leaders last week.

The Kremlin is increasingly targeting its neighbouring states in a reckless bid to pressure the military alliance into pulling its support for Ukraine.

Earlier this week, Nato jets scrambled to shoot down a drone in Lithuania after the latest suspected incursion into the Baltic states.

Just hours earlier chaos broke out in the Baltic sea, where a Russian frigate fired flares at a Danish defence helicopter and another drone washed up on a Polish beach.

The triple overnight threat came amid growing concern about Russian aggression across the Baltic states – Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia.



Just last week Moscow threatened a “devastating” response after Nato activated its Baltic-air policing mission to deter drone incursions near Estonia.

There have been at least a dozen drone alerts along Nato’s eastern flank over the past two months.

Germany explicitly held Moscow responsible for a botched drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport in August.

Close Putin aide and former FSB chief Nikolai Patrushev declared Tuesday that Russia could obliterate Poland in “two or three days”.

Patrushev’s threats came as Poland responded to a Russian drone attack just two miles from its border on Sunday.



Kyiv suggested the attack was targeting a previous “diplomatic” train carrying high-profile figures including former UK PM Boris Johnson.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned: “These coming weeks and months will be a time of very intensified actions on the Russian side, and unfortunately we cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory.”

Several political leaders and intelligence agencies in Nato have warned of an imminent possible escalation against Poland or one of the Baltic states.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Intensifying Russian aggression towards the West this summer culminated in CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Moscow on August 25.

Ratcliffe reportedly warned the Kremlin not to attack Nato member states during his visit.

News.title: Palace in war of words with Earl Spencer over claims in Diana book
News.content:
Buckingham Palace is in a war of words with Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, over a controversial memoir about her life and death.

King Charles is accused of insensitively saying to Earl Spencer, in the wake of Diana's death in 1997, that "we'll forget her soon enough", according to excerpts published in the Daily Mail.

But the Palace has pushed back unusually strongly, angered by the claims and attempting to cast doubt on them.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.

The language is reminiscent of Queen Elizabeth's unexpectedly firm response to claims of racism by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in 2021, with the comment that "recollections may vary".

And the row threatens to overshadow a very crowded day for the royals - with the King, Prince William and Catherine attending events and Prince Harry making his first big appearance since returning to the UK.

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, to be published next week, seems set to reopen a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family - written from the perspective of her own Spencer family.

The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's sudden death. And this book will give an insider's view on those events.

In the published excerpt, Earl Spencer claims the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession.

Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

It's a claim that's being rejected by the Palace, who see it as being entirely out of character for a man with a deeply compassionate nature, who at the time was dealing with his own grief and that of their two sons.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a truck in the Netherlands.

Julian Payne, the monarch's former communications secretary, told the BBC that the King's apparent comments in the book were "just not language that I recognise".

He said the "highly unusual" statement from the Palace demonstrated the "strength of feeling that there must have been for them to feel that they needed to go out there and correct it".

News.title: 'Everybody was as one': Rector reflects on search effort for Noah Woods
News.content:
The love shown by a community who rallied to search for missing three-year-old Noah Woods was a "thread of positivity" amongst the tragedy, a rector has said.

Noah disappeared from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday after becoming separated from a relative.

At least 1,300 people helped to try to find him in the following 24 hours, before a child's body was discovered on Wednesday afternoon at a nearby pond.

The Reverend Chris Willis said: "Everybody was as one... what we saw throughout was a real coming together of people and a willingness to work together which, in spite of the deep sadness, was a thread of real positivity seeing how people cared."

News.title: 'I can get more time - that's everything': Breast cancer patients get life-extending drug
News.content:
The BBC understands that the drug companies Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca have not substantially lowered their prices since the drug was first rejected.

The reason NICE has reversed its decision is largely because of a trade deal with the USA, where the UK government agreed to spend 25% more on medicines.

As part of this, NICE has increased how much the NHS will pay for every extra year of good quality life a medication can give.

This is known as a QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) - and the upper threshold per QALY has gone from Â£30,000 to Â£35,000.

At the end of August, NICE also introduced a different, more nuanced, way of measuring a patient's quality of life.

These two changes were enough to tip the balance.

It is thought that patient campaigns for Enhertu - and other drugs - have helped too.

Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca welcome NICE's decision, but the latter is calling for "strong collaboration" across the healthcare system to ensure "faster, more equitable patient access in the future".

Breast Cancer Now's Claire Rowney says: "We are calling on the government, NICE, NHS England and the pharmaceutical industry to work together to fix this broken system, so that people with incurable metastatic breast cancer are not forced to spend precious months and years campaigning for treatments that could give them more time."

Helen Knight, director of medicines evaluation at NICE, says she is pleased a "commercial solution" means the treatment can be made available on the NHS in England but adds she knows the decision "comes too late for many families".

"Our role is important in ensuring NHS spending on new medicines reflects the benefits they deliver while protecting valuable health resources for other essential patient services," she says.

For Kate, the thought of dying before she had to, "when there was a drug that I just could almost reach but couldn't get", was "so incredibly painful".

"To know that I can get it now is absolutely everything."

News.title: Ed Sheeran asked me to donate $2m in aid, Robert Kraft says after Macklemore backlash
News.content:
Macklemore was removed from the tour on Monday, sparking a backlash that included Sheeran's other support acts dropping out in protest.

Sheeran has said the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoters, Messina Touring Group, not by him.

Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would refuse to let the concerts take place if he performed, meaning the tour would have been cancelled if Macklemore remained on the bill.

Sheeran, who played at Kraft's wedding in 2022, has faced criticism from some for his apparent acceptance of the decision.

In his statement on Tuesday, the singer said he respects "Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes", and that while he doesn't use his own platform for politics, that "doesn't mean I don't care" or "support causes in my own, personal way".

The singer-songwriter also said he did not want to let down his fans or crew by cancelling the tour, which is set to resume in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on Saturday.

Although some artists like Billy Bragg have called for Sheeran to scrap the tour, that would potentially leave the musician and his promoters liable for huge sums for costs including venue hire and ticket refunds.

Sheeran is able to perform solo, even if his set has to be reconfigured to compensate for the loss of Irish folk band Beoga, who previously accompanied him for several songs.

News.title: Inside Singapore's 'Fort Knox' for city's $2bn dirty money auction
News.content:
Singapore has begun auctioning off luxury goods that were seized by police in a sensational $2.2 billion money laundering case that gripped the city state in 2023.

The items are being held inside Le Freeport, a fortified storage facility, where the BBC's Vandhna Bhan was allowed inside for a look.

News.title: Balaclava boys on electric bikes: How to tackle the problem?
News.content:
From the Pentland Hills near Edinburgh to the streets of the country's biggest cities, a common menace is causing irritation, alarm and in some cases even death.

The sight of young men, their identities hidden by black balaclavas, tearing around on electric bikes or scooters is becoming a familiar one.

The picture above was taken by a man who posted on social media about "morons on electric bikes" scaring a nearby horse, external as they rode illegally on public footpaths.

Aside from being showered with gravel churned up by the "gobby" miscreants, no-one came to harm that day, but others have not been so lucky.

News.title: 'My mother apologised': A survivor's journey after genital mutilation
News.content:
Sara Kahsai grew up in Sudan but moved to Birmingham, England, in 2022 after marrying a bus driver from the city.

But as she settled into married life and her new home, she was coming to terms with a life-changing discovery.

Sara realised she was a victim-survivor of Female Genital Mutiliation (FGM), a procedure she had endured as a young girl.

She was floored by the revelation and, not least, the excruciating pain she was now beginning to fully understand.

"The shock was massive," she said.

"It made it difficult with my physical relationship with my husband - but he was very kind and very patient with me."

Warning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilation

Sara turned to the one person she knew must have orchestrated it - her mother - and asked her why.

"I was a baby. It was the culture to do it for everybody," she said her mother, still living in Africa, told her.

"When I spoke to my mum she was really upset and she apologised to me."

News.title: 'My rent was higher than my student loan' - the booming cost of private halls
News.content:
You don't have to walk far in any university city before spotting some form of private Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA).

These large blocks of student housing are springing up in cities across the UK, yet rents continue to soar and young people studying at university say they're still finding it difficult to secure a place to live.

The increase in PBSA has predominantly been driven by private companies, with many developments targeting more affluent international and postgraduate students, who industry experts say are becoming increasingly important to the sector.

Developers say they are meeting a market demand but campaigners argue that they are too expensive for most Scottish students and more affordable housing should be being built instead.

News.title: At least seven months of relentless rain needed to end drought, research shows
News.content:
Above-average rainfall is needed across England for the next seven months for all areas to recover from drought by spring 2027, according to new research.

The Environment Agency (EA) stated that despite some wet weather during the first half of September, almost three-quarters of England remains in drought following an exceptionally dry spring and summer as well as a succession of heatwaves.

It says around 120% of typical rainfall is needed between now and April for all areas to be considered out of drought.

Even under the most likely rainfall scenario - which predicts a wetter autumn than normal based on the latest Met Office forecasts - Devon and Cornwall and East Anglia could still be in drought by the start of spring 2027.

Other predictions suggest there is also roughly a one-in-four chance that around half of England will still be in drought next spring, but currently only a 1% chance of a severe drought in the coming months.

The EA defines severe drought as a situation where water shortages have extensive and lasting impacts on the environment, farming, communities and the economy, and where there may be a serious threat to public water supplies. England has not seen a severe drought since 1976.

News.title: Mum's Facebook kidney plea prompts 'mind-blowing' gift from total stranger
News.content:
A woman who shared a desperate plea for a kidney on Facebook has undergone a lifesaving transplant after a stranger offered to be her donor.

Karen Davey, 41, had exhausted every avenue before turning to social media, where she said she did not "want to leave her family without a mother".

Gary Summerfield saw the mum-of-four's post and, after learning he was a match, donated one of his kidneys via an operation in July.

"I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them," said Gary.

Karen's family said they would never be able to repay Gary for his generosity, adding that it had given her "another chance to be a mum".

The average wait for a deceased donor kidney transplant in the UK is two to three years, according to NHS Blood and Transplant, but if you have a living donor it can be about three to six months.

News.title: Boy abducted by mum has renewed 'sense of purpose'
News.content:
Alex Batty, who disappeared for six years after being abducted by his mother as a child, has described feeling a renewed "sense of purpose" after finding work.

Batty, from Oldham, was declared missing by his grandmother in 2017, aged 11, after his mother and grandfather failed to return him from a holiday in Spain and instead moved to France.

He spent the following years in isolation before he was spotted by a delivery driver in December 2023 in the foothills of the Pyrenees in the south-west of the country.

Batty, who is now 20, said his job at a waste management company had given his young family financial security.

It has been a whirlwind couple of years for Batty, whose teenage years were spent living as a nomad in France.

His mother, Melanie, who was not his legal guardian and was heavily influenced by conspiracy theories, told him to throw away his passport.

They lived off-grid and he did not attend school.

News.title: Metal detectorist finds 3,000-year-old gold bracelet 'worth up to £20k'
News.content:
Having only ever found a silver coin while metal detecting, Idris Thomas was shocked to strike gold - a late Bronze Age gold bracelet which has been declared treasure.

Believed to be about 3,000 years old, the bracelet was found to be 92.8% gold by experts from Museum Wales. Brett Hammond, CEO of Timeline Auctions, estimated its value at between Â£15,000 and Â£20,000. An official value has not yet been given.

Thomas was scanning on farmland belonging to Geraint Edwards, in Llanuwchllyn, Gwynedd, for about 20 minutes when his detector alerted him.

"I thought it was another bit of tin foil to begin with, and I just saw a flash of gold and dug a little bit around it," he said.

News.title: Boy, 13, is new voice of Thomas the Tank Engine
News.content:
A 13-year-old schoolboy has made his voice-acting debut as Thomas the Tank Engine in a new animated series.

Harry Sparkes, from Harpenden, Hertfordshire, stars in Thomas & Friends: Railway Stories alongside Crazy Rich Asians actor Henry Golding, who narrates the series in a role made famous by Sir Ringo Starr.

For nine months, Sparkes kept his weekly recording sessions secret from his classmates by telling them he was attending physiotherapy for a foot injury.

"It feels amazing, because I played and watched Thomas as a kid, and now I get to be Thomas. It just feels insane," he said.

News.title: UK prosecutors file for extradition of the Tate brothers from the US
News.content:
Prosecutors in the UK have lodged a formal request for the extradition of brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate from the US to face charges of rape and sex trafficking.

The US State Department, which received the requests last week, will review the extradition applications to make sure they comply with the existing agreement between the US and UK.

But the lawyer for the brothers, who are dual US-UK citizens, accused British authorities of failing to provide the necessary supporting documents in the request.

The brothers are facing a total of 59 charges in the UK, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child. Both men deny any wrongdoing.

The Crown Prosecution Service originally brought 21 charges, but added 38 more in July for alleged actions spanning between 2010 and 2017.

US authorities took the men into custody in July after the UK announced the new charges. The brothers lost a bid to be released from a Florida jail on bail last week.

UK authorities had until Wednesday 16 September to submit a full extradition request.

Joe McBride, the brothers' lawyer, said he would be challenging the requests, arguing they were not backed up by the information needed under the extradition agreement.

In a statement to the BBC, McBride said the brothers had also not received the extradition requests themselves, nor documents such as "a warrant, a charging document, and information that provides a reasonable basis to believe my clients committed these offences".

"This cloak-and-dagger act speaks to the deception behind these accusations and to their weakness," he added.

Once the State Department completes it review, there are still several legal steps before extradition can be permitted. Applications must go through the US Justice Department which will in turn forward it to the court, where the final decision on their extradition will be made.

During this legal process, the Tate brothers will remain in jail in the US.

An official letter from the State Department details that Andrew Tate, 39, is "wanted to stand trial in the United Kingdom" on a series of charges, including 10 counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm.

He is also accused of making and distributing indecent images of a child and possessing extreme pornography.

Charges levelled against Tristan Tate, 38, include five counts of rape, six counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, three counts of sex trafficking and a sexual assault.

Both men deny any wrongdoing.

In response to the formal request for extradition from the US, a Home Office spokesperson said: "As a matter of long-standing policy and practice, we do not routinely comment on individual cases."

The former professional kickboxers turned divisive social media influencers hold dual US and British citizenship, and had primarily been living in Romania since 2017.

They have been accused of promoting misogyny and toxic masculinity online, which has attracted a large following, particularly from young men.

Andrew Tate, who is a self-proclaimed "misogynist", first rose to fame after a 2016 appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother.

The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025.

Both brothers have denied all charges and allegations.

News.title: Real Madrid keen on Man Utd forward Gabriel, 15
News.content:
Real Madrid are among the clubs trying to sign Manchester United academy player JJ Gabriel.

Earlier this week, the 15-year-old sent United formal notice he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect, but the club can challenge the request.

It is understood a number of major teams across Europe, including Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Bayern Munich, have a firm interest in the forward, but multiple sources have described Real's efforts to sign him as strong.

The Spanish side want to recruit the teenager immediately and position him in Real Madrid Castilla - the club's recognised reserve team.

Unlike in England, Castilla play in senior football and are in the regionalised third league of the Spanish system. Last season, they were coached by Alvaro Arbeloa, who then took over the senior Real side following Xabi Alonso's dismissal and has since moved to Fulham.

Thiago Pitarch, who was 18 at the start of last season, played for Castilla in a Premier League International Cup encounter against Southampton in October, and made 16 senior appearances across the campaign.

Sources close to Gabriel, who turns 16 on 6 October, feel let down by United, arguing promises around the pathway to the first team have not been kept.

The club say it was anticipated Gabriel would become their youngest senior player by playing in Wednesday night's EFL Cup tie with Brighton. Given they lost 3-2 after leading 2-0, it is debatable whether that would have actually happened.

United have not given up hope of keeping Gabriel, though they are unsure precisely why he wants to leave.

It is understood the player is not currently training with the club.

News.title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
News.content:
The man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to being run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack.

He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation.

The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious".

Eddie Hearn has predicted that Conor Benn will soon retire from boxing, after his former ally’s emphatic loss to Ryan Garcia.

Last week, Garcia stopped Benn in the second round, retaining the WBC welterweight title in their Las Vegas main event.

Garcia, 28, dropped Benn with a hard right hook, and although the Briton beat the referee’s count, he was overwhelmed by the American, forcing the referee to stop the fight.

open image in gallery Conor Benn (left) during his stoppage loss to Ryan Garcia ( Getty )

Benn, 29, later said he was unsure what his next move will be, and that his priority is spending time with his family. He had previously suggested, however, that he will move back up to middleweight next.

In any case, Hearn has now discussed the fight, which was Benn’s second after leaving Hearn’s Matchroom promotion in a shocking move in February.

“My last few predictions were that I thought Ryan Garcia would win inside three rounds,” Hearn told iFL TV.

“I just felt [Benn] looked lost. I don’t know, didn’t really look like himself… and in the ring he looked all over the place, he looked like a rabbit in headlights.

“Listen, Conor Benn will be done in the next year or so. He may have one more fight. Who knows? He may not even fight again. He’s made his money.”

Doubling down on the sentiment, Hearn said: “Yeah, I do [think he’ll retire soon]. I think he wants his money, and he’s made a load of money. What else is there?

“He’s not gonna beat anyone of any significance at 160lb [middleweight], so what are you in the game for? He’s in the game to make money, and he’s done that.

“I don’t think he’s gonna wanna hang around in the sport of boxing; he’s got other interests, he’s got family.”

Benn and Hearn’s split was a stunning one, with Matchroom having stood by the “Destroyer” during a drug-test saga that lasted from 2022 until 2024, only for the fighter to join Hearn’s rival Dana White at Zuffa Boxing.

Benn had failed two drug tests in summer 2022 and was provisionally suspended from fighting in the UK, until he was cleared to do so again in late 2024. He maintained his innocence throughout the episode.

open image in gallery Benn dropped Chris Eubank Jr twice in the final moments of their rematch, before winning on points ( Getty )

Benn was reportedly offered $15m to sign with Zuffa on a one-fight deal, and his promotional debut came against Regis Prograis in April. On the undercard of Tyson Fury’s win over Arslanbek Makhmudov, Benn outpointed the former world champion, who was boxing at a career-highest weight and retired after the bout. Benn then extended his Zuffa deal and faced Garcia.

His likeliest next move is a trilogy bout with Chris Eubank Jr, with whom he traded middleweight wins in 2025. Eubank Jr outpointed Benn in April, before his bitter rival returned the favour in November – scoring two knockdowns along the way.

Eubank Jr, 36, was quick to mock Benn after his loss to Garcia, while middleweight champion Denzel Bentley this week offered Benn a shot at his WBO belt.

British doubles specialist Joe Salisbury has announced his retirement from professional tennis at the age of 34.

The six-time Grand Slam doubles champion – with four men’s doubles majors and two mixed doubles triumphs – reached the semi-finals of the US Open men’s doubles last week with long-term partner Rajeev Ram.

Yet four months after returning to the game following a five-month break due to anxiety, the Putney-local has decided to call time on his impressive career and disclosed the news via an emotional post on Instagram.

open image in gallery Joe Salisbury (left) played alongside Andy Murray for Great Britain in the Davis Cup ( PA Wire )

"I’ve decided I’m retiring from professional tennis,” he said. “I’ve been thinking about it for a while and am now very happy with the decision.

"Tennis has been my life for as long as I can remember and I have been incredibly fortunate to have had all the opportunities, experiences and success that I have. To be able to travel the world and call playing tennis my job has been a dream come true and I never believed I could have lived the life and had the career that I have.

“I gave it my all and know I can be proud and look back with no regrets.”

After attending college at the University of Memphis, Salisbury got his big break in 2018 (aged 26) when he reached the semi-finals of the men’s doubles at Wimbledon with Frederik Nielsen.

Salisbury then linked up with American player Ram, with whom he won four Grand Slams: the 2020 Australian Open, followed by US Open victories in 2021, 2022 and 2023. The pair also reached world No 1 in 2022 and won the ATP Tour Finals in 2022 and 2023.

open image in gallery Salisbury (left) won four men's doubles Grand Slams with Rajeev Ram ( Getty )

The Briton also won two mixed doubles majors: the 2021 French Open and 2021 US Open with American player Desirae Krawczyk. Salisbury also represented Great Britain in Davis Cup and at the 2020 and 2024 Olympic Games.

He added: "The best thing about it all has been the people I’ve met along the way and shared these times with and many of them will be the closest people to me for the rest of my life.

“I feel so lucky to have had so much amazing support and there are too many people to mention but I am grateful to you all. A special thanks to my parents, Natalie, Rajeev, Justin, Louis, Dave, TC, Ed and the LTA. Without all of you I could not have done this so thank you.

“I’m not sure what’s next for me but I know I have so much to look forward to and so much to be happy right now and I know that all the highs and lows, good times and bad on this crazy tennis journey have made me a stronger and better person."

The Bank of England has kept interest rates at 3.75 per cent, despite mounting pressure to hike rates after an uptick in inflation.

The vote is the final one before next month’s Budget and marks the sixth time in a row that the central bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) has kept rates on hold.

Most analysts now predict the rise will come in November – 11 months on from when rates last moved, when they were pushed downwards from 4 per cent.

The MPC’s vote was once again 6-3, signalling that several members believe a bump in rates is required to offset the rise in inflation, which has been largely driven by higher energy costs due to the Iran war.

But the wider domestic picture has been tricky for the BoE to navigate this year. While the economy has grown slightly more than expected, unemployment is still hovering at 5 per cent, inflation has pushed up to 3.1 per cent and job vacancies are falling. These factors, as well as slowing wage growth, typically argue the case to send rates in different directions – leaving a tough balancing act.

Many economists are also forecasting the cost-of-living to rise further, with households facing another rise in their energy bills from next month – which could prompt the Bank to raise interest rates in the months ahead.

There continues to be “little evidence” in second-round inflation effects from the rise in energy costs, the BoE noted in its meeting minutes, but that came with a caveat pointing to the likelihood of future hikes: “the risk of such [inflationary] effects, against which [interest rates] policy needs to lean, is greater the longer higher energy prices persist.”

Despite the base rate not moving, a recent spike in two-year gilts and swap rates mean mortgage prices have also risen across most major lenders, with experts continually warning homeowners to secure a new deal early once they are in the final six months of their existing ones.

Money markets are still pricing in three interest rate hikes, but economists do not presently expect that to translate to more than two actual votes to raise them between now and the end of 2027.

“It’s what’s coming down the line that could shake up people’s finances,” said George Sweeney, personal finance expert at Finder.

“We’ve already seen the mortgage market take a turn, with five major lenders raising rates on the same day this week. This has largely happened because of issues in the bond markets, but the current sentiment from the BoE suggests interest rate hikes are very likely in the near future - with some reports suggesting we could hit at least 4 per cent before the end of the year. This could push mortgage rates even higher.

“Unfortunately, price rises are heating up too, and the latest inflation reading will offer no respite for those who were holding out hope for possible base rate cuts. The interest rate climate isn’t in dire straits just yet, but the data appears to be heading in the wrong direction.”

South African police revealed on Thursday that a ninth woman’s body has been discovered in an area east of Johannesburg, and said it could be linked to a series of killings they are investigating.

All nine bodies were found in the Ekurhuleni municipality over the last two months, raising concerns that they were carried out by the same person or people.

Police previously said that some similarities in the killings of the first eight victims were “sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning.”

The discoveries have sent shock waves around the country, sparked a high-level investigation and highlighted the scourge of femicide and high levels of violent crime.

Here's what to know about the murders and the police investigation.

What happened in the latest killing?

Police said the discovery of the latest body early Thursday “will be added to the investigations into the deaths of women in Ekurhuleni.”

Provincial police commissioner Fred Kekana said a passerby found the woman’s body near a construction site and alerted police.

The unidentified woman appeared to be about 30 and had an apparent stab wound to her side, while her throat appeared to have been cut, he said. Forensic investigators had not yet determined the official cause of death.

open image in gallery South African Police Service (SAPS) officers stand guard at the crime scene where the body of a woman was discovered in Boksburg. ( AFP/Getty )

Kekana said police had not established whether her death was linked to the other cases and appealed for information from the public.

He also urged people not to circulate photographs of the bodies or unverified reports on social media, warning that they were spreading fear and could encourage copycat crimes.

A multidisciplinary team of experts has been assigned to investigate the cases and identify those responsible. Police appealed to the public for information.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi said police were pursuing leads and making progress in two or three cases, although he did not provide details. He urged the public to give investigators time to gather sufficient evidence.

“They’ve declared war against the state. We’ll respond,” Lesufi told reporters at the scene. “We’re not going to surrender.”

Police looking into whether a serial killer was responsible

The Gauteng provincial commissioner Fred Kekana said on Wednesday that police are examining whether the cases are linked, but warned against prematurely describing the deaths as the work of one perpetrator or a serial killer.

“Investigators are considering all possibilities, including the possibility of multiple suspects or separate perpetrators,” he said. “Police are comparing the evidence, timelines, locations, victim profiles and circumstances of each case before reaching conclusions.”

open image in gallery People gather and point in the direction of the crime scene where the body of a woman was discovered in Boksburg on September 17, 2026. ( AFP/Getty )

However, he pointed out that the similarities and proximity of the locations where they were found was concerning.

So far, the bodies had been found across several Ekurhuleni communities, including Kempton Park, Pomona, Clayville, Olifantsfontein, Rhodesfield, and Dawn Park.

Some of the bodies discovered more recently were in Olifantsfontein and Kwa-Thema areas, respectively about 25 kilometers (15 miles) and 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Kempton Park, where the first five bodies were discovered.

“While investigations are still underway and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations,” said Kekana.

The victims were all young women

The last eight victims were between the ages of 20 and 38, and all were found either naked or partially clothed with bruises on their bodies, according to the police.

The first body was discovered on 17 July, naked and restrained with cable ties. A suspect believed to have been the victim's boyfriend was arrested and remains in custody, according to the police.

One of the victims was identified as 38-year-old runner Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who went missing last week.

She was reported missing after her 8-year-old daughter alerted family members that she had not returned from her daily afternoon jog, and was found dead several days later.

open image in gallery Members of the South African Police Service (SAPS) Forensic Pathology Services work on the crime scene where the body of a woman was discovered in Boksburg ( AFP/Getty )

The body that was recovered in Olifantsfontein on Tuesday was found naked and in an advanced stage of decomposition.

The youngest victim has been identified as a 20-year-old woman.

High rates of femicide and violent crime

The recent deaths have highlighted high rates of femicide and violent crime in the country and sparked an outcry over the safety of women.

Between April and July this year, the country recorded 5,427 murders, which is an average of about 45 murders per day, according to the latest crime statistics.

Femicide rates in South Africa are among the highest in the world, according to the United Nations' agency for gender equality.

A study in 2022 by a South African think tank found that more than 35% of South African adult women had experienced physical or sexual violence at some point.

Police have offered a cash reward for any information to related to the murders.

Missing In Southern Africa, which supports missing people and their families, urged communities and families to report immediately when they suspected.T

he organization said the discoveries had deepened the anguish of families searching for loved ones and urged people to report disappearances immediately.“

There is no waiting period to report a missing person,” it said. “The moment you suspect that someone is missing, report it immediately to the South African Police Service.”

Nearly 10 years after the publication of the million-selling “Educated,” Tara Westover is returning with a second memoir in which she reflects on the fallout from her celebrated and controversial debut.

Random House announced Thursday that “Brothers and Sisters” will come out on April 13. It's her follow-up to “Educated,” which was released in 2018 and became one of the most talked-about memoirs of its time.

Westover's account of growing up as the youngest of seven siblings in a Mormon survivalist family in Idaho, the physical abuse allegedly suffered at the hands of an older brother and her eventual break from her family spent more than two years on The New York Times' nonfiction bestseller list. Winning wide acclaim, it was chosen by the National Book Critics Circle as a finalist in two awards categories and praised by Bill Gates and former President Barack Obama, both of whom placed it on their lists of favorite books of 2018.

In “Brothers and Sisters,” Westover writes about her parents' disputing her memories and her siblings denying events in “Educated” that they had previously confirmed.

“'Brothers and Sisters' is a story of how memories are held in a family. How someone can know you are telling the truth but still say you are lying,” the publisher's announcement reads in part. “Ultimately, it is a story of what it means to grow up — to outlive the story that made you.”

Westover, who turns 40 later this month, was admitted to Brigham Young University as a scholarship student and later received a doctorate in intellectual history from Trinity College in Cambridge, England. In 2021, then-President Joe Biden awarded her a National Humanities Medal for serving “as a powerful example of how the humanities can set people — and a Nation — free.”

News.content:

Liverpool’s midfield have veered from the maligned to the magnificent. Some of the issues in Andoni Iraola’s start to life at Anfield have come in the centre of the park, but some of the highlights have been provided by the men deployed there.

Dominik Szoboszlai added to his compendium of glorious goals on Wednesday, a half-volley from 30 yards against Tottenham. “I was thinking, ‘why not?’” he said, with a certain understatement. “So I just took a shot and hit it quite well.”

Four days earlier, though, Liverpool had been lacklustre against Fulham. Szoboszlai won only one of his 10 duels that day. Against Atletico Madrid, they had initially struggled in midfield but triumphed with a wonder goal from a midfielder, in Alexis Mac Allister.

open image in gallery Dominik Szoboszlai scored a thunderbolt against Spurs ( PA )

The opener at St James’ Park had featured two Newcastle goals when Liverpool’s midfield partnership of Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch were caught upfield as the ball was lost, but a draw was rescued by the Hungarian’s 99th-minute penalty. Iraola has noted he has goalscoring midfielders and so far they have delivered five of Liverpool’s 11 goals this season.

Szoboszlai feels the men in the middle have been misunderstood; or at least their roles have been. Iraola’s formation is often described as 4-2-3-1, sometimes as 4-1-4-1. Szoboszlai insists it does not have two holding midfielders.

“You guys see a little bit different because we play with one [No] 6, one [No] 8 and one [No] 10,” he explained. “So the [No] 6 and the [No] 8 are not next to each other, the [No] 8 is a little bit higher and the [No] 6 is a little bit deeper and the [No] 10 is a little bit even higher [than the No 8] so it is not two next to each other.”

open image in gallery Andoni Iraola has delpoyed Szoboszlai in a number of different roles ( PA )

Often used as the No 8, he has a licence to get forward. It is certainly what he likes to do and, with 16 goals since the start of last season, something he excels at, but the accusation is that Szoboszlai can lack positional discipline.

After the stalemate with Fulham, his defensive efforts were faulted. Szoboszlai claimed it was news to him. “Was there criticism?” he asked. “I don’t know, I didn’t see but thanks for telling me.”

Nevertheless, he gestured to his ear when he scored against Tottenham. He insisted it was not a pointed rejoinder to his doubters. “Just for myself,” he said. “I just decided before the game and I just did it.”

open image in gallery Szoboszlai pointed to his ear during his celebration of a goal against Spurs ( PA )

There was nevertheless a message. Szoboszlai’s best is so good that it can generate high expectations. His fitness record indicates that he always plays. He argued he cannot always play brilliantly.

“We are also humans so we can have bad games, we can have bad days and I think never ever was [there] a player who played every game of his life [well],” he said. “It’s always balance. There will be games where we are not playing at our best as a team, personally me or somebody else, but, trust me, it is always leave the past and then [move on to] the next one.”

Liverpool, too, are amid a search for balance. Szoboszlai forms part of the conundrum. He has a skill-set that equips him to occupy half of the outfield positions in Iraola’s side. While the Basque has Florian Wirtz as a specialist No 10, Szoboszlai was a title winner in that position and seems Iraola’s second choice to operate off the main striker.

When Mohamed Salah was dropped last autumn, it was Szoboszlai who was shunted to the right wing. He won Liverpool’s player-of-the-year award for a campaign when he was often, and increasingly to his annoyance, at right-back. He finished the draw with Nottingham Forest there.

open image in gallery Szoboszlai and Florian Wirtz may end up competing for the same position ( Getty )

“Last week against Fulham I was a No 8,” he said. “I have been No 2 as well, I have been No 6, No 8, No 10, No 7.” The sense is that his preference is for the role reflected by his shirt number – 8 – but Szoboszlai sounded diplomatic. “I just want to be on the pitch,” he said.

Maybe, though, he is at his best in particular parts of it. In Iraola’s thinking, the defensive midfield role appears to be between Gravenberch and Mac Allister, with Liverpool looking far better with the Argentinian in the side. Szoboszlai’s credentials for the deeper role may have been dented by his display against Fulham.

He can be sardonic and he can be spiky and, after being informed of his statistics on Saturday, remembered them. “Maybe I am not at the best in the [No] 6 position because I win one of the 10 duels,” he said. “Maybe the next game I am going to win eight out of 10, so I am then a good [No] 6?”

Cinema firm Vue is considering a float on London’s stock market or a potential sale deal after a strong summer at the box office.

The company, one of the UK’s largest cinema chains, could be reportedly valued at up to £1.5 billion in an initial public offering (IPO).

Vue confirmed that it has hired advisers from Rothschild to consider strategic options, including a potential private sale or IPO.

A company spokesman added: “No decision has been made so there is nothing further to comment on at this stage.

“Vue enters this period from a position of strength and the global cinema business has broken countless records in 2026.

“We have delivered consistent year-on-year growth in recent years, gaining market share and cementing our position as Europe’s largest privately owned cinema operator.

“Cinema is not just back, it is back for good and Vue is leading from the front.”

It came after the Financial Times reported that the company’s backers, which include asset management firm Barings and hedge fun Farallon Capital, would favour an IPO.

Founder and chief executive of the group Tim Richards indicated that both a float and private sale are being consider in order to provide a potential exit for investors who took control of the chain following a debt restructuring process in 2022.

A decision is expected to take place in the coming weeks.

“If we did [an] IPO, I personally believe in the country and would want to list on the London Stock Exchange,” he told the publication.

“I’m not going into this blindly. I’ve spoken to a number of CEOs who have listed on other exchanges and the grass is not always greener.”

A float would represent a welcome boost for the London Stock Exchange following a dearth in activity so far in 2026, which many firms opting to float in the US or other markets.

The stock market has also been beset by delays to planned listings, such as for Superdrug owner AS Watson and software firm Visma.

A raft of companies, including Intertek and Beazley, have also been snapped up from the London Stock Exchange and taken private by suitors over the year.

Vue has been among cinema operators buoyed by a strong summer for film releases, with bumper audiences for films including The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

News.title: Next-generation antivenom fights India’s deadliest snakes
News.content:
The process to make antivenom has barely changed in a century: snakes are milked, their venom is injected into horses, and their antibodies are harvested to form the basis of the product. The resulting treatments are difficult to administer, can trigger severe side effects, and the quality varies from batch to batch.

“The big four snakes contribute to 70 per cent of poisonous bites [in India]… so 30 per cent of poisonous snakes are not covered, even to begin with,” said Dr Yogesh Jain, a public health physician in Chhattisgarh state and a member of The Global Snakebite Taskforce.

“But there are huge quality and efficacy issues even against these 70 per cent of bites. We’re relying on a 100-year-old technique of getting antivenoms, and at least 50,000 people are dying every year,” he told The Telegraph.

“There’s a real need for new technology. We don’t have a safe and appropriate antivenom for the largest majority of people in rural India.”

Now, scientists are hopeful that they have developed a potential alternative.

In the latest study, published last week, researchers showed that an experimental antivenom cocktail with five components protected mice against lethal doses of antivenom in Indian cobras, even when delayed by up to 20 minutes – a scenario that mimics the real-world lag between a bite and treatment.

“If you go 10 years back, people didn’t think you could make sufficiently simple products with new, modern biotechnology that could cover all these different snake venoms,” said Prof Andreas Laustsen-Kiel, head of the Section of Biologics Engineering at the Technical University of Denmark and co-author of the paper.

“People simply believed it was too complex, too expensive to manufacture, and so on… But the data we are gathering is convincing enough to say this is something that could make a huge dent in the lost lives and limbs snakebite causes every year.”

The antivenom itself was based on lab-made nanobodies – antibodies derived from a group of animals including camels, llamas and some species of shark. Scientists believe their structure means they could be a more potent, more precise, more temperature-stable alternative to man-made monoclonal antibodies – and cheaper to manufacture.

“The latest study builds on an earlier discovery of nanobodies that can protect across a broad spectrum of African snakes,” said Prof Nicholas Casewell, director of the Centre for Snakebite Research and Interventions at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, who has previously collaborated with Prof Laustsen-Kiel.

“In this paper they have iterated and demonstrated that a narrow number of nanobodies can protect against Indian cobras and king cobras. This demonstration brings the nanobody technology closer to market,” he added.

But that is likely still years away, depending on how much funding the researchers can attract. The next steps – a larger animal study, scaling up manufacture, and launching human trials – are expensive.

“If money was no issue, we could probably be testing in humans in 1.5 to three years from now,” said Prof Laustsen-Kiel. “But since money is a big issue, it is more likely that human trials won’t be able to start until 2.5 to four years from now.

“But I really think that this [study shows] there’s no doubt that biotech can deliver better antivenoms. The question is whether people are willing to fund it,” he said.
