Sports.title: Raheem Sterling’s bleak tale a reminder of absurd path young footballers face | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
“What’s your name?”

“Raheem.”

“What’s your surname?”

“Sterling.”

This is how a story ends. At 9.13 on a glorious May morning, by the side of the A327, sitting in the passenger seat of a wrecked Lamborghini, feverishly stashing canisters of nitrous oxide into the back, having to recite one’s name from scratch. A police officer asks him who was driving the car at the time it smashed into a metal pole on a country road in Hampshire. Sterling says nothing. There’s nobody sitting in the driver’s seat.

As it transpired in court in Basingstoke this week, Sterling had been up driving all night by the time police started getting calls from members of the public concerned that someone was bobbing and weaving up the M3 in an unpredictable, uncontrollable manner. And of course there is an acrid and tasteless irony in the fact that this was exactly what Sterling was known for on the pitch: weaving in and out of traffic, no order or reason to it, following a logic that existed only in his own head.

We can, and we should, and the district judge did, take an extremely dim view of the serious and life-threatening crime to which Sterling has admitted. We can also acknowledge that football is the one and only reason any of this remotely registered on our radar. You are not angry at the other dangerous drivers, whose names you do not know and will never look up. You are angry at this one in particular, a £50m footballer four years ago, now facing the possibility of prison and a sporting career that may just have come to a hard stop at the age of 31.

View image in fullscreen ‘The end of Sterling as a going concern really happened much earlier, about the time his Arsenal loan deal ended.’ Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

Yep: younger than Kepa Arrizabalaga, younger than Solly March, younger than Ariana Grande. And let’s be real, the end of Sterling as a going concern really happened much earlier, about the time his Arsenal loan deal ended and Enzo Maresca made clear he had no further use for him at Chelsea and he was made to train on his own after 8pm despite having young children, and Maresca said this was no big deal, because people in the fishing industry also work hard hours.

In a way, Sterling became a victim of the cycle he helped to catalyse. At the age of 15, he became one of the first big-money academy transfers when he moved from Queens Park Rangers to Liverpool for a fee of up to £2m. More than a decade on, the increasing emphasis on one‑on‑one duels, on straight-line speed and dynamic dribbling, on unpredictable and unmapped movement, has generated a kind of fetish for unscarred teenage footballers, a self-perpetuating market in child labour that nobody has ever really begun to question, much less challenge.

The Premier League’s centre of gravity has been shifting younger for years, to the point where last season half its players were 25 or younger. The three youngest Premier League debuts (Jeremy Monga, Max Dowman, Ethan Nwaneri) have taken place since 2022. Farther afield players such as Lamine Yamal (La Liga debut at 15) and Cavan Sullivan (Major League Soccer debut at 14) have begun to normalise the trope of the child footballer, the athlete propelled to global superstardom before they can legally buy a vape.

This week it has been widely reported that JJ Gabriel, a talented and highly coveted 15-year-old attacking midfielder, has demanded to leave the Manchester United academy. Let’s assume for the sake of argument that Gabriel didn’t walk into the offices of the Daily Telegraph and plant this story himself. So what we really have here, in essence, is an entire locus of gossip – briefings, counter-briefings, whispers, internet spume, back-page splashes – centred on a child.

View image in fullscreen It has been widely reported that JJ Gabriel has demanded to leave Manchester United. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

And before we even get into the myriad safeguarding issues, it’s worth reflecting on the financial incentives involved here. As scouting networks broaden and deepen, as clubs increasingly remodel themselves as trading vehicles, the premium on exclusive young talent has become unignorable. Should Gabriel leave United he will undoubtedly have his pick of Europe’s top clubs.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Players and their representatives have also begun to recognise their rarefied value in this market. In a previous era Michael Carrick might have had the luxury of integrating Gabriel gradually into the United first team, taking a long-term view of his development, much as Mikel Arteta has done with Dowman at Arsenal. But of course if Lamine Yamal is playing first-team football at 15, then why not JJ Gabriel? If every big club in Europe is looking for the next big star, then who ultimately holds the power in this relationship: the kid or one of the biggest football clubs in the world?

And this is absurd, and it is intentionally absurd, and it is no defence of Sterling’s subsequent actions to point out that this is basically a ridiculous path upon which to dispatch a human being: festooned with unimaginable riches as a teenager, placed at the very centre of things, cast on to the scrap heap by 29. This is an unbelievably weird life, one that starts so wildly and violently beyond the boundaries of normative society that it’s a wonder anyone manages to stay remotely sane within it.

The life-changing money, the scrutiny, the lack of privacy, the intermediaries and handlers, the winnowing of trust, the noise beyond the windows, the strangers demanding a piece of you, at a time when – remember – you are still a child and this entire lifestyle has been sold to you as the ultimate aspiration. Remember, you’re supporting the whole family now. Gabriel’s original surname, taken from his father and agent, was reportedly changed from O’Cearuill to Gabriel because it was easier to pronounce and therefore more marketable.

I guess the point here is that nobody has as much agency over their career as they might like. The young modern footballer exists at the mercy of forces barely within their control. Their job is contingent on so many others: the coaches who train their skills, the medical staff who manage their workload, the teammates who pass to them, the support network that might just dissuade them from getting into a car with a load of nitrous oxide balloons in the early hours of the morning.

And by any measure, Sterling is one of the lucky ones. The teenager who made it, who scaled the peaks, won 82 international caps, four league titles, worked under one of the greatest managers of all time, who tasted the manna even if it eventually choked him. How many other thousands of lives you will never see have been fruitlessly and callously bent and twisted towards this world: skills you will never witness, names you will never hear? How much humanity are we prepared to fling into this machine in order for it to provide us with entertainment?

Perhaps in the post-Ronaldo/Messi era we are beginning to shake the idea that great individual players can bend the arc of history to their will, a fallacy we may as well call the Ballon d’Or Industrial Complex. Injuries, circumstance, tactical trends, physical shifts, the inevitability of time and tide: these are the handmaidens of talent, its trade winds, its lucky charms. Gaze at any footballing prodigy from afar and you’ll see a seductive blur of gift and privilege. But look closely enough and you’ll notice that the driver’s seat is empty.

Sports.title: ‘We can’t accept that’: Carrick urges Manchester United to respond after cup collapse
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick admitted Manchester United’s Carabao Cup capitulation against Brighton that was greeted by boos at Old Trafford was unacceptable and that answers had to be found at Fulham on Sunday.

United were knocked out 3-2 by Fabian Hürzeler’s visitors after leading 2-0 after 10 minutes through Shea Lacey and Mason Mount. Goals from Charalampos Kostoulas in first‑half added time, Pascal Gross on 65 minutes and Maxim De Cuyper four minutes later eliminated United.

It was the first time United had lost after leading 2-0 at Old Trafford for 50 years and the first time since 1984 they had been defeated there after being ahead at half-time.

Carrick’s side have beaten only Ipswich in the league and Sabah in the Champions League. “Under pressure? That doesn’t bother me one bit,” he said.

“I understand what goes on and how the world works. What bothers me is winning games and I believe we will do, but we have to do it pretty quickly. We can’t accept that [the manner of the defeat] as a group. I take responsibility for it. The performance towards the end of the second half, that’s on me. We have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to go back to winning football matches. It doesn’t feel good at the moment.”

Carrick said of the boos at the end: “I totally understand the feelings of the supporters.”

The manager was asked about JJ Gabriel, the 15-year-old academy player who has informed United he wants to leave. “We have to be a little bit careful on that one. He’s a 15-year-old boy. It’s more about the welfare, the care and the attention of JJ as a child really,” Carrick said. “He’s certainly a young man. The situation is what it is, but we have to be careful about the exposure and how much we jump on that.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Hürzeler, who made six changes, was delighted with the win. “I am not sure how many players on the pitch had experienced winning here, we have a lot of newcomers but when we play to our level we can compete with anyone in the league,” the Brighton manager said. In the next round his side will travel to the winner of the game on Thursday between Manchester City and Norwich. “We want to go as far as possible but if you want to win something you have to win at the highest level,” Hürzeler said.

Sports.title: ‘It is for every fan who has ever followed us’: Bournemouth’s European debut caps journey from the brink
Sports.content:
It is 13 years since Bournemouth, a couple of months after finishing runners-up to Doncaster in the third tier, hosted Real Madrid. It was a balmy summer’s day, officially Carlo Ancelotti’s first match in charge, and, a few hours after checking into the Haven hotel on the Sandbanks peninsula, a wave of galácticos took to the pitch: Cristiano Ronaldo, Luka Modric, Kaká, Karim Benzema, the list goes on.

An early, wayward Ronaldo free-kick broke the wrist of an 11-year‑old boy before Madrid ran out 6-0 winners in a bucket-list friendly.

“I retired a month earlier, and I thought: ‘Yeah, that’s typical, isn’t it?’” says Steve Fletcher, a bona fide Bournemouth legend and now club ambassador who scored 121 goals across 728 appearances, a smile unravelling on his face. “You play for a club for 20 years, and then you go and get the biggest team in the world to come down. I wanted to say to Eddie Howe: ‘Can I have five minutes on the pitch?’ For them to play here was utterly ridiculous.”

It was one of the stranger days in Bournemouth’s recent history and on Thursday they will take another step when they face Real Sociedad in their first competitive game against European opposition. On the final day of last season, Bournemouth’s staff and players celebrated qualifying for the Europa League by gathering around a “Rayanair” flag depicting their Brazil forward piloting a plane, giddy supporters providing the perfect backdrop for the pictures, and those fans have since booked trips to Prague, Oslo and Vigo.

Perhaps it was fate that Andoni Iraola, who grew up in the Basque Country, would guide Bournemouth to San Sebastián. “It is going to be a momentous occasion, an I-was-there moment,” Fletcher says. He has exchanged messages this week with Iraola, who sent best wishes, including for a win.

The scale of the achievement is not lost on Fletcher. Iraola, who will return to Bournemouth with Liverpool on Sunday – with his assistants Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper, both of whom also played for the club in the third tier – was the mastermind. “I always say to people around Bournemouth: ‘Don’t ever take this for granted,’” Fletcher says.

“It is for every supporter who has ever followed Bournemouth: past, present, for the people who passed away, grandparents, great‑grandparents. I think everyone will feel very emotional on Thursday.”

View image in fullscreen Bournemouth reveal their ‘Rayanair’ banner after qualifying for the Europa League. Photograph: Robin Jones/AFC Bournemouth/Getty Images

La Real are playing in Europe for the sixth time in seven seasons but for Bournemouth, coached by Marco Rose, this is new ground. It was not unplanned, though. At the end of 2023, when Bournemouth were 14th in the Premier League, their bullish American billionaire owner, Bill Foley, predicted they would play in Europe within five years. Foley’s motto “Always Advance, Never Retreat” adorns a wall in the boardroom.

“He created the Golden Knights, the ice hockey team in Las Vegas, and they won the Stanley Cup within six seasons,” Fletcher says. “He has obviously got a crystal ball, he can see things and believes in people … I always think there should be a movie made about this time at AFC Bournemouth.”

View image in fullscreen Young fans waiting to catch a glimpse of the star-studded Real Madrid team in 2013. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian

Fletcher was influential in Bournemouth making it this far. His winning goal at home against Grimsby on the penultimate day of the 2008-09 season ensured Bournemouth would not fall into non-league, the club having begun the season on -17 points after failing to exit administration. He subsequently worked in the recruitment department, as first‑team coach to Howe, Gary O’Neil and Scott Parker and then as a player liaison officer. “I’ve still got kit man and groundsman to go,” he says, laughing.

Adam Smith, the 35-year-old Bournemouth captain into his 15th season at the club, including a loan in League One in 2010-11, remembers the days of training at Canford school, round the corner from the state-of-the-art facility they moved into 18 months ago. Did Europe feel plausible when he signed from Tottenham as a teenager? “I would never have believed you; I’d just think it’s bonkers,” Smith says.

Quick Guide Benfica dispatch Amorim's Milan Show Ruben Amorim’s Milan were beaten 2-0 by Marco Silva’s Benfica in the Europa League. Dodi Lukebakio put the Portuguese side ahead at San Siro in the 16th minute and Jakub Kaminski added a second early in the second half. Bayer Leverkusen, finalists in 2024, began their Europa League campaign with a 2-0 win against the Slovenian champions Celje while Lyon were 2-1 winners at Anderlecht. The Cypriot champions Omonia Nicosia stunned the La Liga side Celta Vigo 1-0 while Rangers’ conquerors Jagiellonia Bialystok were denied a point at the Greek giants Olympiacos by Roman Yaremchuk’s late winner. Sparta Prague thrashed Ararat-Armenia 4-1 while Sturm Graz against Rennes and Hapoel Be’er Sheva versus Dinamo Zagreb both ended goalless. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Fletcher references Neil Vacher, the former club secretary and current club historian who grew up as a supporter in the 1960s. “Would he have dreamed that we could even be in the top flight, never mind playing in Europe?”

Bournemouth have been in the top flight for all but two seasons since their promotion in 2015, but Europe hits differently. Most of the squad watched the August draw in the canteen and until this season David Brooks was used to midweek European matches meaning a night on the sofa.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

He watched his Wales teammate Brennan Johnson lift the Europa League and Conference League in successive seasons with Tottenham and Crystal Palace respectively, and another, Neco Williams, excel in the Europa League for Nottingham Forest.

View image in fullscreen Bournemouth’s Steve Fletcher (left) and Burton’s Shaun Kelly battle for the ball in a League Two match in 2010. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

“I was delighted for them, but for selfish reasons you want to be involved in teams like that, competing in Europe,” he says. “Everyone’s raring to go and wanting to showcase their talents, and hopefully we can go far. We always cause the big teams in the Premier League problems and I don’t think it should be any different in Europe. The club’s journey has been well documented and to finish it off with a European trophy would be really nice.”

The Madrid game coincided with Bournemouth opening a stand named after Ted MacDougall, another much-loved striker. At the time the pressure was on to ensure the stadium was ready for the landmark fixture, and if that sounds familiar then that is because this summer Bournemouth had to upgrade their ground to meet Uefa regulations. Their first home game is against Sturm Graz next month; the week after, Milan – whose red-and-black stripes inspired Bournemouth’s kit at the start of the 70s – come to town. “Just to mutter the words Milan, AC Milan, in the same sentence as AFC Bournemouth, in a competitive fixture, is crazy,” Fletcher says. “I think of Maldini, Baresi, Van Basten, Gullit.”

The stand at the other end of the ground has been named after Fletcher since 2010. Viktoria Plzen and Hapoel Be’er Sheva will visit in December and January. “A lot of people might come to Bournemouth and go: ‘Who is Steve Fletcher?’ Because I’m not one of the great footballers, but I’m very proud of the career I had,” the 54-year-old says.

View image in fullscreen More than 11,000 crammed into Dean Court in 2013 to watch Cristiano Ronaldo and co at Bournemouth. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Bournemouth hosted Madrid on a balmy afternoon in 2013. Thirteen years later they are embarking on their first European campaign. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian

“I’ve had Premier League managers before games, an hour and a half before kick-off, look over and say: ‘That’s your stand, very well done.’ People like José Mourinho and Pep Guardiola said that and when I walked away I got straight on the phone to my parents and said: ‘You won’t believe what’s just happened.’”

There will probably be a pervading sense of disbelief among the Bournemouth supporters in San Sebastián and those tuning in from home on Thursday. “There will probably be people coming to our European games in their 80s and 90s who will have watched the club from year dot,” Fletcher says. “For us to be mixing it with some of the giants of European football is magical.

“It’s beyond anybody’s wildest dreams, and we still have to pinch ourselves. But at the same time, we have to enjoy it, embrace it. I hope there’s many more happy times to come. To think we’re playing someone like Milan in a competitive game is incredible. Wouldn’t it be amazing if in the next few years we could play Real Madrid?”

Sports.title: Rancour, road trips and revival: tale of battle for Brighton’s future hits the stage
Sports.content:
It was the tip-off that changed Ian Hart’s life for ever. The funeral director from Worthing was co-editor of the Brighton fanzine Gull’s Eye when he received a phone call from Gordon Lucking, a Crystal Palace director, in July 1995.

“Gordon always wanted to join the Brighton board, but they didn’t want him there,” Hart says. “Ron Noades [the Palace chair] welcomed him with open arms. One of his [Lucking’s] employees had been on this golf day and someone got pissed in the evening and said: ‘You’ll never guess what’s happened – Brighton have sold the Goldstone Ground and are moving to Portsmouth.’ Gordon loved it, because it was another nail in Brighton’s coffin.”

Hart initially struggled to believe that Brighton’s home since 1902 could be in danger, but decided to confront the chief executive, David Bellotti, at his office. “I parked the hearse outside, went in and asked him straight whether they had sold the ground and were moving to Portsmouth,” Hart writes in his book, Brighton & Hove Albion: From Every Angle, which was released last year. “All the colour drained from his face.”

View image in fullscreen Ian Hart is the producer of Stand or Fall, which will be performed at Brighton’s Theatre Royal from 23-26 September. Photograph: James Boardman

The subsequent battle between the supporters and owners was the start of a nomadic period in Brighton’s history that will be revisited this month in a new play to coincide with the club’s 125th anniversary. Stand or Fall, written by the Brighton fan Mark Brailsford, follows a group of fans from the last days at the Goldstone in 1997, their exile 70 miles away in Gillingham and then at the Withdean Stadium in Brighton before the club find a new home at the Amex Stadium.

Hart is a producer for the play that will run for four nights from 23 September at the city’s Theatre Royal. An exhibition, also entitled Stand or Fall, detailing what he describes as the club’s civil war, opened at the Brighton Museum in August and continues until the end of the year.

View image in fullscreen In February 1997, thousands of supporters from clubs across the UK and Europe converged on Brighton’s Goldstone Ground for Fans United day to show their solidarity. Photograph: Andrew Hasson/Alamy

“We were all thrown together, all different demographics: a funeral director, a punk performance poet, a chartered accountant, plasterers and labourers,” Hart says of the action group that included the punk poet John Baine, better known as Attila the Stockbroker.

“A few days after everyone found out the Goldstone Ground was being sold, we had a fans’ meeting at [the pub] Chapman’s, which is now the Railway, in Worthing. There were probably 40 or 50 people from all walks of life and it grew from there.

“A year later, there were 500 people who couldn’t get inside listening on loudspeakers outside the Concorde [nightclub] when things were getting really serious.”

View image in fullscreen Brighton fans dig up the turf to take as a souvenir after Brighton’s last game at the Goldstone Ground. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

In April 1996, 600 spectators ran on to the Goldstone Ground pitch after a win against Carlisle, calling for Bellotti’s resignation. Some fans tore up seats in the directors’ box as attempts were made to storm the boardroom. Then came the meeting with York that has gone down in Brighton folklore, as fans waited until the 16th minute to invade the pitch, causing the game to be abandoned.

“It was not a riot, it was a legitimate protest,” Hart says. “The FA and the Football League were a bit like Neville Chamberlain at Munich, waving a piece of paper saying everything was going to be fine. They thought they could give us a load of bullshit and we would just take it.”

View image in fullscreen Fans leave the Goldstone Ground for the last time. Photograph: Paul Popper/Popperfoto/Getty Images

The Goldstone Ground was demolished a year later after Brighton came within 27 minutes of relegation from the Football League, only to be saved by Robbie Reinelt’s equaliser against Hereford. At one stage they had been 13 points adrift at the bottom of Division Three (now League Two). Brighton finished 91st in the Football League again the following year, playing home games in Gillingham after Portsmouth reneged on their offer to groundshare.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We lost a generation of fans, which we’ve got back now, but for years you used to be driving past parks in Worthing seeing football teams training on a Saturday morning with kits and no Brighton shirts. It was horrible,” Hart says. “I was a coach at Worthing United from under-six to under-16 and I banned anybody not wearing a Brighton or Worthing shirt.”

View image in fullscreen From 1999 to 2011 Brighton played at Withdean Stadium, which had a capacity of 8,850. Photograph: Andrew Cowie/Shutterstock

Bill Archer paid £100 to take control of Brighton via a supporter‑led consortium and steadied the ship as they moved back to the city, albeit at the Withdean, primarily an athletics stadium. It was when Tony Bloom took over as chair in 2009 that Brighton really began to take flight, moving into the Amex Stadium two years later before being promoted to the Premier League in 2017.

The club reached the last 16 of the Europa League in their first European campaign in 2024 and will compete in the Conference League this season. Hart is hoping they could complete the quest for a major trophy.

View image in fullscreen In 2011, the Seagulls moved to the 22,500-capacity Amex Stadium, which opened with a friendly against Tottenham. Photograph: Simon Dack/Alamy

“It would be brilliant and Tony did promise us a trophy at the 1983 [FA Cup final] reunion dinner a few years ago,” he says. “We were having a drink with him in Tromsø [before the Conference League playoff in Norway last month] and as much as he promised us a trophy I don’t want to get weighed down by expectation.

“The great thing about the play is that there are highs and lows, but you can’t really celebrate the highs unless you have the lows. It makes the whole story even more incredible.”

Sports.title: ‘My scar, not your scar’: Tuchel stands by England semi-final subs but admits wrong timing
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel stands by his heavily criticised defensive substitutions in the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina this summer, but the England head coach accepts he made them too early.

Tuchel said England were “waiting for death”, unable to cope with the attacking tactics adopted by Argentina in Atlanta as they chased the game after Anthony Gordon’s opener on the hour. He said fatigue and the success of defending with a back five in knockout games against Mexico and Norway also influenced his decisions to sit on the lead.

That approach proved catastrophic as goals from Enzo Fernández and Lautaro Martínez in the final stages of the game ended England’s dreams of making a first World Cup final since 1966.

“You can try to kill me here. But it’s my scar, it’s not your scar,” Tuchel said in a documentary on the England app. “No one is more hurt than me, no one wanted it more. They can endlessly torture you and think: ‘If I had done different substitutions, then we would have won the match.’ You just don’t know it.

“Of course you could [have made attacking changes]. No one knows what would have happened. We could have done it and maybe lost 2‑1 and could have gone: ‘Is he crazy? He finished the game against Norway with a back five, why didn’t he finish the game with five?’ I think from what I saw and the experience, the information and the level of craziness Argentina put in – change after change after change, it was just one offensive change after the other. That was my solution to the problem.

“That’s what the intervention of a coach is. I try to help, you don’t implement anything for your ego or whatever. You just try to help.”

View image in fullscreen Jordan Pickford is beaten by Enzo Fernández’s shot for Argentina’s first goal. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters

England were on the back foot after scoring, with Djed Spence making a last-ditch tackle and Jordan Pickford making a big save immediately before the hydration break. It was then when Tuchel made his ill-fated decision to replace the goalscorer Gordon with the defender Ezri Konsa.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The German, who faced calls to be sacked in the aftermath of the semi-final defeat, insists the opposition’s gung-ho tactics forced his hand. “Argentina then play very, very quickly. Sorry for the language, [they played] fuck-it football: ‘We have nothing to lose. Let’s fuck it.’ A key moment if I look back at it and what happened to my decision-making, we conceded a big, big chance right before the water break. And I thought: ‘We will not survive. This is waiting for death. We don’t have ball possession, we’re not defending good, we’re not defending properly in our 4-4-2. We need help.’

“I changed to a 5-3-2, we changed the structure. Because I believe we can handle the width better and we still have three central defenders in the middle if crosses still fly in. We changed then to a 5-4-1. Even my mindset is maybe like: ‘Let’s just overcome it.’ And it’s too early. Too early for that mindset.”

Sports.title: Boehly and Walter sell Chelsea shares as Clearlake Capital takes full control of club
Sports.content:
Todd Boehly and Mark Walter have sold their stakes in Chelsea in a deal under which Clearlake Capital takes full control of the Premier League club.

The American billionaire businessmen Boehly and Walter were two of the investors who partnered with Clearlake to buy the club from Roman Abramovich in a sale mandated by the UK government in May 2022. The private equity company Clearlake had previously owned 61.5% of the club, with Boehly and Walter carving up the remaining shares with another investor, Hansjörg Wyss.

A statement issued late on Wednesday night read: “Chelsea Football Club today announced affiliates of Clearlake Capital Group, LP will acquire the ownership interest of Todd Boehly. Hansjorg Wyss will remain an important stakeholder and partner in the ownership group.

“As part of the transition, Clearlake will also acquire Mark Walter’s ownership interest and therefore acquire full control of the club.”

Chelsea said Boehly, the chair, had shown “unwavering commitment” to the ownership group’s belief that the supporters are at the heart of the club. “The owners have worked together with the shared objective of building a sustainable foundation for long-term sporting success,” the statement added.

“Under their joint ownership, substantial investment has been made across the men’s and women’s senior and youth squads, Chelsea’s training facilities at Cobham, medical and player-support resources, academy development and pathways, and the sporting and business leadership of the club.

“Todd Boehly now leaves his role as chairman with Chelsea well positioned for the next phase of development. Clearlake intends to continue building on the strategic course the club is now on and realising the ambition that the ownership group has developed together.”

View image in fullscreen Xabi Alonso has been tasked with reviving Chelsea’s fortunes. Photograph: Dave Shopland/AP

Boehly said: “It has been an honour to serve as chairman of Chelsea Football Club. I would like to thank the many who helped secure a bright future for the club, including the English Premier League, the coaches and players, the talented leadership and staff at Chelsea, and the legions of dedicated fans.

“I have valued my partnership with Clearlake and the wider ownership group, and the collective decisions and investment we have made to support the immediate and long-term success of the club. I am confident that Chelsea is well positioned for continued success under Clearlake’s leadership.”

Behdad Eghbali and José Feliciano, cofounders of Clearlake Capital, said: “Todd has been an important partner throughout our ownership of Chelsea, and we thank him for his time and contribution as chairman. He will always be a part of the Chelsea story and family.

“Clearlake has served as Chelsea’s majority owner since 2022, and as we move to full control our focus is to continue investing in the club’s infrastructure, sporting performance, player development and delivering long-term success for Chelsea and the club’s supporters.”

Chelsea, who appointed Xabi Alonso as manager in the summer and are sixth in the Premier League, say there will be no changes to day-to-day operations, leadership or strategy at the club.

Sports.title: Enzo Le Fée makes amends from the spot as Sunderland overcome AZ
Sports.content:
Granit Xhaka, Sunderland’s captain, believes it is not unrealistic to dream about Régis Le Bris’s side travelling all the way to the Europa League final next spring.

It is rarely a good idea to dismiss Xhaka but reaching that showpiece in Frankfurt will necessitate considerably more efficient finishing on his team’s part than proved evident on a highly evocative night on Wearside.

Thanks to a second-half penalty from the indefatigable Enzo Le Fée – appropriately the game’s outstanding player – the game ended happily for Sunderland as the home side launched their big return to Europe with a morale-boosting win.

Along the way they missed a litany of chances but, in Le Fée, possessed both a high-calibre attacking playmaker and a tireless off‑the‑ball warrior who, time after time, regained possession for his team.

When Le Bris was invited later to agree that a player he first coached as a 12-year-old in Lorient’s academy was Champions League class, the Sunderland manager’s smile lit up the room. “Enzo’s a great player,” he said. “I trust him and his quality. I’m proud and pleased for the players and the fans, AZ are a really good side but we played with heart and togetherness.”

Occupants of the VIP seats included Jimmy Montgomery, the now 82-year-old hero of Sunderland’s 1973 FA Cup triumph against Leeds and their European goalkeeper during that last, albeit fairly short‑lived, adventure in the Cup Winners’ Cup 53 years ago.

View image in fullscreen Sunderland put on an impressive fireworks display before their European comeback. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

Kick-off was prefaced by a spine-tingling, ear-splitting preamble featuring a giant tifo of a sailing ship floating above the message: “New shores to conquer”.

Not that AZ were inclined to surrender lightly. Leeroy Echteld’s team had enjoyed an unbeaten start to the season, winning five and drawing one of their opening Eredivisie games.

Indeed they would have taken an early lead had Robin Roefs not extended a boot and kept out the dangerous Ro-Zangelo Daal’s low shot after he had been played in by the talented visiting No 10 Kees Smit.

The moment had arrived for Le Fée to start raising the home tone and his half-volley duly tested Jari De Busser. Though De Busser was swiftly forced to push Kevin Danso’s fine shot over the bar, Sunderland almost came undone on the counterattack and it took an excellent interception on Trai Hume’s part to halt Ayoub Oufkir.

Quick Guide Benfica dispatch Amorim's Milan Show Ruben Amorim’s Milan were beaten 2-0 by Marco Silva’s Benfica in the Europa League. Dodi Lukebakio put the Portuguese side ahead at San Siro in the 16th minute and Jakub Kaminski added a second early in the second half. Bayer Leverkusen, finalists in 2024, began their Europa League campaign with a 2-0 win against the Slovenian champions Celje while Lyon were 2-1 winners at Anderlecht. The Cypriot champions Omonia Nicosia stunned the La Liga side Celta Vigo 1-0 while Rangers’ conquerors Jagiellonia Bialystok were denied a point at the Greek giants Olympiacos by Roman Yaremchuk’s late winner. Sparta Prague thrashed Ararat-Armenia 4-1 while Sturm Graz against Rennes and Hapoel Be’er Sheva versus Dinamo Zagreb both ended goalless. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Smit and his teammates issued plenty of reminders that AZ are more than merely deft in possession, but Le Bris’s starting XI was hardly shabby either and, after Wilson Isidor conjured a glorious chance, Le Fée’s shot hit the post.

It was not long before another shot, from Hume this time, whizzed just wide of an upright. When, back in January 2022, Hume joined Sunderland, they were still in League One.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Back in the present Le Bris’s team ended the first half thoroughly dominant yet frustrated. The manager later blamed “overthinking”. Oufkir, meanwhile, was arguably fortunate to collect only a yellow card after sliding in recklessly on Le Fée and was replaced by Weslley Patati at the interval.

AZ re-emerged for the second half invigorated and, as Smit wrong‑footed Sunderland’s rearguard before curling a shot inches wide, it was easy to see why he has collected so many admirers across Europe.

View image in fullscreen Le Fée fires home the decisive penalty. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

Perhaps anxious not to be upstaged, Le Fée swiftly regained the limelight courtesy of a stellar pass that Isidor could not quite polish off.

When Hume subsequently missed another presentable chance it seemed that De Busser’s goal must be protected by some sort of magnetic forcefield.

Then Patati felled Le Fée in the area as he shaped to shoot and a player being scrutinised by the France head coach, Zinedine Zidane, stepped up to the spot.

Having seen a penalty against Arsenal saved expertly by David Raya last Saturday, Le Fée looked a little nervous but he sent De Busser the wrong way as he struck a textbook kick low into the bottom corner. “It was important to score,” Le Bris said. “But Enzo stepped up with bravery and courage. He’s resilient.”

Although Nordi Mukiele and Brian Brobbey, on as a substitute, should really have doubled the lead before Patati’s volley almost provided a late equaliser for AZ, that penalty proved just enough to launch Sunderland’s galleon on European waters.

Sports.title: Tammy Abraham’s double powers Aston Villa to Carabao Cup win at Coventry
Sports.content:
For Aston Villa, an overdue drama-free outing as Unai Emery’s side cruised into the Carabao Cup fourth round courtesy of a Tammy Abraham double and a Ross Barkley header.

The satisfaction was detectable in Emery’s voice as he reflected on a night of positives: Abraham’s first goals of the season, Ibrahim Mbaye’s encouraging full debut and another half-hour for the £52m club-record signing, Johan Manzambi. Are things clicking into gear after a summer of changes?

Unfortunately for Coventry, it was a sorry case of more of the same. Frank Lampard’s side have lost five of their six matches in all competitions, across which they have leaked 15 goals. It was hard to know whether Abraham’s tap-in or Barkley’s free header, both from corners, was worse from a Coventry perspective. The sight of Lampard hunched in the dugout, hands clasped, has become a familiar sight. “If you give two set pieces away as simply as we did, it’s quite hard to win against Premier League opposition,” the Coventry head coach said.

Lampard’s side, who have lost their opening league four matches by an aggregate of 10-0 and on Saturday visit Nottingham Forest hoping for lift-off, are yet to score outside this competition. Victor Torp’s sweet free-kick from the edge of Villa’s 18-yard box, to cancel out Abraham’s opener, represented Coventry’s first goal since Torp capped the scoring at Plymouth in the previous round. This victory earned Villa a fourth-round trip to Bournemouth at the end of October.

This was the first competitive meeting between these sides since 5 May 2001, when Coventry’s initial 34-year stay in the top flight came to an end with a 3-2 defeat at Villa Park. When Aurèle Amenda limped off with a calf injury after 10 minutes, Bobby Thomas, wearing the captain’s armband, was the only player left of the starting lineup from Sunday’s 5-0 home defeat against Brighton.

Emery made seven changes himself and George Hemmings, one of those to keep their place, was the architect for Villa’s opener. Matteo Ruggeri fed Hemmings down the left and the 19-year-old sent a sumptuous pass into Abraham with the outside of his right boot.

View image in fullscreen Frank Lampard shows his disappointment as Coventry suffer another defeat. Photograph: Getty Images/Sportsphoto/Allstar

Coventry struggled to retain possession and Villa were enjoying themselves, exchanging crisp, clean passes. But then Barkley was penalised for fouling Caleb Yirenkyi on the edge of the Villa box and Torp stepped up to lift the subsequent free-kick over the Villa wall. John McGinn, the Villa captain reduced to the role of draught excluder, picked himself up from the turf.

Quick Guide Carabao Cup roundup: Fleetwood handed win over Blades Show A 57th-minute Rhys Norrington-Davies own goal sent Fleetwood into the last 16 of the Carabao Cup for the first time as the League Two club stunned their Championship opponents, Sheffield United, 1-0 at Highbury, before pulling a home tie against Arsenal out in the draw. Matt Lawlor’s side, unbeaten now in nine games in all competitions, had another Danny Andrew effort ruled out for offside and twice hit the woodwork in a dominant second-half display. It was a searching left-wing cross from Andrew that Norrington-Davies nodded beyond Michael Cooper to give the fourth-tier club a historic victory. Tom Cannon did get the ball in the net for Chris Wilder’s visitors who lined up with only four starting survivors from last Friday’s 1-0 league defeat by Wolves. But a flag for offside was raised before the striker slid the ball into the net. United started positively and Ollie Arblaster had a goalbound effort blocked after only 36 seconds. But Mark Helm forced Cooper into a seventh-minute save before the former United forward Ched Evans put his follow-up header narrowly wide. Jay Lynch denied Joe Rothwell as the visitors attacked again but Cooper was the busier, saving from Lewis McCann and Crispin McLean. Helm’s dipping right-foot effort from 18 yards grazed the top netting as Fleetwood finished the first half in the ascendancy and they deserved their break from Norrington-Davies’ own goal. United finally came to life in the last 10 minutes with Lynch brilliantly denied Sydie Peck and Ben Brereton Díaz, while Cannon saw a goalbound strike superbly blocked. Everton’s forgotten man Charly Alcaraz stepped up when his side needed some inspiration to score the only goal in the win over Wolves three minutes after coming on. The Argentinian had played just 14 minutes all season but belied his lack of match sharpness with a quick switch of the ball from one foot to the other to guide a left-footed shot past the former Everton goalkeeper João Virgínia in the 80th minute. It also represented a minor success for Tyler Dibling, whose career has not really taken off since his £35m move from Southampton just over a year ago, as he claimed the assist at the end his most encouraging performance for the club. Everton's reward is a home tie against Newcastle. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Suddenly Coventry were full of confidence, a little giddy. Thomas moonlighted as a striker, forcing an error from Tyrone Mings, but then declined a golden opportunity to shoot at goal and the chance fizzled out. Gustavo Hamer then whistled a left-foot shot just past a Villa upright.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Coventry sprung to life but Villa responded. McGinn smacked his hands together after spurning a decent chance and a few minutes later Barkley sent a low drive at goal that Dan Bentley did well to push wide for a corner, from which Villa prospered. Mbaye’s inswinging delivery was on the money and Barkley, totally unmarked in the six-yard box, headed in at the front post.

Coventry had the meanest defence in the Championship last season but have been porous since promotion. More slack marking enabled Villa to extend their lead. McGinn whipped a corner into the six-yard box and Abraham prodded in after walking off his marker, the 18-year-old Coventry debutant Stephen Mfuni, who this month joined on loan from Manchester City.

Abraham’s second gave Villa breathing space. Emery, whose side visit Tottenham on Saturday, felt comfortable enough to withdraw McGinn and Mbaye just after the hour. Zion Suzuki replaced the injured Marco Bizot at half-time, the goalkeeper reporting a back problem. Nicolas Jackson later came on in place of Abraham. Emery cycled through the changes but Alejandro Garnacho, who has played just 31 minutes since signing, remained on the bench.

“He is progressing but we have players in front of him now,” Emery said. “George is playing fantastic, Alysson is understanding a lot of things very good; he needs time but he is giving us things I want. Mbaye responded well. We want a competitive team and the players ready to compete on the standard we have. Of course, he [Garnacho] is a little bit behind because of some circumstances he had in pre-season. It is time to be patient for the time he needs.”

Sports.title: Sunderland tipped to win Europa League with only two teams beating 52-year record
Sports.content:
Sunderland tipped to win Europa League with only two teams beating 52-year record

Sunderland have been told there is 'no reason' they cannot win this season's Europa League.

The Black Cats made a winning return to Europe on Wednesday as they beat AZ Alkmaar at the Stadium of Light.



3 Sunderland have been backed to win the Europa League this season Credit: Getty

Enzo Le Fee's second half penalty proved to be the only goal in the club's first European fixture for almost 53 years.

Regis Le Bris' side will face the likes of AC Milan and Anderlecht during the league phase.

It comes just over four years on from their promotion out of League One in 2022.



They join Bournemouth and Crystal Palace as the Premier League's representatives in this season's Europa League.

Meanwhile, Brighton will fly the flag for English football in the Conference League.



Sunderland backed for Europa League glory

Prior to Sunderland's win over AZ, club legend Micky Gray joined Alan Brazil and Ally McCoist on Wednesday's talkSPORT Breakfast show.

Brazil and McCoist had both backed English clubs for glory in Europe this term.



Gray can also see his old side lifting the trophy in Frankfurt come May.

He explained: "I love your optimism saying they can go all the way, these English sides and win the European trophy as well. They’ve got every chance. There’s no reason (they can’t win it).

"Nobody’s going to know too much about the way Sunderland play, apart from what they saw last season. They’ve given themselves a really good chance."

3 Le Fee's second half penalty secured a victory over AZ on Wednesday night Credit: Getty



Historic return

Sunderland's return to continental competition came 52 years and 313 days after their last European outing.

Prior to facing AZ, the Black Cats had not played in Europe since November 7, 1973.

On that occasion, they were beaten 2-0 away from home by Sporting Lisbon in the second round of the European Cup Winners' Cup.

Only two clubs have ever gone longer between European matches than Sunderland.



Belgium's Union Saint-Gilloise waited 57 years and 336 days, whilst Dutch side Go Ahead Eagles had gone 59 years and 353 days without featuring in a competition proper before last season's Europa League.

3 Sunderland has been 'bouncing' since securing their first European campaign for 53 years, says Phillips Credit: Getty

Sunderland 'bouncing' - Phillips

Former Sunderland striker Kevin Phillips was present at the Stadium of Light for the match against AZ.

The 53-year-old played in the first match at the ground, a friendly against Ajax in 1997.



Reflecting on the atmosphere in the stadium and around the city, he joined Breakfast on Thursday morning.

Phillips explained: "From the minute they qualified for the Europa League in May, the city has been bouncing.

"Coming off the back of an incredible Premier League season and you think things couldn’t get any better at the Stadium of Light.

"To witness that last night, the pre-match show, the fireworks, seeing the fans, it’s stuff that they dreamt about when that stadium opened.



Sunderland's Europa League fixtures September 16 - Beat AZ Alkmaar 2-0 October 15 - Torreense (A) October 22 - Lech Poznan (A) November 5 - Dinamo Zagreb (H) November 26 - Jagiellonia Bialystok (H) December 10 - AC Milan (A) January 21 - Anderlecht (A) January 28 - Levski Sofia (H)

"We came close back in those days, finished seventh twice, but to see them lining up against Alkmaar last night, it was incredible. The game was end-to-end.

"It could have been a 3-3 or 4-4 with the chances that were created, but they managed to hold on to that 1-0 win and it was a celebration. I’m pretty sure most of the fans are still celebrating right now."

Sunderland face Portuguese Cup winners Torreense away from home in their next league phase fixture on October 15.

Meanwhile, their next home match in the competition comes on November 5 against Croatian champions Dinamo Zagreb.

Sports.title: David Beckham picks who should win Ballon d’Or and it’s not Harry Kane
Sports.content:
David Beckham picks who should win Ballon d’Or and it’s not Harry Kane

David Beckham has tipped Lionel Messi to win the Ballon d'Or over England's Harry Kane.

The Inter Miami co-owner thinks the Argentina legend should win the prestigious award after he was nominated on the 30-player shortlist.

3 The 39-year-old moved to the MLS side in 2023 and won his eighth Ballon d'Or.

The 39-year-old has won the Ballon d'Or eight times, and the former England captain believes he should win it again following his brilliant World Cup.

The Argentina international scored eight goals and provided four assists, to help his country reach the final against Spain.

He is the second-highest goalscorer in World Cup history with 21 goals, one behind France's Kylian Mbappe.

Beckham made his comments after Messi scored his 100th goal for Inter Miami on Wednesday in a 2-0 victory in the Campeones Cup final.

Beckham said: "I think when you see him do things like this tonight, when you see him have the World Cup that he's had, it's not luck that he's being considered for the Ballon d'Or again

"It's not luck because he was probably the best player in the tournament. He had an incredible year last year.

"He came into that tournament in the World Cup, and like you've just said, 39 years old, to affect a World Cup and every game the way he did. That's special. There's no one at 39 that's doing that and doing it at that level

"So he deserves to be considered for the Ballon d'Or. He, in my opinion, he should win it.

"You've got great players there like Harry Kane, like Kylian [Mbappé], like Jude Bellingham and other players there, but you know when you're talking about Leo, I'm his biggest supporter."

The Barcelona legend has won eight before; in 2009, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2021 and 2023.

3 Beckham has a special relationship with the forward and even awarded him his eighth award Credit: AFP

Messi has been creating history stateside, becoming the first Inter Miami player to reach a century of goals after he headed home a cross from Luis Suarez in the 24th minute.

He also provided an assist to former Manchester United midfielder Casemiro, as the goal gave Miami their first Campeones Cup.

Following the clash, Casemiro said: "We have to enjoy this because we don't know how long we'll have it."

"What he has done and continues to do for football is incredible. He remains the best. He proved it at the World Cup and continues to prove it in MLS."

His achievement follows his retirement from international football, which he also considered his future in football as a whole following the death of his father.

Who are the Ballon d'Or favourites?

Harry Kane is the bookies' favourite to win the award next month after scoring 73 goals in 61 games for Bayern Munich and England last season.

3 Kane has been one of world football's most prolific goalscorers since joining Bayern Munich Credit: Getty

Real Madrid's Bellingham and Arsenal's Declan Rice join their countryman on the 30-player shortlist.

Lamine Yamal is one of six Spain players that won the World Cup to be included, alongside PSG forward Ferran Torres who scored the winning goal in the final.

The European champions have nine players nominated, including last year's winner Ousmane Dembele.

Real Madrid forwards Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius Jr are also seen as strong contenders for a wide open Ballon d'Or.

The award is celebrating its 70th anniversary, having been created by France Football in 1956.

The winner will be announced at a ceremony in London on Monday, October 26.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi in heated exchange with MLS Commissioner moments after Campeones Cup win
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi gave MLS Commissioner Don Garber an earful following Inter Miami's Campeones Cup win.

The Herons claimed a 2-0 victory over Mexican side Cruz Azul in the early hours of Thursday morning [UK time].

3 Messi bagged his 100th Inter Miami goal in their Campeones Cup win over Cruz Azul

Messi scored the opener midway through the first half, his 100th in an Inter Miami shirt, before Casemiro wrapped up the victory late on.

And as the MLS giants, now managed by Messi's former international teammate Cristian 'Kily' Gonzalez, celebrated their first ever Campeones Cup triumph, the iconic Argentine made a beeline for Garber.

While it's unclear what Messi said to the MLS Commissioner, the 39-year-old didn't look best pleased as he spoke with Garber.

Garber's previous with Messi

Garber and Messi have endured a frosty relationship in recent weeks, which the former feels stems from the latter's decision to skip the 2025 MLS All-Star Game.

The Inter Miami forward was handed a one-game ban as a result.

And Garber believes that Messi holds him accountable for issues with referees in the league.

"We are communicating a little bit more," Garber stated in an interview earlier this year.

"After a game, the president of US Soccer and their CEO and I went down to the officials’ locker room, waited for Ismail to come out, one of our referees, and thanked him for officiating probably the most difficult game of his career.

"I don’t think Leo was too happy during that game.

"I’m not sure that he looks at me as the guy who picks the officials; I don’t, but he’s got to complain to somebody. I’ll take it."

Ballon d'Or 2026 winner?

Messi's Campeones Cup success will reinforce his 2026 Ballon d'Or credentials, with a number of high-profile individuals backing the Argentine to claim the individual award.

The former Argentina international is on the 30-man shortlist for the accolade, which includes Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Jude Bellingham, Rodri and Spain's 2026 World Cup hero Ferran Torres.

And following Inter Miami's win over Cruz Azul, former England and Manchester City star, and Inter Miami co-owner, Sir David Beckham backed Messi for the gong, which will take place in London for the first time next month.

3 Messi deserves a ninth Ballon d'Or triumph according to Beckham

"I think when you see him do things like this tonight, when you see him have the World Cup that he's had, it's not luck that he's being considered for the Ballon d'Or again," Beckham said.

"It's not luck because he was probably the best player in the tournament. He had an incredible year last year."

Beckham isn't the only former pro suggesting that Messi wins the Ballon d'Or with 1998 World Cup adversary Diego Simeone calling for his compatriot to claim the award.

When asked recently who deserved to win the 2026 Ballon d'Or, the Atletico Madrid boss said: "Messi, without a doubt.

"Look at the World Cup he played at his age. No doubt about it! Messi."

talkSPORT verdict

Conversely, talkSPORT's own Ally McCoist was left 'angered' by suggestions that Messi could win the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Speaking on Breakfast earlier this month, it was put to McCoist that Messi could claim the award, to which he replied: "That has angered me. There's no way on this earth.

"He doesn't deserve it. It's for the player of the year, it's the Ballon d'Or, which he wasn't. He has been, but he wasn't this year."

3 Kane, and not Messi, deserves to win the 2026 Ballon d'Or according to McCoist Credit: Getty

Rather, the former Scotland striker threw his support behind Bayern Munich and England star Kane, continuing: "Who are his serious competitors?

"I get (Kylian) Mbappe. Mbappe's goalscoring at Real Madrid was fantastic and goalscoring at the World Cup was great.

"But Harry Kane has been absolutely out of this world. And I don't buy the argument that you cannot win the award unless you win the Champions League or you have a great World Cup."

Sports.title: Man United told to sack Michael Carrick and get Premier League manager now
Sports.content:
Man United told to sack Michael Carrick and get Premier League manager now

Manchester United have been urged not to 'wait until Christmas' before sacking Michael Carrick.

The Red Devils boss saw his side booed off after their Carabao Cup exit on Wednesday night.

3 United have been urged to sack Carrick after their third defeat of the season Credit: Getty

United were beaten 3-2 by Brighton at Old Trafford despite taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes.

It is the first time in 50 years that they have lost a home match after leading by two goals.

The defeat followed a loss to Manchester City on Sunday, with United already losing three of their six matches in all competitions this term.

United told to sack Carrick

However, Carrick's future divided the talkSPORT studio after Wednesday's match as Jamie O'Hara and Jason Cundy reacted to the result.

The Sports Bar hosts were split on whether the Red Devils should part ways with their current manager.

After a caller asked who United would replace Carrick with, O'Hara replied: "Let’s not start talking about new managers.

"We’re not having that conversation. I don’t want to hear Man United fans talking about ‘who can we bring in?’

"You can’t keep changing your manager. You’re the same as Tottenham. You’ve got a problem. You’ve got a mentality problem.

"It isn’t the manager. It doesn’t matter who you bring in, you still have the same problems."

Cundy was convinced a change is needed, though, as he called for Aston Villa's Unai Emery to be appointed.

He hit back: "Unai Emery. Go and get him. Get him out of Villa."

The Spaniard has taken Villa into Europe in four successive seasons, as well as winning the Europa League in May.

However, O'Hara has doubts Emery would be interested in the United job.

Would Emery take United job?

He responded: "I don’t know if Unai Emery wants to be Man United manager. Why would he want to go in there?"

Cundy then admitted: "That’s what I’d do. If I was Sir Jim Ratcliffe, I’d now cut my losses and go and get Unai.

"Don’t wait until Christmas to have the conversation, do it now."

3 Cundy has called for United to appoint Emery as Carrick's replacement Credit: Getty

O'Hara's stance remained unchanged, though, as he argued: "Unai Emery isn’t going to leave Villa now anyway. He isn’t leaving Villa.

"You just said they’re (United) skint. They’ve got to sack Carrick, then you’ve got to buy Unai Emery out of Villa and then you’ve got to pay him £10-15million. You just said they’ve got no money."

The former Tottenham Hotspur midfielder added: "I think, Man United, it’s a bad night, it’s a terrible night and it’s garbage, but they need to just chill the beans."

Carrick was appointed permanent manager in May on a two-year deal through to the summer of 2028.

It followed a successful spell as caretaker boss having replaced Ruben Amorim back in January.

During his time in caretaker charge, Carrick won 11 of his 16 matches to guide United to a third place finish and Champions League qualification.

3 Carrick claims he is not feeling the pressure despite United's slow start to the season Credit: Getty

Carrick responds to pressure

The 45-year-old admitted after the defeat to Brighton he is not fazed by any potential pressure surrounding his job security.

Carrick told reporters: "I don’t feel under pressure. Either way that doesn’t bother me one bit. It genuinely doesn’t bother me one bit.

"I understand what goes on outside and how the world works but genuinely it doesn’t bother me.

"What bothers me is winning games and having a good feeling around the place and a good feeling around the group to know we’re moving in a good direction. That’s ultimately what bothers me."

United travel to Craven Cottage to face Fulham on Sunday afternoon ahead of the international break.

A defeat could see the Red Devils end the weekend in the relegation zone.

Sports.title: Unrivalled Celtic, one team in Manchester and the greatest story – the definitive list of the best fanbases in the UK
Sports.content:
Fan culture is the beating heart of football and every group of supporters believes their club has the best backing.

But there has to be a true greatest fan base out there, right? Well, talkSPORT's Max Scott thinks he has the definitive list.

6 If you were to carve British football's best group of fans into a version of Mount Rushmore, then talkSPORT presenter Max Scott thinks he has the most unbeatable Credit: Getty

In fact, if there was a Mount Rushmore of ultimate fan bases then this is them. Well, it's a Mount Rushmore-or-Less because picking four is simply too hard as he explained in a previous edition where he picked the best football rivalries in the UK.

Everyone will have an opinion and this is who Max has experienced in his time as a match going football fan.

Celtic fans 'unrivalled'

Kicking us off, Scott picked Celtic supporters and it wasn't a hard decision for him at all.

The 56-time Scottish champions are backed by 60,000 fans every time they play at home and they always have a huge following on the road and in Europe, with passion pouring from the stands.

"It's difficult to deny, Celtic have one of the best fanbases in the UK," he explained. "They are undeniably one of the loudest, most passionate fanbases I've ever seen.

"All you need to do is look at the numbers - the Scottish Premiership has 18.5 attendees per 1,000 members of the public that go to football games. This is 70 per cent higher than anywhere else in Europe.

"So, in terms of a nation, Scotland love their football and Celtic without a doubt lead the way.

"Parkhead is an unbelievable stadium, it sets an unbelievable atmosphere and it's the Celtic fans that make it come alive.

"So whilst they might be playing in a league that isn't as competitive as we would like it to be, their fans are unrivalled."

What is Mount Rushmore? The faces of George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Abraham Lincoln are carved into the stone in South Dakota, chosen for their representation of the most important events in the United States' history. As a result, fans use the idea to create their own version to list the most influential or iconic games and people that define their selected categories. Here, though, talkSPORT argues five is not enough, so more or less this is Mount Rushmore.

6 Celtic fans are hugely passionate and create an incredible atmosphere as one of half of the Glasgow rivalry Credit: Getty

Fans fought to create 'unbelievable story'

Wimbledon were once a successful Premier League side before relegation in 2000 and then, in 2003, their owners moved the club 60 miles north to Milton Keynes and rebranded as MK Dons.

But the fans weren't having it, creating their own club instead, starting from the bottom again and remarkably working their way up the English Football League to the third tier in just 13 years.

"One of the greatest stories in recent English football history of fan power - it's that of AFC Wimbledon," Scott started.

"These fans had their football club ripped out the heart of their community by Pete Winkelman and Charles Koppel, who conspired to move the club to Milton Keynes. In many ways, they did it successfully, but it was the fans that rebuilt the club.

"4,000 fans turned up to the try-outs of the newly-formed, fan-owned AFC Wimbledon and today, they're in League One and doing pretty well."

6 AFC Wimbledon were born from the old Wimbledon and formed by fans in 2002 and have risen from the ashes where the fans have remained among the best in the game Credit: Getty

Scott continued: "What those fans achieved should never be underestimated. Millionaires can decide what they do with their football club, but it was Wimbledon fans who stood up and said: 'That's not happening, we're having our football club'.

"Their entire story is because of the fans. An unbelievable story."

Through the good times and the bad

"Far have we travelled, much have we seen. That's what Forest fans sing at the world-famous City Ground on the banks of the River Trent," passionate Forest fan Scott said.

"That Mull of Kintyre song is one of the best songs from British fanbases. Forest fans are one of the greatest in the country."

Nottingham Forest were two-time European Cup/Champions League winners and League champions in the late 1970s, sitting as one of the best clubs in Europe at the time - and fans remain proud.

"In the City ground you've got to different generations," Scott said. "You've got one that witnessed Brian Clough's back-to-back European Cups, the greatest story football has ever experienced and seen.

6 Forest fans saw huge success in the past and a new generation are now witnessing top-flight football Credit: Getty

"And then you've got a set of fans that grew up with their dads and grandads telling us those stories, but all we saw was dross in League One."

The once-successful Forest were relegated to League One in 2005 and wouldn't return to the Championship until 2009 - and the club would remain there until 2022, when a 23-year wait for fans was rewarded with promotion back to the Premier League.

"Now we're back where we belong in the Premier League," he added. "There's this sense of shared pride in our history and what we've been through as a fanbase - and as a result, on it's day the City Ground is one of the most intimidating atmospheres.

"It's because of the fans, it means more to them as they have been outside the Premier League for so long, they've watched the struggles in League One and with dreadful ownership. We appreciate it and that comes out with the fanbase."

Predicting a riot

"You cannot talk about the greatest fanbases in the UK without talking about Leeds United.

"I Predict A Riot, Marching on Together, Don Revie, Dirty Leeds United," he said of the songs at Elland Road.

"The reality is we sing 'We All Hate Leeds Scum' because the fans are incredible.

6 You won't find a tougher atmosphere to play in than away at Elland Road Credit: Getty

"Whether you're going to Elland Road on an away day or they're coming to your ground, you know you are in the presence of Leeds fans. Whether they're winning 4-0 or losing 4-0, the fans are unbelievable. They travel in great number and I admire it.

"I've been to Elland Road many times and it's unpleasant, it's ugly, it's a nasty place to be and that's because that is Don Revie, that's Leeds' culture.

"I love Leeds fans, Elland Road is an amazing stadium and you can't have this conversation without saying Leeds, they're absolutely unbelievable."

Who is the extra pick?

Four isn't enough, so Manchester United fans are the arguable fifth selection on the Mount Rusmore-or-less for football's greatest fans.

"I know that the team and the club and arguably the stadium are a shadow of their former glory, but United fans to this day are some of the most loyal, passionate, well-travelled lot.

"You think about the United fans living in Surrey who have never set foot in Old Trafford, but the reality is, when you go to Manchester itself, it's Man United.

6 Man United fans have always stayed loyal - and loud - despite the club's recent struggles Credit: Getty

"Elliot Anderson may have said Man City are the kings of Manchester...he's a wonderful player, but he hasn't got a clue.

"If you know football and football in Manchester, United are the biggest club there. The fans are a testament to the long-standing history of that football club.

"And what I like about United fans, more than any other big club, is that they don't half stay loyal or patient to some of the dross that they've had since Fergie left.

"They've hardly won anything...and despite all of that, United fans know that it takes time to build an empire."
