It’s Conex’s balance sheet and regional infrastructure, alongside AFC’s financing muscle, that gives AMR’s bid its weight.

What’s actually on the table for Liberia

If the deal closes on the terms in Severstal’s letter, the pitch is substantial: more than 20,000 jobs, government equity carried free of cost, a share offering open to ordinary Liberian investors, and commitments to build out roads, rail, power, and port infrastructure alongside the mine itself — rather than simply exporting raw ore and leaving the rest to someone else.

It’s worth saying plainly, though, that a binding offer is not a closed deal. The Share Sale and Purchase Agreement still has to be finalized, and the same questions about execution capacity that dogged AMR in the spring haven’t entirely vanished just because the sanctions issue has been resolved. Fifteen years of false starts at Putu have taught the southeast to be patient about promises made on paper.

A skeptic’s caution

Not everyone is convinced this reversal changes the fundamentals. Back when Severstal was still lobbying for Planet One, former Minister of Mines and Energy Wilmot Paye warned publicly against treating any change of ownership at Putu as progress in itself.

“I do not believe that a mere change of control is adequate to achieve any more desirable outcome than maintaining the status quo,” Paye said at the time, questioning what had specifically qualified Planet One over other bidders after Severstal had reportedly “concluded” transfer terms with them — the same abrupt reversal now playing out again, in the opposite direction, in AMR’s favor.

Paye’s broader argument was less about which company wins than about the structure underneath the fight. “Mining is not like harvesting a cassava farm,” he said, cautioning that Liberia won’t fully understand what it has agreed to until a real deal is signed — and warning that a successor could eventually seek to extend the existing Mineral Development Agreement through amendment, leaving the country “tied up” again. “The consequence?” he asked. “The vicious circle continues.”

Whether AMR’s newly cleared sanctions status and financing commitments answer that concern, or simply repeat the pattern Paye described with better paperwork, is likely to be argued over for as long as the deal itself takes to close.

The president’s bet

Seen from a few months’ distance, Boakai’s April intervention looks less like picking a side in a corporate dispute and more like buying AMR the runway it needed to clear the objections that were actually holding things up. Whether that reads as prudent mediation or as a government that nearly reversed a fair, competitive process before catching itself is likely to depend on who’s telling the story — and it’s a question this paper’s readers deserve to see asked plainly, not just answered on the government’s terms.

World.title: Liberia: Swedish Ambassador Pledges Continued Support for Post-War Justice, Sexual and Reproductive Rights Among Other Priorities After Embassy Closure
World.content:
Karl Backéus, Sweden’s ambassador to Liberia, presents the embassy’s annual investigative journalism prize to New Narratives/Okay FM senior reporter Fatu Kamara in a ceremony this month. Anthony Stephens/New Narratives.

Summary:

In an exclusive interview, Sweden’s ambassador Karl Backéus has pledged the country will continue to support Liberia’s postwar justice efforts through the U.N., E.U. and other multilateral institutions even as it ends direct assistance to the country.

Backéus said he hopes lawmakers will pass a bill to establish a war and economic crimes court “in the next few months.” He says international backing will depend on a “robust and strong” court, and financial ownership by the government.

Backéus said he sees progress in fight against corruption, but says major problems remain, citing concerns about corruption cases being delayed.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Sweden’s ambassador to Liberia has used an exclusive interview with Frontpage Africa/New Narratives marking the end of the country’s sixteen years of direct bilateral support since the end of the war, to reaffirm his government’s commitment to Liberia’s post war justice and accountability process.

Ambassador Karl Backéus said the Swedish government, which was one of the country’s most generous donors until last month, will continue supporting post-war justice efforts through the United Nations, European Union and other multilateral institutions. And he added his voice to international diplomats urging Liberia’s lawmakers to approve legislation establishing a war and economic crimes court within the next few months.

“I really fundamentally do believe that, as part of the reconciliation process in Liberia, there is a need for accountability,” said Backéus. “And even though it has taken a very long time, I do think it needs to move forward.”

Ambassador Karl Backéus attends a gathering of postwar justice actors in Monrovia in February. Source: Swedish embassy Facebook page.

Sweden’s commitment comes at a pivotal moment for Liberia’s long-running quest for accountability. More than two decades after the civil wars ended, no one has been prosecuted in Liberia for the widespread wartime atrocities documented by the country’s 2009 Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Six competing proposals involving a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court are before the Legislature, while questions remain over how the costly courts will be financed as international development funding shrinks. Sweden has been the major international donor to Liberia’s war crimes court process and was in recent years, the second largest bilateral donor after the United States.

Sweden announced last year that it was ending support to five African countries, including Liberia, in order to bolster support to Ukraine, which has been invaded by Russia. The government sees Russian aggression in Europe as a major threat to its own security.

The decision was a major blow for Liberia. Under its 2021–2025 cooperation strategy, Sweden committed about US$190 million to 39 projects spanning human rights, rule of law, governance, sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender equality, agriculture, infrastructure, independent media and climate and environmental protection. (New Narratives was a recipient of support.)

Liberia could continue to benefit from Sweden’s regional and thematic development programs , covering areas including gender equality, sexual and reproductive health and rights, democracy and human rights, peace and security, climate and sustainable development. Backéus said the European Union would be particularly important because Sweden, as an E.U. member, contributes to its funding. He also pointed to cooperation between Sweden and Liberia at the United Nations, including through the Peacebuilding Commission.

But Sweden’s future commitments to Liberia and Africa in general will depend heavily on the outcome of national elections to elect all 349 seats of the Riksdag held on the weekend. It’s turned into a genuine cliffhanger: early results put the opposition centre-left bloc, led by former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats, narrowly ahead of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s outgoing centre-right coalition. The race is too close to call.

Under Sweden’s outgoing government, Sida — the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency — has faced four consecutive years of cuts, with its 2026 budget reduced by roughly 20 percent as part of a broader shift that abandoned Sweden’s long-standing target of spending one percent of gross national income (GNI) on aid. Aid to Africa is projected to fall by two-thirds between 2021 and 2026.

Across the opposition bloc, the rhetoric is consistently pro-aid, but the near-term budgets tell a different story. Every opposition party still cuts aid in 2026 relative to pre-2023 levels — just less than the government — and none has taken a specific position on reversing the five-country phase-out that includes Liberia.

For now, Backéus said, post war justice and accountability is a priority. Sweden provided nearly $1 million to the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in Liberia, which has in turn provided furniture and technical support to the government office preparing for the proposed court. Backéus said he hopes that will continue.

“If we can be supportive of that, we want to be,” Backéus said. “We want to continue to stay engaged in this.”

Sweden’s “Stories of Change” on social media sites have documented their support for a range of areas in Liberia including small business. Source: Swedish embassy Facebook page.

A recent FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey of 1,150 people across 11 of Liberia’s 15 counties found 91 percent wanted the court, while 89 percent said they would not vote for lawmakers who failed to support legislation establishing one. The survey was not conducted under scientific polling standards. Backéus said it was a strong sign of public sentiment.

Civilians flee Lurd fighters on Bushrod Island in 2003. Credit: Tim Hetherington.

“I think it really shows that this is something that’s there’s broad support throughout society in Liberia, through communities all over the country for this important process,” Backéus said.

But he acknowledged the legal complexity of the competing proposals and said lawmakers needed to be confident that whatever legislation they approved was legally sound.

“But at the end of the day, of course, we want to see progress,” he said. “So I hope that we will see that in the next few months.”

Backéus said the precise model was ultimately Liberia’s decision, but international partners would need confidence in the institution before backing it.

“We need, of course, to have something that’s robust and strong,” he said. “And then, with that, I think the international community will continue to be there.”

He identified one potential obstacle to Swedish support: the possibility that the court could impose the death penalty.

“From the Swedish side. We would struggle, I think, to support any court that could, at least in theory, sentence people to the death penalty,” Backéus said. “That would not be consistent with our principles that we stand for.”

Financing presents another challenge. Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office of the War and Economic Crimes Court, has estimated that establishing and operating the court would cost at least US$20 million .

Backéus warned that international financing for tribunals is far more limited than it was 10 or 20 years ago, pointing to the heavily internationally financed Special Court for Sierra Leone as a model Liberia should not expect donors to replicate.

“Sweden will not be able to provide that kind of funding,” he said. “So there needs to be a stronger ownership for for this also financially from the Liberian side.”

Still, Backéus said he believed political commitment to the court had grown significantly in Liberia and that a less expensive model than some previous international tribunals was possible.

Sweden has been one of Liberia’s most generous donors. Credit: Swedish embassy in Liberia.

Backéus said Sweden had spent years building the capacity of Liberian institutions and organizations and had worked with partners to prepare them for the transition away from Swedish funding. He singled out support for independent media as an example of an investment he expected to endure.

“One example is, and I’m saying this because I’m talking to you right now, but you know, independent quality journalism, that kind of legacy will live on long after Swedish funding will end,” he said.

Backéus said he was confident Sweden had made a lasting difference and hoped its withdrawal would not leave many unfinished programs.

Backéus also praised Liberia’s democratic resilience in a West African region where several countries have experienced democratic backsliding, highlighting freedom of speech and a free press. But he said corruption remained a serious concern. The embassy has had a major focus on anti-corruption and accountability efforts with funding support to groups including the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia and Naymote Partner for Democratic Development.

“I think we are seeing some positive trends in that area, without a doubt,” he said. “A lot of work remains to be done, and I think it’s important to recognize that corruption is still a major challenge.”

He specifically raised concern about delays in corruption cases brought by the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission and expressed disappointment over the limited number of convictions and sentences.

The concern has also been raised by Liberia’s own anti-corruption authorities. The Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission that it conducted 44 investigations in 2025 and completed 29. It secured six indictments, resulting in three convictions and one acquittal during the year. The commission has blamed court congestion and the absence of a specialized anti-corruption court for delays in resolving cases.

“I think that’s part of the challenge with the capacity constraints in the legal system, and that there are too many cases that the Liberian Anti-Corruption Commission is bringing to the courts that are delayed,” Backéus said.

He said the proposed National Anti-Corruption Court could help address those constraints.

Backéus, who has traveled to Harper, Robertsport, Nimba, Lofa and other parts of Liberia, said the country also had enormous potential to build a tourism industry around its coastline, forests and other natural attractions.

“There’s so many beautiful spots for nature and tourist potential. I think is almost endless here,” he said.

But he said realizing that potential would require better roads, reliable electricity, investment and skilled workers.

“So I think potential is there,” he said. “It’s going to take time to develop that as well, but I definitely think it’s there.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: How Liberia’s Milestone Billion-Dollar Revenue Took Shape
World.content:
Monrovia- At a customs desk in Monrovia, a clerk stamps another form before 9 a.m. In a mining camp outside Kokoyah, a payroll officer wires a wage tax remittance she’s processed a hundred times before. In a market stall along Broad Street, a vendor counts out change for a small business tax she’s paid every quarter for six years. None of them made headlines this week. All of them, in aggregate, did.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

As of Wednesday morning, September 16, 2026, the Liberia Revenue Authority confirmed that the country’s domestic revenue collection had crossed US$1,005,638,048.43 — the first time in Liberia’s history that figure has read ten digits before the decimal point.

It is, in the words of Finance Minister Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, a number “assembled dollar by dollar, receipt by receipt, by Liberians.” It is also, underneath the ceremony, a story about concentration, timing, and a handful of institutions that carried outsized weight in getting the country here.

The Shape of a Billion Dollars

Ten taxpayers account for the visible core of this year’s collections:

| Rank | Taxpayer | Contribution |

|——|———-|————-|

| 1 | ArcelorMittal Liberia | $270M |

| 2 | Bea Mountain | $100M |

| 3 | Civil Service Agency | $35M |

| 4 | Orange Liberia | $28M |

| 5 | APM Terminals | $14M |

| 6 | Monrovia Breweries | $12M |

| 7 | LPRA | $12M |

| 8 | Aminata & Sons | $11M |

| 9 | LISCR | $10M |

| 10 | West Oil Investment | $10M |

Two names do most of the heavy lifting. ArcelorMittal and Bea Mountain together account for $370 million — more than a third of everything collected this year. That is not a coincidence of good fortune; it is a structural reality of Liberia’s economy, where iron ore and gold extraction remain the most reliable large-scale sources of taxable revenue. When a mining company settles its annual obligations — as ArcelorMittal did with a $209.6 million signature-bonus payment earlier this year — the effect ripples through the entire national ledger in a single month.

But the milestone isn’t only a mining story. The Civil Service Agency’s $35 million in payroll withholding is, in a quieter way, just as telling: it represents the cumulative tax discipline of thousands of government employees, deducted paycheck by paycheck, month after month, with none of the drama of a corporate settlement. Between the two — the single large payment and the steady payroll drip — lies the real anatomy of how a country gets to a billion dollars.

The Arithmetic Behind the Announcement

The number itself sits inside a larger structure. Liberia’s FY2026 National Budget totals US$1.302 billion — the original US$1.249 billion budget plus a US$53 million supplementary package (US$48 million in World Bank budget support and a US$5 million carryover from FY2025).

Of that, US$312 million is earmarked for public infrastructure spending under the Public Sector Investment Program, funded through a combination of the full US$200 million ArcelorMittal signing bonus, US$23 million in World Bank support, and US$89 million drawn from ordinary domestic revenue.

With roughly three and a half months left in the fiscal year, LRA still faces a US$296 million gap between what’s been collected and what the full budget requires. But officials are quick to note that US$120 million of that gap is already spoken for through committed external financing — US$88 million from the World Bank, US$20 million from the European Union, and US$12 million from the African Development Bank. LRA’s own year-end forecast puts total domestic collections at US$1.42 billion, which would leave the Authority US$140 million ahead of its domestic target by December.

In other words: the billion-dollar headline is real, but it is a waypoint, not a finish line. The harder, less photogenic work — closing a shrinking but still real gap, largely through routine collection rather than one-time windfalls — happens in the months the cameras won’t be there for.

What the Number Doesn’t Say

It’s worth being honest, in the same piece that celebrates the milestone, about what it obscures. A significant share of this year’s total rests on two extraction-sector taxpayers and one large one-time bonus payment. Strip out ArcelorMittal’s signature bonus, and the underlying growth in ordinary tax compliance — the kind that comes from broader businesses, more consistent withholding, and expanding VAT administration — is real but more modest than the topline number suggests.

That distinction matters for how Liberia plans its next budget. A billion dollars built partly on a non-recurring mining payment is a different fiscal foundation than a billion dollars built on a diversified, growing tax base. LRA’s own five-year strategic plan — with its emphasis on digitization, automation, and the pending introduction of VAT — reads like an acknowledgment of exactly that gap: an effort to convert this year’s milestone into next year’s baseline, rather than this year’s high-water mark.

The Human Ledger

Commissioner General James Dorbor Jallah has called LRA staff “Liberia’s unsung heroes” — the officers at ports, borders, and county offices who process the thousands of smaller transactions that never make a top-ten list but that, together, are the difference between a target missed and a target met. Minister Ngafuan’s framing is similar: the billion dollars, he has said, is not a trophy but a toolbox — for clinics, classrooms, and roads that depend on the country’s ability to fund itself.

Whether this particular Wednesday morning belongs to a mining company’s remittance, a government payroll withholding, or the accumulated weight of thousands of smaller filings is, in the end, a less important question than the one the country now has to answer: can it do this again next year, without a $200 million bonus to lean on?

World.title: Liberia: VP Koung Dismisses Brussels Airport Search Report
World.content:
MONROVIA — Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung has pushed back against reports that he was stopped and searched while transiting through Brussels Airport, dismissing the claims as the latest in a pattern of stories he says follow him regardless of how routinely he travels.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

In a statement addressing the reports, Koung said he had used the standard passenger route through the airport — the same one “everyone uses” — to pick up items for his daughter at the Duty Free stores. He said the screening was uneventful.

“No shoes, no jacket was removed,” Koung said, pushing back directly on the specifics of the reports.

The Vice President drew a comparison to an earlier controversy from 2024, when he flew on a private jet belonging to a friend, free of charge — a trip that also generated public discussion and scrutiny at the time. He suggested the pattern was not coincidental.

“Again, this is the effect of the package,” Koung said, referring — without further elaboration in his statement — to what he characterizes as a recurring dynamic around coverage of his travel.

VP Koung was en route to Vienna, Austria to attend the 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

Nuclear Technology Access

At the conference, Koung called for greater and more equitable access to peaceful nuclear science and technology, particularly for developing countries seeking to apply nuclear technology in healthcare, agriculture, environmental protection and radiation safety.

He reaffirmed Liberia’s commitment to the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology, arguing that access to its benefits should not be determined by geography or national income.

“We believe that access to peaceful nuclear technology must not be determined by geography or by national income. Its benefits must reach people in countries with the greatest needs,” Koung said.

World.title: A $200 Million Lost Opportunity: Turning Liberia’s natural-resource windfalls into national wealth
World.content:
THE GOVERNMENT of Liberia recently received a $200 million signature bonus from ArcelorMittal in connection with the extension of its Minerals Development Agreement. Under the agreement, the government is expected to receive an additional $100 million in 2027, $100 million in 2028, and another $100 million in 2029, bringing total signature-bonus payments to $500 million.

THIS IS A SIGNIFICANT windfall for a country whose fiscal resources are severely constrained. The initial $200 million received in 2026 alone represents more than one-fifth of the government’s 2025 domestic revenue. It is therefore legitimate for Liberians to ask a fundamental question: What are we going to do with this extraordinary, once-in-a-generation opportunity?

AVAILABLE INFORMATION indicates that the initial payment has been incorporated into the government’s overall fiscal resources and is being used to support ordinary operations. If the entire amount is absorbed into recurrent and annual budgetary expenditures, then by the end of the fiscal year Liberia may have little or no enduring asset to show for this exceptional revenue.

THAT WOULD be a missed opportunity — not because government spending is inherently wrong, but because a one-time resource windfall should not be treated the same way as recurring government revenue. A signature bonus is finite. Once spent, it is gone.

THE QUESTION therefore, is not simply how much government can spend today. The more important question is how Liberia can transform a temporary windfall from its natural resources into permanent national wealth.

THE CASE FOR A LIBERIAN SOVEREIGN WEALTH FUND

ONE POSSIBLE answer is the establishment and capitalization of a Liberian Sovereign Wealth Fund, or a broader National Investment Fund — a state-owned investment vehicle capitalized from sources such as fiscal surpluses, resource revenues, foreign-exchange reserves, privatization proceeds and other extraordinary receipts. Its purpose can include saving for future generations, stabilizing public finances, and investing in assets that generate long-term returns.

LIBERIA WOULD not be venturing into uncharted territory. Across Africa, countries including Nigeria, Ghana, Senegal, Guinea, Cape Verde, Libya and Botswana have established sovereign or state investment vehicles combining savings, stabilization, infrastructure and intergenerational objectives.

THE IMPORTANT point is that Liberia’s natural resources should create more than temporary government revenue. They should create national capital.

SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS OF IRON ORE: WHAT DO WE HAVE TO SHOW FOR IT?

LIBERIA HAS been commercially exporting iron ore for approximately 75 years. In 1951, the Liberia Mining Company began commercial exports from the Bomi Hills mines, with an initial shipment of roughly 10,000 tons of ore to the United States. Iron ore subsequently became one of the pillars of Liberia’s economy, generating substantial export earnings and government revenue over several decades.

YET CONSIDER Bomi today. Tubmanburg, the capital of Bomi County, bears little resemblance to what one would expect of a community that once stood at the center of a major international mining industry. Its infrastructure remains inadequate, economic opportunities are limited, and the communities surrounding the former mining areas continue to face significant development challenges.

BOMI IS NOT simply a story about one mining town. It forces us to confront a larger national question: After roughly 75 years of exporting iron ore, how much of the wealth generated from our mineral resources has been transformed into enduring national assets?

THE SAME QUESTION applies to our other natural resources. We have mined iron ore, exported rubber, harvested timber, extracted gold, and granted concessions for other minerals. Yet Liberia remains heavily dependent on external financing, development assistance and borrowing to meet many of its basic infrastructure and development needs. We must therefore begin thinking differently.

WHAT COULD $200 MILLION BECOME?

IMAGINE IF a meaningful portion of the $200 million had been placed into a professionally managed sovereign investment vehicle rather than being entirely absorbed by the annual budget. The objective would not necessarily be to lock the money away indefinitely, but to convert a finite resource payment into a portfolio of assets capable of generating value for Liberians for decades.

A NATIONAL INVESTMENT fund could, for example, allocate capital among several carefully governed windows:

A FUTURE GENERATIONAL Fund. A portion could be invested internationally in diversified, professionally managed assets, with the principal preserved while investment returns accumulate. Instead of saying Liberia received $200 million and spent it, future generations could say our generation inherited a national investment portfolio that began with the proceeds of our natural resources.

A LIBERIAN Value-Addition Fund. Liberia produces gold, yet much of the value chain occurs outside the country. A portion of the fund could support the development of gold refining and other value-added infrastructure, subject to feasibility studies, commercial viability, regulatory safeguards and environmental standards — capturing more value domestically and strengthening the country’s financial reserves.

A NATIONAL CREDIT Enhancement Facility. Rather than simply lending government money, the facility could provide partial guarantees enabling credible Liberian businesses to obtain financing from commercial banks and other institutions. A relatively modest amount of sovereign capital could mobilize substantially more private capital.

A LIBERIAN SME/MSME Investment Fund. Liberian-owned businesses routinely face one of their greatest constraints: access to affordable, appropriately structured capital. A dedicated window could finance viable enterprises in agriculture and agro-processing, manufacturing, logistics, tourism, information technology, construction materials, fisheries, renewable energy and import-substitution industries — investing commercially and transparently in businesses capable of creating jobs, paying taxes and generating returns.

A NATIONAL EDUCATION and Human Capital Fund. An education endowment whose investment returns support scholarships and technical training in engineering, medicine, science and agriculture. There is a profound difference between spending on government operations today and investing in the next generation: one buys consumption, the other builds capacity.

INFRASTRUCTURE INVESTMENT: A portion of the fund could co-invest with private investors and development-finance institutions in commercially viable energy, telecommunications, logistics, transportation, water and industrial infrastructure — making government capital catalytic, using limited public resources to attract far larger amounts of private and institutional capital.

THIS IS NOT AN ARGUMENT AGAINST GOVERNMENT SPENDING

LIBERIA HAS enormous development needs. Roads must be built. Hospitals require resources. Schools need support. Civil servants must be paid. The argument is not that government should refuse to spend — it is that extraordinary, non-recurring resource revenues deserve a different fiscal philosophy from ordinary recurring revenues.

IF WE USE a temporary windfall entirely to finance permanent recurrent obligations, those obligations remain after the windfall disappears. If, however, we convert part of it into productive assets, those assets can continue generating returns long after the original payment has been spent. That is the fundamental distinction between consumption and capital formation.

WE HAVE ANOTHER $300 MILLION COMING

PERHAPS THE most important point is that the opportunity has not entirely passed. An additional $300 million is expected over the next three years under the payment schedule. That gives Liberia another chance to make a different choice.

What should Liberia look like in 2040, since we received this money in 2027, 2028 and 2029?

WE SHOULD NOT be satisfied merely because a government has balanced an annual budget. We should ask whether today’s decisions have increased the wealth, productive capacity and economic independence of the Liberian people.

FROM NATURAL RESOURCES TO NATIONAL WEALTH

FOR TOO LONG Liberia’s development conversation has focused on the resources beneath our soil without sufficient attention to the assets we should build above it. Iron ore is finite. Gold is finite. Timber is finite. Even concession revenues are finite. Human capital, productive enterprises, infrastructure, financial assets and institutions can endure.

THAT IS WHY the real measure of natural-resource management should not simply be how much revenue government collects. It should be how much permanent national wealth we create from the resources nature has entrusted to us. Liberia is blessed with considerable natural resources, but natural resources alone do not make a country prosperous — institutions, human capital, investment, sound fiscal management and prudent stewardship do.

THE RESPONSIBILITY OF LEADERSHIP

THE RESPONSIBILITY for this decision does not rest with the President or the Minister of Finance alone. It also rests squarely with the Legislature, which has the constitutional responsibility to scrutinize and approve the national budget and to determine, through legislation and appropriation, how public resources are used. That is more than a legal obligation — it is a responsibility to the Liberian people.

WHEN LEGISLATORS decide whether an extraordinary national resource should finance consumption today or create assets for tomorrow, they are making a decision that can affect generations of Liberians. Will we buy more government vehicles, or help educate the next Liberian doctor, engineer, scientist or entrepreneur? Will our children inherit another story of resources extracted and revenues spent, or institutions, businesses, infrastructure and financial assets built from those resources?

A CALL FOR A NEW ECONOMIC MINDSET

LIBERIA’S MINDSET must mean more than political sovereignty. True independence also requires economic capacity — the ability to increasingly finance our own development, build our own institutions, invest in our own people and reduce our dependence on the generosity of others.

WE CANNOT CONTINUE to appeal to the international community for assistance while allowing exceptional domestic resource revenues to disappear into ordinary consumption without building a corresponding stock of national assets. Our natural resources are a gift from God and a trust from one generation to another. We have a moral and economic obligation to manage them wisely.

THE $200 MILLION should be a wake-up call. More importantly, the remaining $300 million should be an opportunity to change course. Let us establish the mechanisms, governance structures and investment disciplines necessary to ensure that a portion of future extraordinary resource revenues is transformed into permanent national wealth.

LET US CREATE a fund that is professionally managed, independently governed, transparently audited and protected from political interference. Let us invest for Liberia — not merely for today, but for tomorrow.

BECAUSE THE REAL question is not whether Liberia has resources. The real question is whether we have the wisdom to turn those resources into wealth that will outlive us. That is the test of leadership — and the responsibility we owe to the generations of Liberians yet unborn.

World.title: Liberia: Several Females Fishmongers in West Point Receive First Cash Payment Through Government-Led Social Projection Project
World.content:
The West Point Town Hall was on Wednesday, September 16, 2026 overcome by joy as the first beneficiaries of 50 females fishmongers stood to their feet to dance to different musical beats as they received the first disbursement of US$450 intended to improve their business.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Each of the 50 marketers under the program was selected/qualified to receive a total sum of US$900 to improve her businesses after going through a series of vetting and verification processes.

And the joyful day arrived on Wednesday as they were told to gather in the Star of the Sea Town Hall in Monrovia’s densely populated township.

To them, the first payment means their dream and aspiration of expanding their business is being realized through the Recovery of Economic Activity for Liberian Informal Sector Employment (REALISE) Project – a Government of Liberia’s social protection project funded by the World Bank, French Development Agency (AFD), and Swedish International Development Association (SIDA).

The REALISE Project aims to increase access to income-earning opportunities for the vulnerable in the informal sector in response to crises, expand income and livelihood support to poor and food-insecure households, and improve efficiency in managing social protection programs.

It is implemented by Ministry of Youth and Sports (lead coordinator), Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, and Liberia Agency for Community Empowerment (LACE) through a single Project Management Team (PMT).

The project has six components including: Grant Support to Vulnerable Households to Revive or Start Small Businesses; Temporary Employment Support; Community Livelihood and Agriculture Support (CLAS); and Social Cash Transfer.

On Monrovia on June 11, 2026, the REALISE Project officially launched the PROBLUE – an initiative aimed at improving livelihoods of fishmongers and strengthening economic opportunities within Liberia’s coastal communities.

PROBLUE is a multi-donor trust fund administered by the World Bank that supports sustainable and integrated development of marine and coastal resources in a healthy ocean, aligned to Goal 14 of the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Accordingly, speaking at occasion marking the first disbursement of grants to beneficiaries of the ProBlue Program, Mr. Julius K. Sele, Executive Director of the Liberia Agency Empowerment (LACE), pointed out that program is one of the means through which the government is trying to help its vulnerable citizens to in turn be able to help themselves.

“Today we are here to talk about empowerment, how to make our people able to help themselves and help their families. You know every time we pass around people say ‘government find job for the people, government find job for the people.’ But who is the government? The government is you. Why don’t you want to find your own job? And then the people you elected will use their power to help you,” said the LACE bossd.

“Today we came to join the government to address the issue of unemployment. I want to say congratulations to you, because for the last three or four months you have been listening to people, going through the training and everything they told you to do. So I know you are serious.”

Sele among other things called on beneficiaries to use the initial grant for its intended purpose so as to pave the way for the disbursement of the second segment.

With a joint call, they craved beneficiaries of the funds to use it wisely in order to encourage the donors to spread the program across other communities.

For their part, the women (beneficiaries) thanked the government and partners for addressing the needs, something one of the speakers described as realization of their dream. “We are very thankful to the Government of Liberia and the World Bank for this partnership. We want to thank all of the collaborating Ministries and Agencies for making our dream to be realized. We can assure them that we will use these monies wisely to grow our businesses so that others will benefit. Next time they see us, they will see a difference in our businesses. They will see total growth,” stated Princess Blamo.

World.title: Liberia: Women Legislators Hold Roundtable with Media Today to Strengthen Engagement
World.content:
Monrovia – The Women’s Legislative Caucus of Liberia (WLCL) will convene a one-day National Media Roundtable on Thursday, September 17, 2026, as part of efforts to strengthen collaboration and build stronger working relationships between women legislators and media institutions across Liberia.

The roundtable will be held at 10:00 a.m. in the First Floor Conference Room of the Honorable House of Representatives in Monrovia.

The Media Roundtable is intended to create a platform for open dialogue between women legislators and media practitioners, improve media understanding of the mandate and work of the WLCL, and promote regular, accurate, balanced, and gender-sensitive reporting on women’s legislative leadership and contributions to national development.

The activity is being led by the Women’s Legislative Caucus of Liberia, with support from UN Women Liberia The activity forms part of the project, Women Legislators in Liberia: Promoting Voice, Leadership, and Gender-Responsive Governance for Sustainable Development. The IBSA Fund supports the project with contributions from the Governments of India, Brazil and South Africa. The United Nations Office for South-South Cooperation administers the Fund.

The Women’s Legislative Caucus of Liberia (WLCL) serves as a unified platform for women legislators in the Honorable House of Representatives and the Liberian Senate, working to promote gender-responsive legislation, women’s political participation, and policies that improve the lives of women, girls, and vulnerable populations.

Despite the Caucus’ active engagement in legislative oversight, advocacy, constituency outreach, and policy reforms, many of its achievements, interventions, and contributions receive limited media attention. This has contributed to gaps in public awareness regarding the role and impact of women legislators in Liberia’s national development process.

Recognizing the strategic role of the media in informing the public, promoting accountability, and shaping national discourse, the WLCL is convening the Media Roundtable to foster stronger and more sustained collaboration with media institutions.

The engagement will provide an avenue for open dialogue, mutual understanding, improved access to legislative information, and stronger professional relationships between women lawmakers and journalists. It will also encourage balanced, consistent, accurate, and gender-sensitive reporting on the work of women legislators and issues affecting women and girls.

The WLCL believes that a stronger partnership with the media is essential to ensuring that citizens are better informed about legislative processes, policy initiatives, advocacy efforts, and the contributions of women lawmakers to Liberia’s democratic governance and development.

The national media roundtable will be followed by county-level media engagements led by each of the 11 WLCL legislators within their respective constituencies providing opportunities for women lawmakers to interact directly with local media practitioners and strengthen sustained communication at the county level.

World.title: Liberia: Senator Snowe Convenes NPP Leaders, Suspended Partisans in Unity Talks
World.content:
By Wednesday’ evening’s end, Senator Snowe reported that the exchange had been open and respectful, and voiced confidence that the standoff behind the suspensions could be settled within days

MONROVIA – A private residence in the ELWA community in Paynesville became the setting for a pivotal internal conversation within the National Patriotic Party (NPP) Wednesday, as Senator Edwin Snowe convened a closed-door meeting between the party’s top leadership and representatives of partisans who had been suspended amid a lingering internal dispute.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Seated around the table were NPP Chairman Atty. Sylvester George Mulbah, Vice Chairman Mr. Mark Keshen, known widely within party circles as “Fox,” and several members of the Executive Committee, who met face-to-face with a delegation of concerned partisans headed by Mr. Emmanuel Goll, Mr. Doa Metzer, and Ms. Amanda Gannett.

The presence of Chairman Emeritus Sen. James P. Biney lent further weight to the proceedings, with attendees describing his counsel as instrumental in keeping the conversation grounded and forward-looking.

By the evening’s end, Senator Snowe reported that the exchange had been open and respectful, and voiced confidence that the standoff behind the suspensions could be settled within days.

Senator Snowe’s decision to host the gathering is inseparable from his own identity as a member of the National Patriotic Party, a fact that shaped both the tone and the stakes of the meeting. Rather than approaching the dispute as a neutral outsider, Senator Snowe engaged as a partisan with a direct interest in seeing his party heal its internal wounds, lending the discussions a sense of shared ownership over the outcome.

His choice to bring both the party’s executive leadership and the suspended partisans’ representatives into the same room, under one roof, reflected a calculated effort to use his standing within the NPP to force a face-to-face reckoning that had perhaps been avoided for too long.

In doing so, Senator Snowe cast himself not as a mediator parachuted in from outside, but as a party man determined to see the NPP’s internal house set back in order.

Among those who left the meeting visibly encouraged was NPP Chairman Atty. George Sylvester Mulbah, who is understood to have approached the evening’s discussions with considerable warmth and openness despite the sensitive nature of the issues at hand.

Those familiar with the meeting say Mulbah arrived prepared not to relitigate the circumstances that had led to the partisans’ suspension, but to listen carefully and work toward practical solutions that could restore harmony within the party’s ranks.

His conduct throughout the session was marked by patience and a visible desire to keep the conversation constructive, repeatedly redirecting attention away from past grievances and toward the party’s shared future, a posture that reportedly set a cooperative tone for the rest of the attendees.

The chairman’s satisfaction with the meeting was evident in the remarks he is said to have shared with those present, in which he praised the spirit of the engagement and the willingness of all parties to show up in good faith. He is quoted as saying,

“It takes courage for a party to sit down and confront its own internal difficulties, and tonight I saw that courage in this room.” He is further quoted as remarking, “Our unity as the NPP cannot be negotiable, and I am confident that what we started here tonight will carry us toward a full and lasting resolution.”

Party observers say such comments, coming directly from the chairman, have already begun to reassure anxious partisans that leadership remains firmly committed to healing the rift rather than allowing it to fester.

As the meeting drew to a close, both Senator Snowe and Chairman Mulbah reaffirmed that dialogue, reconciliation, and unity would remain the guiding principles as the party works toward resolving the outstanding issues tied to the suspensions.

The active participation of senior figures such as Chairman Emeritus Sen. James P. Biney, combined with the visibly constructive engagement from both Mulbah and the delegation representing the concerned partisans, has left many within the NPP cautiously optimistic that a durable resolution is now within reach. With commitments made on all sides to continue talks in good faith, attention within the party now turns to whether the coming days will deliver the peaceful and speedy resolution both camps say they are determined to achieve.

World.title: Playing AFCON qualifiers with interim coach worrying – Chalawila
World.content:
Kitwe-based football administrator Sydney Chalawila has expressed concern that Zambia is going into the crucial 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers with an interim coach.

Nchanga Rangers coach George Lwandamina is currently drilling the Chipolopolo in an interim capacity alongside Osward Mutapa, the coach of local champions Power Dynamos.

The Football Association of Zambia (FAZ) is yet to hire a permanent Chipolopolo coach, 11 months after the departure of Israeli trainer Avram Grant.

Lwandamina was appointed interim Zambia coach last March, after the departure of Moses Sichone, who led the team at the last Africa Cup in Morocco.

There are suggestions that FAZ would have hired a new coach or confirmed Lwandamina on a permanent basis prior to the AFCON qualifiers.

Commenting on the matter, Chalawila, the former Kitwe United General Secretary, said going into the qualifiers with an interim coach may have a negative impact on Zambia’s performance.

He said it was worrying that FAZ has taken nearly one year without resolving the issue of the vacant coaching job.

“We have to move on at some point. It’s been a year plus since a new FAZ was ushered in and what’s worrying is that up to now they haven’t settled for a permanent coach,” Chalawila said.

“Modern football requires stability to build confidence in players and stakeholders,” he said.

“We can’t wait for the 11th hour whilst the pressure keeps building up. This is a serious administrative concern which may have an impact on results,” Chalawila added.

Zambia plays Algeria in Algiers on 25th September and hosts Togo in Ndola on the 29th*.

“The team may lack confidence, which may be seen on the field of play. First game away against Algeria is crucial,” he concluded.

Zambia is in Group I with Algeria, Togo and Burundi for the 2027 AFCON qualifiers. The finals will be jointly hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.

World.title: ECZ Missed Its Own 24 August Deadline, Says Legal Analysis
World.content:
Legal Scholar Says ECZ’s Month-Long Delay In Publishing Full Election Results Threatens Transparency

More than a month after Zambians voted in the 13 August general election, the Electoral Commission of Zambia has still not published the full official results as its own roadmap for the poll had promised, according to an analysis by law professor Cephas Lumina.

Professor Lumina, writing in his regular legal affairs column, argued that the delay does not prove the election was invalid or that declared outcomes were wrong. He said, however, that measured against the Constitution, electoral legislation, the Commission’s own past practice and regional standards, the prolonged non-publication amounts to a serious and avoidable transparency problem at a moment when public confidence most needs strengthening.

He pointed to Article 45(2) of the Constitution, which requires the system administering elections to ensure not only free and fair elections but also independence, accountability, efficiency and transparency, alongside a simple and practical system of voting and tabulating votes. The ECZ, he noted, is a constitutional institution established under Article 229, mandated to implement the electoral process, conduct elections, regulate candidates and voters, and delimit boundaries, with Article 216 requiring it to remain independent, professional, non-partisan and impartial.

The scholar drew attention to the Commission’s own “Revised 2026 General Election – Roadmap,” which had fixed polling for 13 August, receipt and verification of results for 15 to 17 August, declaration for 17 August, and, separately, “Publication of Election Results” for the period 17 to 24 August 2026. Because the Commission itself treated declaration and publication as distinct stages, he argued, the fact that a winner was declared cannot on its own explain why the publication stage remains incomplete.

As of mid-September, Professor Lumina said, the ECZ’s General Election Results page still directs users to 2021 and 2016 results rather than 2026 publications, while pages on the Commission’s new 2026 results portal continue to display some constituencies as “Results Not Yet Received,” with zero votes recorded. He contrasted this with the 2021 and 2016 elections, when detailed results were published within roughly two weeks, noting that the current delay has gone well beyond both previous practice and the Commission’s own published 24 August deadline.

Professor Lumina cited a range of legal provisions requiring prompt publication, including Section 28 of the Electoral Process Act, which requires the ECZ to compile and publish an election timetable, and Section 117, which provides that where documents must be made available for inspection or copying, the Commission should endeavour to make them available electronically. Read together with sections 72 and 73, which require returning officers to announce and declare results as soon as they are received, he said this supports a clear expectation of prompt and accessible disclosure, even without a fixed universal deadline for every polling-station result.

The scholar acknowledged that the 2026 election process had both strengths and controversies. He noted that the Constitutional Court had dismissed legal challenges over the sequencing of constituency delimitation and voter registration, and had separately upheld the ECZ’s authority over nomination requirements, while the European Union observer mission had described candidate registration as inclusive, transparent and timely.

He was more critical of the Commission’s late guidance on ballot-marking, which he said blurred the distinction between the prescribed cross and other marks that could still indicate clear voter intention, and of the ECZ’s decision on 14 August to suspend counting and announcement of results nationwide. While the legal power to suspend counting existed under the Act, Professor Lumina said observers had questioned the transparency surrounding its exercise, with regional bodies recording the uncertainty and mistrust the pause created and pointing to procedural concerns during tabulation.

Comparative jurisprudence, he argued, is instructive here. Courts in Kenya have emphasised that transparency and verifiability require an auditable record connecting polling station, constituency and national totals, and while Kenya’s statutory scheme differs from Zambia’s, the underlying constitutional logic of verifiability remains relevant to Zambia’s own Article 45. He noted that international instruments, including the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance and the UN Human Rights Committee’s General Comment No. 25, similarly call for transparent, independently scrutinised electoral processes.

He called on the ECZ to urgently complete the unfinished transparency stage by publishing consolidated presidential, National Assembly, mayoral and councillor results with constituency-level statistics comparable to those published in 2016 and 2021, and by clearly identifying any corrections, re-votes or missing returns rather than leaving them to inference.

Professor Lumina said the episode also strengthens the case for a formal, inclusive review of the Commission’s institutional capacity, involving the ECZ, political parties, civil society, Parliament and electoral experts, though he stressed this need not prejudge the validity of the 2026 election itself. “Article 45 does not treat transparency as optional once ballots are counted,” he wrote, urging the Commission to publish the results in full and let the numbers be examined.

World.title: Self-Interest, Not Conviction, Drove Nevers Mumba’s Exit From Politics- Sichinga
World.content:
Sichinga Says Self-Interest, Not Conviction, Drove Nevers Mumba’s Exit From Politics

Veteran politician Bob Sichinga has said the decision by former New Nation Party president Dr Nevers Mumba to quit active politics was driven by self-interest rather than genuine conviction. He argued that Dr Mumba was left with little real choice once a new law barring former presidents and vice-presidents from active politics came into force.

“I must say I feel the move was motivated by personal interest and not that he genuinely wanted to retire,” Mr Sichinga said, adding that he shares a close relationship with Dr Mumba but felt compelled to be candid about his own reading of the decision.

Mr Sichinga said it was evident that Dr Mumba had been forced into the move by the law, arguing that the former vice-president desperately needed the benefits attached to that status in order to continue living comfortably. He said Dr Mumba’s continued relationship with the United Party for National Development made the resignation from active politics necessary if he wished to keep receiving those benefits.

“One thing people should know is that this move has nothing to do with him trying to do the right thing but because he has his personal interests at heart to protect,” Mr Sichinga said. He described it as the most difficult decision Dr Mumba has had to make, framing it as a straight choice between benefits and political office.

Mr Sichinga said there was a need to respect the law regardless of the individual concerned. He drew a direct comparison with former president Edgar Lungu, who had his own benefits stripped over continued involvement in active politics, arguing that if that standard applied to Mr Lungu, it was only right that the same law apply equally to former vice-presidents.

The Action Institute for Policy Analysis Centre has taken a markedly different view of the same decision, welcoming Dr Mumba’s resignation from active politics as a straightforward matter of legal compliance rather than a question of motive.

Executive director Solomon Ngoma said the decision was simply in line with the enactment of the law governing former presidents and vice-presidents. “The law provides that former presidents and vice-presidents shall not engage in active politics or hold party positions once they leave office,” Mr Ngoma said, offering no view on Dr Mumba’s personal reasons for stepping back.

The contrasting reactions from Mr Sichinga and the Action Institute reflect a wider and continuing debate in Zambia over how the newest generation of senior political figures navigates the boundary between public service, party politics and the benefits attached to high office once that office has ended. For Mr Sichinga, the timing of the resignation, arriving only after the law took effect, is itself evidence that pragmatism rather than principle guided the decision.

For the Action Institute, by contrast, the law itself is the relevant fact, and compliance with it need not be read as either virtuous or self-serving. Mr Ngoma’s comments stopped short of engaging with Mr Sichinga’s characterisation directly, focusing instead on the legal basis for the resignation rather than the motivation behind it.

The dispute also touches on the broader precedent set by Mr Lungu’s case, which Mr Sichinga has used as his benchmark for consistency in how the law should be applied. Whether Dr Mumba’s own circumstances mirror that precedent closely enough to draw the same conclusion remains, for now, a matter of political interpretation rather than settled fact.

Neither Dr Mumba nor the New Nation Party had responded to Mr Sichinga’s characterisation of the resignation at the time of publication, leaving his version of events, and the Action Institute’s more neutral reading, as the two competing accounts currently in public circulation.

World.title: Kabesha Rejects Joint CSOs’ Claim That Zambia Has Descended Into Lawlessness
World.content:
Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha has rejected as unsupported a statement by a coalition of civil society organisations alleging that Zambia’s constitutional order is being systematically dismantled. He insists the country remains a functioning constitutional democracy governed by its laws.

Mr Kabesha said political actors and civil society groups have every right to criticise Government, and that such criticism is protected under the country’s constitutional ideals. He added, however, that legitimate criticism must be carefully expressed and backed by evidence rather than sweeping conclusions.

The Attorney General was responding to a statement issued by a grouping calling itself the Joint Civil Society Organisations, which had accused Government of overseeing a breakdown in the rule of law following the 13 August general election. He said the conclusions drawn by the coalition were grave but not supported by established facts and evidence, and rejected outright the characterisation that Zambia had descended into lawlessness or that its constitutional order was being dismantled.

On the cancellation of six Zambians’ passports, cited by the Joint CSOs as evidence of overreach, the Attorney General said the decision was lawful. The action was taken under Section 12 of the Passport Act, Chapter 129 of the Laws of Zambia, which permits the Chief Passports and Immigration Officer to cancel a passport under warranting circumstances. The six affected are former ambassador Emmanuel Mwamba, academic Sishuwa Sishuwa, former MPs Binwell Mpundu and Emmanuel Jay Banda, former State House aide Kaizer Zulu, and social media commentator Lillian Mutambo.

Mr Kabesha said it was misleading and wrong of the coalition to suggest the passports had been cancelled outside the law, adding that those affected retain avenues through which they can appeal. He also took issue with the CSOs’ commentary on cases currently before the courts, warning that such statements risked amounting to sub judice.

The Joint CSOs had raised concerns over the continued detention of National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu, whom the coalition said had been held since 27 August without appearing before a court. Mr Kabesha said Government remained committed to protecting the constitutional rights of all persons, including the right to legal representation, but declined to be drawn further on a matter properly before the judicial process.

Turning to a separate claim, the Attorney General dismissed as speculation the coalition’s assertion that newly elected Mafinga South MP Faith Munthali had been denied her right to legal representation, saying no evidence had been provided to support it. A related claim questioning the independence of key Government institutions was equally rejected as unsupported.

Mr Kabesha said it was in the national interest for key public institutions to operate independently, professionally and impartially. He reiterated that Government remains strongly committed to the constitutional ideals of separation of powers, checks and balances, and the protection of the independence of the judiciary, the Electoral Commission, the defence force and law-enforcement agencies.

While welcoming the coalition’s call for peace, restraint and dialogue, the Attorney General cautioned that any engagement must be conducted in good faith and should promote national unity rather than amplify unverified claims or undermine ongoing judicial proceedings. He said dialogue could not supersede the legal mandate of the courts to try matters brought before them, terminate legitimate criminal investigations, or confer immunity from the application of the law.

Mr Kabesha said Government remains open to engagement with political parties, civil society organisations, faith-based groups, professional bodies and other stakeholders, provided such engagement is anchored in verified fact rather than allegation.

The Attorney General’s statement lands days after seven international and regional lawyers’ organisations issued their own joint statement raising overlapping concerns about court closures, security-force conduct and the treatment of opposition figures since the election, placing Zambia’s handling of the post-election period under scrutiny both at home and abroad.

World.title: Govt empowers 124 CWACs with bicycles in Shangombo
World.content:
The Department of Social Welfare in Shangombo District has distributed 124 bicycles and raincoats to members of the Community Welfare Assistance Committees (CWACs) to enhance their mobility.

Shangombo District Social Welfare Officer, Telas Phiri, handed over the bicycles and raincoats during a ceremony held at the Civic Centre today.

Speaking during the handover, Mr Phiri said the bicycles are intended to ease the movement of CWAC members as they execute their duties in their respective areas of operation.

Mr Phiri explained that the department works closely with CWACs in delivering various social protection programmes to vulnerable members of the community.

“The CWAC members are very important to our department because they are the eyes of our department. They bridge the gap between the community and the department,” Mr Phiri said.

He said the provision of bicycles and raincoats will significantly improve efficiency and service delivery at community level.

Mr Phiri added that government is committed to supporting community structures that play a critical role in identifying and assisting the needy.

And speaking on behalf of the beneficiaries, Mulyata Mukiti thanked government for the gesture adding that said the bicycles will enable them to execute their duties effectively without the challenge of walking long distances.

“With these bicycles, it will be easier for us to execute our community duties considering the vastness of the areas we operate from”, Mr Mukiti said.

World.title: Govt commends TRALARD infrastructure in Isoka
World.content:
Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary Tuesday Bwalya has commended the Transforming Landscapes for Resilience and Development (TRALARD I) Project for constructing crossing points and an embankment in Isoka District.

Dr. Bwalya said the infrastructure has improved connectivity and benefited communities in the area.

He said this when he inspected two crossing points and embankment works along the Nansala Road in Isoka.

Dr. Bwalya called on Isoka Town Council to take over the maintenance of the infrastructure now that the project has ended.

He said periodic maintenance of the crossing points and Nansala Road would help preserve the infrastructure and ensure that it continues benefiting local communities.

“Indeed, there is impact. Our people have benefited from the TRALARD I Project, with infrastructure that Government has put up,” he said.

Dr. Bwalya also inspected a bulking centre constructed under the TRALARD I Project and urged Sansamwenje Cooperative, which operates the facility, to ensure that it functions at full capacity.

Meanwhile, Muchinga Province TRALARD Project Operations Officer Catherine Sakala said the crossing point was previously in poor condition, making it difficult for people, especially children, to cross during the rainy season.

Ms. Sakala said the bridges and embankment have also improved farmers’ access to markets and farming inputs.

“This whole part was actually a dambo area, so from where we started, we had to create an embankment to create connectivity for them to be able to get inputs and also to market their produce,” she said.

Meanwhile, Acting Isoka District Commissioner Kenneth Mwantalasha has urged Sansamwenje Cooperative to lower its bulking fees to attract more farmers.

Mr Mwantalasha said affordable fees would encourage farmers to bring their produce to the centre, gradually creating demand for its services.

“You need to relate with reality and set affordable fees that will attract farmers to bring their produce for bulking and gradually demand will be created,” he said.

World.title: Chipangali records reduction in malaria cases
World.content:
The Department of Health Services in Chipangali District of Eastern Province has revealed that malaria incidents in the district have significantly reduced to a range of about 50 per 1000, compared to 1021 per 1000, about 3 years ago.

Speaking during the malaria task force and epidemic preparedness meeting, District Health Promotions Officer Mutale Musonda noted that Chipangali has had a history of high malaria incidences as high as 1021 per 1000.

Mr Musonda noted that during the year 2025, the district began to experience a significant reduction in malaria cases with notable improvement beginning in the second quarter of 2025.

He said the district noted a significant reduction of 200 cases per 1000 during the second quarter of 2025, and that margins continued to reduce with a significant drop from 200 per 1000 in the second quarter of 2025 to 55.6 per thousand in the second quarter of 2026.

Mr Musonda mentioned that in the first quarter of 2025 the district was ranging at 600 to 800 per 1000 malaria incidents.

He said the reduction is a testament to the interventions put in place to help reduce malaria incidents in the district.

“There is a lot of testing happening at the community level through the community health workers who are conducting tests for malaria. Before any malaria case becomes complicated at community level, we have community health workers in facilities that are conducting testing at community level. So most of the cases are not coming to the health facilities, but tested and treated at community level, and by the time cases get complicated, someone will have already begun malaria treatment. The sooner we start treatment, the better the chance of reducing transmission,” he said.

Mr Musonda added that aside from the community health workers who were trained in malaria testing, government has recruited more Polyvalent Community Based Volunteers (CBVs) that have been infused into the Integrated Community Case Management (ICCM) programme, and are conducting training as well as Social Behavioral Change Communication at Community level.

He added that as of last year, second quarter, 90,853 people were tested for malaria at community level, while 50,037 people were tested during the second quarter of 2026

“Out of the over 90,000 people that were tested, 35,000 were positive. For this year out of the 50,037 that were tested, only 9,000 were positive. So there is a big gap of people that were found to be negative when you compare results for the two quarters. This is a significant drop in malaria cases,” Mr Musonda said.

He further mentioned that there are areas that recorded higher incidences of malaria which include Madzi-a-tuwa which recorded 74 per 1000 incidents of malaria, Mpawa which recorded 70 per 1000, Chakoloma area with 74 per 1000 cases and Mshawa catchment area which recorded 55 per 1000 malaria incidents.

“Our target for each community is to have cases as low as 50 per 1000. Out of 1000 people at least only less than 50 should test positive. But if we find people above 100 with malaria, then we are worried as a district,” he said.

Mr Musonda also noted that the Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) has played a significant role in combating malaria incidents.

He disclosed that the IRS programme will start on September 22nd, 2026, and that all eligible structures and households in the district will be sprayed to prevent malaria incidents from escalating.

World.title: Gamphani Lungu recuperates from injury
World.content:
Chipolopolo forward Gamphani Lungu is back in the Orlando Pirates squad after a two-week injury layoff.

Lungu was injured during Orlando Pirates’4-0 Betway Premiership win over Kruger United at Mbombela Stadium on 1 September.

Pirates have announced that Lungu is available for selection as his club make their return to Betway Premiership by renewing rivalries with Durban City at Orlando Amstel Arena on Thursday night.

“Coach Abdeslam Ouaddou’s squad could be boosted by the return of winger Tshepang Moremi who was kept out of Champions League action by suspension, while Gamphani Lungu is also back after a brief injury spell,” Pirates confirmed on their official website.

This is good news for Chipolopolo ahead of this month’s 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers.

Lungu was this week named in the 27-member Zambia squad for the back-to-back AFCON qualifiers against Algeria and Togo.

Zambia plays Algeria in Algiers on 25th September and hosts Togo in Ndola on the 29th.

Lungu has enjoyed good form after joining Pirates from Siwelele FC in June this year.

The former Power Dynamos player has scored three goals in six appearances for Pirates.

On 8 September, Lungu was voted Orlando Pirates Player of the Month for August.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 17, 2026
World.content:
press review

Sudan Gold Mine Collapse Kills at Least 60

At least 60 people have reportedly been killed after an informal gold mine collapsed in Sudan's West Kordofan region, with dozens more feared trapped underground. The Al-Zaraa mine, an unregulated site where dozens of small-scale miners were working, began collapsing, forcing miners to carry out a difficult rescue operation using basic equipment. The collapse occurred in an area controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, where artisanal miners work in largely unregulated conditions. A lack of heavy machinery and basic safety equipment has severely hampered rescue efforts. The disaster highlights the dangers facing thousands of Sudanese who have turned to informal gold mining amid the country's economic collapse and war. Gold is also a major source of revenue in Sudan's conflict economy, with much of the country's production extracted through small-scale operations and significant quantities reportedly smuggled across borders.



Social Media Censored in Equatorial Guinea After Corruption Claims

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Facebook and TikTok have been inaccessible in Equatorial Guinea for more than two weeks after a video accusing Vice President Teodoro Nguema Obiang, popularly known as "Teodorin", of corruption circulated online. Internet speeds have also been restricted since September 2. WhatsApp and Instagram remain available but with limitations. The woman who posted the video was subsequently arrested. The government has not publicly explained the restrictions. Teodorin, the eldest son of President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, is known for showcasing his luxury lifestyle online. He was convicted in France in 2021 in a case involving "ill-gotten gains." His assets were frozen in the United Kingdom following investigations into alleged corruption. Equatorial Guinea has been ruled by President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo since 1979 and has regularly faced allegations of repression and restrictions on civil liberties. The apparent social media shutdown comes amid growing scrutiny of internet access and online expression in the region.

DR Congo Ebola Outbreak May Have Started Months Earlier

The Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak may have been circulating for months before it was officially declared on May 15, with health authorities facing criticism over delays in detection and response. The first known case was a health worker in Ituri province who developed symptoms in late April, but reports of unexplained deaths in the Mongbwalu area had emerged weeks earlier. Researchers have suggested that transmission may have started as early as February. Genetic analysis cited by the World Health Organization also points to an outbreak beginning around that time. WHO has warned that delayed detection continues to increase the risk of transmission, particularly in communities affected by insecurity, displacement, overcrowding and poor access to healthcare. As of September 7, WHO reported more than 6,700 confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo and more than 3,200 deaths there, with cases also reported in Uganda and France.

Prosecutors Drop Fraud Charges Against Suspended South African Police Chief

South Africa's National Prosecuting Authority has withdrawn criminal charges against suspended National Police Commissioner General Fannie Masemola after determining that there were no reasonable prospects of a successful prosecution. Masemola had faced charges under the Public Finance Management Act linked to a controversial police health-services tender worth about R228 million. The case arose from allegations that he failed to act on warnings concerning the tender, which was later cancelled. The NPA said its decision followed a review of the evidence and cited its requirement that there must be reasonable prospects of success before a matter proceeds to trial. Masemola remains suspended, and the decision has prompted questions about what happens to his position as national police commissioner. The allegations are also connected to the wider Madlanga Commission inquiry into alleged corruption and criminal infiltration within the police.

Namibia Says Same-Sex Marriage Remains Illegal

Namibia's Justice and Labour Relations Minister Wise Immanuel has told Parliament that same-sex couples cannot legally marry under Namibian law. He said a 2023 Supreme Court ruling did not legalise same-sex marriage in the country, but dealt specifically with the recognition of same-sex marriages legally concluded abroad for immigration purposes. Parliament later passed legislation in 2024 defining marriage, although Immanuel said the legislation has not yet been operationalised. His clarification follows renewed confusion over the legal position, including claims circulating on social media about court rulings. The minister stressed that the Supreme Court judgment must be understood within the limited immigration context in which it was issued, rather than as recognition of same-sex marriage inside Namibia.

Nairobi to Host 2029 World Athletics Championships

Nairobi will host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, becoming the first African city to stage the global event. World Athletics announced the decision following its council meeting in Budapest, selecting Nairobi ahead of London, Rome and Munich, while Munich was awarded the 2031 championships. The decision is a major moment for Kenya, a country with a long-standing reputation for producing elite distance runners, and has been welcomed by athletes who say hosting the event at home could inspire younger generations. Kenya is also investing heavily in sports infrastructure ahead of major international events. However, hosting the championships will bring additional scrutiny to the country's doping record: more than 140 Kenyan athletes have been suspended for doping offences since 2017. Kenyan anti-doping officials say the number of suspensions has declined in recent years as efforts to strengthen clean-sport programmes have increased.
