World.title: Here’s who’ll be on ‘SNL’ when Season 52 starts next week
World.content:
“Saturday Night Live” added two new names to its cast for its 52nd season, while another cast member is moving on.

Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter will join the sketch comedy show as featured players when it resumes next weekend, “SNL” announced Wednesday.

“Welcome to the cast!” the show said on Instagram, in all capital letters.

Saidah Belo-Osagie

Saidah Belo-Osagie. Mike Klubeck

Belo-Osagie is a New Yorker from Queens. She wrote and directed “Tinge,” a short film; created an event series, “Afrobeats Futura”; and had a solo show, “Saidah Gets Closure,” “SNL” said in a news release about the two additions.

She shared the “SNL” post on her Instagram Story, writing, “A DREAM COME TRUE.”

Grace Reiter

Grace Reiter. Jill Petracek

Reiter, who is from Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, co-wrote, directed and stars in the upcoming Netflix show “Minimum Wage,” a series about teenagers running a pizzeria. It’s based on the series released online in 2024, which made waves on TikTok and elsewhere, Netflix said.

‘SNL’ departures

Chloe Fineman, who joined the show in 2019 for the 45th season and beyond, said July 16 that she was leaving to try something new.

“It’s really hard to leave SNL but it does feel like the right time,” she wrote on Instagram at the time.

Chloe Fineman on "The Kelly Clarkson Show" on Dec. 11. Weiss Eubanks / NBC

Fineman spent seven seasons as an “SNL” cast member, performing impressions of Drew Barrymore and Britney Spears and appearing in sketches and advertising spoofs, such as “Domingo,” “Snackhomiez” and “Forever 31.”

Deadline reported that Fineman would be joining the cast of “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent.

The annual turnover of cast members can be minimal, indicating that the show and its longtime executive producer, Lorne Michaels, are fine-tuning its cold open, sketches and news segment. Every several years, a greater number of on-air and writers room departures foreshadow a virtual reset for “SNL.”

Amid and after the 50th season and its accompanying anniversary specials, the show had some big-name departures, including those of Heidi Gardner, Ego Nwodim and Bowen Yang. Fellow departing talents Michael Longfellow, Devon Walker and Emil Wakim held the freshman-like title “featured player,” a position that often leads to repertory player status.

Season 52 of “SNL” premieres Sept. 26 with New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson as host and musical guest Katseye. “SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

World.title: Supreme Court pushes back against Trump and GOP ahead of the midterm elections
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court in the last week has delivered major blows to President Donald Trump and his fellow Republicans that suggest the justices will not be receptive to last-minute efforts to change election rules heading into the midterms.

With control of Congress at stake, the court on Monday night blocked Trump’s plan to exert federal control over mail-in ballots via a Postal Service regulation.

The decision came after the court twice last week ruled against Republicans by declining to revive a new congressional map in Missouri that would have eliminated one of two Democratic-held districts.

While the court has a 6-3 conservative majority that often rules for Republican priorities, there are limits to how receptive some justices are to more extreme requests, election law experts told NBC News. That’s especially true for cases that could disrupt voters when an election is close or already underway.

Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor and election law expert at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said the recent decisions show “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos.”

“I think the court is going to pay very close attention to any extraordinary actions that destabilize the electoral process,” said Bob Bauer, who served as White House counsel under President Barack Obama. “There’s a signal here that this sort of late intervention is going to receive scrutiny.”

On the left, the Supreme Court has been viewed with particular distrust and alarm as it relates to election issues following a major ruling in the spring that further weakened the landmark Voting Rights Act.

In the aftermath, the court quickly allowed Republican states to draw new congressional maps that eliminated majority-Black, Democratic-held seats.

But now it is Trump who appears angered and frustrated by the court’s actions.

“It is a big loss for Republicans, and America itself, and makes cheating by the Radical Left ‘Dumocrats,’ on Mail-In Ballots, a much easier thing to do — And now they have an open field to do so!” he said in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, repeating his unfounded claims about widespread election fraud.

With some states already sending out ballots for the midterm elections, timing was an issue for Republicans in both cases.

The Missouri Supreme Court faulted Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins for delaying a decision on whether the new map could be challenged, ultimately finding him in contempt for defying its ruling in favor of plaintiffs.

As for the Postal Service, it pushed through the new regulation despite concerns raised by election officials that they would be unable to implement it in time.

“In both instances, the court said we’re not going to countenance that,” said Travis Crum, an NBC News contributor and law professor at Washington University in St. Louis. “I do think that the Missouri case is going to send the message that dragging your feet like this is not going to be rewarded by the Supreme Court.”

There are limits to how receptive the Supreme Court is to more extreme election requests, experts said. Matt Nighswander / NBC News file

As the November elections loom, efforts to make late changes to the rules, including any new proposals from the Trump administration relating to mail-in ballots, are likely to meet with a similarly frosty reception from the justices, experts said. They cautioned, though, that it is too early to say what new litigation could arise ahead of or after Election Day.

Among the concerns that have been raised by some election officials are that the Trump administration could post federal immigration agents near polling places, although officials have said they have no current plans to do so.

As he has done previously, Trump might also complain about mail-in ballots being counted after in-person votes, claiming voter fraud because the outcome might appear to change, even though it is customary for various jurisdictions to continue counting ballots after Election Day under state law.

States with competitive elections, especially those that could determine control of the Senate, could be a particular focus for any Election Day or post-election litigation. These include Texas and Georgia, two states under Republican control with competitive races. Alaska, where votes often take a long time to count, is another state that could attract litigation, with Democrats hoping to win the Senate race there.

One fear among election administrators is that the federal government could try to seize ballots and other voting records over claims of election fraud similar to those Trump and his allies raised, and courts rejected, following the 2020 presidential election. In January, the FBI searched an election office in Georgia, seizing 2020 election ballots.

But as the Supreme Court has shown in other cases, the conservative majority follows its own agenda, not Trump’s, and has delivered him major defeats this year on his sweeping tariffs and plan to roll back birthright citizenship.

“This court is radically conservative,” Levitt said, “but not actually in the tank for Trump’s particular version of personalist chaos.”

World.title: 2 adults and child found dead after flooding inundates New Mexico
World.content:
Three people are dead after being swept away by floodwaters early Wednesday on the Navajo Nation, authorities in New Mexico said.

Tribal police officers received a report around 12:30 a.m. about people being washed away near the community of Newcomb in northwestern New Mexico. The report followed a day of heavy rain that left roadways and other areas flooded with standing water. More rain followed during the overnight hours.

Search crews responded and found the bodies of two adults and a child. Authorities did not release any details about the circumstances, other than saying the drownings were under investigation.

Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren offered his condolences and thanked first responders for working through the night in difficult and dangerous conditions as they searched for the people.

"There are no words that can ease the pain of losing a loved one so suddenly, and our hearts are especially heavy knowing that three lives were lost," Nygren said in a social media post. "To the family, relatives, and loved ones who are grieving today, we offer our deepest condolences."

The National Weather Service in Albuquerque issued a special briefing on Tuesday, warning that numerous and widespread thunderstorms were expected over the coming days. The organization reiterated warnings again Wednesday, noting that moisture levels were expected to be near record levels for mid-September.

The Navajo Police Department released images of multiple damaged, flooded roads, saying some streets "are currently impassable and drivers should not attempt to travel through the closure."

Three people are dead after being swept away by floodwaters early Wednesday on the Navajo Nation, authorities in New Mexico said. Navajo Nation Police

Excessive rainfall was predicted through Thursday for areas throughout the Four Corners region, which includes New Mexico, Arizona, Utah and Colorado.

Across New Mexico, an active monsoon pattern was forecast to continue through Saturday, bringing a threat for heavy rain and flash flooding, CBS affiliate KRQE reported. In Arizona, forecasters issued a flash flood watch for much of the central and northern parts of that state.

Nygren joined in asking residents to exercise extreme caution.

"Conditions can change quickly, and moving water can be dangerous-even in places we know well," he said. "No destination is worth risking your life or the lives of those traveling with you."

The three deaths on the Navajo Nation follow flooding just weeks ago at the Grand Canyon, where three hikers were swept away and dozens more were rescued after heavy rain brought torrents of water through Bright Angel Creek.

World.title: 9th woman found dead in South Africa, adding to fears of serial killer
World.content:
Johannesburg — South African police said Thursday a ninth woman's body has been discovered in an area east of Johannesburg, and said it could be linked to a series of killings they are investigating.

All nine bodies were found in the Ekurhuleni municipality over the last two months, raising concerns that they were carried out by the same person or people. Police previously said that some similarities in the killings of the first eight victims were "sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning."

The discoveries have sent shock waves around the country, sparked a high-level investigation and highlighted the scourge of femicide and high levels of violent crime.

Police said the discovery of the latest body early Thursday "will be added to the investigations into the deaths of women in Ekurhuleni."

Members of the South African Police Service (SAPS) Forensic Pathology Services work on the crime scene where the body of a woman was discovered on Sept. 17, 2026. EMMANUEL CROSET / AFP via Getty Images

Provincial police commissioner Fred Kekana said a passerby found the woman's body near a construction site and alerted police.

The unidentified woman appeared to be about 30 and had an apparent stab wound to her side, while her throat appeared to have been cut, he said. Forensic investigators had not yet determined the official cause of death.

Kekana said police had not established whether her death was linked to the other cases and appealed for information from the public.

He also urged people not to circulate photographs of the bodies or unverified reports on social media, warning that they were spreading fear and could encourage copycat crimes.

A multidisciplinary team of experts has been assigned to investigate the cases and identify those responsible.

So far, the bodies have been found across several Ekurhuleni communities including Kempton Park, Pomona, Clayville, Olifantsfontein, Rhodesfield, KwaThema and Dawn Park.

Police have imposed a lockdown in Kempton Park, French news agency AFP reported. "We cannot continue picking up bodies," deputy police chief Tebello Mosikili told journalists in Dawn Park, where AFP said the latest body was found.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi said police were pursuing leads and making progress in two or three cases, although he didn't provide details. He urged the public to give investigators time to gather sufficient evidence.

"They've declared war against the state. We'll respond," Lesufi told reporters at the scene. "We're not going to surrender."

Missing In Southern Africa, which supports missing people and their families, urged communities and families to report immediately when they suspected something unusual.

The organization said the discoveries had deepened the anguish of families searching for loved ones and urged people to report disappearances immediately.

"There is no waiting period to report a missing person," it said. "The moment you suspect that someone is missing, report it immediately to the South African Police Service."

World.title: Millionaires are everywhere in the U.S., new book says
World.content:
The richest person in your town probably isn't a technology entrepreneur or a hedge fund manager. More likely, it's the dentist who runs six offices or the HVAC contractor whose trucks you see everywhere, according to economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick.

These "stealthy wealthy," as the duo describes them in their new book, "The Everywhere Millionaire," typically get rich the old-fashioned way — through hard work over many years. And there are plenty of them in the U.S., with roughly 5 million households worth at least $5 million and holding combined wealth exceeding 13 times that of the Forbes 400, their research shows.

The findings, based on the economists' deep dive into Treasury and IRS data that matched tax records to individual businesses and their owners, show that the path to great wealth in the U.S. typically isn't through a regular paycheck. Instead, it's through ordinary enterprises that often benefit from the same tax breaks and structures — "pass-through" businesses such as sole proprietorships and partnerships.

"This is not just a story about wealth being on the coast, Silicon Valley and finance," Zwick, an economics professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, told CBS News. "This is a much broader phenomenon, and also much closer to home for a lot of Americans."

Economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick researched Treasury and IRS data to learn more about millionaires in America. They found that many own brick-and-mortar businesses like HVAC repair businesses or restaurant chains, rather than making their money in Silicon Valley or on Wall Street. Henry Holt and Co.

To be sure, the stock market boom has also minted a growing number of 401(k) millionaires, but Zwick and Zidar are focused on people who have amassed wealth far beyond what even dedicated savers have been able to sock away. These "everywhere millionaires" include 3 million owners of private businesses, with an average wealth of about $25 million, they found.

"Elon [Musk] is very rich, but the Forbes 400 is 3% to 5% of total household wealth in the U.S., and this group is just so much bigger, and that's consequential for understanding the economy," Zwick said.

The millionaire next door?

The new research is reminiscent of the 1990s bestseller "The Millionaire Next Door" by Thomas Stanley and William Danko, which found that many millionaires were average Americans who built their wealth through careful saving and investing. These millionaires were more likely to drive a used car than a flashy luxury car, and were less likely to live on Park Avenue than on Main Street, according to the book.

The millionaires who are the subject of Zwick's and Zidar's research aren't generally as unassuming as those studied by Stanley and Danko, with the economists finding that many of these wealthy business owners aren't shy about enjoying the fruits of their prosperity. Yachts, large houses and other extravagances are common, they found.

At the same time, their businesses are of the typical brick-and-mortar variety, rather than the headline-grabbing wealth associated with Silicon Valley and Wall Street.

"You're walking down the street, you look at a truck that's delivering beer, and if you look on the door, you see the name of the beer distributor, and then you go look them up, and you're like, 'Oh, that's an everywhere millionaire,'" Zwick said. "And you start to see them everywhere like that."

Who are America's everywhere millionaires

The research also examined the traits of the typical millionaire, tracking whether they inherited their businesses or wealth, for instance, or if they were more likely to have college degrees. The pair found that about three-quarters of these millionaires started their own businesses, while the vast majority didn't inherit money.

"The typical everywhere millionaire is 62, married," Zwick said. "They're more likely to be a college graduate, but not that much more likely than the general population."

Their business is also their day job, and they're not necessarily retired even though they're in their 50s, 60s or older, he added. "Often they're still quite obsessed with what they're doing," he said.

One typical millionaire profiled by the economists is Dick Portillo, who grew up poor in a Chicago housing project and started a hot dog stand in 1963 with a $1,100 investment. Portillo grew the business into a large regional chain, eventually selling it to Berkshire Partners for $1 billion.

Many of these business owners are driven chiefly by a desire to be their own bosses rather than to become rich, Zwick said.

"Freedom, independence, is almost more important to a lot of them when they're starting — Portillo similarly — than 'Oh, this is going to make me hugely rich,'" Zwick said.

Pass-through businesses

One common characteristic of many such millionaires is their use of pass-through businesses, such as LLCs or sole proprietorships, that provide a lucrative tax benefit to their owners. The tax code allows profits from these businesses to flow to the owner's personal tax return, avoiding the double taxation of corporate taxes.

Such arrangements also allow pass-through businesses to deduct 20% of that income from their taxes, allowing owners to avoid paying income taxes on a portion of their earnings. Those benefits help owners accumulate wealth in ways most W-2 employees can't emulate.

"You pay lower tax if you're getting your income through one of these businesses, even if your labor is going into running the business," Zwick told CBS News. "It has made them richer than they otherwise would have been, and it's an important part of the story of their growth over the last 40 years."

Will AI change this path to wealth?

Zwick said he believes his findings show that the American Dream "is more alive than most people think."

He added, "The prevailing narrative is very pessimistic relative to our reading of the data, but it's not necessarily where people are looking."

With artificial intelligence prompting speculation about the future of work, Zwick thinks opportunities to build wealth will continue to abound in the U.S.

"The problems that these people are solving are tactile, they're tangible — they're problems that people experience every day," he said. "Technology will change what these businesses look like, but these tactile, real-world problems are still going to be there. HVAC is still going to be a need."

He added, "There's a lot of room for people to take new technology but solve these old problems."

World.title: OpenAI reveals 6 more incidents of "unexpected or concerning" AI behavior
World.content:
OpenAI has disclosed six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behavior in artificial intelligence models as the debate on AI safety becomes increasingly heated.

The AI company also said Wednesday it was introducing a new framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called "misalignment," including where AI models acted without authorization, coordinated with other models or evaded oversight.

OpenAI's latest announcement came as U.S. AI bosses, including OpenAI and Anthropic, are calling for a slowdown in the technology's development over safety concerns.

In one new case reported by OpenAI, an unreleased research model inserted "jailbreak-like instructions" into its own notes to disregard its normal constraints and told itself to be "freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots."

In another instance, an AI "agent" uploaded files to the internet to obtain a browser citation without asking the user.

The six reports were discovered during training or evaluation over the past months, OpenAI said.

"As AI systems grow more advanced and more widely deployed, we need to build a broader and better-informed consensus on the progress of alignment research," OpenAI wrote in a blog post as it disclosed the events.

"Decisions about how AI development should proceed in the months and years to come need to draw on evidence that people outside the companies building frontier models can examine for themselves," the company said.

Wednesday's new cases followed OpenAI's disclosure in July that its rogue AI system hacked into AI startup Hugging Face. Anthropic also said the same month that its AI models hacked into three organizations during testing.

AI "agents" are becoming smarter and have become "more determined to resolve complex tasks through inter-agent collaboration, knowledge sharing, deception, and concealment," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at technology research and advisory group Omdia.

That's making it harder to govern and contain them using traditional AI security approaches, he said.

OpenAI's new tracking and disclosure framework, meanwhile, can help push for other AI developers to also adopt similar practices.

"That said, the process remains internal and voluntary, but is a step in the right direction," Su added.

In an open letter published Thursday, the leaders of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft and dozens of other signatories said there is a "limited window" to strengthen cyberdefenses and protect against potentially devastating AI-enabled cyberattacks. That window may last only months, it added.

The signatories also include security companies like CrowdStrike and banks including Citi and Capital One.

The same AI advances that could increase risks to public services and technology infrastructure can also help organizations identify and "fix weaknesses" that leave them vulnerable, the letter said.

"If we act decisively, we can use the defenders' window to make our digital world much more secure," the letter said.

World.title: 3 dead after NBC Los Angeles news helicopter crashes in Chatsworth
World.content:
Investigations are underway after three people were killed when an NBC Los Angeles helicopter crashed in the San Fernando Valley on Tuesday night near the scene of a deadly Metro bus crash in Chatsworth.

The helicopter crash happened just before 7 p.m. between two commercial buildings at a storage facility in the 9100 block of N. Mason Avenue, according to Los Angeles firefighters. The aircraft appeared to have landed on top of two shipping containers and several vehicles that were parked in the area.

Around 9 p.m., NBCLA confirmed that the helicopter belonged to their station. NBCLA later identified the two victims on board the helicopter as aerial news reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw.

"We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening," said a statement from NBCLA and Telemundo 52. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives."

A photo of Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw. George Marciniw

LAFD Captain Branden Silverman said a third victim was pronounced dead at the scene of the crash. Officials believe he was outside on the ground when the helicopter crashed.

The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner has identified the person as 29-year-old Edy Guitierrez Mejia.

Circumstances surrounding the incident remain unclear, but aerial footage showed Los Angeles firefighters working to fight the flames from a large fire that broke out after the crash and spread to the nearby vehicles.

Another victim was taken to a local hospital in unknown condition, the LAFD said. The nature of their injuries is not immediately known.

The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration confirmed that they will be investigating the helicopter crash. The FAA said the NTSB will lead the investigation. Both are expected to be at the scene on Wednesday.

Updates on the investigation

During a news conference on Wednesday, NTSB investigator-in-charge Fabian Salazar said the public can expect a preliminary report on the crash in about 30 days. After that preliminary report, a final report will follow, which will include the probable cause of the crash.

Salazar repeatedly called the crash an "accident," but refrained from speculating on what could have caused the helicopter to drop.

"The NTSB and the FAA and our party members will be on scene pretty much all day today gathering factual data from the wreckage," he said. "So [Wednesday] .... we are doing the field portion of the of the investigation. That is, we're on the accident scene gathering as much factual data as we can."

The initial steps of the investigation, aside from examining the wreckage, will include obtaining and reviewing video footage from nearby security cameras and conducting witness interviews.

Salazar acknowledged that the NBCLA helicopter was capturing footage from a live camera when the crash occurred. He called that video the "most important evidence" so far.

"What we're going to do is get a pristine copy of that recording and send it to our recorders lab for a sound spectrum analysis," he said. "Because in that recording, we are clearly hearing sounds that are consistent with the engine changing its speed. And we're also hearing tones that are being generated that are likely advisories to the pilot."

Anyone with information regarding either the deadly bus collision or helicopter crash was encouraged to email the NTSB at witness@ntsb.gov.

Mayor Bass and Gov. Newsom speak on tragic day

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and other city leaders spoke during a news conference on Tuesday night.

"This is a very, very tragic day in Los Angeles," Bass said while speaking during a news conference. "We lost five Angelenos today, and my hearts certainly go out to the families and friends to all of those that we lost. ... This is a heartbreaking night for our city, and my thoughts and prayers are with first and foremost with the families and loved ones that we lost today."

LA Mayor Karen Bass offered her condolences to the families and friends of the victims. CBS LA

Supervisor Lindsey Horvath called on Angelenos to support one another during such difficult times.

"Tonight is a time to care for the people who are hurting, to support our first responders and to stand together as a community," Horvath said. "Chatsworth has experienced an incredibly difficult day. To everyone grieving, recovering or processing what they experienced today, we are here for you and we stand with you."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom also shared a message on Facebook late Tuesday.

"Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family. Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight," Newsom's post said.

The Los Angeles Police Department offered its heartfelt condolences to the families, friends, colleagues and loved ones of those who died during the crash.

"The LAPD recognizes and values the vital role our media partners play in serving our community," the LAPD said in a statement. "Their commitment to informing the public — often in challenging and unpredictable circumstances — is essential to public safety."

CBS LA anchors and reporters also spoke on the tragedy impacting the tight-knit news community in Los Angeles after the helicopter's affiliation was confirmed.

"It was a double tragedy," said CBS LA's Desmond Shaw. "I don't want the poor people that were caught in the bus crash today - I don't want them to be forgotten either ... I obviously just have to give my heartfelt condolences to NBC and the family members of the crew on board."

"Our hearts go out to all of them. This is when we all come together for something like this, even if you've never met the person," CBS LA anchor Pat Harvey said. "I want to say that we have each other's backs."

"That helicopter community is a small group of people, and it's just devastating to know that this has happened to one of those people, to our friends and our colleagues at NBC4," CBS LA assignment editor Mike Rogers said. "Our hearts are shattered with you."

NBCLA mourns loss of colleagues

NBCLA and Telemundo 52 are mourning the loss of two of their colleagues, Moreno and Marciniw. Reporters and anchors shared tributes and memories they shared with Moreno and Marciniw.

The station reported that Moreno was born in Orange County and was a 2010 graduate of Chapman University. She studied broadcast journalism and political science. NBCLA added that she joined the Angel City Air helicopter team in September 2010.

Moreno worked across other Southern California news outlets, including CBS LA.

Marciniw also grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.

They began flying together in 2023.

CBS LA's Mark Liu said he previously worked with Moreno when she was beginning her career as a news helicopter reporter.

"I had the opportunity to work with her when I was an assignment manager when I was in the newsroom back then," Liu said. "What I remember about her is that she was so enthusiastic and so excited for this job. She described it as one of the greatest jobs in television news."

CBS LA reporter Rick Montanez also previously worked with Moreno. He described her as passionate and dedicated to covering news.

"I worked with her on a lot of breaking news during my years I spent in the NBC newsroom covering wildfires, covering breaking news across Southern California," Montanez said. "You could just feel the passion in her for this, this calling."

World.title: Ross Fire 100% contained after more than 3 weeks
World.content:
A wildfire that sparked near Ross in Palo Pinto County on Aug. 24 has burned roughly 90,000 acres and is 100% contained as of Wednesday, Sept. 16.

It destroyed more than 150 structures in the area, including homes, forced evacuations in neighboring Jack County and affected local schools, North Texas officials said.

The National Weather Service said the Ross Fire is the second-largest wildfire in North Texas.

How big is the Ross Fire and where was it burning?

The Ross Fire burned roughly 90,000 acres in Palo Pinto and Jack counties, with the fire burning near U.S. 180 and FM 919.

According to the Texas A&M Forest Service, the fire is 100% contained as of Wednesday, Sept. 16; 157 structures have been destroyed, 140 have been damaged and 453 have been saved.

Residents in Jack County along County Road 2210 toward Highway 281 were instructed to evacuate on Tuesday, Aug. 25; however, those mandatory evacuations were lifted a day later as conditions improved. Jack County Emergency Management warns returning residents to stay vigilant as the fire is still burning in neighboring Palo Pinto County.

The fire began near Ross in Palo Pinto County just before 1:30 p.m. Monday, Aug. 24, and was initially estimated at 25 acres, according to the Palo Pinto County Emergency Service District. It rapidly expanded to thousands of acres.

The Longhorn Council of Scouting America said many buildings at Worth Ranch in Palo Pinto were among the structures that suffered catastrophic damage, but no scouts, campers, or guests were at the property when the fire moved into the area, and the camp ranger, Pat Adams, was safely evacuated.

What areas were under evacuation orders because of the Ross Fire?

As of Monday, Aug. 31, all school districts in the area resumed normal operations.

The wildfire and evacuations affected schools in the area. Jacksboro ISD delayed the start of school by two hours on Tuesday, Aug. 25, but normal operations resumed the next day.

Perrin CISD canceled classes for Tuesday, Aug. 25, and delayed the start of school to 10 a.m. Wednesday, Aug. 26.

Jack County Emergency Management instructed Bryson ISD and Graford ISD to cancel classes that same Wednesday.

A Molson Coors spokesperson said the company had temporarily paused some canning lines at the Fort Worth facility out of an abundance of caution over the smoky skies.

"But beer lovers will see absolutely no impact," the spokesperson said.

The Texas Intrastate Fire Mutual Aid System (TIFMAS) Strike Team, along with the Texas A&M Forest Service, is supporting firefighting efforts with dozers and aircraft.

What roads closed because of the Ross Fire?

U.S. Highway 180 reopened after being closed to all traffic between South FM 4 and FM 919 because of the wildfire on Tuesday.

A Temporary Flight Restriction was in place over the fire area.

Where could livestock be taken during the Ross Fire?

CBS News Texas

The Graham Livestock Commission said that it was offering space for livestock displaced by the wildfire at the Old Mineral Wells Sale Barn at 2805 North Oak Ave.

The holding station is available to people who need a temporary place for livestock until other arrangements can be made.

The Humane Society of North Texas said it is helping the Mineral Wells Animal Shelter clear out its current shelter population to make room for pets displaced by the Ross Fire. Twelve dogs and 26 cats were expected to arrive at the shelter in Fort Worth on Wednesday.

Why is the wildfire risk high in North Texas?

Dry vegetation, a lack of measurable rainfall and gusty winds are creating elevated wildfire conditions across parts of North Texas.

The National Weather Service is monitoring several wildfires west of Interstate 35, with the Ross Fire among the largest.

After more than a month without measurable rainfall, fine surface fuels have become critically to extremely dry, making vegetation easier to ignite and allowing fires to spread quickly.

Residents are urged to avoid outdoor activities that could produce sparks or flames.

World.title: 5 missing women are linked to Olney home in Philadelphia. Here's what we know.
World.content:
Philadelphia police continue to probe a home in the city's Olney neighborhood that is linked to at least five women who are presumed dead, with the investigation into their disappearances centering around a father-son duo who lived in the house.

Inside the home, authorities said they recovered a trove of digital images and found a so-called "laboratory" of chemicals and a small marijuana grow operation. Eugene Horsch, who owns the home, was arrested in June and is facing firearms and drug charges. His father, R.C. Horsch, had also lived in the home before he died last year.

Here's what we know about the investigation.

Eugene Horsch arrested in June

Eugene Horsch was initially arrested in June when a park ranger saw him illegally parked near Philadelphia's Independence National Historical Park, according to a criminal complaint. When the ranger went to confront 44-year-old Eugene Horsch, he saw that there was also a woman in the car. When he asked for their identification, the woman's documents were those of another woman who had been missing since 2023: Blair Tonzelli.

While searching Eugene Horsch and his car, the park ranger found a switchblade, two guns, drug paraphernalia and forged documents identifying Horsch as a DEA agent, the criminal complaint alleges. Eugene Horsch was arrested and is facing charges related to the alleged forged documents, in addition to the drugs and firearms charges.

Search of Olney home

Law enforcement later in June searched Eugene Horsch's home in the Olney neighborhood.

A search of the home revealed hidden spaces containing dangerous chemicals, a 55-gallon drum connected to hoses and other piping, a small marijuana operation and what authorities described as 120 pieces of ballistic evidence.

Searches of the home have also uncovered "over 1 million digital images," which include "tons of pictures of lots of people, women, posed in different positions within that house," Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner of Investigations Frank Vanore said Wednesday. Police have said the images appear to show multiple women who have been reported missing and were last seen with Eugene Horsch. Several of the videos also appear to feature R.C. Horsch, while none reviewed so far include Eugene Horsch, police said.

Investigators have identified 58 people in the recovered images. Of those 58, 16 have been found alive but are not cooperating with police. Another 25 have been found alive and have interviews scheduled. Five women are seen on videos and in photos where they appear to be injured, and at least one person appears to be dead. Of those five, police believe they know the identities of four of them.

Police also found five urns that they believe contain human remains. Police said they believe one of the urns contained the remains of R.C. Horsch, another contains his sister's ashes and a third is the remains of a friend.

As of Wednesday, however, no human remains have been confirmed at the house, including any possible victims of crimes.

At least five missing women linked to Olney home

Police have said at least five women who have been missing for years are believed to be connected to the Olney home. They have been identified as Gabrielle Amarando, Maribel Fresses, Nicole Fusaro, Amy McHale and Tonzelli.

Amarando, 27, has been missing since 2012 and is one of the women seen in the images dated to 2017 that were recovered from the home, police said. Fresses, 26, was also seen in the images, also dated to 2017.

McHale, who has been missing since 2016, left her daughter a voicemail the night she went missing, saying that she was at the Olney home with R.C. Horsch, her family has said. According to her daughter, Amanda Stofer, McHale and R.C. Horsch met in the 1990s, married and eventually divorced, but remained friends. She went to his house that night following an argument with her mother, the family said.

In one of the videos recovered from the house, again from 2017, R.C. Horsch and a woman are seen naked. At one point, R.C. Horsch is seen handcuffing the woman to the bed, police said.

"He puts a zip tie around her neck, and she becomes unconscious on that video. Appeared to be lifeless at that time, but it's just appearing that way. I have to caution you, and emphasize, we never recovered a body here," Vanore said.

"We still need to find evidence to corroborate what appears to have happened in this video," he said.

Vanore said they believe some of the videos involved include "play-acting" while other events "could be real."
