World.title: Carney nods to Trump, says Canada, Europe not 'fair-weather allies' in speech to European Parliament
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says a "deeper partnership" between Canada and Europe is necessary to hedge against great powers encroaching on the sovereignty of smaller nations.

"Together, Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive," Carney said in an address to the European Parliament on Thursday morning.

"This is about sovereignty. Our ability to live as we wish. It is about the freedoms we must fight for every day. Sovereignty requires resilience — the ability to withstand shocks."

The prime minister called for an "alliance of the future" between Canada and the 27 countries that make up the European Union. Carney has been trying to forge closer ties with Europe amid Canada's ongoing trade war with the United States.

The prime minister nodded to U.S. President Donald Trump's tactics in his speech, saying economic integration has been used as leverage and suggesting that Europe can be a more reliable ally.

"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals," Carney said. "We hold common values, for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant."

WATCH | Trump says closer Canada-EU co-operation is 'laughable': Trump says closer Canada-EU co-operation is 'laughable' | Duration 0:25 U.S. President Donald Trump threatened the European Union with 'very serious tariffs' or to 'stop trading' if it makes a trade deal with Canada 'with bad intentions.'

As Carney stepped up to deliver his address, someone began a "U.S.A." chant. Others in the room booed in response.

When the U.S. president was asked about Canada and the EU seeking to strengthen their partnership on Wednesday, Trump called the idea "laughable" and threatened the European Union with "very serious tariffs" if it makes a trade deal with Canada "with bad intentions."

Carney offered a rebuke of Trump and other hegemonic powers in his address on Thursday, suggesting that an alliance between Canada and the EU will be a "beacon for other democracies."

"I want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners," he said.

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

Over the last year, Canada has signed several new partnership agreements with the EU. It was also the first non-European country to become a member of Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which provides €150 billion in loans for defence spending.

WATCH | EU chief talks about Canada in her state of the European Union address: 'We see the world with the same eyes,' EU chief says of Canada | Duration 2:57 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, after highlighting the shifting international order in her state of the European Union address, spoke of the potential of the Canada-Europe relationship. 'This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength.'

During his address, Carney proposed that Canada join Erasmus+, the EU's program ⁠supporting education, training, youth and sport.

"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," he said.

Carney's speech comes after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her state of the European Union address on Wednesday that the door is open for Canada to become an "associate member" of the bloc.

"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen said, drawing a standing ovation.

Carney then nodded, rose from his seat, approached von der Leyen and embraced her. He briefly waved to the chamber before returning to his seat.

The EU chief said the two must "urgently reimagine" their partnership, and move beyond just a free trade agreement.

Carney said he "welcomes the ambition" of that proposal, but he has preferred to use a different term, calling it an "alliance for the future."

"Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities," he said.

Carney and his team have been downplaying the idea of using "associate member" to describe a new partnership since it was first floated in a story in the Wall Street Journal last week that cited unidentified sources.

The prime minister said Sunday that Canada was "not looking to become a member" of the EU, a point reiterated by Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's incoming EU ambassador, on Wednesday following von der Leyen's speech.

WATCH | Ambassador focused on 'results' in deepened EU alliance: Canadian ambassador focused on 'results' after EU chief opens door to associate membership | Duration 1:33 Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's incoming ambassador to the European Union, says 'we're not there' after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered to open the door to associate membership. 'What we're focused on is actually driving results,' he said, adding the government will 'eventually' turn to how to describe the relationship.

"There are a bunch of different things people have used to describe what this [new relationship] could be. I think we've actually got to get to the point where we actually know what we're describing," Wilkinson told reporters following von der Leyen's address.

"It's nomenclature; I mean, at the end of the day, there's lots of different ways you could describe it."

Carney had a meeting with von der Leyen on Wednesday and the two discussed sectors where both leaders feel they can deepen ties, according to a readout from the Prime Minister's Office. Those sectors include critical minerals, AI, defence, energy and finance.

World.title: 911 services gradually being resolved after outages affect Ontario and other parts of Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Access to 911 service is down across parts of Canada and Ontario, including in Toronto, Waterloo region, and across Nova Scotia, according to emergency response services.

Residents in need of emergency services and unable to contact 911 are being urged to contact any available non-emergency lines.

Bell 911 service is down across Ontario, a spokesperson with Toronto paramedics told CBC News. They said typically 911 calls are filtered and transferred by dispatchers with the Toronto police.

CBC News has reached out to Bell for more information.

Service across Nova Scotia has also been disrupted and anyone unable to reach 911, should try using a landline, Wi-Fi calling or another carrier, said the province's Department of Emergency Management in a Facebook post.

They said people can also try calling non-emergency lines for their nearest emergency facility or the service they are trying to reach for immediate assistance.

Winnipeg police posted on social media platform X that their 911 service issue has been resolved after being disrupted for over 30 minutes on Thursday.

How to reach Greater Toronto emergency services

All emergency services in Toronto, Durham Region and through the Ontario Provincial Police across the province are still experiencing an outage of their 911 services as of 5:40 a.m. Thursday, according to their posts on social media platform X.

Toronto paramedics said anyone needing their assistance Thursday morning should still call 911, as some calls have still been coming through this morning.

Toronto police shared on X that anyone needing emergency assistance should reach out to their non-emergency line at 416-808-2222 or directly contact their local division.

Toronto Fire said on X they can be contacted through their non-emergency line at 416-338-9000.

Durham police requested on X that residents unable to access 911, should instead call their non-emergency line at 1-888-579-1520 for any emergency support.

Police in York and Peel region in the Greater Toronto Area, shared on X that their service is back up and running.

How to reach Waterloo, other parts of Ontario services

Waterloo Regional Police said on X that their service is also disrupted at this time. They said anyone requiring police, fire or ambulance services can call 519-570-9777.

Niagara regional police said on X that emergency services can be reached at 905-688-4111 or by reaching out one of their eight local district offices.

The OPP said in a news release there has been reports of "intermittent 911 outages across the province" and that they are working to expedite the service's restoration.

They urged residents to not call 911 for information, updates, or to test the phone line if they are not in an emergency.

The OPP said their non-emergency line at 1-888-310-1122 is fully operational and members are still responding to calls.

More to come.

World.title: Toronto cop charged in Project South allegedly didn't care if selling information harmed people
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Unsealed Project South court documents reveal new details on the police corruption probe, including allegations one officer knew confidential information he sold could help facilitate ‘serious violence’ but didn’t care.

Toronto police Const. Timothy Barnhardt knew the information he sold to a civilian from police database searches could help facilitate "serious violence and explicitly stated that he did not care if individuals were harmed," according to an Information to Obtain (ITO) application supporting more than 50 warrants in the Project South investigation.

The sweeping corruption probe began in June 2025, when York Regional Police thwarted an alleged plot to kill a senior corrections official from Toronto South Detention Centre (TSDC).

Investigators subsequently discovered Barnhardt allegedly ran an unauthorized search on the official's licence plate less than a month before the attempted hit, and he is accused of then sharing confidential information about that official with civilian Brian Da Costa. The identity of the senior corrections official is covered by a publication ban for their safety.

Both Barnhardt and Da Costa are in custody facing several charges in the probe, which have not been tested in court. Their lawyers declined to comment for this story.

The unauthorized query on the jail official was one of 17 times Barnhardt allegedly accessed the Ministry of Transportation server to do searches while off-duty in the first six months of last year, according to the ITO. Police-intercepted communications revealed to investigators that Barnhardt "routinely sold confidential database information to known criminal associate Da Costa, often at Da Costa's direction."

A publication ban was lifted on those revelations, and many others, from the Project South ITO on Wednesday in a ruling from Ontario Superior Court Justice Laura Bird.

Brian Da Costa is one of four civilians charged in Project South who investigators connected to Toronto South Detention Centre inmate Gurpreet Singh, according to the ITO. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Other new details include why investigators believed TSDC inmate Gurpreet Singh ordered the hit on the senior jail official, along with his alleged connections to a corrections officer and four men charged in Project South, including Da Costa.

Neither Singh nor the corrections officer have been charged in this investigation.

CBC News was part of a group of media organizations fighting to lift a publication ban on the ITO in court. Bird previously lifted the ban on some details earlier this summer. In her decision this week, Bird lifted the ban on the majority of the rest of the court record.

"Permitting the media to publish the vast majority of the ITO while maintaining a temporary publication ban over limited portions of it strikes an appropriate balance between the court openness principle and the fair trial rights of the criminal defendants," wrote Bird.

An ITO is a legal document from a police officer laying out the evidence they have of a criminal offence in order to request judicial authorization for a warrant or production order from a judge or justice of the peace. The allegations in the ITO have not been tested in court.

The search warrants were executed as investigators arrested and charged seven Toronto police officers, one retired cop and 19 civilians in Project South. The charge against one of those civilians has since been stayed, and one of the officers retired and pleaded guilty to two charges in July.

The charges against the others accused in Project South have not yet been tested in court.

Police believed Singh behind attempted hit: ITO

Elsewhere in the ITO, police say Singh had motive to harm the senior corrections official who was targeted, and that he was named by that official as one of a handful of inmates who'd expressed hostility toward them. The official told police that Singh and his former cellmate were angry after the official seized cellphones and steroids from their cell and then separated the pair.

CBC News previously reported that Singh and correctional officer Nishwant Dosanjh were investigated for potential involvement in the alleged conspiracy.

TSDC inmate Gurpreet Singh had motive to harm the senior corrections official who was targeted and was named by that official as one of a handful of inmates who’d expressed hostility toward them, according to the ITO. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California)

The ITO also states Dosanjh was Singh's former romantic partner and she allegedly took the photo of the senior corrections official's licence plate in the employee area of the jail. The photo was allegedly later provided to Da Costa and then shared with Barnhardt, who's accused of using the image to search a police database on May 27, 2025.

The results of that query were allegedly provided to Da Costa, then shared with a gun-for-hire group accused of conspiring to kill the senior corrections official the following month.

The allegations in the ITO concerning Dosanjh and Singh have not led to charges, nor have they been tested in court.

Nishwant Dosanjh's lawyers provided this photo of their client and told CBC News in a statement that Dosanjh has co-operated with police, maintains her innocence and had no part in the attempt on the senior corrections official's life. (Submitted by Kim Schofield and Miranda Brar)

In a statement, Dosanjh’s lawyer, Kim Schofield, told CBC News her client has co-operated with police, maintains her innocence and had no part in the attempt on the senior corrections official's life.

Schofield says she hired an independent digital forensics expert to review the "data dump" she received of Dosanjh's seized cell phone. The lawyer says the expert found no photos or chat discussions relating to the attempted hit.

"There is absolutely nothing to connect her to that incident," wrote Schofield.

Singh has been held at TSDC since his October 2024 arrest amid allegations he acted as an accomplice in a drug-smuggling organization led by accused cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

CBC News contacted Singh's lawyer for comment, but did not receive a response before publication. In an emailed statement in June, Singh's lawyer, Brian Greenspan, said his client had not been charged with any offence in Canada, months after the execution of the February warrants.

Singh has been held at the Toronto jail since his October 2024 arrest amid allegations he acted as an accomplice in a drug-smuggling organization allegedly involving killings and led by accused cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding.

Singh is fighting extradition to California.

Inmate connected to 4 men charged in Project South: ITO

Investigators also connected Singh with others charged in Project South. According to the ITO, Singh was associated with four of the civilians charged in the corruption probe, including Elwyn Satanowsky, Da Costa and Dequon Lemonious.

Satanowsky is accused of arranging several shootings connected with the probe. He deposited money into Singh's inmate trust account and he spoke to Singh on the phone more than 300 times between the beginning of January and mid-September 2025, according to the ITO.

Elwyn Satanowsky is charged with arranging this September 2025 shooting at a house in Vaughan, Ont., as part of the Project South investigation. (York Regional Police)

Police intercepted communications between Da Costa and Singh through TSDC's inmate telephone system.

Lemonious is charged with conspiracy to murder the senior corrections official. The ITO identifies him as someone "who plans and structures violent criminal activity" within a gunmen-for-hire group.

In an intercepted phone call, Keajean Doman, an alleged enforcer in the group also charged in the conspiracy, blames Lemonious for "plays" that resulted in his incarceration. Doman was arrested last September after allegedly carrying out a shooting related to Project South in Vaughan, Ont.

Other intercepts connect Singh and Lemonious by way of them both speaking to, or about, a former cellmate of Singh's who's in custody on a different range at TSDC, according to the ITO.

CBC News contacted lawyers for Satanowsky and Lemonious for this story but neither provided a comment before publication.

World.title: New arrest, troubles delaying investigation into 2022 Manitoba smuggling deaths revealed in warrant documents
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Newly obtained search warrant documents reveal police arrested a driver this year believed to have been involved in a human smuggling scheme that led to the deaths of a family of four in Manitoba in 2022.

The documents also provide a closer look into the years-long investigation — and shed light on some of the reasons why RCMP say it's taking so long.

It's been nearly five years since the frozen bodies of 39-year-old Jagdish Patel, his 37-year-old wife, Vaishali, and their two kids — 11-year-old Vihangi and three-year-old Dharmik — were found 12 metres from the U.S. border. They were trying to walk from Manitoba into Minnesota in January 2022 and became separated from a larger group of migrants.

In a trove of search warrant documents obtained by CBC News, RCMP said the unnamed driver arrested in February 2026 — one of the most recent updates made public in the case — is believed to have helped bring the Patels and other migrants to Winnipeg before their treacherous journey to the border.

"Investigation is ongoing to determine if they will be a witness or subject to prosecution in either Canada or the United States," an affidavit filed by an RCMP sergeant in May said.

The documents also paint a picture of why the RCMP say the investigation has progressed so slowly.

Though Canadian "person of interest" Fenil Patel — whom the documents allege was responsible for organizing the smuggling and drove the migrants to the border — was arrested last year after a U.S. extradition request, no charges in the investigation have been laid in Canada.

WATCH | The Fifth Estate questions Fenil Patel: The Fifth Estate questions Fenil Patel | Duration 2:01 Steven D'Souza, host of The Fifth Estate, questions Fenil Patel over allegations from Indian police that he was one of the smugglers responsible for transporting the Patel family (no relation) to the Canada-U.S. border in January 2022.

The RCMP affidavit from May 2026 said U.S. law enforcement told Mounties they'd gotten a sealed indictment for six charges against Patel, who is not related to the Patel family.

In the months before his arrest last year, an earlier affidavit filed by an RCMP constable said the unit responsible for border-related cases in Manitoba had been "plagued with resourcing challenges and competing priorities."

"Due to resourcing issues and deployments to the border beginning in January 2025 as a result of the recent spotlight on the international border by the new President of the USA, RCMP investigators have been unable to follow up on new developments of the Investigation," including search warrant results and information from U.S. Homeland Security Investigations, the May 2025 affidavit said.

The delays were also blamed on the relatively small border unit being responsible for newly reported human smuggling investigations that needed to be prioritized for prosecution, and on staff members not being immediately replaced after leaving the unit.

Though the documents reveal more about the case — including information about the Patel family's final days, details about Fenil Patel's alleged activities before their deaths and a 2025 reference to other potential "unidentified co-conspirators" — much of the information they contain remains redacted after a ruling from a Manitoba judge last week .

CBC News fought in court to unseal the search warrant documents, including the unredacted portions.

Provincial court Judge Tracey Lord found disclosing the redacted information "would create a serious risk to the integrity of the ongoing investigation.

"While the investigative decisions left to be made in this case are few at this stage, they are nonetheless significant in terms of how or if the case may proceed," Lord wrote.

Some identities remain unknown: documents

As RCMP investigated the case, they applied for more than 40 warrants for everything from bank and phone records to information about car rentals and email accounts, the documents said.

That investigation also included details provided by people who interacted with the Patel family in their final days, including the manager of a hotel where the family stayed in Mississauga, Ont., an acquaintance they stayed with in Welland, Ont., and an Uber driver who gave them a ride in-between.

The Welland acquaintance, whom the documents said grew up with Jagdish Patel in Gujarat, India, later gave the family a ride to another Mississauga hotel, where he said he saw two men meet them outside.

"The identity of these 2 males remains unknown," the documents said.

The documents also said the Patel family was in Canada on a visitor's visa that named a Mississauga woman as the person they were visiting. That woman later told police she didn't know the Patels or why her name was on their documents "and was concerned that her identity had been stolen," the documents said.

The other migrants who travelled with them were issued work or study permits, or both.

"Information received from [from the Canada Border Services Agency] indicated that the [visas] obtained by these Indian [nationals] were done so via fraudulent documents, such as student records and providing false visitor names," the documents said.

Booking hotel rooms back to 2018

Police also spoke to two managers at a hotel where the Patel family stayed, who recognized a photo of Fenil Patel as a man who would book rooms for people he said were students, the documents said.

One of the managers said Patel had once mentioned to her that "he had an agency 'back home' and that was how he was bringing the students into Canada," while the other said she remembered him booking hotel rooms as far back as 2018.

The students would stay for anywhere between a day and over a week, paying on a day-by-day basis.

"When asked about who the people were, he simply stated that they were students from India who did not have a place to live and he was looking for accommodations for them," the documents said.

Fenil Patel remains in custody in Canada and is scheduled to appear in court next month for a disclosure application in his extradition case, court records show.

World.title: Millions of fish tested Canada's largest nuclear plant. The incident points to a growing climate risk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Almost two years after a freak fish event at Canada's largest nuclear power plant "challenged reactor safety," newly obtained documents show how extraordinary the event was — as experts warn unusual ecological conditions are becoming a growing challenge for nuclear plants around the world.

In February 2025, millions of gizzard shad overwhelmed cooling systems at Bruce Nuclear Generating Station near Tiverton, Ont., shutting down one reactor, reducing power at another and leaving dead fish washing ashore along Lake Huron for days.

CBC News obtained more than 1,200 pages of federal and provincial records that reveal how an environmental phenomenon involving a small, cold-sensitive fish tested Canada's largest nuclear power plant in ways its operators had not anticipated.

Bruce Power, the private company that operates the plant, declined a broadcast interview. The company later provided a written statement, but did not answer CBC News's specific questions.

Dead fish 'challenged reactor safety'

Bruce Power's own root-cause investigation concluded the plant had encountered "a novel environmental event." Canada's nuclear regulator described an "uncharacterized and unanticipated volume of gizzard shad" — enough to overwhelm defences meant to keep fish out of the plant's cooling water system.

Gizzard shad gather beneath the ice in the warmer waters of Lake Huron by the millions near Bruce Nuclear Generating Station. The cold-sensitve fish seek out warm water refuges in winter, including the thermal discharge from the plant. (Zack Melnick/Inspired Planet Productions)

Another company investigation concluded in June 2025 that the two fish runs, on Feb. 1 and Feb. 13, "challenged reactor safety."

David Novog, a professor at McMaster University and Canada Research Chair in Nuclear Safety, said the phrase has a specific meaning in an industry where plants are protected by multiple layers of defence.

"When we talk about a challenge to reactor safety, what it usually implies is that one of those defences has been reduced in effectiveness or taken offline. And when that happens, nuclear power stations are required to shut down," he said.

There was no risk to reactor safety, in my opinion. - Douglas Boreham, former principal scientist and manager at Bruce Power

Douglas Boreham, a professor of medical sciences at Northern Ontario School of Medicine University who previously worked as a principal scientist and manager at Bruce Power, said the reactors responded as designed when their cooling systems were disrupted.

"Maybe the wording in that document should have been slightly modified to say it was operations that were impacted, but there was no risk to reactor safety, in my opinion," he said.

"There was no safety issue. I mean, it's designed to do that. You shut things down when the system isn't optimal."

Nuclear regulator warned of worst-case scenario

The potential consequences are laid out in an April 2026 report by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) prepared for the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The forebay at Bruce Power holds water drawn from Lake Huron before it enters the plant's cooling water system. Millions of gizzard shad congregated around Bruce A in February of 2025, with large numbers that became trapped and died in the intake system. (Bruce Power)

On Feb. 13, 2025, the mass cold-water fish die-off disrupted cooling systems serving two operating reactors. Bruce Power was forced to shut down Unit 2 and reduce power at Unit 1.

Less than two weeks earlier, on Feb. 1, the fish event affected cooling at Unit 4, which was already shut down for refurbishment. Even after a reactor is shut down, its fuel continues producing heat and must be kept cool.

In formal regulatory correspondence sent to Bruce Power on May 5, 2025, the CNSC warned that "the potential consequences of this event could have resulted in all [four Bruce A] units being shutdown."

8.1 million fish in a single day

The scale of the fish event was enormous.

In a March 2026 report to Fisheries and Oceans Canada, Bruce Power estimated that 8.1 million gizzard shad were in the vicinity of Bruce A on a single day in February 2025 — far exceeding any counts made public at the time.

A school of gizzard shad gathers in the warm water near Bruce Nuclear Generating Station in Lake Huron, near Tiverton, Ont. (Inspired Planet)

The report said severe winter conditions, including significant snowfall and a sharp drop in air temperature, pushed water temperatures close to freezing, causing cold shock among the fish. The surviving gizzard shad, a species poorly adapted to cold water, congregated around the warmer water discharged by the nuclear plant.

Ryan Lauzon, a fisheries biologist with nearby Saugeen Ojibway Nation, whose traditional territory includes the Bruce Peninsula and surrounding Lake Huron shoreline, co-authored a report on the 2025 fish kill. He said warmer winters in the years leading up to 2025 — including record-low ice levels in 2024 — may help explain how such a large population developed.

"It is a reasonable hypothesis," he said. "It potentially allowed these fish to develop larger populations" before colder conditions in 2025 left large numbers of fish vulnerable.

A dead gizzard shad lies on a Lake Huron beach. Large numbers of dead gizzard shad washing ashore in 2025 raised concerns about whether disease could be involved. (Lee Brintell/Facebook)

Federal records estimate between 3.8 million and 4.95 million gizzard shad became trapped and died at Bruce A between Jan. 30 and March 26, 2025 — several times the previous record of roughly 800,000 set in 1977.

The number was so enormous Bruce Power brought in a crane ito help remove them, according to emails obtained by CBC News from Ontario's Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks. The carcasses were hauled to a landfill.

Reactor shutdown 'a big hit to the grid'

Novog said a reactor shutdown isn't simply a matter of clearing out the dead fish and flicking a switch. Restarting a reactor in Canada would take at least three or four days.

An aerial image of the Bruce Power site located near Tiverton, Ont. (Submitted by Chad Richards)

"That's not trivial. Each nuclear station is generating hundreds of megawatts of electricity every hour of the day, so to lose them for multiple days even, is a big hit to the grid," Novog said.

Internal provincial records obtained by CBC News show Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator said the province's electricity supply was "tight" while Unit 2 remained offline. It assessed a "medium risk" that another Bruce reactor could go offline, but said the grid could remain reliable using electricity imports and other domestic generation.

Nuclear power's climate paradox

What happened at Bruce Power is not the only recent case of environmental conditions disrupting the cooling systems nuclear plants depend on.

The Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant in Romania, seen here next to Danube-Black Sea channel on September 3, 2025. Its Candu reactors depend on water from the river for cooling. In July 2026, severe drought brought the Danube to unprecedentedly low levels, forcing the plant to shutdown Unit 1 and later Unit 2 as a precaution. (Daniel Mihailescu/AFP via Getty Images)

Novog said he has seen such events become more common over the course of his career, pointing to events that disrupted nuclear cooling systems in Romania and France.

In the summer of 2026, reactors were forced offline by record-low water levels on the Danube River in Romania. At France's Gravelines nuclear plant, massive influxes of jellyfish clogged cooling systems for two consecutive summers, forcing reactors offline in 2025 and 2026.

Nuclear plants are being forced to adapt to a changing climate, even as governments increasingly rely on them to help fight it.

"It just appears to me that over time, these kind of events have been increasing," Novog said.

'Organizational failure' to adapt

Bruce Power's investigation identified inadequate real-time environmental monitoring and what it called an "organizational failure" to recognize emerging problems associated with changing environmental conditions and make design changes to protect the plant from cooling water blockages.

A few jellyfish lie on a beach near the Gravelines nuclear plant in northern France. In August, a massive influx of jellyfish clogged filters in the plant's seawater pumping stations, automatically shutting down four reactors. (Reuters)

Since the event, Bruce Power has said it spent nearly $10 million on mitigation measures and research aimed at preventing another mass fish event from disrupting the plant.

In a statement received after CBC News' deadline, Bruce Power said it has strengthened its defences since the fish event and is preparing for emerging risks associated with climate change, acknowledging that "we cannot anticipate every future event."

The measures include new physical barriers to keep fish away from the cooling-water intakes, underwater acoustic deterrents, sonar and video monitoring and an artificial intelligence system intended to provide earlier warning when large numbers of fish approach.

Novog said preventing those disruptions will become increasingly important as nuclear plants are relied upon to provide low-carbon electricity.

"The best solution is to have no fish congregate there and keep the units running and so that's why I think over the years to come, you'll see more on mitigation and prevention measures at Bruce and other stations around the world."

World.title: 'Blood is on our hands': Haitian honour student's death sparks outcry over ICE ankle monitors
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of suicide.

Decorated with academic and athletic awards, Pierre Damas Bel was well on his way to fulfilling his dream of becoming a neurosurgeon.

Described by teachers as a " student of the highest calibre " and a " deeply dedicated " member of his community, Bel was an honour student, captain of the varsity soccer team and volunteer at a food bank in Springfield, Ohio.

But this summer, Bel lost the protected immigration status that allowed him to legally live in the U.S. after fleeing the ongoing instability in Hait i in 2024.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) fitted the 20-year-old Wright State University student with an ankle monitor in late July as an "alternative to detention." But the device prevented him from playing soccer, and he reportedly began to be bullied by classmates and felt he was " treated like an animal ."

"I came here to study, to build my future … not to be treated like [a] criminal," he wrote in a post.

Bel was one of about 350,000 Haitians living and working in the U.S. who lost temporary protected status (TPS) after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowed the Trump administration to revoke the humanitarian protection.

Homeland Security's deportation campaign began immediately.

"Those with terminated TPS are in our nation illegally," it posted alongside a video showing Haitian migrants in chains , escorted onto a repatriation flight on Aug. 27.

Bel was a proud member of the Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps at Springfield High School, earning the rank of lieutenant. (scsdoh/Instagram)

Once a lieutenant in his high school's Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps (JROTC) program and described as a " natural leader " who would become a " great American ," Bel was the only one in the Wright State ROTC program not to be given a uniform because of the monitor, his father says .

The following Monday, Bel walked into traffic on a nearby highway and was struck by a semi-truck, according to Ohio State Highway Patrol .

He died on the scene. His family believes it was a suicide.

'100% preventable'

In the following days, memorials were held in his honour in Ohio and across the U.S. , including New York City. Many held ICE's immigration crackdown responsible for his death.

"Racist anti-Haitian campaign murdered Pierre Damas Bel," one woman's sign in New York read.

A woman holds a sign during a vigil for Bel in Brooklyn, New York, on Sept. 4. (David (Dee) Delgado/Reuters)

Asked to respond to advocates' allegations that the shame of the ankle monitor drove Bel to suicide, ICE told CBC any attempts to blame the agency for his death are false.

"No one is required to stay in the United States illegally and wear a GPS monitor," the agency wrote, adding that self-deportation is an option.

But Yola Lamarre, a friend of Bel, says ICE's response oversimplifies Bel's mental health crisis and blames the young man for his own death.

"We have to be honest in where blood is on our hands," she told CBC News.

Yola Lamarre, a friend of Bel who considered him a little brother, says he was a bright and determined individual whose 'story was cut short' because of harsh immigration policies. (Yanjun Li/CBC)

Lamarre, who saw Bel as a little brother, said his death was "100 per cent preventable" if he had been treated more humanely.

"He told me how he would try to wear a certain wardrobe to hide the ankle monitor," she said.

"He just wanted belonging. He just wanted acceptance."

Haitians were granted TPS after the 2010 earthquake that killed more than 300,000 people in the Caribbean country. Other crises, including cholera outbreaks , Hurricane Sandy and the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse , prompted further extensions.

After failed attempts to end Haiti's TPS in Trump's first term, the Department of Homeland Security announced in June 2025 it was ending it, saying the situation had "improved enough that it is safe for Haitian citizens to return home." Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department tells its citizens not to travel to Haiti due to the risk of "crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited health care."

Carl Ruby, right, pastor of Springfield's Central Christian Church, comforts Bel's father at his home on Aug. 31, as he reels from the loss of his son earlier that day. (Carol Guzy)

The ankle monitoring program Bel was subjected to appears to be part of a larger strategy by ICE to "make life so miserable" that Haitians will self-deport, said Carl Ruby, senior pastor at Central Christian Church in Springfield, Ohio, a city where at least 10,000 of its roughly 60,000 residents are Haitian.

"They're afraid to go outside of their homes," said Ruby, whose church saw its Haitian attendance plummet from about 50 people to two.

Residents 'shackled'

Ruby said hundreds of Springfield residents — including teenagers, elderly and pregnant people — have been "shackled" with ankle monitors, often leading to deep shame and social isolation.

"Their old friends start to pull back from them because they're afraid that if they're with a person who has an ankle monitor, that they might be apprehended."

Critics lik e Ohio Dem ocratic congressman Greg Landsman say the electronic monitoring program also unfairly humiliates law-abiding migrants.

"They aren't criminals," wrote Landsman . "It's all so wrong and cruel to pick on anybody, especially a group this vulnerable."

WATCH | The struggle to come to Canada: Canadian immigration 'very difficult' for Haitians in U.S., says advocate | Duration 0:52 Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, Ohio, does not encourage Haitians living in the U.S. to go to Canada because of the risk of being turned away and handed over to American law enforcement.

Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield, said his community members are caught in a catch-22: no longer safe in the U.S., they also have nowhere to go.

"There is no country that is willing to welcome us," said Dorsainvil, who lost TPS himself. "We cannot go to work. We live in fear and anxiety on a daily basis."

The end of TPS has had a chilling effect across the wider Haitian diasp ora in the U.S.

At a Springfield strip mall, once a hub of economic activity with several Haitian-owned businesses, storefronts were locked or shuttered altogether when CBC visited last week.

One store employee, who asked not to be identified because of his immigration status, described the situation as a "catastrophe."

"There are many people who don't have enough to eat, who are sick, who don't have access to medical care … and no way to get to a doctor," the asylum seeker told CBC in French.

WATCH | Haitians staying home: 'There's no life for them,' restauranteur says of Haitians who lost protected status | Duration 0:55 Business has slowed for Claucia Dossous, a Haitian American who runs T-Co Islands Restaurant in Columbus, Ohio, after the Trump administration ended temporary protected status for Haiti, leaving many of her customers out of work.

Other businesses are struggling to pay their bills.

Claucia Dossous, a Haitian American who runs T-Co Islands Restaurant in Columbus, Ohio, said ending TPS has "broken everybody's life" after Haitians who frequented her restaurant were forced out of work.

"I pay for the price, too."

Looking to Canada

The climate of fear has led some Haitians to try moving to Canada.

More Haitian nationals file for asylum at the land border than any other country so far this year, according to the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA). Figures from the Immigration and Refugee Board show that more than 27,000 Haitians are awaiting decisions — about 1/10th of all pending asylum claims.

Haitian American activist Guerline Jozef wants Canada to open more humanitarian pathways for Haitians who no longer feel safe in their country.

"We find ourselves in a place where we cannot leave, we cannot stay. And the only option they are giving them is to be kidnapped and be deported to the same place that they have fled," said Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance in San Diego, Calif.

WATCH | 'We cannot leave; we cannot stay': Canada returning Haitian asylum seekers to U.S. immigration authorities, says activist | Duration 1:04 Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance in San Diego, Calif., says Canada is turning away vulnerable Haitian asylum seekers entering from the U.S., leaving them at risk of deportation to the country they fled.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada told CBC it "cannot speculate on future policy decisions" but highlighted temporary measures for Haitian nationals in place until October.

But for those outside Canada, those measures are only available to family members of Canadian citizens and permanent residents.

Ruby described the case of one family who was a part of their congregation who survived several kidnapping attempts in Haiti.

WATCH | Haitians in U.S. too scared of ICE deportation risk to go outside, advocates say: Haitian student in Ohio ended his life over 'humiliating' ICE ankle monitor, family believes | Duration 2:06 The family of a Haitian college student in Ohio says they believe the humiliation of being forced to wear an ICE-ordered ankle monitor, combined with the fear of deportation, led to his suicide after temporary protected status for 300,000 Haitians was revoked in July.

Because one of them had a sister in Canada, they were able to join her. The day they arrived in Canada, they received letters from ICE telling them their TPS was over and to self-deport.

"They got out just in time," he said. "But that option just isn't available to very many people."

Instead, Jozef said many of the people who try to flee the U.S. into Canada are turned away.

Under the Safe Third Country Agreement, refugees who first arrive in the U.S. are barred from seeking asylum in Canada, barring certain exceptions . More than 1,100 asylum seekers were returned to U.S. immigration authorities under this agreement so far this year, according to the CBSA.

Frantz André, a community organizer and advocate for asylum seekers in Montreal, says the Safe Third Country Agreement effectively allows for 'deportation by proxy' when Canada hands over migrants to the U.S., where they will be sent back to their home countries. (Romain Schué/Radio-Canada)

Montreal migrant advocate Frantz André said the agreement now effectively allows for "deportation by proxy" when Canadian agents turn back Haitian migrants knowing they will be deported by the U.S.

"The United States is no longer a safe country for hundreds of thousands of people," he said. "People are in despair."

World.title: Republican senator warns Carney against tightening Canada's links to European Union
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A long-serving Republican senator from a border state is warning Prime Minister Mark Carney against strengthening Canada's economic and political ties to the European Union.

Sen. Susan Collins of Maine — facing a re-election battle in November's midterms in a state highly dependent on cross-border trade — says it's unfortunate that Canada is turning toward the EU in response to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs.

"That doesn't help rebuild the good relationship that we once had and that I want us to have again," Collins told CBC News correspondent Katie Simpson at the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday.

In a speech earlier Wednesday in Strasbourg, France, with Carney present, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Europe wants to open the door for Canada to become an "associate member" of the EU.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: Is Canada more like Europe than the United States? What’s at stake for you if Canada builds closer relations with the EU?

Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

(It's not clear what that would mean, as "associate member" is not currently a legal designation in the EU. Although Canada's ambassador to the EU says the two sides are "a ways away" from formalizing anything, Carney has said he wants a "unique alliance" with Europe.)

In response to a question Wednesday evening about the prospect, Trump called it "laughable" and threatened to punish Europe.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," he said. "If it's a good intention, that's fine."

WATCH | Canada's plan to deepen European ties draws U.S. backlash: Trump threatens new tariffs over Canada-EU alliance if it's 'a hostile act' | Duration 2:32 U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at a possible Canada-EU trade alliance, threatening new tariffs if he finds it to be 'a hostile act.' Meanwhile, Democrats in Washington expressed sympathy for Canada and said trade talks should resume.

Collins says she believes Canada deepening its ties with Europe could make it harder for the Carney government to reach a deal with the Trump administration to end the escalating trade war.

"I believe that both Canada and the United States should return to the bargaining table. I do not support this tariff war," Collins said.

WATCH | What Europe's top official has in mind for Canada: EU chief opens door to Canada becoming associate member | Duration 4:41 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed opening a path for Canada to become the European Union's first associate member, a status that doesn't currently exist.

Collins has long tried to distance herself from Trump's tariff policies, in part because Canada accounts for roughly two-thirds of Maine's imports and about 40 per cent of its exports.

She claimed credit last week when the Trump administration announced it was exempting cement and road salt — two products Maine imports from Canada in significant quantities — from its list of Canadian goods facing new tariffs of 50 per cent.

'Not in the interest of our country'

Collins's comments come amid growing signs of unease among some Republicans in the U.S. Congress over Trump's trade tactics toward Canada, particularly as the Nov. 3 midterm elections grow nearer.

The Republicans hold narrow majorities in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate and stand to lose control of Congress if the Democrats can flip a handful of districts or states.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who has occasionally broken with Trump on policies, told CBC News he's opposed to the trade war.

"I think it is wrong to have a trade war with Canada. It is not in the interest of our country to have a trade war with Canada," Cassidy said.

U.S. Sen. Chris Coons, a Democrat from Delaware is pictured at the U.S. Capitol on May 19. Coons told CBC News on Wednesday that he is organizing a 'bipartisan trip to Canada' for his fellow lawmakers. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)

Meanwhile, Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware says it will be "a tall order" to halt Trump's trade war on Canada even if the Democrats win the midterms.

"We won't be able to reverse his direction immediately, but at least with a new majority in Congress, should we be successful in the November elections, Canadians will begin to recognize their neighbours again," Coons told CBC News.

Coons says he has spoken with "personal friends" in Carney's cabinet about action that he and other members of Congress could take to win back allies in Canada.

He says he's working on "a bipartisan trip to Canada by American lawmakers to say, we hear you, we get it, we're acting."

Coons declined to say who in the Canadian cabinet he was speaking with, and his office had no further details about which lawmakers are interested in the trip or when it's likely to happen.

His initiative is part of a movement among Democrats to try to seize on the concerns of many Americans that Trump's tariffs are driving up the cost of living, which polls suggest is a top issue in the midterms.

This week, Senate Democrats formally introduced a bill that seeks to repeal and refund all tariffs the Trump administration has levied under Section 338 of the Tariff Act, including the 50 per cent duties imposed on Canadian products in August.

The bill, first tabled in the House by congressman Brad Schneider of Illinois, is called the BAD DEAL Act, an acronym for Banning Antiquated Duties and Delivering Equitable American Levies.

What's not clear is whether any such Democrat bill has any chance of becoming law with Trump in the White House for another two-plus years.

Even if the Democrats win control of both the House and the Senate, the U.S. president holds veto power over legislation unless it's approved by a two-thirds majority of both houses.

World.title: What does Carney’s investment summit mean for clean energy?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of deep-pocketed investors have descended on Toronto for the first-of-its-kind summit. CBC’s Clara Pasieka breaks down Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pitch — and the pushback from critics.

Despite big-ticket fossil fuel projects, the two-day investment summit did also feature dozens of clean energy and climate tech projects in its deal book. Where will the money land?

While proposed fossil fuel projects got more attention at Prime Minister Mark Carney's investment summit in Toronto this week — from the $35 billion-plus West Coast oil pipeline to the $28.5 billion Ksi Lisims LNG terminal — there was a lot of climate tech on the agenda as well.

Energy storage, upgrading the electricity grid, nuclear projects and renewables like wind and solar were all sprinkled throughout the summit's deal book.

It's a throwback to Carney's career before he became prime minister when he spent years making a business case for climate-friendly policies in the global financial world, and could be a nod to what international investors increasingly want.

"What we've seen is that clean energy investment is roughly double that of fossil investment globally," said David Pickup, director of the electricity program at the Pembina Institute, an energy transition think-tank.

Industry watchers hope bringing large investors to Canada can help boost interest in Canadian renewables and raise the billions of dollars that will be needed. But where the money will land is still unclear.

Protesters demonstrate against the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

Climate advocates critical of summit

Even before it started, the summit attracted massive criticism from some of the most prominent voices in the climate movement.

David Suzuki, the longtime environmentalist and journalist, blasted the summit in an interview with the CBC, saying a financial system that does not see the environment as the source of its wealth is doomed.

"Yeah, we have a crisis right now," Suzuki told the CBC’s David Common, referring to the current trade conflict with the U.S. which is driving Carney to diversify investment into Canada.

"But I don't think the solution is to call these people together and say, 'Look, invest in Canada, and we will continue the destruction of the biosphere that supports us.'"

WATCH | Suzuki takes aim at investment agenda: Suzuki: U.S. trade crisis no excuse for ‘destruction’ of Canadian biosphere | Duration 2:15 Canadian environmental activist David Suzuki says current trade tensions between Ottawa and Washington shouldn’t be reason enough for the exploitation of natural resources that would lead to ‘the destruction of the biosphere’ in Canada. His comments come as Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting 100 of the world’s biggest investors, pitching Canada as a place to do business in the fields of conventional and clean energy, AI, as well as mining and metal projects.

The investment opportunities include dozens of clean energy and climate tech projects, such as wind and solar farms, carbon capture facilities, electricity grid upgrades and energy storage. But the issue is what else is getting pitched.

"The No. 1 problem with [the investment summit’s] deal book is the amount of oil and gas projects that are proposed," said Richard Brooks, climate finance director at advocacy group Stand.earth. "It features $100 billion of new oil and gas projects that Mark Carney is seeking investment in."

Pickup pointed out that the recently-announced West Coast oil pipeline could be up to 90 per cent funded by the federal and Alberta governments, which the Pembina Institute says is a signal that it's a risky investment that may not end up paying off for taxpayers. It also shows that private investors are not as interested in fossil fuel projects.

"The trends are pretty clear globally that clean is the thing that people want to invest in and in particular, clean is the thing that private investment really wants to bring forward," Pickup said.

After Carney's rollbacks on key climate policies, such as electric vehicle mandates and the consumer carbon tax, Canada is now more than 20 years behind on its climate targets , according to the latest analysis by the Canadian Climate Institute. On the current course, Canada's emissions in 2050 will be 460 megatonnes of carbon, rather than the goal of net-zero emissions by 2050, a commitment enshrined in law.

Investors consider Canadian renewables

Vittoria Bellissimo, president of the Canadian Renewable Energy Association (CanREA), says interest is growing in the Canadian clean energy sector. Her association hosted a finance summit back in May that attracted hundreds of investors and developers, and Canadian utilities are busy procuring renewable power to expand electricity production.

"I think at a very high level, the message that ... is being communicated through this investment summit is that Canada is open for business and Canadian infrastructure is an area that looks attractive and is a stable investment," she said.

CanREA estimates that there's 25 gigawatts of installed solar, wind and energy storage capacity in Canada right now, a more than 50 per cent increase since 2020. That's enough to power about 18 million homes. And they’re tracking another 24 gigawatts that provinces are looking to procure in the future.

Bellissimo said bringing investors to Canada is important to get more interest flowing into some of these projects.

"All in, it's a $200-billion opportunity, and investors are sitting up and taking notice," Bellissimo said, pointing to the newly established major projects office and federal efforts to make project approvals easier.

That's important because the federal government has an ambitious electricity plan , Pickup said, which aims to double electricity generation throughout the country by 2050 by using clean sources. “We're talking a big amount of investment that needs to go into our electricity system. And the real question here that I have is, is this investment that we're bringing for today, does it align with that?”

WATCH | Carney's electricity plan: Carney announces national strategy to double Canada's electricity grid by 2050 | Duration 6:47 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Powering Canada Strong, a new national strategy aimed at doubling Canada's electric capacity by 2050 and lowering electricity costs for seven in 10 households by expanding the role of natural gas in the country's energy mix. The plan will be fine-tuned during four months of consultation with provinces and stakeholders.

Pickup pointed to certain solar and wind projects in the investment summit’s deal book as positive signs. But investment alone won't be enough; the government also has to come through with strong policies that will lead to both future supply and demand for this electricity, he said.

That includes things like an electric vehicle strategy that would lead to more clean electricity use in the transportation sector rather than gasoline, and speeding up home and building retrofits that will get fossil fuels out of Canadian homes.

“So the question really becomes, you know, are we moving towards this future economy that Carney and others in the federal government talk about?”

World.title: Frank Stronach to be sentenced today for 1977 indecent assault
World.content:
Article content

The trial started provocatively, as the Crown sought to use each case to bolster the credibility of the others. But by trial’s end, only three complainants remained. One woman had an emotional breakdown on the witness stand and gave evidence so garbled and disjointed the judge decided no conviction could flow from it. Another gave such self-contradictory evidence, especially over the year the alleged crime occurred, that Molloy decided she could not convict. One woman tried to apologize after lying on the witness stand about whether she had read another complainant’s account in the media. Another was revealed in cross-examination to have an extensive history of controversial business litigation involving what a judge described as her deceit and dishonesty, and a more recent instance of allegedly falsely reporting to police that a man she had a dispute with threatened to kill her. All those charges failed.

World.title: Adam Pankratz: Mark Carney’s worthwhile plan for privatizing airports
World.content:
Article content

It is a well established fact that markets and private enterprise are far more efficient than government at running companies and organizations. The reason is simple: corporations and private companies have a clear profit incentive to which they respond. This benefits everyone and is the magic of the market at work. Adam Smith, the father of capitalism, recognized this in his totemic work, The Wealth of Nations back in 1776. “It is not,” Smith wrote, “from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer or the baker that we expect our dinner but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves not to their humanity but to their self-love.” Smith’s recognition that by looking out for their own profit interests, individuals, without any formal coordination, would all move towards producing better products more efficiently and at a lower price. This is the famous invisible hand of the market which makes capitalist societies tick.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of
