Colombian president Abelardo De la Espriella said his government has approved 85 extraditions since taking office on 7 August 2026. He announced the figure in a post on X on 16 September. Most of the cases go to the United States on drug trafficking charges.

What Was Announced

De la Espriella put the count at 85 extraditions in one month and ten days of government.

He said he continues signing without rest and that there is no leniency with crime.

The announcement came through his own social media account rather than a justice ministry release.

No names, destination courts or case numbers were published with it.

How Extradition Works in Colombia

A request arrives from a foreign government, usually the United States.

The Supreme Court reviews it and issues a non-binding opinion on whether the formal requirements are met.

The president then signs or refuses the resolution that authorises the handover.

The presidential signature is the final political step, which is why a count of signatures is a policy statement.

Why the Number Is Political

Gustavo Petro suspended extradition for members of armed groups who joined his peace negotiations.

That policy was among the sharpest points of friction with Washington during his term.

De la Espriella campaigned on reversing it, and the count is how he demonstrates the reversal.

The figure also lands days after Washington kept Colombia on its list of countries failing anti-drug cooperation.

What the Count Does Not Tell You

A signature is not the same as a person boarding a plane, and the two can be months apart.

The figure includes cases prepared under the previous government and inherited at the signing stage.

Without a published list there is no way to see which organisations the 85 belong to.

Nor has the government given a comparable figure for the same period in earlier administrations.

The announcement came days after Washington renewed Colombia’s decertification. Photo: Stefhaniapl95, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

The Washington Angle

The United States renewed Colombia’s decertification on anti-drug cooperation this week.

It kept economic support in place, which softened the practical effect of the decision.

Extradition has historically been the clearest signal Bogotá can send to Washington.

However, decertification is judged on coca cultivation and seizure data, not on extradition counts.

What It Means Inside Colombia

For armed groups, the end of the suspension removes a bargaining chip from any future negotiation.

For the peace process built under Petro, it narrows what the state can offer.

For prosecutors, extradition can remove a defendant before Colombian victims see a domestic trial.

That last point is the standing objection from victims’ organisations, raised under every government that has used it.

De la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026 after a campaign centred on security. Photo: Petruss, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Six Weeks So Far

De la Espriella took office on 7 August 2026 after a campaign centred on security.

He has clashed publicly with Petro, now his predecessor, over the fiscal deficit.

His government has also backed the resumption of air strikes against dissident groups.

The through line is a harder security posture, delivered quickly and announced directly.

What to Watch

Whether the justice ministry publishes a verifiable list of the 85 cases.

The number of those signatures that result in actual transfers by the end of the year.

Any response from armed groups still in talks under the previous framework.

And next year’s certification decision in Washington, which uses different measures entirely.

More: Latin America news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many extraditions has Colombia approved?

President De la Espriella says 85 since he took office on 7 August 2026.

Where did he announce it?

In a post on X on 16 September 2026, not in a formal government release.

Where are they sent?

Mostly to the United States, mostly on drug trafficking charges.

What changed from the previous government?

Gustavo Petro had suspended extradition for members of armed groups taking part in peace talks.

Does a signature mean a transfer?

No. The presidential signature authorises the handover, which can take months to carry out.

Is the list public?

No. The government has not published names, case numbers or destination courts.

Sources: Statement by President Abelardo De la Espriella on X, 16 September 2026, as reported by El Heraldo; Colombian Supreme Court extradition procedure.

World.title: Colombia Court Lifts Air Strike Ban, Sets Rules on Minors
World.content:
COLOMBIA · SECURITY

Key Facts — What happened A Bogotá court lifted its own suspension of air strikes in areas where recruited minors are present.

— Which court The 34th family court of Bogotá, in a ruling dated 16 September 2026.

— What replaced the ban A reinforced standard of precaution: more intelligence checks, a search for less harmful options and a written proportionality test.

— How it started A constitutional action filed by lawyer Ower Jimmy Borda Parra after a strike in Guaviare on 27 August killed three minors.

— The military view The armed forces argued the ban would encourage armed groups to keep children in their camps as protection.

— What is not settled The ruling can be appealed, and the court has not said who verifies that the new conditions were met.

The ban is gone. The conditions that replaced it are stricter than what existed before the ban.

A Bogotá court lifted its suspension of air strikes in areas where minors are present. Photo: Petruss, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A Bogotá court lifted its suspension of Colombian air strikes in areas where recruited minors are present. The 34th family court issued the ruling on 16 September 2026. It replaced the ban with a stricter set of conditions the military must meet before it strikes.

What the Court Had Stopped

The same court had ordered a halt to bombardment wherever reliable information placed recruited minors in the target area.

That was a precautionary measure taken while a constitutional protection case was heard.

Lawyer Ower Jimmy Borda Parra brought the case.

The trigger was an operation in Guaviare on 27 August against the dissident group led by alias Calarcá.

Three minors aged 15, 15 and 16 were killed in that strike.

What the Court Now Requires

The judge lifted the blanket suspension and imposed what the ruling calls a reinforced standard of precaution.

Where information about minors is certain, objective or reasonably verifiable, the military must intensify intelligence verification.

It must assess alternatives that carry less risk before choosing an air strike.

And it must carry out a concrete proportionality assessment rather than a general one.

Why the Government Fought the Ban

The armed forces and the government argued that a public ban creates an incentive.

If a camp with children cannot be struck, armed groups have a reason to keep children in every camp.

Recruitment of minors by dissident and guerrilla groups has risen through the past three years.

The counter-argument, accepted by the court in August, is that the state cannot bomb children to reach commanders.

The Incidents Behind the Case

On 10 August an ELN bombing in Catatumbo killed a 16-year-old.

On 27 August, Operation Amón against Calarcá’s group killed three minors in Guaviare.

On 30 August a strike against the group led by Iván Mordisco recovered two people who said they were minors.

Those three episodes in one month turned a long-standing legal question into an urgent one.

The government argued the suspension would let armed groups shelter behind children.

An Old Argument in Colombia

The same dispute surfaced under previous governments whenever air strikes killed recruited children.

Colombian law treats minors in armed groups as victims of recruitment, not as combatants.

International humanitarian law allows strikes on military targets but requires proportionality and precaution.

The tension between those two positions has never been resolved by legislation, only case by case.

What Changes in Practice

Air strikes can resume immediately, which was the government’s main objective.

Commanders now carry a documented burden they did not carry before the case.

A written proportionality record creates evidence that can be reviewed later by courts or prosecutors.

However, the ruling does not say which body checks compliance, or what happens when it is not met.

The case was brought as a constitutional protection action before a Bogotá court.

Who Is Affected

The military regains a tool it uses against dissident commanders in remote terrain.

Families of recruited children gain a procedural standard, though not a guarantee.

Armed groups lose the shield the suspension effectively handed them.

And prosecutors gain a paper trail for any future case about a strike.

What to Watch

Whether the ruling is appealed by either side.

The next air operation against a dissident camp, and how the new standard is documented.

Any figures published on minors recruited or recovered this year.

And whether Congress attempts to write the standard into law rather than leaving it to courts.

More: Latin America news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Bogotá court decide?

It lifted its suspension of air strikes in areas where recruited minors are present and replaced it with stricter conditions.

Which court issued it?

The 34th family court of Bogotá, on 16 September 2026.

What are the new conditions?

Intensified intelligence verification, assessment of less harmful alternatives and a concrete proportionality test before striking.

Why was the ban imposed?

After a strike in Guaviare on 27 August killed three minors aged 15, 15 and 16.

What did the military argue?

That a public ban gives armed groups a reason to keep children in their camps.

Can the ruling be appealed?

Yes. The ruling can be appealed, and it does not name the body responsible for checking compliance.

Sources: Ruling of the 34th family court of Bogotá, 16 September 2026, as reported by El Tiempo, El Heraldo and El Colombiano.

World.title: Milei Reaches 1,000 Days With His Worst Poll Rating Yet
World.content:
ARGENTINA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Javier Milei reached 1,000 days as president of Argentina on 16 September 2026.

— The poll Explanans found 58.2% rate his government negatively and 41.8% positively, his worst reading so far.

— The mood 57.4% of those surveyed say government measures have left them worse off. 21.9% say better off.

— The floor holds In a first-round vote he still leads with 38.5%, against 24% for Axel Kicillof.

— The ceiling does not In a head-to-head runoff the same poll puts Kicillof at 43.1% and Milei at 41.9%.

— The fieldwork 7,015 responses gathered between 2 and 9 September across 91 cities.

The worst approval numbers of his presidency, and he is still the leading candidate. Both things are in the same poll.

Javier Milei reached 1,000 days in office on 16 September 2026. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

Javier Milei passed 1,000 days as Argentina’s president on 16 September 2026. A survey by the consultancy Explanans put his negative rating at 58.2%, the worst of his term. The same survey still shows him leading a first-round vote with 38.5%.

The Numbers

Explanans surveyed 7,015 people between 2 and 9 September across 25 urban clusters in 91 cities.

Negative assessments of the government reached 58.2% and positive ones 41.8%.

The average score fell to 4.4 out of 10, down from 4.6 in June.

Nearly half of respondents, 47.5%, gave the government the lowest possible score of one.

The Economy People Feel

57.4% said government measures had left them worse off.

21.9% said they were better off and 20.7% saw no change.

Inflation has fallen sharply since 2023, which is the government’s central claim.

Wages, pensions and employment have not recovered at the same pace, which is the counter-claim.

Why He Still Leads

In a first round the poll gives Milei 38.5% against 24% for Buenos Aires governor Axel Kicillof.

Myriam Bregman takes 10.4%, Sergio Massa 6.1% and Mauricio Macri 3.7%.

Around 17.3% are undecided, blank or name someone else.

A fragmented opposition lets a leader with a 58% negative rating stay first past the post.

Where It Turns

In a head-to-head runoff the same survey puts Kicillof at 43.1% and Milei at 41.9%.

Blank votes account for 8.8% and non-responses 6.2%.

That gap is inside the margin of most surveys, so the pairing is effectively level.

The pattern is a hard electoral floor and a low ceiling, which is what a polarising presidency produces.

Milei took office in December 2023 with a devaluation and deep spending cuts.

What the 1,000 Days Contain

Milei took office in December 2023 with a devaluation and deep cuts to public spending.

Monthly inflation fell from the peaks of early 2024, and the fiscal accounts moved into surplus.

Subsidies, public works and transfers to provinces were cut to get there.

The cost has landed on pensioners, universities and public-sector employment.

The Warning Signs Around Him

The Universidad Torcuato Di Tella index put the probability of recession at 82% in August.

The Fundar think tank counts more than 31,000 employer companies lost since he took office.

Poverty rose again in the first half of 2026.

However, country risk and the exchange rate have both been steadier than in the first two years.

Country risk and the exchange rate have been steadier than in the first two years. Photo: Pablorosario2013, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons.

What a Single Poll Can and Cannot Tell You

Explanans is one consultancy, and Argentine polling has missed badly in recent cycles.

The fieldwork is urban, which under-represents rural and small-town voters.

No margin of error was published with the release.

The direction of travel, from 4.6 to 4.4 since June, is the more reliable signal than any single percentage.

What to Watch

Whether other consultancies show the same runoff pairing in the coming weeks.

Real wage and employment data, which move approval numbers with a lag.

The 2027 budget negotiation in Congress, where Milei has no majority.

And whether Kicillof consolidates the opposition vote or splits it with Massa.

More: Latin America news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the poll find?

Explanans put negative assessments of Milei’s government at 58.2% and positive at 41.8%, his worst reading so far.

Who was surveyed?

7,015 people between 2 and 9 September 2026, across 25 urban clusters in 91 cities.

Does he still lead?

Yes. In a first round the poll gives him 38.5% against 24% for Axel Kicillof.

What about a runoff?

Kicillof takes 43.1% and Milei 41.9%, a gap small enough to call the pairing level.

How do people feel about the economy?

57.4% say government measures left them worse off. 21.9% say better off.

When did the 1,000 days start?

Milei took office in December 2023 and reached 1,000 days on 16 September 2026.

Sources: Explanans survey published 16 September 2026, reported by Infobae and Los Andes; Universidad Torcuato Di Tella recession index; Fundar company data.

World.title: Storm Cuts Power to 120,000 in Brazil’s Vale do Aço
World.content:
BRAZIL · MINAS GERAIS

Key Facts — What happened A storm hit the Vale do Aço region of Minas Gerais on the evening of 16 September 2026.

— The power cut More than 120,000 customers lost electricity, according to the utility Cemig.

— The measurements Ipatinga recorded 38.8 millimetres of rain in one hour, with wind gusts of 76.2 kilometres an hour.

— The damage Uprooted trees, torn roofs, fallen water tanks and loose cables. The BR-381 highway was blocked by trees and poles.

— Casualties Civil Defence reported no serious injuries or deaths as of late that night.

— What follows Four municipal schools in Ipatinga cancelled classes on 17 September.

An hour of rain took the lights out of an industrial valley that makes much of Brazil’s steel.

More than 120,000 Cemig customers lost power in the Vale do Aço on 16 September. Photo: Nonato III, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

A storm struck the Vale do Aço region of Minas Gerais in the early evening of 16 September 2026. More than 120,000 customers lost power, according to Cemig. Ipatinga recorded 38.8 millimetres of rain in a single hour with gusts of 76.2 kilometres an hour.

What the Storm Did

The worst of it fell on Ipatinga, Coronel Fabriciano, Timóteo and Santana do Paraíso.

Trees came down across streets, roofs were torn off and rooftop water tanks were knocked loose.

The BR-381 highway, the main road between Belo Horizonte and Espírito Santo, was blocked by fallen trees and utility poles.

Civil Defence reported no serious injuries or deaths as of 23:30 that night.

Why the Power Went Out

Cemig said wind and rain threw branches and roofing material against the network.

That caused short circuits and broke cables across several neighbourhoods.

The worst-affected districts of Coronel Fabriciano included JK, Belvedere, Melo Viana, São Domingos and Planalto.

Cemig forecast gradual restoration through the night, with harder repairs running into Thursday morning.

The Emergency Line Failed Too

The fire service emergency number 193 stopped working in the region during the storm.

Residents were directed to a mobile number and to Civil Defence on 199.

A communications failure during a weather emergency compounds the risk rather than causing it.

The line was a casualty of the same network damage that cut the power.

The Vale do Aço is one of Brazil’s main steel-producing regions.

Where This Happened

The Vale do Aço, the steel valley, sits in eastern Minas Gerais around the Piracicaba river.

Ipatinga is home to the Usiminas mill, one of Brazil’s largest flat-steel producers.

Timóteo holds an Aperam stainless plant, and Vale’s Vitória-Minas railway runs through the valley.

About half a million people live in the four municipalities affected.

A Region With a Memory

The same valley flooded severely in 2025, when the Piracicaba burst its banks and displaced thousands.

That episode led to new drainage work and a stricter alert system.

This time the damage came from wind and the electricity network rather than from rising water.

However, the pattern of short, violent storms in the spring transition has become familiar here.

Cemig said branches and roofing thrown against the network caused short circuits.

What It Means for Industry

Large steel mills run their own substations and do not lose supply at the same moment as households.

The immediate industrial risk is road and rail access rather than the power feed.

Neither Usiminas nor Aperam has reported a production interruption.

Blockages on the BR-381 matter most for trucking of finished steel and inputs.

What Has Not Been Published

Cemig has not said how long the last customers waited for restoration.

No municipal damage assessment has been released.

The number of homes that lost roofing is not confirmed.

Those figures usually arrive with the formal Civil Defence report several days later.

What to Watch

The Civil Defence damage assessment and any request for emergency status.

Whether the BR-381 reopens fully to heavy traffic.

Further INMET alerts, which had flagged storms in the region through Thursday.

And the restoration timeline Cemig publishes for the last affected neighbourhoods.

More: Brazil news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in the Vale do Aço?

A storm on the evening of 16 September 2026 cut power to more than 120,000 customers and blocked roads with fallen trees.

How heavy was the rain?

Ipatinga recorded 38.8 millimetres in one hour, with gusts reaching 76.2 kilometres an hour.

Which cities were hit?

Ipatinga, Coronel Fabriciano, Timóteo and Santana do Paraíso.

Were there casualties?

Civil Defence reported no serious injuries or deaths as of late that night.

Why did so many lose power?

Cemig said wind threw branches and roofing against the network, causing short circuits and broken cables.

Are schools open?

Four municipal schools in Ipatinga cancelled classes on 17 September.

Sources: Cemig statements, Ipatinga municipal administration, Minas Gerais Civil Defence, O Tempo and Rádio Educadora reporting of 16 and 17 September 2026.

World.title: Guyana Opens Its Oil Economy to Ibero-American Investors
World.content:
GUYANA · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened President Irfaan Ali invited Spanish and Latin American companies to invest in Guyana’s oil, mining and infrastructure.

— Where At the CEAPI business congress in Madrid, where he received the council’s medal of honour in September 2026.

— What he said “Our ambition is not simply to be richer. Our ambition is to transform our economy and our society.”

— The growth The IMF projects Guyana growing about 23% in 2026 and 21% in 2027, the fastest rate in the world.

— The roads Ali cited 130 kilometres of new highway built, 35 more under contract and talks on the Kurupukari bridge.

— What is not settled No company signed anything in Madrid, and no investment figure was announced.

The fastest-growing economy on earth went to Madrid looking for partners who are not American or Chinese.

President Irfaan Ali invited Ibero-American companies to invest in Guyana.

Guyanese president Irfaan Ali invited Spanish and Latin American companies to invest in his country’s oil, mining and infrastructure. He spoke at the CEAPI business congress in Madrid, where he received the council’s medal of honour. CEAPI is the business council for the Ibero-American region.

What He Offered

Ali asked investors to treat Guyana as a platform rather than simply a place to park capital.

He named oil, mining and infrastructure as the sectors open to partnership.

CEAPI president Nuria Vilanova presented the medal. Madrid mayor José Luis Martínez-Almeida attended.

No company signed an agreement at the event, and no investment total was announced.

The Numbers Behind the Invitation

The International Monetary Fund projects Guyana expanding about 23% in 2026.

It projects a further 21% in 2027.

That makes Guyana the fastest-growing economy in the world in percentage terms.

The base remains small, so a large percentage covers a modest absolute sum by regional standards.

How a Country of 800,000 Got Here

ExxonMobil announced the Liza discovery offshore Guyana in May 2015.

Production began in December 2019 and has expanded through a series of floating production vessels.

The Stabroek block has become one of the most productive new oil provinces of the past decade.

Guyana went from one of South America’s poorest economies to its fastest-growing in under ten years.

What the Money Is Building

Ali pointed to 130 kilometres of completed highway with bridges.

A further 35 kilometres are under contract.

Negotiations continue on the Kurupukari bridge, a crossing on the route toward the Brazilian border.

He put the timeline for regional road integration at roughly four years.

Ali spoke at the CEAPI business congress in Madrid. Photo: "2026-09-03 - Puerta del Sol in Madrid Spain" by Matt Joseph, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Why Madrid and Why Now

Guyana’s oil sector is dominated by American and Chinese contractors and financiers.

Spanish and Latin American firms bring construction, ports, water and power experience.

Spreading the supplier base is a way to reduce dependence on any single partner.

It also gives Georgetown more room in a neighbourhood where Venezuela disputes two thirds of its territory.

The Risks Investors Weigh

Guyana has few engineers, few contractors and a small civil service for the scale of money arriving.

Absorbing oil revenue without inflating costs is the standard problem of a sudden resource boom.

The Essequibo dispute with Venezuela remains unresolved at the International Court of Justice.

However, oil output has continued to rise through every round of that dispute so far.

Venezuela disputes two thirds of Guyanese territory, a case still before the International Court of Justice. Photo: "Essequibo River" by Dan Lundberg, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

What Guyana Wants From Partners

Ali framed the pitch as transformation rather than extraction.

That language points to processing, training and local supply chains rather than only drilling contracts.

Whether contracts follow the language is the test, and none were signed in Madrid.

Guyana has said the same to investors in Washington, Beijing and New Delhi.

What to Watch

Any Spanish or Latin American contractor announcing a Guyanese project in the coming months.

The Kurupukari bridge tender, which is the nearest concrete opportunity.

Guyana’s 2027 budget and how much of the oil revenue it commits to infrastructure.

And the next IMF country report, which will test the 23% projection.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Guyana’s president offer?

He invited Spanish and Latin American companies to invest in oil, mining and infrastructure.

Where did he say it?

At the CEAPI business congress in Madrid in September 2026, where he received the council’s medal of honour.

How fast is Guyana growing?

The IMF projects about 23% in 2026 and 21% in 2027, the fastest rate in the world.

What infrastructure was cited?

130 kilometres of completed highway, 35 more under contract and talks on the Kurupukari bridge.

Were any deals signed?

No company signed an agreement at the event, and no investment figure was announced.

Why look to Spain and Latin America?

Guyana’s oil sector already leans on American and Chinese firms. A broader supplier base reduces that dependence.

Sources: CEAPI congress coverage by El Observador, El Independiente and Infobae, September 2026; International Monetary Fund growth projections for Guyana.

World.title: Panama Economy Grows 5.5% in the First Half of 2026
World.content:
PANAMA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Panama’s statistics institute reported growth of 5.5% for the first half of 2026.

— The quarter The second quarter alone grew 6.4% against the same period a year earlier, the strongest since 2023.

— The two numbers They do not conflict. One covers six months, the other covers three.

— What drove it Transport, storage and mail rose 12.8%. Wholesale and retail trade rose 11.6%. Canal toll revenue rose 13.6%.

— The size Second-quarter output came to US$20.07 billion at current prices, according to INEC.

— The catch Economist Carlos Araúz says the growth has not moved into formal employment at the same pace.

Panama is growing faster than almost anywhere in the region. Where that growth lands is the harder question.

Panama grew 5.5% in the first half of 2026, according to the national statistics institute.

Panama’s economy grew 5.5% in the first half of 2026, the national statistics institute INEC reported on 16 September. The second quarter alone expanded 6.4% year on year. Transport, trade and the canal carried most of the increase.

The Numbers, Sorted Out

Two figures have circulated from the same release, and both are correct.

The 5.5% covers January to June 2026 against the same six months of 2025.

The 6.4% covers April to June alone, again against the year-earlier quarter.

A stronger second quarter pulling up a softer first quarter produces exactly that gap.

Where the Growth Came From

Transport, storage and mail grew 12.8%, the fastest of the large sectors.

Wholesale and retail trade grew 11.6%, which points to domestic demand as well as re-export activity.

Agriculture grew 9.6%, a strong showing for a sector that rarely leads.

Canal toll revenue at current prices rose 13.6%.

The Canal Is Working Again

The waterway moved 9,568 high-draft transits in the first nine months of fiscal 2026.

That splits into 6,888 through the Panamax locks and 2,680 through the Neopanamax locks.

Transits were 6.3% above the year before.

The recovery matters because the drought years of 2023 and 2024 forced Panama to ration daily crossings.

Canal toll revenue rose 13.6% at current prices. Photo: "Desde Gatun canal de panama" by Sa, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What Did Not Grow

Information and communications contracted 1.8%.

Construction managed 1.3% in the second quarter and 4.5% across the half year.

Construction is the sector that usually carries employment in Panama, so a weak reading there is felt on the ground.

The release does not break out the effect of the closed Cobre Panamá copper mine.

Growth and Wages Are Not the Same Thing

Economist Carlos Araúz argues that sector gains have not translated into formal jobs at the same rate.

Panama has a large informal workforce, and logistics growth does not automatically hire at scale.

That gap is why headline growth of 5.5% can sit alongside public frustration over the cost of living.

The statistics institute publishes output, not household income.

Panama’s dollarised economy is tied closely to global shipping volumes. Photo: "Cinta Costera de Panamá" by JAVR2020, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Regional Comparison

Most of Latin America is growing between 1% and 3% this year.

Panama’s dollarised economy and its position on the canal give it a different engine from its neighbours.

Those same features tie it closely to global shipping volumes and to United States demand.

When world trade slows, Panama feels it earlier than the rest of Central America.

What Is Still Missing

INEC has not published the methodology notes that would show how much of the gain is price rather than volume.

The half-year figure is also subject to revision when the third quarter lands.

No employment series accompanied the growth release.

Those are the numbers that would settle whether the expansion is reaching households.

What to Watch

The third-quarter reading, which tests whether the second quarter was a peak or a trend.

Any decision on the future of the Cobre Panamá mine, which alone moved several points of GDP when it operated.

Canal transit volumes through the dry season.

And the labour market data, which is where the argument about this growth will be settled.

More: Latin America news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How fast did Panama grow?

5.5% in the first half of 2026, and 6.4% in the second quarter alone, according to INEC.

Why are two different figures circulating?

They measure different periods. One is the six-month total, the other the second quarter on its own.

What drove the growth?

Transport and storage at 12.8%, wholesale and retail trade at 11.6%, and canal toll revenue at 13.6%.

How big is the economy?

Second-quarter output was US$20.07 billion at current prices.

Did anything shrink?

Information and communications fell 1.8%. Construction grew only 1.3% in the quarter.

Is the growth reaching workers?

Economist Carlos Araúz says formal employment has not expanded in proportion. No employment series came with the release.

Sources: Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censo (INEC) release of 16 September 2026, Panama Canal Authority transit data, La Prensa and Forbes Centroamérica reporting.

World.title: Bolivia Court Orders Luis Arce Moved From Prison to Cancer Hospital
World.content:
BOLIVIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened A Bolivian judge ordered the immediate transfer of former president Luis Arce from prison to an oncology hospital.

— Who ordered it Judge Carlos Alberto Moreira of the 15th criminal sentencing court of Santa Cruz, on 16 September 2026.

— Where he was San Pedro prison in central La Paz, where Arce has been held since December 2025.

— Why he is there The Fondo Indígena corruption case, which concerns public transfers authorised during his years as economy minister.

— The medical grounds The court cited a cancer diagnosed in 2017 and a kidney condition. The request came from his family and defence lawyers.

— What is not stated The ruling does not say how long the hospital stay will last, and no treatment schedule has been published.

A former president leaves a prison cell for a hospital ward, and the case against him continues.

A judge ordered Luis Arce moved from San Pedro prison to an oncology hospital. Photo: "Bolivia - La Paz 01" by P. Hughes, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

A Bolivian judge ordered former president Luis Arce transferred immediately from prison to an oncology hospital. Judge Carlos Alberto Moreira of Santa Cruz issued the order on 16 September 2026. Arce has been held at San Pedro prison in La Paz since December 2025.

The Ruling

The order came from the 15th court of criminal sentencing, anti-corruption and violence against women in Santa Cruz.

Arce’s family and defence lawyers had filed a constitutional action seeking the move.

The court accepted that he needs specialist monitoring and treatment outside the prison system.

Bolivian reporting names the Arco Iris hospital in La Paz as the destination.

The Medical Grounds

The ruling refers to a cancer diagnosed in 2017 and to a kidney condition.

His last full medical review was carried out in October of the previous year, according to the filing.

Prison health care in Bolivia is thin, and San Pedro is among the most crowded facilities in the country.

The court did not set an end date for the hospital stay.

Why Arce Is in Prison

The case is the Fondo Indígena affair, a long-running corruption investigation.

Prosecutors allege that public money was transferred to private accounts of peasant leaders for projects never carried out.

The charges relate to the period when Arce was economy minister, before his presidency.

He has denied wrongdoing throughout, and the case has not reached a verdict.

Arce governed from November 2020 to November 2025 and did not seek a second term.

How Bolivia Got Here

Arce governed from November 2020 to November 2025 and did not seek a second term.

His years in office were marked by a dollar shortage, fuel queues and a collapse in gas export earnings.

The movement that carried him to power split bitterly between his supporters and those of Evo Morales.

He was detained in December 2025, weeks after leaving the presidency.

A Familiar Pattern

Bolivia has jailed or prosecuted a long line of former leaders across changes of government.

Jeanine Áñez spent years in detention after the 2019 crisis and the trials that followed.

Each side describes the other’s cases as political and its own as justice.

However, the courts themselves have been criticised by international bodies for both delays and pliability.

What the Transfer Does and Does Not Change

Arce remains in custody. A hospital room under guard is still detention.

The criminal case continues on its own timetable, unaffected by the medical order.

Prosecutors can appeal the transfer, as has happened in earlier cases involving senior figures.

For his defence, the ruling is an acknowledgment that the prison could not provide the care.

Arce remains in custody, with a hospital room replacing a prison cell. Photo: "2017 Lima - Centro Cívico - Av Bolivia 109, Cercado de Lima 15001, Perú" by Felipe Restrpo Acosta, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Why It Matters Beyond Bolivia

Detained former presidents are a recurring feature of South American politics rather than an exception.

Investors read these cases as a signal about how contracts and decisions are judged after a government changes.

The pattern raises the cost of holding office and shortens the horizon of policy.

It also keeps the previous administration in the news long after it has left.

What to Watch

Whether prosecutors appeal the transfer order.

The next hearing date in the Fondo Indígena case.

Any statement from the prison service or the health ministry on his condition.

And whether his detention is converted to house arrest, which his defence has sought before.

More: Latin America news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Bolivian court order?

The immediate transfer of former president Luis Arce from San Pedro prison to an oncology hospital in La Paz.

Who issued the order?

Judge Carlos Alberto Moreira of the 15th criminal sentencing court of Santa Cruz, on 16 September 2026.

Why is Arce in prison?

He is held in the Fondo Indígena corruption case, which concerns transfers authorised while he was economy minister.

Is he free now?

No. He remains in custody, and the transfer moves him to a hospital rather than releasing him.

When was he detained?

In December 2025, weeks after leaving the presidency.

How long will he stay in hospital?

The ruling does not say, and no treatment schedule has been published.

Sources: Ruling of the 15th criminal sentencing court of Santa Cruz, 16 September 2026, as reported by Infobae, Opinión and Bolivian wire coverage.

World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

LATIN AMERICA · HUMANITARIAN, 17 SEPTEMBER 2026

Key Facts —Cuba 3.2 million people lack reliable access to safe water; rotavirus and norovirus outbreaks are spreading. —Haiti 5.83 million people, 52 percent of the population, face acute food insecurity; nearly 1.9 million are in emergency conditions. —Colombia More than 1,300 people newly displaced or confined by armed groups in Bolívar, Antioquia and Nariño. —Ecuador 4,882 murders from January to July, down from 5,295 a year earlier; 27 attacks on schools in the first half of 2026. —The source UN OCHA regional reporting for the week to 11 September 2026.

The UN’s latest humanitarian readout for Latin America and the Caribbean describes four emergencies moving in the wrong direction at once: disease in Cuba’s water system, record hunger in Haiti, fresh displacement in Colombia and a school-year under fire in Ecuador.

Havana. Cuba’s water network now fails 3.2 million people, and waterborne disease is following.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Cuba: The Water Crisis Turns Epidemiological

The number that defines Cuba’s emergency is 3.2 million — the people who no longer have reliable access to safe drinking water, according to the UN’s latest regional reporting. What changed this month is what flows instead: health authorities are now confronting outbreaks of rotavirus and norovirus, the classic signature of a failing water and sanitation chain.

The deterioration moves fast. On 5 September the US Embassy in Havana warned its citizens about contaminated water and medicine shortages. The UN data published since confirms the warning was not caution but description. For households, the crisis is a daily logistics problem of buckets, tankers and boiling; for the health system it is becoming an epidemiological one.

Haiti: Hunger at Levels the Region Has Not Seen

Haiti’s figures have crossed a threshold. Some 5.83 million people — 52 percent of the population — now face acute food insecurity. Of them, nearly 1.9 million sit in IPC Phase 4, the “emergency” classification one step below famine.

Displacement drives the hunger. Around 1.47 million Haitians are internally displaced, more than 300,000 of them in Port-au-Prince alone, where armed groups control most of the capital and its access roads. Food cannot move in, people cannot move out, and the transitional government’s collapse this month has left the state absent exactly where the crisis is deepest.

Haiti’s crisis is now measured in millions: 5.83 million acutely food insecure, 1.47 million displaced.

Colombia: Displaced and Confined as Peace Tables Close

Colombia’s post-agreement fragility shows in the UN’s incident log. More than 1,300 people were newly displaced or confined in recent weeks: around 880 in Montecristo, in the southern Bolívar coca region; 339 in Ituango, Antioquia; further cases in Tarazá. In Nariño, on the Pacific border with Ecuador, another 1,500 people are assessed at risk.

The timing is not accidental. Bogotá has now closed its last remaining peace tables and stripped armed groups of their political status, ending nine negotiation tracks. The groups’ answer, in the territories, is written in displacement figures.

Ecuador: Better Numbers, Same Emergency

Ecuador offers the report’s only comparative improvement — and it is a grim one. The country recorded 4,882 murders between January and July, down from 5,295 in the same period of 2025. Violence is falling from its peak, not from its crisis.

The figure that should worry policymakers most is 27: attacks on schools in the first half of 2026. Extortion of students, teachers and parents has turned education into a revenue line for the gangs, and classes in the affected districts keep emptying.

Why It Matters Beyond the Four Countries

All four crises export people. Cuban, Haitian, Colombian and Ecuadorian migration flows meet at the same borders and the same routes north, and each deterioration adds pressure to neighbours already managing their own emergencies. The UN’s ask is unchanged and unmet: funding for the regional response plans runs far behind the needs its own reports document.

Frequently Asked Questions How bad is Cuba’s water crisis in September 2026? The UN reports 3.2 million people without reliable access to safe water, with rotavirus and norovirus outbreaks now spreading. The US Embassy warned about contaminated water and medicine shortages on 5 September 2026. How many people are going hungry in Haiti? Some 5.83 million people, 52 percent of the population, face acute food insecurity. Of them, nearly 1.9 million are in IPC Phase 4, the emergency level one step below famine. How many people are displaced in Haiti? Around 1.47 million people are internally displaced, including more than 300,000 in Port-au-Prince, where armed groups control most of the capital. Where is displacement rising in Colombia? In southern Bolívar (around 880 people in Montecristo), Ituango in Antioquia (339), Tarazá, and Nariño, where some 1,500 people are at risk. The surge follows the government’s closure of its remaining peace talks with armed groups. Is violence in Ecuador falling? Slightly. Murders from January to July 2026 totalled 4,882, down from 5,295 a year earlier. But gangs carried out 27 attacks on schools in the first half of 2026, and extortion of students and teachers is spreading.

Sources: UN OCHA Latin America and the Caribbean reporting, week to 11 September 2026; IPC; US Embassy Havana.
