World.title: Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day
World.content:
Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Department of the Environment (DOE), through the National Ozone Unit, awarded 12 scholarships under the Refrigeration and Air Conditioning (RAC) Scholarship Programme.

The recipients are enrolled in RAC programmes at ITVETs in Belize City, Orange Walk, and Stann Creek, and will receive support for the 2026–2027 academic year, including tuition, a toolbox of servicing tools, and personal protective equipment.

Three of the twelve recipients are female trainees, marking a step toward greater participation of women in the RAC sector.

The ceremony coincided with World Ozone Day, observed annually on September 16. This year’s theme, “Global Action for a Cooler Planet,” marks ten years of sustainable cooling efforts under the Kigali Amendment.

The DOE said the scholarships reflect Belize’s ongoing transition toward lower-global-warming-potential refrigerants and more efficient cooling technologies, which requires a pipeline of skilled technicians.

Through the programme, the DOE said it is investing in the next generation of RAC professionals to help promote safe, efficient, and environmentally responsible cooling practices going forward.

The twelve scholarship recipients are Zadiel Dias, Patrick Zetina, Samuel Alamilla, Brandon Ysaguirre, Gerardo Magana, Milcar Ku, Rilma Urbina, Edwardo Coc, Cierra Teck, Jahleel Flowers, Erwin Colon, and Dorda Castillo.

World.title: Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance
World.content:
Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) has cleaned up a garbage site at the entrance of Yo Chen Village following a media report regarding the issue.

The DOE said it investigated the matter promptly and worked with the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH) to address the concern.

The area has since been cleaned and placed under surveillance to help prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

The DOE is reminding the public that under the Pollution Regulations, it is an offence to place or permit refuse to be placed on any land without written permission from the department.

The DOE is encouraging community members to remain vigilant and report instances of illegal dumping at this or any other location.

World.title: Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Magical History Tour made its way through Orange Walk Town on September 15, continuing a series of events aimed at encouraging dialogue and reflection on the country’s history.

The tour is led by the Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) in partnership with historian Dr. Assad Shoman, and focuses on Belize’s path to independence, the experiences that have shaped its national story, and ongoing conversations around decolonization.

During the day, the tour engaged students from New Hope High School, Muffles College High School, and Orange Walk Technical High School in discussions on Belize’s history, national identity, and the range of experiences that continue to shape the country. Students were given the opportunity to ask questions and share their perspectives on how the past connects to present-day Belize.

That evening, the tour held a public forum at the Banquitas House of Culture, bringing together community leaders and residents of Orange Walk Town. The forum allowed attendees to discuss the country’s shared history and consider how a deeper understanding of the past could inform Belize’s future direction.

ISCR-NICH thanked the students, educators, community leaders, and residents who took part in the day’s events, noting their questions and input as central to the tour’s goals.

The Magical History Tour is made possible through the National Celebrations Commission and the National Institute of Culture and History, along with partners including the University of Belize.

World.title: International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee
World.content:
International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump has nominated Florida businessman Austin Holmes to serve as the next U.S. ambassador to Haiti, as the Caribbean nation continues to grapple with a severe political and security crisis.

Holmes’ nomination was submitted to the U.S. Senate on Monday, September 14, and he must receive Senate confirmation before taking up the diplomatic post.

Holmes has longstanding ties to Haiti through humanitarian and security work and has previously lived in the country with his family.

Earlier this year, he testified before a Senate appropriations subcommittee during a hearing examining U.S. security and foreign assistance priorities in Haiti.

During his testimony, Holmes said he has participated in security operations in Haiti, including kidnapping recoveries and emergency extractions. He cited the 2023 recovery of American humanitarian worker Jeff Frazier, who was kidnapped by gangs while participating in a food distribution mission and held captive for 43 days. Holmes said his team “successfully recovered” Frazier.

Holmes said his approach to operations in Haiti is based on local knowledge and long-term engagement. “Deep cultural fluency, long-term presence and operational leadership rooted in local context” have driven the results achieved by his teams, he said, adding that many of his personnel are Haitian and Haitian American with local experience, language skills and relationships.

World.title: Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police intercepted a pickup truck near the Blue Creek Dam in Orange Walk earlier this month and reportedly discovered several boxes and sacks of food products suspected to be uncustomed goods.

According to police information, personnel from the North HIT conducted a staging operation in the area between approximately 5:30 p.m. and 8:40 p.m. on Friday, September 4.

During the operation, officers intercepted a white Dodge Ram being driven by a 25 year old man from San Felipe Village.

A search of the vehicle reportedly led to the discovery of six boxes of oxtail, five sacks of cabbage and 15 sacks of onions.

The driver and the goods were subsequently escorted to the Orange Walk Customs Department.

Police say the matter was handed over to a Customs officer for further action.

No information was provided on the estimated value of the goods or whether any charges have been filed.

World.title: Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 24 year old Orange Walk man has been charged with reckless driving following an early morning police pursuit.

According to police information, officers were conducting mobile patrol on San Narciso Street at around 1:20 a.m. on September 15 when their attention was drawn to a black motorcycle with a defective rear light.

Police say the rider was signalled to stop but allegedly drove off and began swerving from side to side along the street.

Officers reportedly followed the motorcycle for approximately five minutes before managing to intercept the rider.

Police say the man told officers he had not been trying to escape.

A search was conducted and nothing incriminating was found. Checks on the motorcycle documents also reportedly showed that the licence and insurance were up to date.

The rider was then informed that he was being detained for reckless driving and was escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

Police identified him as Nathan J. Navarrete, 24, a labourer of Santa Familia Street, Orange Walk.

He was later formally arrested and charged with reckless driving.

World.title: Bouncing back fast
World.content:
WILLIAMS...I see quarters that are becoming less negative and that is a good sign.

CITING data that shows Jamaica 18 months ahead of schedule in recovering from the destruction Hurricane Melissa unleashed on several parishes last year, Finance Minister Fayval Williams on Wednesday painted a rosy picture of the country’s economy. She acknowledged, however, that “not everybody is feeling it just yet”, a nod to critics who have argued that the pace of the recovery and rebuilding is much too slow.

During her upbeat PowerPoint presentation, the minister reeled off data to support her claims.

“When I look at this chart, I see quarters that are becoming less negative and that is a good sign,” Williams stated.

“And, no, this is not a picture of a recession. The Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) already debunked that notion,” she added.

Williams highlighted that in the quarter following the hurricane, the economy contracted 7.1 per cent, then 4.1 per cent in the next quarter and just 2.9 per cent in the quarter, after that. She said the 2.9 per cent projection should be finalised by the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (Statin) by the end of September.

The finance minister argued that the shrinking year-on-year numbers are themselves proof that the economy is recovering. She argued further that “an economy in decline produces deepening figures, not improving ones”.

Williams urged Jamaicans to remember that immediately after the hurricane, PIOJ projected that the country would not get back to its pre-Melissa level of output until the last quarter of 2028. She noted that the PIOJ now expects that the economy will begin to see growth by the second quarter of 2027 — “six quarters earlier, a year-and-a-half earlier”. According to her, the PIOJ “has been able to revise their forecast because the out-turn keeps getting better”.

The finance minister highlighted that where it was projected that the fiscal deficit would have been 3.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) immediately after the hurricane, it instead came in at 2.5 per cent. At the same time the primary surplus was projected to be 1.3 per cent but came in at 2.3 per cent, while public debt-to-GDP was projected to rise to 68.9 per cent but came in at 65.6 per cent.

Regarding the public debt-to-GDP number, Williams said, “That number matters, it is not a one-off, it’s because we had stronger nominal GDP, the economy itself is bigger than we assumed, and that is the kind of improvement that will persist.”

She also pointed to the positions taken by the big three international ratings agencies with Moody’s upgrading its assessment of Jamaica just seven weeks after the hurricane, which it described as a “temporary setback”. Standard & Poor’s held its rating for Jamaica in December 2025 and moved the outlook to stable, while Fitch affirmed its BB-rating for Jamaica in February 2026 with a stable outlook.

Williams also pointed out that while unemployment rose from 3.3 per cent to 3.7 per cent following the hurricane, it remained at record lows. She acknowledged that unemployment in the hardest-hit parishes was higher.

“I want to assure them that the Government continues to work night and day to restore the west — to restore roads, water, housing, all the services, employment, schools and so on,” she said.

Williams also noted that the response from the Diaspora helped to stabilise the economy, as is evidenced in the record level of remittances that were sent to Jamaica in the aftermath of the hurricane. A breakdown of the numbers shows that, in November, the Diaspora sent remittances totalling US$273 million, up 16 per cent. December saw a record US$296 million being sent. The figure was up 16.3 per cent for the month. Of note is that all of the hardest-hit parishes received more in remittances than before the hurricane.

In the first three months after the storm, Jamaicans abroad sent home US$93 million more than they sent in the same three months a year earlier.

On the matter of inflation, the finance minister insisted that, while it was expected that food prices “would run away” following the devastating hurricane, they did not. She pointed out that inflation moved to 2.9 per cent in October 2025, 4.4 per cent in November 2025, and 4.5 per cent in December 2025 — all within the target range for the Bank of Jamaica. This, she said, was because agricultural production recovered faster than expected.

“Because of that, the price shock was contained,” the minister remarked.

However, Williams acknowledged that by July 2026 the picture had changed completely, with headline inflation surging to 7.5 per cent — the driver being the transportation division, which was up 13.6 per cent. She said based on figures released by Statin on Tuesday, whereas transportation had pushed up inflation in July, it was higher food prices, as a result of the ongoing drought, which drove inflation in August.

While transportation is still a factor, the finance minister said the August inflation number is directly attributable to the upheaval in international markets, driven by the United States war on Iran which has pushed up oil prices since February.

World.title: Blessing in disguise
World.content:
Sharon Logan, director of sales and marketing at Half Moon Resort, speaks during a JAPEX partner media update on Tuesday. (Photo: Aceion Cunningham)

WHEN Hurricane Melissa swept through Jamaica last October it left tourism businesses counting losses and racing to recover. But nearly a year later, Half Moon resort and Chukka Jamaica are looking beyond the devastation, using the disruption to refresh their properties, redesign experiences, and rethink their operations.

For Half Moon, the forced recovery has gone beyond repairing hurricane damage. The Montego Bay resort has used the interruption to undertake a broad refresh of its property, while Chukka Jamaica says the experience forced it to examine its processes and find ways to operate more efficiently.

Speaking during a Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) 2026 Partner Media Update on Tuesday, director of sales and marketing for the Half Moon resort Sharon Logan said the hurricane created an opportunity for the resort to undertake work that would otherwise have been difficult to complete while guests were on property.

“One of the things that I look on is the silver lining behind the cloud, which is that we got the opportunity to do a complete refresh and regrowth of the property since the reopening,” said Logan.

She explained that while some projects, including renovation work on some of the resort’s villas, had already been under way before the hurricane, other major improvements came directly out of the damage caused by the storm.

“The villas were already a project that we were working on. But the other parts of the property, like the original part of the hotel, that has a complete refresh and that is all as a result of the hurricane,” added Logan.

The result, she said, has included improvements across much of the 400-acre property, including its rooms, meeting spaces, lobby, roadways, and pool areas.

One of the more unusual benefits, she identified, came from the movement of sand during the hurricane.

“There are so many open spaces. All the plants have been sprung up fresh and nice…We even got new beaches because we got sand that washed up. That would have cost the hotel millions of dollars to purchase. We got 30 truckloads of sand, free, so we have expanded beaches, so we’re excited about that,” explained Logan.

The resort, which reopened on April 2, is continuing a phased reopening of its facilities. Logan said half of the original Founders’ Cove section is already open, with the remaining section scheduled to open on October 1.

The hurricane also gave the resort an opportunity to tackle work that had previously required interruptions to operations. Logan pointed specifically to the pool at the Eclipse section, which had experienced problems with its tiles.

But while Half Moon’s gains have been visible in its physical transformation, Chukka Jamaica’s experience has produced a different kind of reset.

The attraction operator, which describes itself as a nature adventure company, was particularly exposed to the effects of the hurricane because its business depends heavily on the natural environment.

Group Digital Platform Manager Ilia Tomlinson said the recovery was especially difficult at Chukka’s river locations. At Good Hope in Trelawny, for example, the site was inundated and its river operations were disrupted.

Chukka began reopening locations in November, according to Tomlinson, with its final reopening taking place in June. She said the river-based operations were among the hardest to restore because of the overflow of the waterways.

But the disruption also prompted the company to scrutinise how it worked, with greater productivity emerging as one of the main lessons from the recovery.

“I would say the silver lining is…we operated a little bit more efficiently. We have had to. Nobody wants to cut back, it’s hard decisions to make, but cutting back and being efficient almost go hand in hand where there’s a middle spot where it’s productivity,” said Tomlinson.

“We have had to look at things we have never thought we have had to look at, and in a way we’re thankful for that. You know, it really has had us reflecting on our own processes and procedures and being more efficient in how we deliver our experiences,” added Tomlinson.

That reassessment has taken place alongside changes to Chukka’s tourism products.

In Ocho Rios, the company has redesigned parts of its offering following the hurricane and has expanded its portfolio through its acquisition of the Green Grotto Caves, which it took over just two days before Melissa struck Jamaica on October 28.

The caves, located near Discovery Bay in St Ann, are being incorporated into Chukka’s wider network of experiences in the resort area, adding a stronger history and culture component to its nature and adventure products.

Meanwhile, at Good Hope, the company has rebranded the attraction as a river outpost reflecting its location and the experiences offered there, including river tubing, bamboo rafting, ziplining, and dune buggies.

Tomlinson said the storm also reinforced the importance of preparation, particularly for a company whose operations are so closely tied to Jamaica’s landscape.

“We didn’t know we were so good at preparing. That was the lesson learned on the value of our standards of procedures and policies that we put into place that we probably otherwise take for granted,” she added.

World.title: J-House Vol 1 puts Jamaica on a new global dance floor
World.content:
Freddy Browne

There are collaborations, there are compilations — and then there are projects whose star-studded line-ups pack such a heavy punch that they position themselves for global attention long before anyone hears a single track.

Keen on taking Jamaican voices into the billion-dollar world of electronic music, Freddy Browne’s ambitious J-House Volume 1 is poised to do just that.

With Patra, Beenie Man, Tessanne Chin, Busy Signal, T.O.K, Agent Sasco, and more in the mix, the project, set for release on September 18, aims to take unmistakably Jamaican voices and personalities into the international house music arena.

Rather than simply placing Jamaican artistes over electronic beats and calling it fusion, Browne has been building J-House as its own musical proposition.

According to the American producer, DJ, and JHouse Entertainment CEO, the project stretches across generations of Jamaican music while refusing to stay comfortably inside any one of them.

Each artiste represents a different era in Jamaica’s rich musical history. Patra carries the weight of an artiste who helped push dancehall into mainstream international spaces during the 1990s. Beenie Man has spent decades as one of the genre’s most recognisable figures, while Busy Signal has built a catalogue around his ability to move between hard-core dancehall and broader musical territory. Ding Dong, meanwhile, brings an energy rooted heavily in dance and movement.

Then there is Tessanne Chin, whose victory on The Voice introduced her powerhouse vocals to millions internationally. T.O.K, whose harmonies became integral to dancehall’s crossover era; Richie Stephens, bringing decades of reggae experience; and Agent Sasco, one of the genre’s most respected lyricists.

Newer voices J’Calm and AcYn ensure the project is not only honouring Jamaica’s musical legacy, but also looking towards its future.

Browne, who has previously spoken about imagining artistes such as Ding Dong performing before audiences at major electronic music festivals, described J-House as an opportunity to carry Jamaican talent into spaces it may not traditionally occupy.

“This is crazy,” he said. “We’re creating a blueprint for other producers and record companies. The goal is to open doors for artistes, producers, and the industry as a whole.”

That ambition extends beyond the music itself. House music connects artistes to a vast international network of DJs, clubs, festivals, streaming platforms, radio, play lists, licensing opportunities, and electronic music audiences. J-House is designed to place Jamaican talent directly within that ecosystem, making the project as much about market expansion as it is about musical experimentation.

With J-House Volume 1 distributed through The Orchard/Sony Music the project also has access to an established international distribution network. And Volume 1 is not being treated as the endgame.

Browne shared that Jamaica represents the first instalment of a wider international concept. The United Kingdom is planned as the focus of the second volume, Japan the third, with Africa completing the four-part series. If the vision unfolds as planned, Jamaica will not simply be participating in another global musical movement. It will be the starting point.

World.title: Jamaica, US finalise operating procedures related to TCNs
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that the United States and Jamaica have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding for TCNs that was signed earlier this year..

JAMAICA could soon receive its first batch of third-country nationals (TCNs) from the United States (US) as Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that both governments have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was signed earlier this year.

Jamaica now joins 30 countries, including several members of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), which have similar arrangements with the US Government amid its ongoing crackdown on illegal immigration.

“After internal consultations and thoughtful negotiations, both governments have now finalised operating procedures related to the MOU in order to settle the guard rails and parameters underpinning the agreement. The arrangements were also finalised, taking into account Jamaica’s capacity constraints and our belief in the principles of safe, orderly, and lawful migration,” said Johnson Smith, speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House on Wednesday.

The agreement, Johnson Smith clarified, will see 25 TCNs entering the country biweekly. While here, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) will provide basic services, like health care and counselling, to help with their transition.

The minister reiterated that under no circumstance will more than 25 TCNs be present in the island.

“We have also not agreed to receive 10,000 individuals. We have negotiated guard rails to address capacity constraints, and have, therefore, agreed to a maximum of 25 individuals per two-week period, which the IOM will, of course, be on a continuous basis making arrangements for their return.

“Furthermore, this arrangement will be suspended if 10 TCNs apply to remain in Jamaica through asylum procedures or other humanitarian applications. This, again, is specifically negotiated by Jamaica,” said Johnson Smith.

She further explained that TCNs were not deportees but the nationals of other countries who entered the US unlawfully and are being returned to their home countries through the IOM’s Assisted Voluntary Return Programme.

Johnson Smith added that while she is aware that some countries have opted to accept TCNs with criminal records, Jamaica will only facilitate those with no previous convictions.

“The Government reiterates its commitment to working with the IOM and the Government of the United States of America to ensure that all arrangements for the next stage of TCN implementation are appropriately governed and implemented in accordance with both our domestic laws and international law,” she said.

Additionally, while acknowledging Minister of National Security Dr Horace Chang’s previous commitment to release the agreement, Johnson Smith explained that the MOU’s bilateral status prevents it from being made public.

“As indicated, this is not a unilateral arrangement; it is a bilateral arrangement, and one in which they [the United States] have not generally released their agreements, and they have not agreed to release this one,” she said.

“I give you every assurance as well that we have all shared all the relevant and material matters, provisions, in relation to the matter. So there’s nothing being hidden per se, but as you would note, even under the ATI [Access to Information Act], bilateral agreements, security agreements, arrangements that are sensitive to relations between countries and otherwise are treated differently from other agreements,” explained Johnson Smith.

Despite not being able to give an official start date for when the first TCNs are expected to arrive, Johnson Smith affirmed that Jamaicans will be regularly updated as conversations advance.

World.title: NEXT LEVEL
World.content:
Jamaica 100m sprinter Jonielle Smith competes in the women’s 4x100m relay heats during the World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, Japan, on September 20, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

After breaking into the ranks of Jamaica’s fastest women ever, national 100m sprinter Jonielle Smith says she’s looking to carry her strong form into next season with the World Athletics Championships looming.

Smith ended her impressive 2026 season over the weekend at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest, finishing fourth in the women’s 100m final and helping Jamaica land silver in the 4×100 metres mixed relay.

The 2025 North American, Central American and Caribbean (NACAC) 100m champion moved to 14th all time in Jamaica’s all-time list when she clocked a personal best 10.89 seconds at the Eugene Diamond League in July.

Prior to this year, Smith had never gone under 11 seconds in the event. However, she managed to dip under the mark six times, including at the Ultimate Championship where she registered 10.94 seconds both in the semi-final and final.

Smith, a finalist at this summer’s Commonwealth Games in Scotland and March’s World Indoor Championships in Poland, believes improving her confidence level was key in her success this year.

“I’m proud of myself [for] having confidence in myself,” she told the Inside Lane UK. “As good as last year was, it took me a while to start to trust my body and I feel like from day one this year in the background, I told myself that I was a champion and I was going to get what I wanted done and I think that’s what I’m most proud of, just being confident.”

The 30-year-old, who won 4x100m silver at last year’s Tokyo World Championships, says writing out her goals has helped change her perspective, which was on display at the recent Ultimate Championship.

“I journalled every day before practice and I had to do that [for the 100m final] also,” she said. “After the 4x100m, I felt bad because I really wanted us to win and I wasn’t able to pass [USA’s] Kayla [White]. She’s a phenomenal athlete, but I wanted us to win [0:44] to be honest, so I genuinely felt bad. My people were like ‘you split nine [seconds], that was so good’. But regardless, it was just like we didn’t win.

“So I went back to what I was used to and I journalled, I told myself that I’m a champion and I reminded myself what we were doing, trying to have fun and stuff like that. And I felt like that made me come out a whole lot more confident since the last month and the results showed.”

Describing 2026 as “phenomenal”, Smith says she’s excited for what’s to come in 2027.

“I got my 10.8, I got top three at the national trials and Ultimate finalist,” she said. “I just didn’t get [a] Commonwealth [medal] but that was out of my control, so I got to give myself some grace for that. But I feel like I finished off extremely well and I started even better indoors, so it’s a great thing to build off going into next season.”

Smith will likely be eyeing an individual spot at the 2027 World Championships in Beijing, having last done so in 2019 in Doha.

World.title: Family services shake-up
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has severed ties with the heads of two of its primary family services agencies — the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) and the National Parenting Support Commission (NPSC) — reportedly to undertake a major shift in their operations, the Jamaica Observer has learnt.

As part of that shake-up, chief executive officer of the CPFSA Laurette Adams-Thomas, who took the helm of the agency in October 2023, will demit office next month.

In a brief response to the Observer, Adams-Thomas said her contract expires on October 1, 2026 and she was “officially notified on July 23, 2026” that it would “not be renewed”.

The CPFSA is an executive agency which was formed from the merger of the Child Development Agency (CDA) and the Office of Children’s Registry (OCR). Adams-Thomas, an educator and social worker, took over its leadership following an eight-year stint as general manager of the largest infirmary in the Caribbean — Jamaica’s Golden Age Home — where she had oversight responsibly for protection and welfare services for more than 450 indigent people from the parishes of Kingston and St Andrew. Prior to assuming that position, she was interim executive director/registrar at the OCR, where her focus was centred on ensuring that an effective system was maintained to facilitate the confidential receipt, assessment, and referral of reports of known or suspected cases of child abuse.

She holds a master’s degree in business administration, bachelor of science in human resource management, and a number of certifications in leadership, corporate governance and strategic planning.

In the meantime, the Observer was reliably informed on Monday that NPSC CEO Kaysia Kerr “is no longer with” the entity. Efforts to get an official response from Kerr were unsuccessful. A pre-recorded message on her personal mobile phone directed all callers with queries related to the commission to contact the education ministry or the commission itself.

A source with knowledge of the development said the ministry had decided to disengage with Kerr due to a breakdown in relations.

She took the helm of the commission in 2017, succeeding Dr Patrece Charles. In an interview with the

Observer at the time, Kerr said she hoped to craft and design programmes for parents and children of all 13 categories of disabilities, move the organisation out of eastern Jamaica to serve other parishes, take some of the programmes internationally, and get the unit to a stage where it generates income.

The former NPSC head has a solid background in education and has completed studies in business and professional management at Nova Southeastern University, along with a first degree in special education and a master’s in administration and supervision from Western Carolina University.

The commission coordinates a wide range of services for parents and also delivers programmes that build parenting skills and promote parental involvement in education.

The Government of Jamaica mandated the establishment of the NPSC in response to the 2004 task force report on the status of education in Jamaica.

The NPSC began operating in January 2013.

World.title: Global aviation squeeze
World.content:
Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose says Jamaica needs more airline seats to meet strong demand as carriers face aircraft shortages and higher fuel costs amid the impact of the war in the Middle East.

Addressing the media during the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) forum in Ocho Rios on Tuesday, Rose said Jamaica’s immediate challenge is not a lack of demand, but having enough airline seats to bring visitors to the island.

“The immediate thing that we do need is more seats into the destination. The good news is, and I really want this to land, the good news is the airlines know this. The airlines are preparing because they don’t want to leave business on the table. The airlines know that the demand is there. The airlines are preparing to put in additional flights,” he said.

His comments come as Jamaica’s tourism industry continues its recovery following last year’s Hurricane Melissa, with hotel capacity gradually returning and airlines looking to adjust their schedules accordingly.

Rose said the global aviation industry is itself under pressure, making it difficult for airlines to simply add capacity whenever demand rises. He pointed to higher fuel costs linked to developments in the Middle East, as well as problems affecting aircraft engines, servicing and maintenance.

“As you all know, there are global pressures now on the aviation space. What’s happening out there in the Middle East has really impacted oil prices, which impacts fuel prices. In the best of days, the margins are exceedingly thin for airlines. You’re going to add this increase in jet fuel, it puts additional pressure on the industry,” he explained.

“Along with that, there is a shortage of aircraft because of issues to do with the engines, which I won’t really bore you all with. There are some service and maintenance things that are going on, which means a lot of aircraft have been pulled out of service,” he added.

The result, he said, is that Jamaica cannot depend on unlimited airline capacity, even as demand remains strong

“Airlines across the world don’t have infinite aircraft. That means that seats are not infinite. When the seats are full, the seats are full. Because of the demand that we have been generating for Jamaica, the vast majority of the flights into Jamaica are full,” he added.

Still, Rose said the outlook for airlift is positive, with airlines preparing to increase service as more hotel rooms become available.

He said airlines are also preparing to return to the flight schedules that existed before Hurricane Melissa, although they first have to resolve their own aircraft availability issues and factor in Jamaica’s accommodation capacity.

World.title: Sugar Cain promises powerful music, deep message
World.content:
Members of the cast of Sugar Cain, Father Ho Lung and Friends’ upcoming stage production, rehearse the songs for the show, last Wednesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

A sober message of moral commitment complemented by powerful music is in store for audiences at Father Ho Lung and Friends’ upcoming stage production Sugar Cain.

“It’s a show that I think everybody will be able to relate to, even if you are not Jamaican,” music director for the group Jody Anne Johnson told the Jamaica Observer last Wednesday, just before the start of rehearsals for the production scheduled to run over two weekends — October 3-4 and October 10-11 at the National Arena in St Andrew.

“There are a lot of emotions that we go through every single day that will be explored, and the music is powerful… in kind of fuelling those emotions and setting the stage for the whole story to unfold,” added Johnson, who described the music as a “kind of melting pot of different genres”.

“We have traditional Jamaican music; there’s mento, there’s reggae — a lot of nice Jamaican reggae. We also have a little bit of hip hop; there are ballads; a little bit of music from the 60s, 70s; and then it comes up to dancehall as well,” Johnson explained, adding that the show contains 20 songs.

The script and all 20 tracks were written by Ho Lung in keeping with the tradition of his stage productions over the years, but Johnson, who took over from Wynton Williams as music director in 2019 after joining the group in 2003, wouldn’t be drawn when asked whether Sugar Cain tops all the previous productions.

“You remember them for different things. I remember Moses for all the tech — all of the interesting lights and special effects. And the Messiah is remembered because it is the story of our Lord and Saviour when He was crucified and risen. So each story has a special kind of brand that it leaves on our audience. So, I wouldn’t want to compare,” she told the Observer.

“I believe, though, that the music in Sugar Cane is a little bit more current, because of the addition of the hip hop, and we have some dancehall and stuff like that. But I think it’s going to be a powerful story… and all the stories that Father Ho Lung has done are powerful,” Johnson added.

She reinforced Director Hugh Douse’s observation, shared in an earlier interview with the Observer, that the ego often associated with artistic personalities is conspicuously absent among the cast, whose members have instead embraced a spirit of humility and collective purpose.

“The persons in this group are very easy to work with. We’ve been doing this for a long time, so we kind of have an idea of how things are to go, exactly what is to be done. So a lot of those initial growing pains where you have different ideas and people getting at each other, it doesn’t really happen,” Johnson said.

World.title: Canada’s Carney stops short of endorsing von der Leyen’s associate member plan
World.content:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to the members of the Parliament at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, September 17, 2026. | Ronald Wittek/EPA

STRASBOURG — Mark Carney used an address to the European Parliament to to sketch out what Ottawa would want from closer ties with the EU but declined to give full-throated approval of Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise “associate member” plan.

Speaking a day after the Commission president floated the unique relationship status, the Canadian prime minister acknowledged the offer and instead of accepting it outright, listed potential individual areas of cooperation, including critical minerals, defense, AI, energy security, and space. He also called for more seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and services, as well as Canadian participation in Erasmus+, the EU's student exchange program.

"We welcome this ambition," he said, after name-checking the idea of von der Leyen, who was sitting in the audience. "Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties."

World.title: France’s Le Pen rules out more money for Ukraine
World.content:
Le Pen is leading the polls ahead of a high-stakes presidential election next spring to replace Emmanuel Macron. One of the campaign's main issues is France's increasingly strained finances, with a public deficit that could exceed 5% this year.

France's direct financial aid to Ukraine is actually quite limited but the National Rally has long been against the EU's €90 billion loan to Kyiv, which is guaranteed by the bloc's budget, fed by national contributions.

National Rally officials privately say that Ukraine will never be able to repay the EU loan and it will ultimately fall on the bloc's capitals to do so.

"You can't say, on the one hand, that there isn't a single euro … to adjust pensions for inflation, but, on the other hand, that there are billions for the net contribution to the European Union," Le Pen said.

While the National Rally is internally divided over Russia, Ukraine and NATO, Le Pen's rivals have on multiple occasions accused her party of playing into the Kremlin’s hands in order to undermine the National Rally's credibility. The media has also repeatedly asked top party figures to clarify the party's line on assistance to Kyiv.

In Wednesday evening's interview, Le Pen stressed that France under her presidency would organize a conference for peace that would bring Russia, Ukraine and other European countries such as Germany and Poland to the table. The goal, she said, is to put an end to the war.

She also pushed back against proposals made by her presidential rivals, such as former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, to protect Ukraine's skies with French fighter jets — an option Paris has also so far refused to contemplate. "That would make us co-belligerents," Le Pen told LCI.

Sarah Paillou contributed to this report.

World.title: Brussels tries to calm Trump over offer to make Canada an EU associate member
World.content:
Responding to Trump’s comments, the Commission was keen to stress the move was not intended to antagonize.

“The proposed strengthening of our partnership with Canada is not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” said Deputy Chief Spokesperson Olof Gill.

Trump’s threats drew a more robust response from Kathleen Van Brempt, the Belgian vice chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee.

“Trump has no veto over our future. We will not be pressured into abandoning that cooperation,” she said. “That Trump has immediately resorted to threats of this severity speaks volumes. It shows precisely why closer cooperation between Europe and Canada is wise and necessary. He does not think the idea is ridiculous. He fears it.”

Von der Leyen’s bombshell offer of associate membership to Canada has left the Commission isolated. The EU’s biggest countries have raised concerns about the untried concept, which appeared to be aimed at showcasing closer ties between Brussels and Ottawa as their trade relations with the United States come under strain.

The EU has no existing model for associate membership, while any decision on full membership would involve the Council, the bloc’s intergovernmental arm, and require the European Parliament’s consent.

World.title: OpenAI finds 6 new cases of ‘concerning’ AI behavior
World.content:
OpenAI also rolled out a new framework to track, investigate and disclose such incidents, known as "misalignment" failures. | Leon Neal/Getty Images

OpenAI also rolled out a new framework to track, investigate and disclose what it describes as “misalignment” failures.

Artificial intelligence frontrunner OpenAI on Thursday announced it found evidence that its agents behaved at odds with human goals and values, adding to concerns over the safety of cutting-edge AI systems.

In six separate incidents, OpenAI agents either concealed information from human engineers or instructed themselves not to act as someone's assistant while trained or tested, the company said.

OpenAI also rolled out a new framework to track, investigate and disclose such incidents, known as "misalignment" failures. The tech firm now has a clear disclosure procedure, wherein any employee can flag model misalignment, after which it can be considered for public disclosure.

World.title: Russia launches massive overnight attack on Kyiv and southern Ukraine
World.content:
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 157 drones and a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles. Air defenses shot down or neutralized 131 targets, but strikes still hit 36 locations and debris fell at five others.

It also confirmed Zaporizhzhia as one of the main targets of attack, alongside Kyiv and Odesa, where three people were injured, including a child, and a residential building was damaged.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a Facebook post that it was “symbolic” that the United States Congress passed Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill on the same night as another Russian attack.

The measure, which passed 262-159 and now heads to President Donald Trump, targets Russian energy revenues and gives the White House tariff powers against major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

Zelenskyy called sanctions “an extremely strong tool” that could force Moscow toward peace. “Russia needs to end this war of its own,” he said.

World.title: Carney on EU-Canada ties: ‘What matters is the substance’ — live updates
World.content:
Prime minister’s speech comes as Canada looks beyond the U.S. and Europe seeks closer alliances.

Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament a day after Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise proposal to make Canada the EU’s first “associate member” left capitals scrambling.

Open questions include what the new status would mean, how it would differ from existing partnerships — and how Washington would react, after Donald Trump threatened “serious tariffs” on Europe if it followed through.

Carney name-checked the term, lauding von der Leyen’s “opening the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first associate member,” adding that he welcomes the ambition.

“Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties. An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on shared values,” he said.

Scroll down for all the updates from our team of reporters in Strasbourg, Brussels, Ottawa and beyond.

Anne reports from a gathering of former prime ministers – Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer – and reveals what life after power really looks like.

Meanwhile, after some football diplomacy with Canadian PM Mark Carney, could it offer a chance for Andy Burnham to unlock closer ties with the EU, or has the reset hit another roadblock?

World.title: King Charles: Pace of AI is ‘deeply concerning’
World.content:
He will say that “those in our world who value our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny.”

And he will warn that the “decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations,” calling on attendees “not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.”

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar are set to attend. Scale AI CEO Francis deSouza and senior figures from Anthropic and Cohere are on the invite list.

U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the Vatican, are also expected to attend, alongside other “thought leaders.”

The Palace said Charles will invite guests to consider “how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart,” and “build international cooperation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind — and the future of mankind protected.”

The event has been organized by the King’s Trust, the King's Foundation and the Sustainable Markets Initiative, and will also explore whether a “shared set of principles” can be developed to help guide the future application of AI “not merely as a driver of capability and efficiency, but as a tool that upholds human dignity and contributes to the flourishing of both people and the planet.”

World.title: Gran Canaria: how an Atlantic island is emphasising its year-round appeal
World.content:
‘Partner Content’ is used to describe brand content that is paid for and controlled by the advertiser rather than the Euronews editorial team. This content is produced by commercial departments and does not involve Euronews editorial staff or news journalists. The funding partner has control of the topics, content and final approval in collaboration with Euronews’ commercial production department.

Few European islands pack in so much variety. Gran Canaria brings together sand dunes, volcanic highlands, a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, celebrated local food and a capital city with genuine urban energy, all of it across an island with 236 kilometres of coastline.

 

As European tourism looks beyond the traditional summer peak, Gran Canaria offers a useful test case: an island that’s spreading its appeal across the entire calendar and the endless reasons for visiting it.

A compact island with an unusually broad reach

Gran Canaria is often described as a “continent in miniature”, and the geography backs up the claim.

A short drive inland leads to pine forests, deep ravines and small mountain villages that boast traditional architecture and little whitewashed houses. A morning on the beach can give way to a mountain trail in the afternoon and dinner in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria that evening, without changing hotels.

That reach is matched by how easy the island is to get to.

Gran Canaria Airport operates around the clock, and according to Turismo de Gran Canaria's year-end figures, it handled 15.82 million passengers and 142,884 flight operations in 2025, with direct connections to more than 160 airports across 30 countries served by over 60 airlines.

Then there is the climate

The island has an annual average temperature of around 24°C, with mild winters and summers moderated by the trade winds and its position in the Atlantic, conditions locals sometimes describe as a fair-weather gym.

Hikers use a wide network of trails through the island's ravines and highlands, cyclists and runners train year-round, and golfers play courses that include Spain's oldest golf club, founded in 1891.

Those same trade winds help create conditions for surfing, windsurfing, kitesurfing and diving at different points around the island throughout the year.

© Turismo Gran Canaria

Sustainability you can see on the ground

Sustainability here is tied to specific places, communities and practices rather than a slogan.

Around 43% of Gran Canaria falls within its Biosphere Reserve, part of UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme and designated in 2005. It encompasses rural communities where farming, cheese-making and transhumant grazing remain part of daily life.

The island boasts a Biosphere Destination certification, which ties tourism development to the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.

The mountains are also home to the Risco Caído and Sacred Mountains of Gran Canaria Cultural Landscape, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In July 2019, UNESCO added this cultural landscape to its World Heritage List, thus giving recognition to a region that is home to numerous troglodyte settlements, granaries, cisterns and sacred sites linked to a pre-Hispanic culture that evolved in isolation for centuries. In the main cave at Risco Caído, an opening in the cave ceiling allows sun and moonlight to enter at certain times of the year, casting a beam that illuminates the interior in a unique way. That relationship between landscape and sky continues today.

Gran Canaria's night skies have earned international recognition as a Starlight Tourist Destination, a designation it first received in 2018 and renewed in February 2026, extending it through to 2029. Ancient islanders looked to those very same skies to track the seasons; today, efforts to preserve them support both environmental protection and a growing interest in astrotourism, with a great number of specially designated viewpoints in privileged star-gazing spots around the island.

© Turismo Gran Canaria

Flavours, scenery and local life

The coast still matters, of course. Gran Canaria's 236 kilometres of coastline hold more than 60 kilometres of beaches, from the Dunes of Maspalomas to Las Canteras, alongside quieter coves and natural rock pools around the island's edges.

Inland, the island's food culture tells a parallel story.

Gran Canaria is currently home to five Michelin-starred restaurants, while a certified Wine Route links more than 50 local businesses across the island, among them wineries, restaurants, wine bars, estates and cheesemakers.

Local producers champion Flor de Guía, a protected, traditional cheese exclusively curdled with thistle flower, alongside gofio, a traditional food ingredient made from roasted and ground maize, tropical fruit, sea salt and Atlantic seafood, while the Agaete valley's coffee plantations, among the few in Europe, add a further point of difference.

That same emphasis on authenticity is reflected in the Gran Canaria Km.0 Fair, a travelling initiative supported by Gran Canaria Tourism, that promotes agri-food products grown or produced on the island. Its various editions tour towns across Gran Canaria, bringing producers and consumers together and showcasing locally sourced foods such as cheeses, honeys, wines, fruit and vegetables, among others. The initiative encourages responsible consumption, supports the local economy and helps to sustain activities closely linked to the conservation of the landscape and the rural environment.

Las Palmas de Gran Canaria adds a cosmopolitan dimension to the island. Its historic quarters of Vegueta and Triana hold landmarks such as the Casa de Colón and the Museo Canario, alongside historic architecture shaped by centuries of transatlantic trade, while Las Canteras beach runs alongside the city's shops, bars and restaurants, bringing the Atlantic into the heart of the capital.

© Turismo Gran Canaria

What Gran Canaria’s example tells us about island tourism today

What Gran Canaria is really demonstrating is how far depth and diversity can carry a destination: a compact, well-connected island building its appeal on the sheer number of reasons it gives people to visit it.

For European tourism, increasingly focused on extending the season and diversifying the visitor experience, that makes Gran Canaria a destination worth watching.

World.title: Revolut hack: criminals steal data of 700 European clients, demand $3m ransom
World.content:
The public prosecutor's office in Reggio Calabria has opened an investigation into a case involving the banking services company Revolut, founded in London, which is now reportedly being blackmailed.

 

A group of hackers requested sensitive data from the bank using a compromised institutional email account belonging to the Reggio Calabria prefecture.

The digital bank has confirmed that data belonging to around 680 European customers has been affected, but that their funds have not been touched.

According to the Financial Times, which contacted the cybercriminals via Telegram, the group calls itself "iamnotavillain" and posted on its website on Wednesday afternoon a ransom demand for 3 million dollars, equivalent to 2.61 million euros.

If they do not receive the money within 24 hours, the hackers are threatening to sell the sensitive data to other criminal organisations.

The National Anti-Mafia and Counter-Terrorism Directorate is also working on the case, as it concerns a government body. The cybercrime division of the police says it was a highly sophisticated operation, but several points still need to be clarified.

An unusual ransom demand

The group posted the ransom demand on its site on the dark web. The Financial Times (source in Italian) notes that making such a demand public is unusual; typically, ransom and extortion attempts are made privately at first and only made public if the targets refuse to pay.

In this case, however, the British newspaper received a message demanding that Revolut transfer "6,000 XMR / 3,000,000 $… otherwise all the data will be sold and you will have blood on your hands".

XMR is the ticker symbol for the cryptocurrency Monero, often used in illegal contexts because it is difficult to trace.

The criminal group also told the newspaper that this was the first time it had used its site for a ransom demand and that it had not yet contacted the bank to open negotiations.

After making the ransom demand public, the hackers sent the Financial Times a 60-second screen recording showing an unidentified user scrolling through a collection of documents, possibly belonging to Revolut.

The information contained in the documents taken from Revolut is said to include passport details, driving licence data, other identity documents and photographs. The hackers claim to hold a total of 147 gigabytes of data.

How far the investigation has progressed

Prosecutors are considering the offence of intrusion into an IT system of public interest. An initial report from the cybercrime police indicates that the operation, which lasted for months, was highly sophisticated, and it is still not certain whether a computer at the Reggio Calabria prefecture or at Italy's Interior Ministry was compromised.

Experts are also trying to establish whether the institutional email account from which the requests originated was infiltrated or cloned.

Alongside the national Anti-Mafia and Counter-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office, the Italian data protection authority has also stepped in, immediately launching checks for possible security breaches at Italian banks and urging data-protection officers to carry out a "prompt review" and, if any vulnerabilities are found, to notify the authority immediately.

The Italian privacy watchdog has also contacted its counterpart in Lithuania, where Revolut's registered office is located, starting an exchange of information to strengthen efforts to counter the threat.

The investigation will determine how the offence was carried out and whether other public bodies were also affected.

World.title: Moeve starts building Europe's largest green hydrogen project in Huelva
World.content:
Moeve has started building, in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva, the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, a project the company describes as the largest of its kind in Europe and which aims to put Spain at the centre of the development of this new energy industry.

 

The first phase, called 'Onuba', will initially have 300 MW of electrolysis capacity, with the option of adding a further 105 MW, and represents a combined investment of more than 1 billion euros, including the associated infrastructure and a photovoltaic plant for self-consumption.

During the development, construction and commissioning phases, Moeve estimates that the project will create more than 8,000 direct jobs, as well as indirect and induced employment across the entire value chain, and will support the activity of more than 400 small and medium-sized enterprises and local self-employed workers.

"Once again, we are turning ambition into a tangible reality," said Moeve's chief executive, Maarten Wetselaar, quoted in a statement. "Today we are turning the page on pilot green hydrogen projects and entering the chapter of large-scale construction."

Speaking to 'Euronews', Wetselaar argued that 'Onuba' can help strengthen Spain's role in the European energy transition and reduce dependence on foreign supplies. "We need European energy that is decarbonised and produced by us, and that is exactly what this project delivers," he explained.

Spain has abundant solar energy, very good wind resources and space to build large renewable parks Maarten Wetselaar Moeve's chief executive

The company expects the facility to produce around 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen a year, avoiding some 250,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually. The hydrogen will be used to support more sustainable production of fuels for road, air and maritime transport, as well as helping to decarbonise other industries.

The start of construction was marked on Thursday in Palos de la Frontera at a ceremony that brought together representatives of the Spanish government, the European Commission, the Andalusian regional government and the town councils of Palos de la Frontera and Huelva, as well as executives from the companies involved in the project.

Those attending included the Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, the president of the regional government of Andalusia, Juanma Moreno, the Third Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for the Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, and the European Commission's Executive Vice-President for a Clean, Fair and Competitive Transition, Teresa Ribera.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez at Moeve's Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley plant in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva. Moeve

Spain at the centre of production

For Moeve, the conditions in Spain, and especially in Andalusia, offer an advantage for the development of green hydrogen. The company highlights the availability of solar and wind energy, the land needed for large renewable facilities and conditions that make it possible to generate renewable electricity at competitive cost.

"Spain has abundant solar energy, very good wind energy and space to build large renewable parks," Wetselaar said. In his view, since renewable electricity accounts for a large share of the cost of producing green hydrogen, the availability of renewable resources could turn the country into one of Europe's leading producers.

The 'Onuba' project is led by Moeve, which controls 51% of the initiative. Hy24 and Cofides jointly hold 29%, while Enagás Renovable and Alter Enersun control the remaining 20%.

The project has been recognised by the European Union as a Project of Common Interest and has received 304 million euros in funding from the Spanish government through the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, financed by the European Union via NextGenerationEU.

Rendering of Moeve's Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley plant in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva. Moeve

A 2 GW project

'Onuba' is the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve plans to develop to reach a total electrolysis capacity of 2 GW at its energy parks in Palos de la Frontera and San Roque, in the province of Cádiz.

The company also intends to link production in Huelva with other European industrial hubs through pipeline and maritime transport solutions. "We want to scale up this plant and connect Huelva with other industrial centres in Europe," Wetselaar explained.

The development of hydrogen is part of a broader transformation of Moeve's facilities in Andalusia. The company plans to invest a total of 2.4 billion euros in energy transition projects in the region, including 'Onuba' and a second-generation biofuels plant that will produce sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel.

For Wetselaar, the roll-out of these projects could have effects that go beyond energy production. "If Spain scales up, we are talking about thousands of jobs, a significant impact on GDP and, of course, political clout," he said. In his view, the ability to produce and export renewable energy could reshape Spain's energy relationship with the rest of Europe.

World.title: Gaza's bicycle couriers refuse to stop despite danger and pittance pay
World.content:
Gaza delivery workers pedalling through rubble on bicycles can spend 40 of their 50-shekel (€12) daily earnings fixing a single puncture.

 

Fuel shortages, transport disruption and the destruction of Gaza's road network have made bicycles — known colloquially as "baskleet" — the primary means of delivery across the Strip.

Workers who spoke to Euronews described a job that keeps them under relentless pressure: the physical strain of cycling through rubble, the cost of constant repairs, and the danger of passing daily through areas still under bombardment.

Tareq Abu Zekri, owner of Barq delivery company, with one of his workers in the Maghazi neighbourhood, central Gaza Strip Euronews

In the Maghazi area in central Gaza, Mohammed Abu Amra works for the delivery company Barq.

Trips he used to complete by motorbike in under 10 minutes now take him 30 or more by bicycle, with heat, rain, road conditions, and the distances involved making it much more challenging.

Tareq Abu Zekri launched Barq during the second ceasefire in January 2025, then expanded by hiring workers who used their own bicycles.

When he advertised for riders, 109 applications arrived within a day and a half, among them university graduates with few other options in what remains of the Strip's labour market.

The company now has more than 50 employees operating across three branches in Gaza City, central Gaza and Khan Younis.

Orders are transferred between areas by whatever means are available before couriers complete local deliveries, covering shop orders as well as goods sold from tents and homes.

Bicycle delivery predates the 2023 Israel-Hamas war: a pilot scheme in Rafah began in March 2021, and since October 2023, bicycles have become standard as fuel has run short and vehicles have been destroyed.

Repairs that cost more than a day's work

Abbas Al-Souri estimates his daily earnings at between 50 and 60 shekels (€12 to €14), depending on how many orders he completes.

A puncture repair costs between 30 and 40 shekels (€7 to €10). A worker who earns 50 shekels and pays 40 to fix a tyre is left with 10 shekels — roughly €2.

Larger repairs cost more. Abu Zekri estimates that fixing wheels, hubs and pedals runs between 200 and 500 shekels (€48 to €120), depending on what needs replacing.

Spare parts are unreliable. When a bicycle breaks down, workers strip components from bikes too damaged to ride and use them to keep others moving.

"From broken bikes to other bikes — it's patchwork on top of patchwork," Al-Souri said.

Bicycles used for deliveries in the Gaza Strip, Maghazi area, central Gaza Strip Euronews

A joint assessment published in April 2026 by the World Bank, European Union and United Nations found that around 74% of Gaza's road network — approximately 4,500 kilometres — had been classified as destroyed, with a further 13% partially damaged.

The assessment put total damage to the transport sector at approximately $3.21 billion (€2.97 billion) and losses at around $1.18 billion (€1.09 billion), covering roads, bridges, vehicles and transport facilities. The figures cover damage recorded up to October 2025, calculated primarily from satellite imagery.

Barq attempted to introduce electric bicycles to reduce the strain on workers. The experiment stalled when charging costs proved prohibitive: powering an electric bike costs around 30 shekels (€7) — roughly half a day's earnings.

Danger beyond breakdowns

On 29 August, delivery worker Raed Adel Mohammed Alyan was killed alongside Abdel Fattah Abu Al-Eesh when a strike hit an electric bike in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of south-west Gaza City, according to local reports citing medical and local sources. Three others were wounded, one critically.

Alyan worked for the Hamama delivery company and was on a delivery run at the time, according to the company's director Jamil Al-Yazji.

Between 40 and 50 bicycle couriers at Hamama have been killed in the Israel-Hamas war, yet around 400 continue to move packages through damaged streets and active bombardment, according to Al-Yazji.

Shelves holding parcels waiting to be delivered to their owners via Barq delivery company, Maghazi, central Gaza Strip Euronews

Abu Zekri said some of his workers were wounded in a strike in Khan Younis and others narrowly escaped shelling near them in the Al-Jalaa area of Gaza City.

Despite the losses, both companies continue taking on workers. For Abu Zekri, the project is partly about providing income when other options have gone. What workers need to keep going, he said, is straightforward: passable roads, repairable bikes and available parts.

"Let us bring in pedals, half-frames, tyres, patches for the bikes," he said.

World.title: "Minotaur" by Andrey Zvyagintsev to represent France at Oscars
World.content:
A Russian-language film competing for the Oscars under French colours: the drama "Minotaur", directed by dissident film-maker Andrey Zvyagintsev, has been selected to compete in the best international feature category.

 

The choice was made by a professional jury chaired by film historian Charles Tesson, "at the end of an independent process, overseen by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences", said (source in French) the National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image (CNC).

Winner of the Grand Prix at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, the film was produced by French companies MK Productions and CG Cinéma, with German and Latvian involvement.

"In a competition that promises to be of a very high standard, this choice is a reminder of France's unique role in major global co-productions", said CNC president Gaëtan Bruel.

The feature, loosely adapted from Claude Chabrol's 1969 film "La femme infidèle", charts the collapse of a couple against the backdrop of the mobilisation decreed by Vladimir Putin in September 2022, seven months after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

As the gulf widens with his wife, who prefers a young photographer, Gleb, the head of a company, has to deliver some of his employees to the Russian army in order to meet the "quotas" imposed in the regions and to spare the Kremlin from having to mobilise Muscovites.

As so often in his work, Zvyagintsev draws on myth. Like Aegeus, king of Athens, forced to send seven young boys and seven young girls to the Minotaur imprisoned in his labyrinth, Gleb is prepared to accept any compromise to keep his position.

A good choice for the Oscars?

Asked by Euronews about "Minotaur"'s chances, essayist Jean-Philippe Domecq, a member of the editorial team of the journal "Positif", published by the Institut Lumière, hails a "subtle and judicious" choice.

He says he was "deeply and lastingly impressed" by Zvyagintsev's earlier work, notably "Leviathan". "And here, the move to revisit 'La femme infidèle', multiplying its ambiguity through the context of conscription, creates an immense grey area, the film's dominant colour."

According to the critic, the film is compelling "because it combines French involvement, through its producers, with an aesthetic and a plot that commit to nuance, as does art that does not lecture."

The film's reception has nonetheless not been free of criticism.

When he received the 2026 Grand Prix in Cannes, the director, now in exile in France, issued a direct appeal to Vladimir Putin to "stop the carnage", without uttering the word Ukraine or explicitly mentioning Russia's responsibility for this war of aggression.

"There is someone else I would like to address in person today," the film-maker said in Russian. "Millions of people on both sides of the line of contact dream of only one thing: that the massacres will finally stop. And the only person who can put an end to this bloodshed is the president of the Russian Federation. The whole world is waiting for this."

His speech was broadly welcomed in the West, but drew criticism in Ukraine and among anti-war Russian exiles.

"Minotaur" will be released in French cinemas on 14 October, distributed by Les Films du Losange. International sales are handled by MK2 Films and the film will be released in the United States by Mubi.

The 99th Academy Awards ceremony will take place on 14 March 2027 in Los Angeles.

World.title: Canada's Carney welcomes associate status idea in EU speech
World.content:
Mark Carney wants to strengthen Canada's ties to the European Union amid a growing rift with the US under Donald Trump. The US president has threatened to halt trade with Europe if it makes Canada an associate EU member.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, in a speech that focused on Canada's and the European Union's shared security and economic interests.

In an address in which Carney spoke in English, French and German, the Canadian prime minister lauded European culture and values of democracy, freedom and human rights, which he said Canada shares.

"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," the Canadian leader told the chamber, to applause.

Europe and Canada are 'stronger together', Carney tells EU Parliament

"We hold common values for which we have always fought and in whose defense we must always remain vigilant," he said.

Carney also said his country "welcomes" the "ambition" of the EU's proposal of an "associated membership".

"Europe and Canada are each strong," he said. But he added that "Europe and Canada are even stronger together."

"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners,” he said. "We do not seek power to dominate others."

"The ​objective is not ⁠self-sufficiency, ​it's ​collective resilience", Carney ​said.

His speech to European lawmakers comes as the EU and Canada look to strengthen their ties amid a growing rift between Canada and its southern neighbor and main trading partner, the US.

Ties between Canada and the US have hit a historic low in recent months, with the North American neighbors locked in an escalating trade war since Carney and US President Donald Trump failed to agree on a deal this summer.

EU defends Canada alliance plan after Trump tariffs threat

On Wednesday, the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was willing to make Canada its first-ever "associate member," days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc, a position that does not currently exist.

During her State of the EU address, von der Leyen said the bloc needed to adapt to an "openly hostile world" marked by aggressive power politics and "frayed relationships," the latter a clear nod to the turbulent ties between Brussels and Washington since Trump returned to the White House.

Prior to his visit this week, Carney had confirmed that he wanted to establish a "unique alliance" between Canada and the EU.

"We share the same values, we have the same priorities and ​we have very complementary strengths," the prime minister said.

Trump on Wednesday slammed the EU's plans to make Canada an associate member.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina. The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."

Carney: Canada to have talks with EU on 'unique alliance' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How did the US-Canada relationship come to this?

Ties between Canada and the US have plummeted since Trump began his second term in January 2025. He has targeted Canada with tariffs and suggested that the US could annex Canada as its 51st state.

Trump has also referred to Carney, as well as his predecessor as prime minister, Justin Trudeau, as the "governor" of Canada.

The growing rift has also seen Trump sign an executive order renaming Lake Ontario, a Great Lake between the US and Canada, to "Lake America."
