World.title: Budapest-Belgrade railway passenger services within sight, says minister
World.content:
Passenger services on the Budapest-Belgrade railway line could be launched in the near future, according to Hungary’s Minister for Transport and Investment, Dávid Vitézy.

Budapest-Belgrade line soon to become fully operational

In a Facebook post on Tuesday, Vitézy said the project had reached an important stage following months of testing and preparations involving the Hungarian and Chinese construction companies, the investment joint venture, MÁV and railway authorities.

A full-load test is scheduled for 3 and 4 October, when trains will operate without passengers for several hours at speeds of up to 160 kilometres per hour, following the daytime peak-hour timetable. The final decision on the launch of scheduled passenger services will only be made after the tests have been completed and their results evaluated.

Safety checks continue

According to Vitézy, stringent safety checks have been carried out on the Budapest-Belgrade line since the summer. Minor problems and faults have emerged, but most have already been corrected, while work on some issues remains ongoing.

Tuesday’s meeting brought together representatives of MÁV, the Hungarian and Chinese construction companies, MÁV Pályaműködtető, independent experts and the railway authority. Vitézy said the parties confirmed that no safety-critical fault had been identified in the train control system, including during the most thorough testing so far.

He nevertheless stressed that passengers would only be allowed to use the new line once all safety checks had produced positive results and these had been confirmed by the relevant authorities and independent experts. “The launch of passenger services is now within sight,” Vitézy wrote, while stressing that safety requirements would not be compromised.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

Warning to residents

The October tests of the Budapest-Belgrade line will simulate a high level of traffic, with trains running for several hours according to the daytime peak timetable. Vitézy also warned residents living along railway line 150 that passenger facilities along the route will still be construction sites during the tests. Only authorised testing personnel and staff will be allowed to enter these areas.

He urged the public to exercise particular caution at railway level crossings as the number of trains using the line increases in October. Residents were asked to cross the railway only at designated crossings, obeying signals and following the applicable safety rules.

In case you missed it: Volánbusz scandal – what we know about why one of Hungary’s wealthiest was detained

Launch date not yet confirmed

The October full-load test represents another important stage before passenger operations can begin, but it does not guarantee that services will start immediately afterwards. The final decision will depend on the test results and their assessment by the relevant authorities and independent experts.

Vitézy’s announcement indicates that the Budapest-Belgrade railway is moving closer to passenger operation, but the exact launch date can only be decided after the successful completion of the remaining safety checks.

Read also: Travel across Hungary for less than EUR 3 during European Mobility Week’s Car-Free Day

World.title: Turkey Blocks Social Media Accounts, Arrests 80, as LGBT Crackdown Expands
World.content:
An Istanbul court on Wednesday ordered access blocks on 419 social media accounts that it claimed had “shared obscene content”, as Turkish authorities continued a broad crackdown against LGBTQ+ groups in the name of “protecting the family”.

Turkey’s state-led Anadolu Agency reported that, under the coordination of the Cyber ​​Crimes Investigation Bureau, the Istanbul Police had conducted a study aimed at protecting families, children and young people from all forms of abuse.

“Within this scope, access was blocked to 419 social media accounts and links deemed to contain obscene content that were found to have been shared on social media platforms,” it wrote.

The blocked accounts include those of journalists, activists, media houses and women’s civil society groups. It is not clear which content was deemed obscene.

“If you think that banning journalists and shutting down accounts will solve the problems, unfortunately you’re very mistaken,” commented Sirin Payzin, a veteran journalist whose account was blocked on Wednesday. X immediately made his account invisible from Turkey. She has 1.8 million followers on X.

Raids, arrests and internet restrictions have targeted these groups as well as independent journalists and human rights organisations reporting on the police operation.

On Wednesday night and Thursday morning, courts ordered at least 80 formal arrests of LGBTQ+ rights activists, their supporters and journalists. However, 106 people detained earlier in a protest against the operation in Istanbul were released.

LGBTQ+ and human rights groups argue that the operations target freedom of expression, freedom of association and human rights advocacy. The authorities insist the investigations are being conducted within the framework of criminal law.

Gurkan Ozturan, Monitoring Officer at the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom, told BIRN that the operations instigated by the conservative Islamist government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan “show that the authorities are criminalising both identity and information”.

World.title: Ownership Changes Unsettle Serbia’s Critical Media Ahead of Elections
World.content:
Branislav Sovljanski said he had yet to receive a call from his news channel’s new owners telling him to pull this or that story, invite or deinvite a certain guest. He expressed hope it would remain that way.

Three months after a change of ownership at Adria News Network, ANN, which owns the Serbian N1 news channel where Sovljanski is director of news, journalists are holding their breath.

Broadcasters N1 and Nova S, the news website Nova.rs, daily newspaper Danas and weekly Radar have long been a collective thorn in the side of Serbia’s government, alone in criticising the country’s democratic backsliding under President Aleksandar Vucic and the ruling Progressive Party, SNS, since they first came to power in 2012.

On May 29, when it was announced that United Group would sell Adria News S.à r.l - the Luxembourg–based company under which Adria News Network operates – to Alpac Capital, it sent shockwaves through part of Serbian society, amid fevered speculation that Vucic would call elections for the autumn. He subsequently did, setting the date for October 25.

Alpac Capital, a Portuguese investment fund, previously bought pan-European broadcaster Euronews in 2022; subsequent reporting by Le Monde and Hungarian investigative media Direkt36, revealed that the acquisition was heavily financed by Hungarian state capital and companies close to the powerful propaganda apparatus of then Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

In Serbia, there are already signs of a shift.

World.title: North Macedonia ‘Putting Youth at Risk’ by Scrapping Sex Education Rollout
World.content:
The abandonment of sex education lessons in schools in North Macedonia will put young people at greater risk of sexual- and gender-based violence, civil society campaigner Velimir Saveski told BIRN after the conservative government cancelled the rollout of optional classes to all ninth graders.

Sex education was introduced in 2021 as an optional topic for ninth graders in four schools in North Macedonia, under a pilot project approved by the then ruling Social Democrats.

It was due to be rolled out as an option for ninth graders in all general secondary schools in the country as of next year, before Education Minister Vesna Janevska announced this month a “deep revision” of the programme.

Janevska comes from the ranks of the conservative VMRO DPMNE party, which came to power in 2024; she insisted her move was based on public disquiet over the programme.

World.title: Bosnia’s Elections Offer New Technologies, But Old Politics
World.content:
The campaign ahead of Bosnia’s October 4 elections started with a bang – literally, as a Serbian army honour guard fired a three-volley salute at the funeral of the Bosnian Serb wartime commander and convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic.

Most Bosnian Serb politicians, ruling and opposition alike, used the occasion of Mladic’s September 7 funeral in Belgrade to display their nationalist sentiments and glorify the man convicted by a UN tribunal of war crimes and genocide during Bosnia’s 1992-5 war.

Bosniak and Bosnian Croat politicians responded in kind, pledging to protect their ethnic kin and reiterating accusations that Serbs were a “genocidal people”, even though only individuals, not entire ethnic groups, can be held responsible for that.

World.title: Kosovo Slams ‘Unjust’ Conviction of Hashim Thaci; Serbian Minister Applauds
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Kosovo’s Prime Minister Albin Kurti condemned the guilty verdict handed down to four wartime leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army in The Hague on Wednesday as “an unacceptable injustice”.

In a video on Instagram, Kurti declared that the war crimes ruling “must undoubtedly be overturned and rectified on appeal”.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci, former parliament speakers Kadri Veseli and Jakup Krasniqi and former MP Rexhep Selimi – all senior Kosovo Liberation Army officers during the 1998-99 conflict – were convicted of war crimes. Their lawyers say they will challenge the judgment.

Kurti’s statement was echoed by other senior Kosovo politicians, including Acting President, Albulena Haxhiu, who called the verdict handed down by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers “shocking”.

The opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK – which has been led by both Hashim Thaci and Kadri Veseli – also condemned the verdict, calling it “a great injustice, because it is based on claims and materials that we consider fabricated and nurtured over the years by the state apparatus and Serbian propaganda to criminalise the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army [against Serbian forces]”.

Kosovo’s former Prime Minister Ramush Haradinaj, who was found not guilty of war crimes by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia in 2012, slammed the verdict as “unacceptable and unjust”.

“The KLA carried out a liberation war. The battle for justice should continue. This battle should be won,” Haradinaj said in a Facebook post.

Kosovo Albanians who gathered to hear the verdict livestreamed in Pristina and The Hague were also furious. In Pristina, they rallied in front of the government building and some threw stones, shattering some windows, as well as tearing down some barriers and pushing police officers.

Thousands of Albanians who had travelled to The Hague for the verdict erupted in anger when the convictions were announced. There was a brief clash with Dutch police, who prevented them marching towards the Specialist Chambers.

In neighbouring Albania, President Bajram Begaj expressed “deep sadness” about the verdict. “For Albanians, no one and nothing tarnishes the KLA!” Begaj declared in a Facebook post.

Albania’s Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has repeatedly criticised the trial as unjust, posted a graphic on Facebook showing barbed wire over a European map and the one-word message “Marre” (“Shame”).

Head of Milosevic’s old party says verdict confirms KLA were ‘terrorists’

Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder. His co-defendants Krasniqi, Veseli and Selimi were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years in prison respectively.

Serbia’s Interior Minister Ivica Dacic welcomed the guilty verdict, saying it represents a “clear, though long-overdue, confirmation of what Serbia and the Serbian people have been saying loudly for more than a quarter of a century – that the so-called KLA was a criminal and terrorist organisation”.

Dacic is the leader of the Socialist Party of Serbia, the party once headed by Slobodan Milosevic, who led a bloody campaign of ethnic cleansing and repression against Kosovo Albanians in 1998-99.

Dacic added that he thought it was a “direct insult to the victims” that the trial chamber had dismissed other charges against the KLA leaders that accused them of committing crimes against humanity.

During the delivery of the verdict, presiding judge Charles Smith III stressed that the case was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army”, saying that individuals were on trial, not the guerrilla force itself.

Some of Kosovo’s allies echoed this statement. The UK’s Minister for Europe, Lord Wood, said that “the court’s findings concern individuals and should not be used to inflame tensions between communities or across the region”.

Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, wrote on X that the verdict “is about individual accountability and justice for victims and their families from all communities in Kosovo”.

Responding to the verdict, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic told a press conference that it should not be received with “any kind of euphoria”, condemning the fact that the trial chamber had dismissed charges relating to crimes against humanity.

He compared the differing Western reactions to the verdict convicting the KLA leaders and the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic in Belgrade last week. EU officials have repeatedly condemned the glorification of Mladic at his funeral, which was held with military honours.

Vucic cited statements by Kosovo officials claiming the defendants were innocent liberators, saying: “My question is – imagine if we had said that, about any accused or convicted person? How many resolutions and declarations would have been adopted against our country in various regional, European and international parliaments?”

During the Kosovo war, Vucic was serving as Serbia’s information minister in the government appointed by nationalist strongman Milosevic.

Meanwhile in neighbouring Croatia, which has a strained relationship with its wartime foe Serbia, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that the verdict “does not alter the historical context of the war in Kosovo, nor the fact that Kosovo and its population were victims of repression and grave crimes committed by the Milosevic regime”.

World.title: Turkey Stages Wide-Ranging LGBT Crackdown for ‘Family Safety’
World.content:
Chanting “Long live the struggle for freedom!”, supporters of recently detained LGBTQ+ campaigners gathered outside Istanbul’s Caglayan courthouse on Tuesday, demanding their release.

Some reportedly unfurled a banner with the slogan: “Being LGBTQ is not a crime.”

The response was harsh: police moved in to detain more than 100 protesters, including activists and journalists.

The protests comes after Turkish authorities launched one of the country’s toughest ever clampdowns on LGBTQ+ groups.

Police have raided organisations, homes and entertainment venues. Activists have been detained and websites and social media accounts blocked.

World.title: North Macedonia Opposition Urges Deeper Probe into Independence Day Spending
World.content:
Spanish tenor José Carreras performs at an independence event in Skopje in September 2026. Photo: EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI.

North Macedonia’s main opposition Social Democratic Union, SDSM, said on Wednesday that the State Anti-Corruption Commission’s decision to examine a possible conflict of interest over independence celebrations involving the composer and producer Nikolche Micevski was insufficient.

It instead called on the Public Prosecutor’s Office to investigate the whole financing and organisation of more than month-long celebrations marking the anniversary of September 8’s Independence Day.

“The opening of a case by the Anti-Corruption Commission for a possible conflict of interest involving one person is not an investigation into the 5.5 million euros,” the SDSM said, referencing the disclosed total cost of events.

Micevski was among three outside experts involved in evaluating the programme submitted by Stardust, the company selected to organise the celebrations. He later appeared in the programme himself as a performer and was involved in the musical arrangements for a concert featuring Spanish tenor Jose Carreras.

The state anti-corruption body has stressed that its case is limited to the possible conflict of interest and does not amount to an investigation into the entire 5.5 million euros expenditure. It said it was, nevertheless, monitoring other aspects of the organisation of the celebrations.

The SDSM said prosecutors should secure the full documentation concerning the spending and establish who authorised the use of the money, how payments were made and whether all procedures were followed.

It specifically questioned the use of some 4.9 million euros from the State Lottery’s undistributed profits to finance the celebrations. It asked whether the lottery’s shareholders’ assembly had approved the allocation and which institution had authorised the expenditure.

The SDSM also called for scrutiny of the contract with Stardust, the payments made to the company, the reported involvement of Avalon production, which is owned by Stardust, and the arrangements for the appearance of French DJ and producer David Guetta at the main September 8 concert in the capital, Skopje.

The government has said the celebrations, comprising 16 events, cost around 5.5 million euros, 4.9 million euros of which came from the State Lottery, which it completely owns. The rest was provided by companies described by the government as socially responsible.

It insists no money was taken directly from the state budget to finance the celebrations.

The government initially provided limited information about the overall cost of the celebrations – until BIRN reported that the state-owned lottery had played a key role in managing events.

The SDSM said questions raised by the Anti-Corruption Commission over Micevski’s role should not divert attention from the broader issue of how millions of euros were allocated and spent.

The anti-corruption body, meanwhile, has said other competent institutions should take action if they establish grounds for criminal or other legal proceedings.

Faced with prolonged public scrutiny, on Sunday Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski again defended the celebrations, dismissing the opposition’s criticism as “political theatre” and saying the events were on a world-class level that promoted North Macedonia internationally.

World.title: Hague Court Convicts Kosovo Liberation Army Leaders of War Crimes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Rexhep Selimi, Hashim Thaci, Jakup Krasniqi, and Kadri Veseli in court on September 16, 2026. Photo: Screenshot/Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

Kosovo’s former head of state Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague on Wednesday for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed from April 1998 to June 1999 during the Kosovo war.

“In the names of the people of Kosovo, the panel finds you, Hashim Thaci, guilty of arbitrary arrest and detention as a war crime against at least 385 persons; cruel treatment against at least 49; torture as a war crimes against at least 303 persons; murder as a war crimes committed against 96 persons,” presiding judge Charles Smith III announced.

Thaci’s co-defendants Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years in prison respectively. All four men were found guilty of bearing responsibility for the crimes while they were senior officials of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA during the war with Serbian forces.

The four men were found not guilty of the crimes against humanity of persecution, imprisonment, other inhumane acts, torture, murder and enforced disappearances because the crimes were committed after the end of the Kosovo war.

Thaci, along with former parliament speakers Veseli and Krasniqi, and former MP Selimi, had all pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Thousands of supporters of the defendants, who had travelled to The Hague for the verdict and listened to the livestream in a public park, erupted in anger when the convictions were announced. There was a brief clash with Dutch police, who prevented them marching towards the court.

The Specialist Chambers found that Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi were part of a joint criminal enterprise that aimed to exert control by targeting perceived opponents of the KLA.

These opponents included people associated with other political or military groups that had not pledged their loyalty to KLA – in particular the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK party – as well as individuals alleged to be associated with the Serbian authorities and members of non-Albanian ethnic groups like Roma people and Serbs.

Hundreds were imprisoned and some killed, according to the verdict. “Some detainees died because of severe beatings from their KLA captors,” judge Smith said.

During the trial, the defence insisted that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have genuine control over lower-ranking fighters. However, judge Smith said the court found that the KLA’s political directorate, which Thaci led, had huge authority over the guerrilla force.

The presiding judge said that the accused worked together with others to set up detention facilities and establish a military police force, intelligence service and special units, and tasked them with carrying out their “criminal plan” to establish their authority in Kosovo. They also “secured impunity for the perpetrators of these crimes as a matter of policy”, the judge added.

The time that the defendants have spent in detention since November 2020 will be counted against their sentences. They have the right to appeal.

This is the highest-level case to be heard at the so-called Kosovo Special Court and has been marred by delays and controversy, as well as a series of protests staged by supporters of the defendants in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague.

Many ethnic Albanians consider the court biased against the KLA’s war against repression by the Serbian authorities.

Delivering the verdict, judge Smith insisted that the case was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army”.

“This case is not concerned with crimes of Serbian army and paramilitaries that undoubtedly committed against the Albanians in Kosovo. This case is not concerned with any claims of self-defence. Instead this case is exclusively concerned if the crimes alleged in the indictment were committed,” he said.

The lengthy trial was marred by accusations of witness-tampering. As a result, Thaci faces judgment in another case for obstruction of justice. Judge Smith lamented that the trial had taken place in “climate of witness intimidation”, saying that some witnesses lied or changed their previous accounts in court, and that some may have been afraid due to concerns for their safety or out of loyalty.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. The court is part of Kosovo’s justice system, but based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters, who are seen by many in the country as heroic liberators from Serbian oppression.

World.title: Dubrovnik Mayor Claims “Most People Don’t Even Know Where Istria is”
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković has caused a stir and claimed that “most people don’t even know where Istria is”, adding that “Dubrovnik is the only tourism champion in Croatia”.

Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković assessed the tourist season as excellent at a session of the City Council and claimed that Dubrovnik is “the only champion of tourism in Croatia.” Index reports that in his review of the results, which according to him exceed expectations, he directed criticism at the “Istrian lobby,” reports Dubrovački dnevnik.

“The season has been excellent, and what is ahead of us looks very good. So far it looks above expectations,” Franković said.

He also expressed satisfaction that the number of visitors in the historic centre is not exceeding critical levels, after which he sent a message to the competition. “We’re the only champion of tourism in Croatia and no one can measure up to us. Istria with its lobby is trying to present itself as successful. People exclusively from Istria, such as Veljko Ostojić, comment on tourism and they push it. We are alone, but we have shown that we are above everyone,” Franković said, concluding with the statement: “Most people don’t even know where Istria is.”

4.7 million people have come to dubrovnik so far in 2026

On Facebook he was answered by the president of IDS and mayor of Poreč, Loris Peršurić. Peršurić replied to Franković that Dubrovnik is one of the symbols of Croatian tourism and that one should be proud of its successes, but he ironised the claim that people do not know where Istria is.

“Just this year 4.7 million people successfully found it, and we’re only in the 9th month because the season with us lasts almost the whole year,” he wrote. He emphasised that Istria’s reputation was not created overnight, but was built over decades by private renters, owners of agritourism facilities, taverns and wineries, olive growers, caterers, hoteliers, craftsmen and farmers. He also pointed out that in tourism it is not only the numbers that matter, but quality, sustainability and the preservation of space for the people who live in it.

Peršurić added that Dubrovnik also has strong state and tourism tools for promotion at its disposal and concluded that one can be proud of one’s own successes without diminishing those of others. “I therefore invite you to personally convince yourself of the qualities of Istria, but hurry with the reservation because these days quite a few people manage to find us,” he said to Franković.

World.title: Russian Ambassador Summoned for Talks in Croatia Following Russia’s Threats
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – The Russian Ambassador has been summoned for talks in Croatia following Russia’s recent threats against various European countries.

Russian Ambassador to Croatia Alexander Nurizade was summoned today for talks at the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs, where the Croatian side expressed concern over security threats from Russia towards European countries, the Russian Embassy in Zagreb announced. Index reports that according to the Russian side, Croatian representatives mentioned incidents in the airspace, territorial waters and on the infrastructure of EU member states, including in Denmark, Lithuania, Romania and Germany. The Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs lists Nurizade on its official website as the current Russian ambassador to Croatia.

the russian ambassador has rejected all accusations

The Russian Embassy states that Nurizade “firmly rejected” the accusations as unfounded. He described them, according to the embassy’s statement, as a “coordinated provocation” aimed at further worsening relations with Russia. He also expressed regret that Croatia, as the Russian side claims, “is pandering to the Kyiv regime and its foreign patrons interested in the continuation of the conflict.” These are the claims of the Russian Embassy. During the talks, Nurizade also repeated the official Russian positions on the causes of the war in Ukraine and accused the West of turning Ukraine into an “anti-Russian project.”

an attempted leipzig drone attack was discussed

Among the cases that the Croatian side, according to the Russian Embassy, cited was the incident in Leipzig. At the beginning of September, the German government officially accused Russia of being behind an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport on 4 August. A drone with explosives was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. Berlin claims that the investigation traces the point to the Russian state, while Moscow rejects responsibility. After that case, the European Union and several member states summoned Russian diplomatic representatives for talks. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas said at the time that the incident had the characteristics of state-sponsored terrorism, while Russia claimed that Germany had not provided evidence for its accusations.

a russian vessel fired signal rockets at a danish aircraft

Tensions rose further this week after an incident out in the Baltic Sea. The Danish military announced that a Russian frigate, during routine surveillance, fired two signal rockets at a Danish military Fennec helicopter. One passed at a short distance from the helicopter. Denmark therefore summoned the Russian ambassador for talks. The Russian side countered with an accusation that Danish military helicopters had performed dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships.

nato had to shoot down a drone over lithuania

In Lithuania a couple of days ago, an Italian fighter jet as part of a NATO mission shot down a drone that had entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus. Lithuanian authorities announced that the drone was carrying explosives. Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said it “most likely” came from Russia, but Lithuanian authorities warned that the investigation into its origin is still ongoing and that a final conclusion has not yet been reached. A similar incident was recorded last week in Romania, where a drone that Romanian and Moldovan authorities linked to Russian attacks on Ukraine entered deep into Romanian airspace before returning towards Moldova.

The Russian ambassador in the talks in Zagreb, according to a statement from his embassy, also spoke about Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. He conveyed that Moscow considers railway junctions, trains and other facilities in Ukraine used for the transport of the army or cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces to be “legitimate military targets.”

In recent days Russia has further intensified attacks on Ukrainian railway infrastructure, including areas near the border with NATO members. Ukrainian authorities claim that civilian trains and infrastructure have also been hit in the process. The summoning of Nurizade for talks comes at a time of heightened warnings from European and NATO officials about incidents involving drones, sabotage and other hybrid threats. The European Commission today also proposed a new mechanism for a coordinated response by EU members to such security incidents. An inquiry was also sent to the Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs about today’s talks with the Russian ambassador. We asked for confirmation of the meeting, the specific reason for his summoning, and clarification of which incidents Croatia cited and whether it plans further diplomatic steps after the talks.

World.title: Croatia to Get a New Road Worth Over €200 Million
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – Croatia is set to get a new road worth over €200 million, and it’s being widely compared to Pelješac Bridge.

The project includes two interchanges, five viaducts, four overpasses and two bridges. Poslovni reports that the Chinese company China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) is building a 16-kilometre expressway that will finally directly connect Požega with the A3 Zagreb – Lipovac motorway. The new road will link Požeški Brestovac with the Godinjak interchange, where it will then connect to the motorway.

This is one of the largest infrastructure projects in Slavonia, which should significantly improve the transport connectivity of Požega-Slavonia County with the rest of Croatia. The route of the expressway runs south of Daranovci, after which it enters the forested area of Babja gora. There, a single-tube tunnel 1,650 metres long will be built, and the route then descends along a natural valley towards Tisovac and Godinjak. The project includes two interchanges, five viaducts, four overpasses and two bridges. The construction deadline is 48 months, meaning the new road should be completed by the end of 2029.

požega will get a faster link towards both zagreb and slavonski brod

The expressway is being built along the route of the existing state road D51, which has so far been the main transport link between Požega and surrounding settlements with the rest of the country. The new road should bring a safer and higher-quality connection to the A3 motorway, and thereby also to Zagreb and Slavonski Brod.

“This expressway represents the largest single project of Croatian Roads after the Pelješac Bridge. This is a big day not only for Croatian road construction, but also for Požega-Slavonia County, because it will be better and more safely connected to the motorway,” said Transport Minister Oleg Butković at the ceremonial introduction of the contractor into the works in Godinjak in November last year. For the residents of Požega-Slavonia County, the project represents the end of long-standing transport isolation. Due to frequent landslides and damage, the D51 does not fully meet modern standards of safety and traffic flow, so the new expressway will take over an important share of the traffic.

the požega interchange on the A3 motorway is also being built

At the beginning of February, a contract was also signed for the construction of the Požega interchange on the A3 motorway. The Požega interchange is part of the integral project for the construction of the expressway, which will connect to the motorway precisely at that point. The investor for that part of the project is Croatian Roads. When the works are completed, after decades of waiting Požega will finally get a direct fast road link with the A3 motorway, which should further improve the transport accessibility of the city and the entire Požega-Slavonia County.

World.title: Saudis Halt Oil Deliveries to Europe. What Does This Mean for Croatia?
World.content:
September the 17th, 2026 – Saudi Arabia has stopped oil deliveries to Europe following a drone incident, but what exactly does this mean for Croatia specifically?

Saudi Arabia has cancelled crude oil deliveries to European refineries after drone attacks damaged a key Saudi oil pipeline leading to the Red Sea. As a result, Europe’s largest buyers are urgently seeking replacement oil. Index/Neven Barkovic reports that hehind the halt in deliveries is the closure of the East-West pipeline, through which the Saudis transport millions of barrels of oil daily to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea in order to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. After the 10 September attack, which Saudi Arabia blames on Iraqi militias, the pipeline was shut down. Since 11 September, not a single tanker carrying oil has left Yanbu for Europe.

The interruption immediately created a major problem in Europe, which, after imposing sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, has relied heavily on Saudi oil. At least three European refineries have been left without their agreed shipments for the end of September, with deliveries postponed as far as November. Polish oil giant Orlen, which covers around 40 percent of its needs with Saudi oil, is now rapidly buying stocks from the North Sea and the United States to keep its refineries in Poland, the Czech Republic and Lithuania running.

The market reacted to this disruption with a rapid rise in prices. While Brent crude futures are trading at around $108 per barrel, on the physical market in Europe the price of the benchmark barrel has reached as high as $122.

croatia has stocks… but they’re getting pricier

What does this mean for Croatia, specifically? There will be no physical shortages of oil at domestic petrol stations. Croatia supplies itself with crude oil by sea via the terminal in Omišalj and the JANAF system, sourcing it from various origins – from Mediterranean and North African to American. The domestic refinery in Rijeka is not directly dependent on the Saudi port of Yanbu in the way that refineries in northern and eastern Europe are.

However, expensive European oil will inevitably affect prices at Croatian pumps. Retail fuel prices in Croatia are calculated on the basis of quotations for petroleum products on the Mediterranean market (CIF Med). When the physical barrel price in Europe jumps above $120, this automatically raises Mediterranean quotations, meaning that in the next calculation cycle the input price of fuel for Croatia will be significantly higher.

can the government do anything?

Whenever fuel prices at the pumps rise significantly, citizens’ first question is – why doesn’t the state lower the levies? In every litre of fuel that drivers put into their tanks in Croatia, state levies – the fixed excise duty and VAT – make up more than a third of the total price. Croatia has a general VAT rate of as much as 25 percent, one of the highest in the entire EU, which is moreover calculated on the total amount after the excise duty has already been included. In other words, the state systematically charges tax on tax. As the price of the raw material on the exchanges rises, the budget automatically collects more and more money from VAT on every litre sold, without ministers having to lift a finger.

Although those in power regularly defend themselves with claims that their hands are tied by European directives on minimum excise duties and that they have already used the room for intervention, the real reason for refusing greater tax relief lies in the habit of filling the state coffers. Excise duties and taxes on energy products bring in hundreds of millions of euros of clean, secure and rapid revenue that the state uses to finance a huge public sector, the growth of the administration and political compromises.

cheap political manoeuvres and more and more money…

Any serious discussion about the state permanently forgoing part of that money is interrupted by the thesis of a “budget hole”, even though that shortfall could easily be made up by rationalising public spending, cutting unproductive costs and reducing the oversized state apparatus. Instead of taking that path, the authorities prefer to protect budget revenues at the expense of citizens’ living standards and the economy’s business operations.

That is why the Croatian Government has for years primarily relied on the cheapest political manoeuvre: pressure on distributors’ commercial margins. But margins make up only a smaller part of the final fuel price, and their administrative cutting pushes small private petrol stations towards the edge of profitability and creates the risk of some sales points closing. By shifting the burden onto traders and customers, the state retains its own lion’s share of every bill, while at the same time serving citizens the story that it is doing everything in its power. Economy Minister Ante Šušnjar justifies the rise in oil prices solely by the crisis around the Strait of Hormuz and global disruptions, claiming that the Government skilfully uses the tools at its disposal and that Croatia, despite the price rise, has the cheapest fuel in the region.

“Security of supply comes into question if exchange trends are not followed. Government decisions are balanced so as not to endanger security of supply, while still keeping petroleum products affordable,” Šušnjar said, repeating that Croatia has already used the EU exception and lowered excise duties below the prescribed European minimum. But the minister thereby conceals that with every new wave of price increases the state collects more and more money per litre through VAT, while in practice almost entirely shifting the burden of the crisis onto the backs of citizens and the cutting of distributors’ margins.

World.title: Autism Centre: 35 Million Euro Zagreb Project Gets Underway After 20+ Years
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – The long awaited Autism Centre is an enormous 35 million euro Zagreb project that is finally getting underway after a long 20+ year wait.

After over 20 years of announcements, the City of Zagreb has finally obtained a building permit for the construction of a new Autism Centre in Oporovec. It will provide modern and adapted conditions for learning, development and professional support for around 200 children, and will bring together programmes that are currently run at multiple locations across Zagreb.

Poslovni reports that the estimated value of the new Autism Centre in Oporovec is around 35 million euros, of which 19.3 million euros will be financed from EU funds through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), while the remaining amount will be secured from the City of Zagreb budget. Once the building permit becomes final, the preparation of project documentation and the public procurement procedure for selecting the contractor will follow. Construction is planned to start in the summer of 2027, with a planned duration of 18 months.

The new school will have 48 classroom departments and educational groups, as well as three preschool education and care groups. Specialised spaces are also planned for music and art therapy, household skills and aquatic therapy with a pool, sports halls and other facilities adapted to the needs of users.

According to the project by the architectural office SODA-ARHITEKTI, the centre will cover more than 9,600 square metres on three floors, with 60 parking spaces, nine of which are designated for people with disabilities. Attention has also been paid to the outdoor landscaping, with a main square featuring a sensory park, fountains and facilities for developing motor skills planned. “This is another of the projects that have been promised in Zagreb for more than twenty years, and now it is finally going into realisation,” said Zagreb Mayor Tomislav Tomašević.

Deputy Mayor Danijela Dolenec stressed that the new school will represent a major step forward in the quality of spatial and programmatic conditions for the education and upbringing of children and young people with autism. The Autism Centre currently cares for around 300 users through preschool programmes, primary education, full-day and half-day stay programmes, and organised housing, she said.

Dolenec added that the City of Zagreb continues to invest in the existing capacities of the Autism Centre. A public procurement for the renovation and arrangement of the sports hall in Ljevakovićeva Street, worth 250,000 euros, was recently launched, and around 750,000 euros has been invested in the renovation of the Centre’s existing facilities in recent years.

By the end of the year, the opening of a new Centre space in Juraj Dalmatinac Street is also planned, where early developmental and psychosocial support services will be provided for 40 children, as well as a stay programme for 30 adults with autism spectrum disorders. The City of Zagreb has also stated that 24 new special classroom departments and educational groups have been established in the new school year, increasing existing capacities by almost a quarter.

The number of special classroom departments has grown from 64 back in 2021 to 126 in 2026, while the network of schools implementing these programmes has been expanded to 55 schools across Zagreb, according to the City of Zagreb press release.

World.title: Zadar Mobile Boat Pharmacy is in the Final for the Best EU Project Award
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – The very commendable Zadar mobile pharmacy on a boat is in the final for the Best EU Project Award.

The Zadar project “Mobile Pharmacy – boat for the islands of Zadar County” has secured a place in the final of this year’s competition for the best EU project in the category Contribution to the Local and Regional Community. Morski reports that this very commendable initiative is primarily aimed at introducing a mobile pharmaceutical service in the island area in order to significantly facilitate residents’ access to medicines and professional advice, especially those in more traffic-isolated places.

The competition is organised by the Croatian Association of Counties, the Office of the European Parliament in Croatia and the portal Župan.hr, under the auspices of the Ministry of Regional Development and EU Funds. In strong competition from almost 50 projects submitted from all over Croatia, the expert jury selected a total of 36 finalists, with the Zadar mobile pharmacy competing among the 18 best in its category.

The winners in the readers’ choice category are decided by the public, and public voting officially ran from the 8th to the 15th of September, 2026.

World.title: Croatia to Get Most Modern Thermal Spa in Historic €42 Million project
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – Croatia is set to get its most modern and largest thermal spa as a historic 42 million euro project finally nears completion.

Works on Wellovar in Veliki Korenovo, the largest construction project in the history of Bjelovar worth €42 million, have entered the final stage. Poslovni reports that the enormous complex with a total of ten pools is already taking on its final appearance, and finishing works and system checks are currently underway before opening. Bjelovar Mayor Dario Hrebak regularly visits the construction site and emphasises that the focus is now on the details and on balancing and calibrating one of the most complex and modern heating, cooling and hot water systems in Croatia.

“Works on the largest thermal spa in Croatia, our Wellovar, are nearing completion. Only minor details remain, but this is one of the most complex and modern heating, cooling and hot water systems in Croatia. We now have to ensure that the entire system is balanced and calibrated. It is hard to say when we will open the doors. Our great wish is that it will be on the 29th of September, on the Bjelovar City Day, but it is very difficult to predict,” said Hrebak. He added that at this moment the exact opening date is not crucial; the most important thing is that the project is completed to a high standard.

“What matters is that everything we see is heading towards its final stage and that the people of Bjelovar will get a standard that 95 percent of other cities in Croatia do not have. Croatia will also get an excellent centre for the development of water sports,” he stressed. In addition to tourist and recreational facilities, Wellovar is also expected to play an important role in the development of sport. According to Hrebak, the facility has been designed to meet the standards for hosting national and international swimming and water polo competitions. “We are truly looking forward to it soon opening its doors and delighting our citizens, as well as all tourists and visitors with its facilities,” Hrebak concluded.

With the completion of this massive €42 million project, Bjelovar is set to gain a major new sports, recreational and tourist complex. Although the official opening date has not yet been confirmed, the city administration’s wish is for Wellovar to welcome its first visitors as early as the 19th of September, on Bjelovar’s City Day.

World.title: Croatia to Make Changes to ENC Usage as of March 1st, 2027
World.content:
September the 16th, 2026 – Croatia will make significant changes to ENC usage as of March the 1st, 2027, and drivers with multiple vehicles need to pay particular attention to what is coming.

The much anticipated new Croatian road toll collection system will use ENC technology, but also automatic licence plate recognition via cameras. Poslovni reports that for years now, ENC has been one of the simplest ways to pay motorway tolls across Croatia. You put the device in your car, drive through the marked lane, and the system automatically handles the payment. However, with the introduction of the new electronic toll collection system, one thing becomes much more important than before: the ENC will also be linked to the vehicle’s registration plate.

From the 1st of March 2027, when the new system starts operating, the vehicle’s registration number, data on the ENC device, and a valid means of payment will have to be registered in the system for the ENC model to be used. The law expressly stipulates that a driver using ENC must pass through the toll point in a vehicle whose registration plates are identical to those linked in the system to the ENC device in the vehicle. This means it will no longer be enough simply to take a working ENC device and put it in any car. Before driving, it will be important that the vehicle being used on the motorway is properly registered in the new system.

this is particularly important if you use one enc for multiple cars

The change is especially significant for those who currently use the same ENC in several cars. Under the current rules of Croatian Motorways, an ENC device for vehicle categories IA, I and II is not tied to a single registration number. It can be used in multiple vehicles of the same category, provided the same device is not used simultaneously in more than one vehicle. The new system introduces a different principle: the registration number becomes an integral part of the data linked to the ENC device. Therefore, drivers who currently simply move the ENC from one car to another will have to make sure that the registration of the vehicle they are using is correctly linked to the device in the Electronic Toll Collection System.

The law itself does not currently stipulate that one ENC can necessarily be linked to only one registration number. The detailed rules on use and changes to data will be regulated by the rules of the new system. However, it is clear that the previous practice of simply transferring the device without checking the registration will no longer be sufficient. The good news for existing users is that current ENC devices will not become unusable. The law obliges motorway operators to include ENC devices purchased before the establishment of the new system into the new ESNC no later than its start.

the new cameras will read license plates

The new toll collection system will use ENC technology as well as automatic licence plate recognition via cameras. For passenger cars and other light vehicles, drivers will be able to choose between the ENC model and a model based solely on the registration number and a registered means of payment. When using ENC, the system will therefore have data on both the device and the vehicle’s registration number. Cameras will record the vehicle’s passage and read the licence plates in order to identify the vehicle and verify payment. For drivers, this brings a new habit: before driving, it will no longer be enough simply to check whether the ENC is in the car and whether there are sufficient funds on the account. They will also have to make sure that the vehicle’s registration number is correctly registered in the system. This is precisely what could be particularly important for those who currently use one ENC in multiple cars.

World.title: Viru Prison inmates learn to do traditional Estonian handicraft
World.content:
Inmates at Viru Prison taught themselves to weave traditional Estonian patterned belts. They have become so skilled that their work is now sold at the Estonian National Museum.

Viru Prison was looking for a way for inmates with restricted movement rights to work in their cells. Weaving traditional patterned belts was found to be a suitable option, with the looms also made at the prison. A year ago, one inmate taught himself to weave the belts using a book and a video and now teaches other inmates as well.

"When the first practice belt was finished, I asked him how it was going. His eyes lit up and he said, you know, it's like a jeweler's work: It requires concentration, it requires precision and it requires patience," said Taavi Puusepp, head of Viru Prison's second unit.

The prison asked the Estonian National Museum (ERM) to assess the work and also received valuable advice from the museum's Center for Folk Culture and Information. The patterned belts have now even gone on sale in the ERM store.

"We are very grateful for every contact with someone who makes authentic patterned belts. We don't accept just any patterned belt; we have our own committee that reviews the quality. The belts that were offered to us were of very high quality and we are very happy to have been able to add them to our selection," said Liina Kuzemtšenko, ERM's head of sales and services.

Patterned belts are very popular items at the ERM store. "Especially when a Song or Dance Celebration is approaching, the situation tends to be that we cannot offer as many as there is demand for, so we are always looking for artisans who make authentic patterned belts," Kuzemtšenko said.

Belts made at the prison are not separately labeled at ERM, but Kuzemtšenko said that if a customer specifically wants one made there, staff can find one for them.

Külli Valk, a curator at the Estonian National Museum's Center for Folk Culture and Information, said museum staff were very surprised and excited when the prison contacted them this spring to show them the patterned belts made by inmates and ask them to assess their quality.

"They brought a lot of pieces with them and the quality varied. But the woven belts had complex patterns and were technically of very high quality. We were able to take original items from our collection and compare them with the work made at the prison. We recommended where they could buy yarn in a more authentic warp shade and emphasized that they should pay attention to the colors of the yarn in the original belts," Valk said.

"Looking at the belts now on sale in the store, I can see that they really are top-notch. It's surprising that they've managed to make the belts so authentic. We're very happy about that," Valk added.

In addition to ERM, there are plans to sell patterned belts made by inmates through an online store operated by the prisons' business center, which is due to open soon. The prison sees this as an opportunity to make its own contribution to Estonia's cultural heritage.

"A patterned belt isn't just an object. It carries Estonia's story and at the same time, it represents one person's opportunity to change their own story for the better. You're not only getting a handmade belt; you're also helping someone develop good work habits and return to society, while preserving cultural heritage," Puusepp said.

A total of five inmates at Viru Prison weave patterned belts. According to Puusepp, one inmate makes an average of two belts a month, while the most industrious make four.

World.title: Northeastern Estonian hospitals join forces to attract new doctors
World.content:
Hospitals in Ida-Viru County are teaming up for a joint campaign to attract doctors to the understaffed region.

The northeastern region's medical institutions are short about 100 doctors. Ida-Viru Central Hospital (IVKH) in Kohtla-Järve, the county's largest, could hire up to 30 immediately, but applicants aren't exactly lining up for the job.

The hospital plans to target med school students early, hoping internships will encourage them to consider careers in the region after graduation.

"If they come here for an internship and like it, they'll talk to others about their experience," said Pille Letjuka, chief physician at IVKH. "And once that connection has been established, it's much easier to get that doctor or nurse to come back and work for us later."

The state offers doctors taking jobs at hospitals outside Estonia's main population centers a relocation bonus of up to €30,000, but money alone has proven not to always the problem.

"I've made salary offers that have left people in Tallinn gasping, but unfortunately, I still haven't found anyone willing to come here for that money," said Narva Hospital board member Üllar Lanno.

He said years of distrust have made doctors reluctant to consider the border city, thus prompting the new campaign.

Ida-Viru Central Hospital (IVKH) in Kohtla-Järve. Source: Dmitri Fedotkin/ERR

Ida-Viru hospitals say the shortage is actually nationwide and competition for new doctors is fierce. Lanno said the state should increase medical school enrollment to address the shortage.

"I think the best solution for Estonia today would be to train 30 percent more doctors to make up for the 33 percent who never complete their residency," he said.

That, he added, would significantly increase the likelihood of future doctors eventually ending up in hospitals.

Unrivaled experience

Doctors already working Ida-Viru County, meanwhile, point to the unique experience they gain there.

"A doctor who works 24-hour shifts in the Emergency Department or ICU at Ida-Viru Central Hospital could go anywhere and work in any hospital in the world," said Neeme Somma, head anesthesiology and intensive care at the hospital. "They have the experience to cope with whatever situation comes their way."

Hospitals in the region have also relied on temporary assignments to fill staffing gaps, with more than a third of specialist doctors working in Ida-Viru County also working elsewhere in Estonia.

World.title: Handcuffed runners cross Tallinn half marathon finish in record time
World.content:
Four friends from England ran the Tallinn half marathon handcuffed together last Saturday, setting a world record for the fastest half marathon by a group of four in restraints.

This was no jog around the course in fancy dress though – the quartet finished the 21-kilometer course in just under 90 minutes: 1:29:29, a well above average time even for an unshackled runner.

Meanwhile, the attempt now awaits confirmation that it is an official record, while the tale of how they got to the event is worth telling.

"We actually didn't practice with the handcuffs on," Joshua Lally, one of the four that pulled off the feat, told ERR News. "We had planned to, but rather embarrassingly the handcuffs were confiscated at the airport. So we had to buy some more on arrival and only got chance to warm up together with them all locked, so we were very unsure whether it was possible."

The group had trained together, including interval running but without using the arms – among other things these are usually central in counterbalancing leg rotation, maintain balance, and save energy.

Even with the training, coordination on the day proved challenging. "We didn't want to get in anyone's way so we started quite far back, and going in and out and avoiding obstacles was challenging," Lally explained. "Not having any arm movement meant the arms and upper body quickly tired."

The four were also decked out in stripy "prisoner" outfits, which drew attention along the route.

"I've run a lot of different races and it's the most cheers I've ever heard," Lally said. "The spectators seemed to find it quite funny — a lot were recording and shouting things like 'the police are chasing you.' Even other runners were giving support."

In fact spectators on the day can help with the record ratification process, too. To secure it, the group needs as much footage as possible. Lally recorded every two kilometres, but said the quality of the clips isn't sufficient on its own. Anyone who took photos or video on race day, Saturday, September 12, can send them to Joshua Lally here or to ERR News here.

Swedbank Tallinn Marathon 2026 start line, Sunday, September 13. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Estonian records topple

Race weekend in Tallinn saw more conventional records falling too, in both the full and half-marathons. This included several Estonian veterans' records getting broken. Aleksandr Kuleshov ran a marathon in under two and a half hours for the first time, setting a new Estonian record in the M45–49 age group with a time of 2:29.29 — breaking his own record in the process.

Among the women, Siiri Kaaver set a new Estonian record in the W60–64 age group with 3:30.30, more than five minutes faster than the previous mark.

Aimi Pihel also set what should be a new Estonian record in the W75–79 half marathon category with 2:09.03. However, as Marathon100 does not have access to runners' dates of birth, there is some ambiguity over whether Pihel is in that age group or is still competing in the W70–74 category. Esmeralda Lille, also born in 1951, was a couple of minutes faster at 2:07.09, but her 75th birthday was reportedly still a few days away at the time of the event.

Evans Kimtai Kiprono and Vivian Cherotich, both of Kenya, won Sunday's marathon, while two Kenyans, Vincent Kiptoo and Regina Wambui Ndungu, also took victory in the men's and women's half marathon the day before.

World.title: Estonia short on field electricians
World.content:
A new training facility for electrical grid technicians at Tartu Vocational College could help ease a severe shortage of electricians qualified to work in the field.

There has been no state-level training for electrical grid technicians since 2004. Skills related to electrical grids are currently taught through continuing education courses. However, this does not produce enough new specialists to meet demand driven by upgrades to the power grid, electrification and the construction of new generation capacity.

"Training has been left to employers. It's a huge burden and until now we simply haven't been able to hire a qualified specialist straight out of school," said Riho Laanemets, administrative manager at E-Service.

Until now, Tartu Vocational College has only trained electricians to work on indoor electrical systems, while work on outdoor electrical grids was covered only in theory. This fall, however, the college opened southern Estonia's first training facility for electrical grid technicians where students can actually climb utility poles.

"What does theory give us? We stand next to a pole and look at it and think, wow, that's high. But actually climbing it physically — that's the experience they get here," said Katrin Vaher, a mentor at Tartu Vocational College.

"Looking at it, it seems easy, but in reality it really isn't. You have to lean back a little to give yourself enough room to climb and you also have to take into account that the pole moves and starts to sway," said Bryan, a second-year electrical student.

The training facility could eventually make it possible for students in Tartu to specialize as electrical grid technicians.

"Those who go on to work in the field will already have received sufficient training here. This training facility was established here in southern Estonia and our biggest dream now is to create a competence center for the electrical field here, with the capacity to administer professional qualification exams — in other words, an exam center," Vaher said.

"This facility makes it possible to conduct the Level 4 professional qualification exam. Everything required for the exam can be done here, so this is where future electrical grid technicians can start coming from," Laanemets said.

World.title: Teachers to hold nationwide warning strike September 22
World.content:
The one-hour strike will be held at preschool institutions from 8 a.m. to 9 a.m. and at general education and vocational schools from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m., with staff halting their work duties for one hour. It will take place across the country, though it was initially announced by the local Tallinn teachers' union.

Reemo Voltri, chairman of the Estonian Education Workers' Union (EHL), said the action was a last resort, and that negotiations had not brought salary targets closer.

"Since our negotiations have not been successful enough, the teaching staff has found that words alone are not enough and that they do not want to listen to us through negotiations and speaking meetings," Voltri said. "Consequently, we decided that since the state budget is still being drawn up, now is the time to hold this warning strike."

The union is demanding that the minimum salary for teachers at general education and vocational schools rise to at least €2,312 in 2027, the projected level of Estonia's average wage. The salary of kindergarten teachers must be at least 90 percent of that, or €2,081, it said, referring to monthly gross pay.

According to Voltri, the government has indicated it is highly likely the promised goal will not even be approached at this point. "Then the teaching staff felt that we needed to respond to this somehow quickly. We decided that we needed to respond now and immediately," he added.

Education workers have stressed the governing parties have repeatedly promised for years to hike teachers' salaries to a competitive level by 2027, yet not done so.

"In reality, over the past few years the minimum salary for teachers has fallen 6 percentage points behind the national average salary, and even during the latest salary negotiations we received no assurance that teachers' salaries would rise at all next year," the union said.

Reemo Voltri Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Schools to decide how strike hour is handled

Voltri said striking teachers cannot decide on their own initiative how the institution organizes its day.

"If it is known that the majority of employees are going on strike, one must think very critically about whether it is possible to ensure the safety of children and young people or whether it is more reasonable to inform children and parents that the institution will open later that day," Voltri said.

Schools are still preparing their plans. Jüri Käosaar, principal of Tallinn Gustav Adolf Gymnasium, said on Thursday it was not yet known how the strike would be organised at his school.

"The draft version is that since our school day starts a little later on Tuesday anyway, students will probably come to school at 10:01 and we will start classes at 10:01," Käosaar said.

Union chief: education cuts a threat to internal security

Asked about the debate over defense spending, which has led to cuts elsewhere, Voltri said educators understand the need for national defense but that internal security must not be neglected.

"If we no longer have good and qualified teachers or educated people, there is no hope for any economic growth. Soon there will no longer be any point in protecting anything from a foreign enemy if people leave due to lack of education and economy," Voltri said. "Defending the country is important, but the use of money must be transparent and purposeful."

The EHLsays it hopes the government will heed the warning strike and that further, longer protest actions will not be needed.

Teachers joined rescue personnel in picketing the Riigikogu Monday, protesting low public sector wages.

Editor's note: This piece was updated to include comments from union chairman Reemo Voltri and details on strike-day organisation in schools.

World.title: Triple murder case closed just as new DNA clue ties former police officer to the scene
World.content:
A promising lead emerged thanks to DNA evidence in a triple murder case that had remained unsolved for 25 years, but the investigation was subsequently closed under extraordinary and unusual circumstances.

In April 2001, three people — a father, his daughter and her former partner — were killed execution-style in a Tartu apartment. The case drew nationwide attention, not least because one of the victims was a senior Estonian Defense Forces officer.

For decades, the case remained cold. Then new DNA testing produced an unexpected suspect. But before investigators could establish how his DNA got to the crime scene, prosecutors concluded that the statute of limitations had expired.

The victims' families are left asking why the investigation ended just as a potential breakthrough appeared within reach.

"It was such a brutal murder that none of us went on living the lives we had before it happened," said Andra Lätt, the sister of victim Tiina Lätt.

"This is our small Estonia, and we have a crime like this that remains unsolved. Inevitably, you start wondering: Is it possible that someone simply doesn't want this case solved?" said Relika Alliksaar Williams, a friend of the victims and their representative.

The family link

Victims Tiina Lätt and Urmas Aal connected the two families.

Aal, the second-oldest of 10 children from Uhtna, had dreamed of a military career from childhood. After Estonia regained independence, he joined the Defense Forces, became an officer, wrote military textbooks and rose to acting head of the Estonian National Defense College.

"He was the pride of his hometown," his mother, Valeria Aal, recalled.

Tiina, the oldest of three children from Jõgeva, studied dentistry at the University of Tartu. Her longtime friend Alliksaar Williams described her as a "soulmate, sister, best friend and family."

Tiina met Urmas during her first year at university. He was 10 years older, legally married and the father of a young daughter. Their relationship eventually became strained, and in early 2001 Tiina moved into a two-room apartment on Põllu tänav that her family had bought for her studies. She and Urmas nevertheless remained on friendly terms.

Their families last saw them over Easter weekend in April 2001. On Good Friday, both visited Tiina's parents' farm in Laiuse. Tiina had planned to remain there until Sunday but unexpectedly returned to Tartu with Urmas.

"That was the last time we saw her," Andra Lätt said.

On Saturday evening, April 14, Tiina attended a party at a friend's apartment on Jaama tänav in Tartu. A photograph taken there is the last known image of her.

During the party, Tiina's handbag disappeared from near the apartment door. After several people searched for it, the bag mysteriously reappeared — but cash, Tiina's keys and her temporary driver's license, which listed her home address, were missing.

"In theory, someone could have taken the keys and known exactly which apartment they opened," Alliksaar Williams said.

Tiina called police and, the following morning, asked her father, Elmo, to come to Tartu with a spare key and change the lock.

At around 11:30 a.m. on Sunday, April 15, Elmo entered his daughter's apartment. Within the next hour, Tiina and Urmas arrived as well.

Then all three stopped answering their phones.

Their families searched Tartu through the evening. Eventually, they authorized friends to break into the apartment.

Alliksaar Williams called a mutual acquaintance who arranged for a locksmith to open the apartment.

"The locksmith drilled out the lock cylinder and said he didn't want to be the next person to see the bodies. I opened the door, turned on the hallway light and went into the living room, which was Tiina's room. That's where I saw Elmo's body," Alliksaar Williams recalled.

She said she was in shock, with everything seeming to happen in slow motion. Alliksaar's friend came out of the kitchen and pushed her back outside, telling her she should not see what was inside.

"No one dared tell us," Andra Lätt said. "My cousin's husband at the time was finally able to tell my mother over the phone that they were all dead."

Urmas' mother learned what had happened early the next morning.

"My other son called. He asked me to sit down and told me that three people had been found dead in the apartment in Tartu and that one of them was our Urmas," Valeria Aal recalled.

Early investigation

Even against Estonia's crime rate at the time, the killings were exceptional. A special Central Criminal Police task force was assigned to the case.

"It was the No. 1 story nationwide," former investigator Ain Balder said.

The apartment itself offered few obvious clues. There were no signs of a struggle and little disorder.

"At first glance, it gave me the impression that the bodies had been brought from somewhere else and placed in a clean apartment," Balder recalled in 2002.

The two men had been shot in the chest and then in the back of the head. Tiina had been shot in the temple. Five shots were fired, yet neighbors reported hearing nothing. The cartridge cases had been collected and the apartment door locked when the killer left. Investigators found virtually no unidentified fingerprints or DNA.

Theories ranged from personal motives and military connections to a burglary gone wrong. One possibility was that someone had stolen Tiina's keys intending to burglarize the apartment and killed the three when they unexpectedly arrived.

But several people involved in the case doubted that explanation.

"How many ordinary burglars did we have in Tartu who walked around with a suppressed gun tucked into their waistband, ready to kill the occupants at any moment?" former investigator Vallo Koppel said.

Balder said investigators thoroughly examined possible motives connected to Urmas, including military angles, without finding evidence that explained the murders.

Whatever the motive, police increasingly focused on one question: Who stole Tiina's keys?

A possible breakthrough

A few years later, they appeared to get an answer.

In 2005, a drug user named Aleksandr, imprisoned for other crimes, admitted stealing Tiina's handbag. He said he took the money and gave the remaining contents, including the keys, to an acquaintance named Aleksei.

"I don't remember exactly, but he said he wanted to go to the apartment and steal something. I think the apartment keys were in the bag," Aleksandr told police.

He also said Aleksei possessed an illegal gun.

Aleksei became a suspect in the triple murder but denied visiting the Põllu tänav apartment. He claimed he had instead passed the keys to another man, Radik, who had moved to Estonia from Russia.

Investigators could not question Radik: He had been stabbed to death in a dispute among drug users in late 2001 and buried in Russia.

Police used methods including hypnosis and a polygraph, but no one confessed and no physical evidence linked the men to the apartment.

"They pursued the stereo theft and those drug users relentlessly, but they could never prove that any of them had actually made it to the apartment," Alliksaar Williams said.

The investigation remained open but effectively dormant for nearly two decades.

New clue emerges 24 years later

That changed in 2022, when prosecutor Mari Kartau arrived in Tartu and discovered the case was still formally active.

"For a crime like this to remain unresolved for so long is very, very rare," Kartau said. "We thought there might still be something we could do, because it was extremely difficult to accept that this triple murder would simply remain unsolved."

Kartau was skeptical of the burglary theory. In a 2023 procedural document, she wrote that the evidence instead suggested "a planned serious crime."

Investigators retrieved evidence stored since 2001 and submitted it for modern forensic testing.

This time, they found something.

Male DNA recovered from a fork taken from the apartment kitchen matched a former police officer.

The discovery was particularly puzzling because the man had worked at the other end of Estonia at the time of the murders and had no known connection to the victims or the crime scene.

"To our knowledge, this person had not been at the crime scene and should not have had any connection to the people who were murdered," Kartau said.

The former officer was named a suspect and detained in early 2025. He denied involvement in the murders and could not explain the DNA.

"DNA doesn't lie," Urmas' sister Ursula Aal said. "So how did his DNA get into that apartment?"

The man's name is being withheld because he was never charged.

Investigators also discovered that in 2002, despite having no role in the murder investigation, he had accessed police database records concerning Urmas Aal and several other people connected with the case. He could no longer remember why.

There was, however, another possible explanation for the DNA: contamination.

Maarja Sadam, head of the DNA department at the Estonian Forensic Science Institute, said contamination in the DNA laboratory itself was not possible because the man's reference sample and the fork were analyzed almost two decades apart in different laboratories.

Earlier contamination elsewhere could not be ruled out. The fork had undergone fingerprint testing in 2001 under nonsterile conditions. But Sadam noted that the amount of DNA recovered from it was high enough to make accidental contact more than 20 years earlier "relatively unlikely."

Investigators therefore faced two possibilities: They had found a significant new lead, or an extraordinary forensic error.

Before they could establish which, the case took another unexpected turn.

Kartau discovered that the murders were subject to a statute of limitations.

Estonia abolished the death penalty in the late 1990s, while a new Penal Code took effect in 2002. Because of the interaction between the laws, murders committed during a brief period around that time were subject to a 10-year statute of limitations.

For decades, investigators and prosecutors had operated on the assumption that murders of this kind did not expire. As recently as November 2024, a chief prosecutor publicly said the Põllu tänav triple murder was not subject to a statute of limitations.

But in spring 2026, around the 25th anniversary of the killings, the families were informed that the investigation was being closed. Police returned evidence that had been stored for a quarter-century.

"It was a complete shock," Ursula Aal said. "We found out that they had DNA and everything, and then it turns out the case had already expired long ago. How can something like this be time-barred?"

Kartau acknowledged how troubling the timing appeared.

"To ordinary people, and especially to the victims directly affected by this, it seems terribly suspicious: You have just found a new, very intriguing lead, and then you suddenly discover that the statute of limitations has actually expired?" she said.

She stressed that the suspect's status as a former police officer had no bearing on whether charges could be brought.

Kartau nevertheless remains troubled by the case.

"As prosecutors, we don't come across cases like this every day — cases that stay with you — and this is unquestionably one that I would have liked to continue investigating," she said.

For the families, the legal end of the investigation has not brought closure. They hope renewed public attention might still uncover information about what happened inside the Põllu tänav apartment 25 years ago.

"It has torn apart several families here in Estonia and affected an enormous number of our loved ones, and now even their loved ones," Andra Lätt said.

"Many years have passed, but you still wonder what he would be doing or where he would be," Ursula Aal said. "How would all of our lives as a family have turned out?"

Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact "Pealtnägija" or the police, even though the investigation has reached a legal dead end.
