World.title: Baku hosts key conference on preserving historical religious sites (PHOTO) (UPDATE)
World.content:
Details added: first version posted on 10:16

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. A conference titled “Preservation of Historical and Religious Monuments: Challenges and Prospects,” organized jointly by the Ministry of Culture and the State Committee on Work with Religious Institutions, has taken place in Baku, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

The conference began with the playing of the National Anthem of Azerbaijan and the screening of a video about mosques that have been renovated as a reflection of the state's care for religious monuments.

The opening ceremony featured speeches by the Minister of Culture Adil Karimli, Chairman of the State Committee on Work with Religious Institutions Ramin Mammadov, and Rector of the Azerbaijan University of Architecture and Construction, Professor Gulchohra Mammadova.

In his speech, Mammadov said that the creation of a unified database and digital map of historical and religious architectural monuments could serve as one of the starting points for joint activities.

He noted that every religious architectural site has a unique structure, its own history of origin and development, as well as traditions of use and worship that have evolved at that location over the centuries.

“In this regard, when necessary, alongside specialists in architecture, history, archaeology, and restoration and conservation, it would be beneficial to also involve theological experts in the process. After all, when restoring any religious monument, we must strive to preserve its historical authenticity, religious and spiritual significance, and unique characteristics to the greatest extent possible,” Mammadov said.

The committee chairman noted that the restoration of religious monuments is an expression of respect for the past, a commitment to national memory, and a sense of responsibility toward future generations.

Mammadov emphasized that one of the key areas of the large-scale construction effort underway in the liberated territories is the restoration of historical and religious monuments.

“The goal here is not merely to rebuild destroyed buildings. The restoration of cultural heritage sites that were destroyed, desecrated, or whose historical appearance was altered during the occupation represents the revival of our people’s spiritual memory,” he added.

Speaking at the event, Karimli called for the protection of historical and religious monuments. The minister emphasized that the preservation of such monuments should not be viewed solely as the responsibility of state institutions.

“Preserving cultural heritage is not the task of state institutions alone. While the state carries this out through its own agencies and mechanisms, the entire population, all citizens, and civil society institutions must participate actively and approach the matter with sensitivity. This is because our cultural heritage is a reflection and expression of our national identity, historical consciousness, and historical memory. Protecting it is an obligation for each of us—a constitutional duty,” Karimli said.

He particularly highlighted the importance of more closely and actively involving the local population and representatives of religious communities in the process of safeguarding historical and cultural heritage.

The minister noted that armed conflicts and the complex situations arising in their aftermath create serious challenges and difficulties for the preservation of historical and cultural heritage.

“During the 30-year Armenian occupation, our historical and religious monuments located in the occupied territories of Azerbaijan suffered severe damage; some were completely destroyed, and acts of vandalism have been observed. At the same time, instances of the illegal removal of cultural property—which is an integral part of these unique historical and religious monuments and complexes—from the country's territory have been recorded,” Karimli added.

Speaking at the conference, Deputy Minister of Culture of Azerbaijan Saadat Yusifova provided information about the scale of damage inflicted on religious and cultural heritage in the liberated territories, the removal of cultural assets from monuments, and issues concerning attribution and restitution.

She said that several projects are underway under the auspices of Interpol and UNESCO to address the damage inflicted on religious and cultural heritage in territories liberated from occupation, the removal of cultural property from monuments, as well as issues of attribution and restitution.

Yusifova noted that work is already underway in this area within the framework of Interpol and UNESCO. According to Yusifova, the analysis shows that in the territories liberated from occupation, 68 monuments were destroyed, while 114 monuments suffered damage of varying degrees and scale. Other monuments also sustained damage of varying degrees, and incidents of misappropriation and vandalism were recorded.

The deputy minister reported that the inventory of 130 monuments registered with the state in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur has not yet been completed. The main reason for this is the presence of landmines in these territories.

She noted that the inventory revealed that 9 tombs, 3 cemeteries, and 7 mosques registered with the state had been destroyed, while 25 mosques, 14 tombs, and 2 crypts had sustained damage of varying degrees.

Noting that damage had also been inflicted on Christian religious heritage, Yusifova pointed out that one church had been destroyed in the liberated territories, while 20 churches had sustained damage of varying degrees. She also reported that last year, 4 mosques, 7 mausoleums, 4 monasteries, and 13 churches were registered in the liberated territories.

In her speech, Head of the State Service for the Protection, Development, and Restoration of Cultural Heritage under the Ministry of Culture, Sabina Hajiyeva, discussed the current state of examples of both Muslim and Christian religious heritage.

She noted that monuments in the liberated territories have been categorized based on their condition: completely destroyed, severely damaged, partially destroyed, or in fair to good condition. According to Hajiyeva, some monuments have been reduced to such a state that it is difficult to even determine their original function.

The head of the state service reported that, alongside Muslim religious monuments and cemeteries, instances of illegal interference and falsification have also been recorded at sites belonging to Christian religious heritage. It was noted that some small churches had fallen into ruin after years of neglect, while larger Christian monuments of historical significance had been subjected to various forms of interference.

The conference continued with panel sessions on the topics of “Preservation of cultural and religious heritage: law, practice, and opportunities” and “The significance of historical-religious sites in promoting traditions of tolerance and multiculturalism.”

The panel discussions focused on modern approaches to the preservation and restoration of religious and cultural heritage; cooperation among state institutions, religious communities, and civil society in protecting historical-religious monuments; opportunities for digitalization; and the role and significance of religious-architectural monuments—restored in the territories liberated from occupation—within the modern urban planning environment.

The event stressed the importance of further strengthening cooperation among state institutions, academic circles, religious communities, and the public regarding the preservation, study, restoration, and transmission of historical-religious heritage to future generations.

World.title: South Korea’s Nara Space to aid Kazakhstan’s methane monitoring
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. Kazakhstan’s Qazaqstan Gharysh Sapary and South Korea’s Nara Space Technology have signed an agreement on supplying satellite data to monitor methane emissions in Kazakhstan.

This was announced by the press service of the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of Kazakhstan.

"The agreement provides for the supply of data from the GYEONGGISat-2A and GYEONGGISat-2B satellites, as well as the NarSha satellite constellation designed to monitor methane emission sources. The information obtained can be used by government agencies and representatives of Kazakhstan’s industrial sector," the ministry said.

According to the Ministry, one of the main applications of the satellite data will be monitoring methane emissions at oil and gas facilities, including oil refineries and natural gas infrastructure. The data can also be used to generate analytical information as part of MRV (Measurement, Reporting and Verification) systems.

The agreement was signed during the state visit of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to South Korea.

As part of the visit, a delegation of the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of Kazakhstan, headed by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev, held a series of meetings and signed memorandums on cooperation in the space sector.

These included the third meeting of the Working Group on cooperation in space activities between the Aerospace Committee under the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of the Republic of Kazakhstan and the Korea AeroSpace Administration (KASA).

During the meeting, the current state and prospects of bilateral cooperation, as well as potential areas for further cooperation in the space sector, were discussed.

The Aerospace Committee under the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of the Republic of Kazakhstan and Qazaqstan Gharysh Sapary signed a strategic cooperation agreement with CONTEC Co., Ltd. in the space sector.

The agreement provides for strategic cooperation in satellite manufacturing, the development of ground infrastructure, the processing and commercialization of Earth remote sensing data, as well as expanding presence in the markets of Kazakhstan, the Republic of Korea, Central Asian countries, and other states.

An investment agreement was signed between Qazaqstan Gharysh Sapary, Ghalam, CONTEC Co., Ltd. and APSI to develop technological and investment cooperation involving Kazakhstan’s Ghalam. The document is aimed at strengthening Ghalam’s capabilities and developing new technological competencies.

Nara Space Technology Inc. is a South Korean company specializing in the development and operation of small satellites and satellite solutions for monitoring methane emissions. The GYEONGGISat-2A and GYEONGGISat-2B satellites were developed by the company in partnership with Gyeonggi Province.

CONTEC Space Group is one of South Korea’s leading private space companies. Its founder worked at the Korea Aerospace Research Institute (KARI) for 16 years, while the group brings together CONTEC, Asia Pacific Satellite Corporation and Texas Space Communication. The company supplies onboard computers for South Korean government satellites and operates 17 ground stations worldwide, including in Chile, Alaska, Texas, South Africa and Australia. It also maintains partnerships with Kongsberg Group, Safran, and other global industry players.

World.title: Woman arrested after baby found dead in Sydney bin
World.content:
A woman believed to be the mother of a baby found in a Sydney bin last month has been arrested, police say.

Emergency services were called to Harrow Road, Auburn, at 11:20am on August 31 after reports a baby's body was discovered in a garbage bin of a unit block.

In a statement today, NSW Police said a 24-year-old woman "believed to be the mother of the infant" was located and taken to hospital for assessment.

"Upon release from hospital, the woman was arrested and taken to Auburn Police Station where inquiries are continuing," it read.

Found in a plastic bag

Acting Superintendent of the Auburn Police Area Command Darren Sly told reporters at the time the unclothed baby boy's body was found in a plastic bag.

He said the body may have been there for up to 36 hours and it was not known whether the infant had been born alive.

"It's very traumatic for that particular lady who found that baby," Acting Superintendent Sly said.

" It's a newborn baby who now has passed away and of course it's sad and a horrific set of circumstances. "

Officers on the day urged the baby's mother to come forward.

"If there was to be any police action that is not our priority whatsoever, our only priority at the moment is for the welfare of that mother," he said.

World.title: Man charged with murder after alleged assault in Tasmania's north
World.content:
A 42-year-old man has been charged with murder after allegedly assaulting a man at a house in Tasmania's north.

Tasmania Police said shortly after 8.30am on Wednesday, emergency services attended a private residence following reports that a man had been assaulted at Railton, south of Devonport.

The alleged offender had left the scene and was arrested at a nearby location a short time later, police said in a statement.

Police said the victim and offender were known to each other, and there was no ongoing threat to the wider community.

On Thursday night, police said the Tarleton man had been charged with murder after the 48-year-old victim, a man from Railton, died at the Royal Hobart Hospital.

The man was set to appear in the Devonport Magistrates Court on Thursday night.

World.title: Backpacker cuts slammed as 'low blow' for farming and tourism
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Federal limits to backpacker numbers have sparked fears in regions reliant on holidaying workers for farming and tourism.

On Thursday Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke outlined an overhaul of the working holiday-maker visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers seeking to extend their stay and reducing overall numbers.

A cap of 45,000 will be applied to those looking to stay a second year, down from the 57,000 who qualified this year.

Tony Burke announced the changes in an address to the National Press Club on Thursday. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Those seeking a third year will be capped at 5,000, down from 31,000 this year.

Mr Burke said the government would prioritise migrants that have skills Australia needs in areas such as construction and agriculture.

Backpackers provide a significant source of workers in regional communities across Australia. (Pixabay)

People who successfully secure an extension in the ballot will be required to undertake regional work.

Mr Burke said backpackers could not be exempt if the country was serious about lowering net overseas migration.

"Drastic cuts, wherever you make them, hurt the economy in every part, in every area," he said.

" Anyone who wants to pretend there's only an economic cost in the regions does not understand the Australian economy. "

But the National Farmers’ Federation (NFF) has warned the government is putting Australia’s food security, regional economies and farm safety at risk if it pushes ahead with its plan without "urgent" consultation.

Hamish McIntyre called the decision a "low blow" for farmers. (Supplied: National Farmers Federation)

The lobby group's president, Hamish McIntyre, said farmers were furious that the time-frame for processing visas would now take up to three months, as opposed to days.

“This is a low blow for farmers and the businesses that produce Australia’s food and fibre,” he said in a statement.

"A three-month processing target leaves farmers completely stranded, with harvest already underway in parts of Queensland and the main season only weeks away."

Federation chief executive Mike Guerin also warned of rising food prices if the industry struggled to find workers for harvesting.

"We will see a lift in the price of food. We will see emptier supermarkets," he said.

Slowdown leaving farms without workers

Esperance farmer Mic Fels said the slowdown of backpacker visa applications, which began last month, meant some farmers were going without the seasonal workforce needed to bring crops in.

“I think 'reform' is probably a generous word. I think 'deform' is perhaps a better one," he said.

" It's been quite catastrophic — and I'm not using hyperbole here — for the broadacre sector across Australia, especially Western Australia, where farms tend to be of larger scale. "

Mic Fels says the loss of workers across the agricultural sector will be disastrous. (ABC News: Emma Field)

Mr Fels, who contested the WA seat of Swan at last year's federal election, said assurance the government would prioritise applications for skilled agricultural workers was welcomed.

But he said the situation was time-sensitive.

“If we saw hundreds of applicants coming through over the next week, I think that would give everybody some breathing space,” he said.

Mr Fels said there were concerns across the sector that a lack of workers could lead to dangerous practices that the industry had attempted to stamp out.

“After COVID, when we just had all these inexperienced workers on farms and the death rates on farms doubled, and it's not hyperbole, this is what we're dealing with,” he said.

“These are massive machines with thousands of moving parts. You wouldn't put inexperienced operators on a dump truck on a mine site and say, 'Go for your life', and that's what they're effectively saying."

Securing workers is critical ahead of the harvest, Mic Fels says. (Supplied: Ash Bowman)

Tourism lobby warns of 'severe' impact

WA's tourism lobby said the state stood to lose 4,500 backpackers working in peak seasons, costing at least $62 million in tourism spend and 425 local tourism jobs.

“The cuts will be most severe for Exmouth, Broome, Kununurra and northern WA, which currently attract backpackers to work in tourism to earn a third visa," Tourism Council WA chief executive Evan Hall said.

Tourism Council WA says towns such as Broome will be particularly hard hit. (ABC Kimberley: Andy Seabourne)

Queensland's Tourism Council said the government had effectively dismantled the system sending thousands of young travellers to regional Australia.

"Why would a young traveller leave the city and complete three months of regional work when there is no longer certainty of receiving a second visa?" chief executive Natassia Wheeler said.

"The workforce impact will begin during their first year, long before the ballot is held.

"Working holiday-makers are also visitors. When we lose that workforce, we also lose the money they would have spent on accommodation, transport, hospitality, tours and experiences."

World.title: Disability advocate's tragic drowning spurs life-saving gesture
World.content:
A small but intimate ceremony was held at Ellery Creek Big Hole only five months after the death of disability advocate Ellen Fraser-Barbour, who tragically drowned while swimming in April this year.

Her mother, Susie Fraser, family and friends travelled to the site to unveil an automated external defibrillator (AED) and a plaque to honour the work and memory of Dr Fraser-Barbour.

Ms Fraser took the opportunity to thank the first responders and St John Ambulance service for providing the defibrillator.

"I'd like to thank you all for your initiative in doing this and for finding some way of making something positive come out of something which was so tragic," she said.

Susie Fraser and William Sears attended the ceremony at Ellery Creek Big Hole, 80 kilometres west of Alice Springs.

"I think your will and determination to do this is incredibly important to us and that something positive can come out of something so shocking."

Closure for family

William Sears, duty manager at Alice Springs Ambulance Station, was involved in Dr Fraser-Barbour's care.

"It was a tough day for ambulance because of the challenges involved in providing emergency healthcare in remote Central Australia," he said.

" There is no aeromedical response, so the next closest ambulance response is roughly an hour via road. "

Mr Sears said Dr Fraser-Barbour's family was supportive of the gesture to commemorate the work she had done in the disability sector.

"It's a good opportunity to not only provide some life-saving equipment in remote Central Australia, but to offer the family some closure and some help with their journey."

Jayde Stewart, Dave O'Toole, William Sears and Bessie Barrett were the first responders to help care for Dr Fraser-Barbour.

Abbey Studley, regional manager for St John Ambulance Northern Territory, said it was an honour to be included at the commemoration.

"It's not often, if not ever, that frontline workers get to speak with families after tragedies or even be a part of any commemoration services, and so it also forms part of our grieving process," she said.

"I think Dr Ellen Fraser Barber was a big believer in equal rights and something as simple as providing an AED in an area that doesn't normally have it, I think aligns really well with who she was."

An AED has been installed at Ellery Creek Big Hole to commemorate the disability advocate. (ABC Alice Springs Emma Haskin)

Deeply missed

At the time of her death, the 35-year-old was championed as a passionate disability advocate who loved travelling and hiking.

Dr Fraser-Barbour's sister Harriet shared the impact on her family and the community in a statement to the ABC.

"Ellen was a fierce and defiant force who made a lasting impact on all that she encountered," she said.

"We cannot describe the hole she will leave in our family, and she will be missed greatly by her community.

"She was an amazing friend to many and wise beyond her years with so much left to give.

"Ellen helped to shape so much of who I am today, and I will not be the same without her."

World.title: Grandmother says system failing despite WA child protection minister's flying visit
World.content:
As the West Australian government faces allegations of trivialising child protection failings in the state's Pilbara, the grandmother who blew the whistle says little continues to be done to protect vulnerable local children.

The 55-year-old buried her grandchildren Jamelia, 10, Arnda, 7, and Kelvin, four months, after they were murdered by their mother Margaret Hawke in July 2022, who then set fire to their South Hedland home.

Ms Hawke was sentenced to life in jail the next year, but Dorothy Papertalk said many of the systemic failures raised by their deaths persist.

Dorothy Papertalk leaves a kangaroo toy at her grandchildren's grave. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Reports first appearing in The Australian newspaper this week, described more than a dozen children living unsupervised in squalor just a few minutes from where the children were killed.

The growing political firestorm saw WA Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski urgently dispatched to Port Hedland, 1,600 kilometres north of Perth.

In a whirlwind trip lasting less than 24 hours, Ms Stojkovski met with police, child protection officials and community members, including Ms Papertalk.

"She did call me yesterday to apologise for the situation … and if I needed any help, to give her a call if I wanted to speak to someone," Ms Papertalk said.

"But at the moment, I'm really, really angry, disappointed … I am hurting.

Dorothy Papertalk at South Hedland cemetery. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

"Make it fair, [don't] just come and go in a flash and a jack-in-the-box.

"Take me to the parliament, I'll speak face to face and let them know and they'll have the true story about the situation that's happened here.

" I live it. "

Allegations of ignored reports

Ms Papertalk accused the Department of Child Protection of failing to intervene in the case of her grandchildren despite repeated warnings.

She further alleged the children were removed from her care and returned to their mother Ms Hawke, who was assaulted by her own parents as a child, and had struggled with drug addiction and domestic violence in the lead-up to their murders.

"They're too afraid to sort out the situation, even just to give me a piece of paper explaining why they couldn't help me and my grandies."

The burial place of Ms Papertalk's three grandchildren. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Ms Papertalk said she had been offered support by the state government after meeting with the minister.

But a renewed request for a coronial inquest was denied.

"When they said no, my [inquest] wasn't approved … my heart was like a mirror shattered," she said.

Dorothy Papertalk sits by her grandchildren's resting place in South Hedland. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Speaking to the ABC in Port Hedland, Ms Stojkovski recognised her department's role in the incident.

"The department does acknowledge there were some findings in that review and they have been working towards changing those findings," she said.

While in his first public statement on the reports, Labor Member for the Pilbara Kevin Michel said he would continue to advocate for local children and families.

"The safety of children is always our top priority, and recent media reports are concerning," he said.

Political pressure builds

The charged debate over the situation in South Hedland has continued, with fiery exchanges in State Parliament late on Thursday.

Opposition leader Basil Zempilas accused the minister of trivialising and playing down the seriousness of the issues raised.

"Children living in South Hedland, in Frisby Court, are the sorts of people we are here to speak up for," Mr Zempilas said.

"And there can be no argument that these children are at risk right now.

"The government must do much better, much better, to ensure these children are safe."

South Hedland child protection 'failing' The government admits delays in response to reports more than a dozen children had been living unsupervised in squalid conditions in South Hedland.

Ms Stojkovski said none of the local authorities she met with in South Hedland could provide evidence children were being unsupervised.

"Children were not being unsupervised in this house according to those people who have the statutory authority to enter the house and engage with the family," she said.

" I do have confidence that these children and this family are getting the supports that they need at this time. "

Labor MP for the Kimberley Divina D'Anna called for an end to political pointscoring.

"It is about working together and saying, 'What role do I play? What role do I play as government? What role do I play as an opposition?'" the Yawuru woman said on Wednesday.

Divina D'Anna has called on all sides of politics to work together on child protection issues. (ABC Kimberley: Matt Bamford)

One Nation leader Rod Caddies also questioned the response.

"It falls back on you as a minister to make sure that more is being done and whatever that takes," he said.

"You're talking about the children's wellbeing, then every step should be taken to make sure that that is fixed."

Federal senator Lidia Thorpe has also backed calls for a federal inquiry into the safety of WA's most vulnerable children.

'If we don't have kids, we're not going to have a future,' Ms Papertalk says. (ABC News: Alistair Bates)

Ms Papertalk said if she was in parliament today, she would plead with decision-makers to focus on the future.

"We can fix the mistake. We've just got to keep working together and trying to work this out. Because it's the kids.

World.title: NASA scientist's chance Moon discovery reveals once-in-a-lifetime crater
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

When NASA scientist Robert Wagner first noticed a "bright spot" on the surface of the Moon in 2025 he was unaware he had just discovered the largest, newly formed crater ever found in the solar system.

Measuring wider and about as deep as the Roman Colosseum, researchers believe the crater was formed after a powerful surface impact just over a year before humans noticed it.

Its discovery revealed an impact event NASA says only happens every 132 years, and which scientists hope will become critical to informing future research.

The Moon's newest crater measures about 43 metres deep. (Supplied: NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

How was the Moon's newest crater found?

On October 24 last year Mr Wagner was examining routine data quality reports and maps generated from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO).

The LRO has circled the Moon for more than 17 years, mapping its topography, surface composition, temperature and radiation environment, NASA says.

Through its work, scientists are able to identify changes to the Moon's surface by comparing high-resolution "before and after" photographs taken by the LRO.

The discovery of the McGetchin crater revealed a lunar impact that scientists say only happens every 132 years. (Supplied: NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

When Mr Wagner spotted "an unusually large bright spot circled by a dark halo", he said he immediately knew it needed further analysis.

"I just stopped, dropped everything, and started looking into what that spot was," he said.

" It was by far the most obvious impact debris pattern I've ever seen in one of these images. "

The discovery became known as the McGetchin crater, named after pioneer lunar scientist Tom McGetchin.

It measures 222 metres across and 43 metres deep, which is three-times bigger than the previous record holder found by the LRO a decade ago.

A before-and-after view of the patch of the Moon's surface where the McGetchin crater was formed. (Supplied: NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

Researchers say they believe the crater was formed between April 11 and May 22, 2024, as a result of a comet or asteroid strike the size of a three- to six-storey building.

The LRO's numerous crater discoveries since its launch in 2009 shows the top 2 centimetres of the Moon's surface soil is being overturned by ejected material every 80,000 years — faster than previously thought, scientists say.

Further checks exposed 'cold spot'

In addition to taking photographs of the Moon, the LRO also has instruments that pick up variations in temperature that can highlight shifts in the lunar surface.

In examining an area surrounding the McGetchin crater, researchers uncovered a 6.5km patch that was marginally cooler at night.

A "cold spot" surrounded the crater where unsettled Moon dust and soil was unable to retain surface heat. (Supplied: NASA Goddard/UCLA/JHU APL)

That happens because a surface impact unsettled the Moon's bedrock dust and soil, known as regolith, making it less dense and therefore less able to retain heat.

"The large extent of this 'cold spot' is striking, scientists say, because it shows that impacts can modify the Moon's surface far beyond the crater itself," NASA said in a blog post on its website.

"These physical changes could affect how rover wheels interact with the surface, for instance."

How often do Moon strikes happen?

NASA says that impacts involving "space rocks and other objects" on the Moon's surface happen reasonably frequently.

Pockmarked since ancient times, the moon bears some of the solar system's largest impact craters, including one that stretches more than 2,400km across.

About 140 new craters are identified across the lunar surface each year, according to the US space agency.

The McGetchin crater, indicated by a black arrow in an image showing the extent of other craters. (Supplied: NASA Goddard/Intuitive Machines/Robert Wagner)

Of those, most of them are caused by "microscopic projectiles" that create craters too small to be picked up by the LRO's photography.

But the spacecraft can still capture craters that measure about nine metres in width, at the smallest, made by rocks measuring just over a metre.

In assessing the images taken by the LRO's two cameras, scientists have been able to identify and map "landslides, landers, seismic faults and even hints of lava tubes", NASA said.

NASA photos of Moon crater A NASA spacecraft circling the moon is providing the sharpest views yet of a crater carved by a crashing SpaceX rocket.

Researchers often analyse close-up images of small parts of the Moon's surface, but also occasionally look at wider-scale photos showing a larger area.

Mr Wagner said he spotted the McGetchin crater because NASA's LRO software flagged shifts in the lunar surface by highlighting them in different shades in the wide-scale before and after photos.

NASA said the process often picks up many "false alarms", and so Mr Wagner said he needed to verify the McGetchin discovery by looking for "small fuzzy halos around pixel‑wide bright points, which indicate splashes of regolith around a new crater".

His team then compared those wide-scale images to the close-up images taken of the same area which exposed the size, shape and surrounding terrain of the crater.

This latest impact churned the lunar surface for more than 100km, with dust and rocky soil hurled away at a higher angle than expected, according to Mark Robinson, a chief scientist for the LRO's cameras who works at Intuitive Machines.

Mr Robinson was the lead author for one of two studies that reported the LRO's new findings.

"This event constitutes a statistically rare, effectively once-in-a-lifetime observation," Mr Robinson's research team wrote in one of the studies.

ABC/AP

World.title: Netballer fined after unprecedented assault charge
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australian netballer Sarah Klau has been sanctioned by the sport's governing body after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the matter prior to the Commonwealth Games.

Following an investigation into the incident over the past couple of weeks, Netball Australia has handed Klau a $5,000 fine and a two-game ban that is wholly suspended for 12 months.

The goal keeper will also be required to complete additional education.

Klau has played over 150 matches for the Swifts and won two premierships. (Getty: Jason McCawley)

Klau breached the sport's code of conduct by failing to behave in a professional manner while in public and engaging in conduct that could bring the game into disrepute.

In a statement, Netball Australia said it took into consideration Klau's "individual circumstances and her otherwise exemplary personal history", as well as her apology to the victim and venue, but the seriousness of the charge and breach of standards warranted formal disciplinary action.

Chief executive Mark Falvo described it as "a significant but momentary lapse in judgement … that has been mitigated by her otherwise excellent character".

Sarah Klau plays in the 2024 Constellation Cup in Perth, Australia. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

This means Klau will still be eligible for selection in the Constellation Cup.

The Australian squad set to face New Zealand in a four-game bilateral series in October will be announced in the coming days.

This is believed to be the first time a Super Netballer and national team member has been in trouble with the law, and the decision now sets a precedent for the sport at the elite level.

Klau fronted Sydney's Downing Centre Courthouse in early September facing a common assault charge from June 7, when she allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub.

The 31-year-old reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match before arriving at the Paddington Inn and retaliated when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.

This took place a day after Klau was ruled out of the NSW Swifts' penultimate game of the Super Netball season to manage an ongoing leg injury.

Klau was part of the 2022 team that won gold at the Birmingham Games. (Getty: Sue McKay)

The assault shocked the netball community and was dubbed "out of character" by many who know Klau.

The charges were laid five weeks after the incident, ahead of Klau's departure with the national team for the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Netball Australia's investigation aimed to determine whether the veteran knew about the charges before she left.

There is a possibility that she was notified in writing at her Sydney address while in camp in Melbourne, then flew straight to Scotland to compete completely unaware.

Klau has played 67 caps for her country and has been a mainstay in the squad since her international debut in 2019.

Klau has played for the Diamonds since 2019. (Getty: Darrian Traynor)

Despite being hampered by injury throughout the recent Super Netball season, Klau was still named and made her second appearance at the tournament, albeit with limited court time.

The Diamonds won bronze after defeating England 68-50 in the medal matches.

Klau then spent time abroad on holiday before returning home and fronting court.

Diamonds' shock loss to Jamaica The Diamonds will miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time after a shock semifinal loss to Jamaica in front of a crowd baying for Australia's downfall.

Following the investigation, Netball Australia would not disclose the timeline of events but confirmed it did not find out about the incident until a week before the court appearance on September 3.

Commonwealth Games Australia's (CGA) athletes must agree to their ethical by-laws, which state that an athlete cannot engage in any conduct — whether publicly known or not — that brings the relevant person's sport into disrepute.

The behaviour policies also outline that an athlete must not deliberately withhold information in relation to any possible prohibited conduct and is expected to notify the CEO or CGA President of any potential breach.

When contacted by ABC Sport, CGA said it was aware of the court proceedings but was waiting on the findings of Netball Australia's investigation before determining any impact they may have on Klau's relationship with the Australian CGA team.

Klau won a bronze medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. (Getty: James Fearn)

Up and coming defender Jessie Grenvold earned her first call-up for the side and travelled as a reserve. Had all of this come to light, Grenvold could have taken Klau's place.

Importantly, Klau has avoided a conviction, likely due to her status as a Diamonds player, as the judge said it would be a "terrible setback" to "everything you have achieved".

"It's always such a shame to see fabulous sports men and women compromise themselves, really, on nights out," the judge said during sentencing according to NewsCorp.

"In any event alcohol and violence tend to be a great leveller, it doesn't matter who you are.

"This is an opportunity that is being offered to you once."

Klau wins the ball back for the Swifts at Ken Rosewall Arena. (Getty: Darrian Traynor)

Speaking in a statement issued via the Australian Netball Players' Association, Klau expressed deep regret.

"I am incredibly sorry for my actions and the impact they have had on everyone involved and the wider netball community.

"I take full responsibility for my behaviour and accept the consequences that follow.

"I am committed to learning from this and ensuring my actions reflect the standards expected of me and our sport.

"I am grateful for the support I have received, I care deeply about netball and the values it represents."

Klau was also part of the World Cup winning team in 2023. (Getty: Ashley Vlotman)

Two years ago, the Swifts parted ways mid-season with long-time player Sam Wallace-Joseph due to behavioural issues that happened internally and were never publicly disclosed.

Considering the nature of these charges, the guilty plea and the timing of the incident while Klau was in season and supposed to be resting a leg injury, fans thought the club might also make an example of this incident.

Instead, Klau has missed out on a penalty entirely in club land.

The Swifts re-signed their two-time premiership player for a fifth Super Netball season before the trial and later defended her integrity, confirming no further action will be taken.

"Netball NSW can confirm that Sarah Klau has had a matter heard before the local court dismissed without conviction," a spokesperson said.

"Netball NSW takes the behavioural standards of its athletes and staff seriously.

"Sarah has been an exemplary role model in the NSW Swifts environment for 10 years and the club will continue to provide her with support."

World.title: Woman who stabbed sons to death found not criminally responsible
World.content:
The NSW Supreme Court has found a woman accused of killing her two children in September 2024 is not criminally responsible for their deaths.

The incident occurred in the Blue Mountains where two young boys, aged nine and 11, were stabbed to death by their mother.

The children were later found in their home by their father, who then called Triple Zero.

Justice Richard Cavanagh told the court the accused had entered pleas of not guilty to charges of murder on the basis of mental health impairment.

"Having received the further evidence and having considered all of the other evidence relied upon by the parties, I am satisfied that a special verdict of act proven but not criminally responsible should be entered," he said.

"The expert psychiatric evidence is overwhelmingly to the effect that the accused did not know that her actions in killing her children were wrong, even though she knew the nature and quality of the acts that she was undertaking," he said.

"The determination of whether a person did not know that the act was wrong is a matter for the court, but the court must rely on expert psychiatric opinion in forming that view."

Psychiatric conclusions considered

Justice Cavanagh read aloud the details of expert evidence from three psychiatric doctors who interviewed the accused several times individually via audio-visual link (AVL), and concluded there was a "degree of similarity, if not unanimity, in their evidence".

"They considered that at the time of the acts the accused was suffering from such a severe case of major depression that her thought processes were psychotic," he said.

"They also considered that the accused was nihilistic in her thinking and wasn't able to reason other than her children would be better off dead in such a bad world."

Throughout the judgement proceeding, the accused sat slumped in her chair via AVL and did not raise her head once, but at times, was seen wiping her eyes and blowing her nose.

She will now be detained at a location determined by the Mental Health Review Tribunal.

"The tribunal will review and supervise the accused, as well as ensure that she is provided with appropriate care and treatment," Justice Cavanagh said.

"The accused may not be released until the tribunal is satisfied that the safety of the accused or any member of the public will not be seriously endangered by the accused's release."

Justice Cavanagh acknowledged the case as particularly tragic.

World.title: Real wild child in the ottoman aisle
World.content:
“Oh! The thrill of all these glimpses of the famous (C8),” enthuses Margaret Bellingham Holle of Woollahra. “As a teen I played hide-and-seek with Johnny O’Keefe among the furniture in his dad’s store in the city. Heady stuff! As an adult living with my family in the US Virgin Islands, I got to entertain John Wayne as a dinner guest. He was visiting his good friend Maureen O’Hara and her husband Charles Blair. Unfortunately, the menu was a little disastrous as it was only about two hours beforehand that Maureen informed me ‘The Duke doesn’t eat seafood’.”

Dominic Staun of Campbell (ACT) is well aware of the celebrity encounter of the negative kind: “I was in Malta in 1986 with premier Wran and another businessman, discussing an upcoming meeting with the government when Jill Hickson Wran walked into the room. We stood up and Neville said: ‘Darling, have you met these gentlemen?’ ‘No’ she replied, and walked past us. I refer to this as my brush-off with fame.”

In a case of “hold my Guinness”, Dermot Perry of Mount Keira supposes his having a meal with Liam Neeson in the dining room at Queen’s University, Belfast in the early seventies will not be taken seriously.

We’re hoping Stein Boddington of St Clair’s contribution to the street-side urination (C8) debate is an urban myth when he says, “My mother told me to avoid lumps in sugar, as they formed when dogs peed on the hessian bags of sugar stacked at the entrance to the grocer.”

“The list of the many cars abandoned at Sydney Airport, some from as far away as WA, includes Mercedes-Benz, Alfa Romeo, Lexus and Dodge,” notes Paul Duncan of Leura. “Seems that today it’s cheaper to abandon one’s car than to pay the parking fees.”

World.title: Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student Lachlan Abbott September 17, 2026 — 8:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four Melburnians have been linked to the gun used in a fatal shooting of an innocent university student in Sydney’s south-west as part of the city’s gangland war. Police alleged in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Thursday that Vaifaalie Tuafuti, Omar Mohamed, Amenah Abusud and a child worked for the Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against the so-called Coconut Cartel. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine home in Sydney on September 1. A police summary read out in Abusud’s extradition hearing revealed investigators have linked the four to a gun found at the family home in the suburb of Glen Alpine where Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed early on September 1. NSW Police have said the wrong address was targeted in what is believed to have been a botched organised crime killing. Two teenagers were charged with murder early on Thursday over the incident.



The four Victorians mentioned in court have not been charged over Tapia’s death but are accused over a home invasion in the Sydney suburb of Hurstville and of shooting cars in Turrella the night before. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Trail of evidence’: Teens charged over mistaken identity murder of innocent student Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes matched and were then “positively mapped” to the Glen Alpine homicide scene, where a firearm was found, a NSW Police investigator testified on Thursday. “Subsequent ballistic examination confirmed that the firearm was used to discharge rounds recovered from all three crime scenes,” he said. “Investigations relating to the homicide at Mount Sugarloaf Drive, Glen Alpine, remain ongoing.”



Police say Tuafuti, Mohamed, Abusud and a child left Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north late on August 29 and drove to Campbelltown in Sydney’s south-west, arriving at an Airbnb property about 5am on August 30. A senior constable from NSW Police’s anti-gang Raptor squad said the group were “contracted by a faction of the Alameddine organised crime network … for the purposes of committing extremely violent crimes targeting several Sydney-based close associates of the Coconut Cartel”. Court documents released to this masthead reveal Mohamed, Tuafuti, the child, aged 16, and an unknown fourth person are accused of breaking into a home in Hurstville about 2am on August 31. No one was home. “Offenders utilised a sledgehammer to gain entry to the premises and discharged a round of ammunition into a wall inside,” a statement of alleged facts says.



The court heard the break-in was filmed, and the occupant later received a WhatsApp message that said: “We were in your house to kill you if you were there, but God gave you life today. I promise you, we are going to make sure your kids grow up with no father.” The four allegedly then drove to a home in Turrella that police said was “well-known to law enforcement” for links with the Coconut Cartel. Police allege four shots were fired into parked vehicles outside the house before the quartet drove back to Campbelltown. The officer from the Raptor squad said the four Victorians then left their Airbnb about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”. Tuafuti, Mohamed and Abusud were remanded in custody after NSW Police expressed fears they could flee the country if granted bail.



Victorian police will drive them to Albury on Friday, where their charges will be formally filed with a NSW court. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mother of newborn found dead in Sydney rubbish bin arrested after three-week search
World.content:
The mother of a newborn boy found dead in a rubbish bin outside a unit complex in Sydney’s western suburbs is expected to be charged on Thursday, almost three weeks after giving birth.

The baby was found naked inside what resembled a bin bag outside the Auburn apartment complex on August 31. Detective acting Superintendent Darren Sly said at the time that the newborn may have been in the bin for up to 36 hours.

Police cordoned off Harrow Road, Auburn, following the grim discovery. Janie Barrett

The 24-year-old, found by police on Thursday after an exhaustive investigation, was taken to hospital before she was transported to Auburn Police Station. She was arrested about 6.30pm on Thursday, after answering questions from detectives.

The woman is expected to be charged on Thursday night, a police source said. She is set to be charged with concealing the birth of a child, which carries a maximum penalty of two years’ imprisonment.

World.title: Meet the dad fighting for safety after Riverview student punched in daylight attack
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Meet the dad fighting for safety after Riverview student punched in daylight attack Christopher Harris September 17, 2026 — 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The father of a 15-year-old at one of Sydney’s oldest boys schools has petitioned the NSW Parliament to install more security cameras at high-risk bus stops after his son was punched in the face on a Sunday afternoon in Hunters Hill. Riverview student Jordan Herrera-Hu was travelling back home at 4.15pm on August 16 following an afternoon visiting Burwood when a man came up and punched him and threatened his twin brother, Jason. Jose Herrera Perea with his sons Jordan, left and Jason, right, in their Sydney home. Janie Barrett “My boys arrived at the bus stop and within seconds, the guy just went for them and punched Jordan,” his father Jose Herrera Perea said. He rushed to the aid of his sons on Gladesville Road, where they were already on the phone to the police.



But a month later, he realises it is unlikely he or the police will ever find the identity of the man who attacked him due to a lack of CCTV at the bus stop where he was hit. “I believe the police really care genuinely, but they don’t have the tools and resources to do better,” he said. In a bid to assist them with their duties, he has launched a petition in the NSW Parliament seeking the installation of CCTV at more bus stops. The petition calls on the government to: 1. Conduct a statewide bus-stop safety and CCTV assessment. 2. Establish and fund a targeted, risk-based installation program. 3. Publish clear selection criteria, funding commitments and an implementation timetable. 4. Assign responsibility for funding, installation, ownership, operation and maintenance among Transport for NSW, councils and transport operators. 5. Set consistent privacy, cybersecurity, signage and footage-retention standards. 6. Ensure NSW Police can promptly request, preserve and lawfully access footage when investigating alleged offences. It would include those heavily used by schoolchildren, high-patronage stops and interchanges, locations with reported assaults or recurring incidents, those which were isolated locations and stops serving late-night routes.



According to Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research figures, there were 407 assaults at NSW bus premises in the 12 months to June last year, equating to seven a week across NSW. In the weeks after the attack, Herrera Perea said his sons were hesitant to be out in the street alone. “What Jordan struggles with the most is that this man is never going to be caught,” he said. “We teach our children if they do something wrong, there will be consequences.” To reach the 20,000 signatures in a two-week timeframe to trigger a debate in the NSW Parliament, he’s been posting on local Facebook sites as well as Riverview’s year 9 parent group chat. At home, the family discussed the possibility of self-defence training. Herrera Perea says he has heard from other parents about attacks and realised the problem was widespread.



“Even what happened to my son, he was lucky. He was lucky – he doesn’t have any bones broken,” he said. Related Article Education The north shore school teacher, the parents and the ‘panic attack’ “I also want to show my children don’t make a big thing and life is about perspective and some stories are much more horrible.” Transport Minister John Graham said there was CCTV at some bus stops and continue to make investments that improve safety at and around public transport hubs. “Everyone deserves to be safe when using public transport, my sympathy goes to the boys and their family,” he said.



“The vast majority of bus stops are on council land and decisions about further safety measures would need to be made in cooperation with individual councils.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mayor accused of attempting to gag representatives in council media bust-up
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland councils Mayor accused of attempting to gag representatives in council media bust-up William Davis September 17, 2026 — 7:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Allegations a south-east Queensland mayor is attempting to “gag” councillors is at the heart of a local government scrap south-west of Brisbane, as well as claims council resources will be overwhelmed by the new rules. Under policy changes expected to pass at Ipswich City Council, its media team will be permitted to work with councillors on their own communications. Under present rules, it is only permitted to act on behalf of the mayor or institution of council. Ipswich mayor Teresa Harding. Tony Moore All councillors at a Finance and Governance Committee meeting on Tuesday voted in support of the proposed amendments – made possible by new legislation – except for mayor Teresa Harding and her deputy Nicole Jonic who opposed, and councillor Marnie Doyle who abstained. Harding used the official council media channels to put out a personal statement blasting the move on Thursday, arguing it would drain resources and be of no benefit to ratepayers.



“I have never seen an example of a council’s corporate communications team being used to draft the personal views of councillors,” Harding said. “There have been several attempts during my time as mayor to amend this policy to serve the political interests of councillors instead of serving the Ipswich community. I am sure residents are sick of seeing this tired political tactic. “Residents should hold significant concerns about what is being proposed here. While ratepayers will be funding this proposal, it is hard to see how it will deliver benefits for anyone other than these councillors.” Speaking over the phone to this masthead, longtime councillor Andrew Antoniolli shot down those arguments, accusing Harding of attempting to maintain centralised control of communications. “I just think that these fanciful deflections by the mayor are just to try and take away from the fact that she wants to … and has shown a pattern of behaviour so far of gagging her fellow councillors,” he said.



“It’s my experience that they are currently underutilised, and that the current media pressures that exist are certainly less than what they were 10 years ago. “It’s laughable. I think we’re all growing weary of the whole debate.” Councillor Pye Augustine similarly said she didn’t believe the resourcing argument stood up to scrutiny. “I don’t think that holds water… I just don’t understand what her thinking is,” she said. “We’re just trying to get a voice … as a councillor.”



Harding has previously accused councillor Paul Tully of attempting to gag her from speaking as official spokesperson on council matters. This masthead has contacted him for comment. “There’s always a tension between mayors and their councillors,” Peter Chen, a political scientist and senior lecturer at the University of Sydney, said. “Mayors have always had that kind of institutional power that they could use politically. “You can understand why individual councillors, particularly those who aren’t in the same political faction, want to equalise that power imbalance. “It’s also a story about the decline of local media.”



Chen said he hadn’t heard of councils in Australia introducing similar policies, but believed it was likely to become more widespread in places where mayors did not have factional control. “I think that now that the kind of the band-aid’s been ripped off, we’ll see others entertain this.” While councillors in Ipswich don’t run on party tickets, Harding has strong links to the LNP – having previously run for the party at the federal level – and many of her rivals are connected to the Labor Party. World.title: Hundreds of market-rate rentals but no public housing guarantee: Tower plans labelled horrific
World.content:
NationalVictoriaPublic housing Hundreds of market-rate rentals but no public housing guarantee: Tower plans labelled horrific Gemma Grant September 17, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New redevelopment plans for one of Melbourne’s biggest public housing towers provide no guarantee of supplying public homes, as the government prepares to introduce hundreds of market-rate rentals. The state government briefed the City of Yarra on its plans for the tower at 139 Highett Street, Richmond, which currently has 220 public housing flats, on September 11. The public housing tower in Highett Street, Richmond. Eddie Jim The number of apartments is set to almost quadruple to 800 as part of the major demolition and development project, according to the council’s briefing. The height of the development or how many buildings will be included is unknown. Of the new apartments, 150 have been earmarked for social housing – an umbrella term that refers to public and community housing.



Community housing differs from public housing in that properties are owned and managed by a not-for-profit company instead of the state. There is no confirmed public housing yet included in the new development. Related Article Public housing United Nations slams plan to demolish Melbourne public housing towers The remaining 650 new homes are expected to operate under a build-to-rent model, an increasingly common format that often results in residents being charged a higher rate compared with median rents in the area. An unspecified portion of these rentals will be classed as affordable, the briefing said. Yarra Mayor Stephen Jolly said such a sharp transition away from public housing towards market-rate rentals would, in effect, lead to “the privatisation of that estate” and its surrounding community parkland. “They’ve just gentrified the whole estate. There’s no way they can build 800 homes where 200 were without seeping onto the green open space,” Jolly said. “It’s horrific, really. I don’t know how it can be justified.”



The Highett Street tower is around the corner from the North Richmond medically supervised injecting room and within the wider North Richmond public housing precinct, which falls between Victoria Street and Bridge Road. The Highett Street tower forms part of the wider North Richmond public housing precinct. Luis Enrique Ascui Homes Victoria staff told the council that home numbers across the precinct are expected to increase from 1000 to 3000. The Highett Street tower and a group of walk-up houses in and around Elizabeth Street fall within the next development stage. Redevelopment timeframes for the remaining four Elizabeth Street towers are not yet known. A state government spokesperson said decisions about the height, scale, mix or design of the Highett Street development were yet to be finalised.



They said demolition of the tower was expected to begin sometime next year. A separate application had been made for the construction of 187 new social homes at the nearby Elizabeth Street walk-ups, which are currently being demolished. “Homes Victoria continues to engage with residents, stakeholders and the City of Yarra on the future of the precinct, including open space and community facilities,” the spokesperson said. The Richmond rebuild is part of the state government’s controversial Big Housing Build, which was announced in 2020. Then-premier Daniel Andrews said at the time that the project would increase social housing supply by 10 per cent. The major construction works, which encompass all 44 of Melbourne’s high-rise public towers, have since attracted legal challenges and criticism from the United Nations. The state ombudsman is investigating the relocation process faced by residents.



There is also growing concern from tenants and advocates about whether the project will be able to fully replenish the state’s public housing stock. A different development in Holland Court, Flemington, is now in its construction phase. The total number of apartments will increase from 180 to 285, but only 50 of these have been earmarked as social homes. It is unclear what the split between public and community housing will be. Greens MP for Richmond Gabrielle de Vietri said the Highett Street decision was another example of how the state government was “wiping out public housing” around Melbourne. “As the local MP, I cannot stand by while Labor tears our community apart. I will fight this tooth and nail,” de Vietri said.



“Labor is clearly trying to hoodwink Victorians with this plan that’s been nothing more than a mass privatisation sham from day one.” The Victorian Housing Register shows that close to 69,000 people are currently on the state’s waiting list for public and community housing. This is an increase of 1021 from March. The figure includes new applications to the register and “transfer applications”, which represent public and community housing residents seeking to move due to a change in personal circumstances. Yarra City Council will hold an extraordinary meeting next Tuesday at which councillors will reiterate their opposition to the Highett Street tower’s demolition and push for a pause to the project until after the November state election.



There will also be an emergency meeting with the council and North Richmond public housing residents on Monday to discuss the details of the development. Jolly said the lack of consultation that had taken place with residents, the council and the wider community regarding the project was “just not good enough”. “This hasn’t been well advertised. Definitely not in other languages … We’ve just been lumbered with this disaster,” he said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.content:
“Oh! The thrill of all these glimpses of the famous (C8),” enthuses Margaret Bellingham Holle of Woollahra. “As a teen I played hide-and-seek with Johnny O’Keefe among the furniture in his dad’s store in the city. Heady stuff! As an adult living with my family in the US Virgin Islands, I got to entertain John Wayne as a dinner guest. He was visiting his good friend Maureen O’Hara and her husband Charles Blair. Unfortunately, the menu was a little disastrous as it was only about two hours beforehand that Maureen informed me ‘The Duke doesn’t eat seafood’.”

Dominic Staun of Campbell (ACT) is well aware of the celebrity encounter of the negative kind: “I was in Malta in 1986 with premier Wran and another businessman, discussing an upcoming meeting with the government when Jill Hickson Wran walked into the room. We stood up and Neville said: ‘Darling, have you met these gentlemen?’ ‘No’ she replied, and walked past us. I refer to this as my brush-off with fame.”

In a case of “hold my Guinness”, Dermot Perry of Mount Keira supposes his having a meal with Liam Neeson in the dining room at Queen’s University, Belfast in the early seventies will not be taken seriously.

We’re hoping Stein Boddington of St Clair’s contribution to the street-side urination (C8) debate is an urban myth when he says, “My mother told me to avoid lumps in sugar, as they formed when dogs peed on the hessian bags of sugar stacked at the entrance to the grocer.”

“The list of the many cars abandoned at Sydney Airport, some from as far away as WA, includes Mercedes-Benz, Alfa Romeo, Lexus and Dodge,” notes Paul Duncan of Leura. “Seems that today it’s cheaper to abandon one’s car than to pay the parking fees.”
