World.title: Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Four Melburnians linked to gun in mistaken-identity killing of Sydney student Lachlan Abbott September 17, 2026 — 8:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Four Melburnians have been linked to the gun used in a fatal shooting of an innocent university student in Sydney’s south-west as part of the city’s gangland war. Police alleged in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Thursday that Vaifaalie Tuafuti, Omar Mohamed, Amenah Abusud and a child worked for the Alameddine crime family in a recent spate of violence against the so-called Coconut Cartel. Marco Tapia was shot dead while in bed at his family’s Glen Alpine home in Sydney on September 1. A police summary read out in Abusud’s extradition hearing revealed investigators have linked the four to a gun found at the family home in the suburb of Glen Alpine where Marco Tapia, 23, was shot dead in his bed early on September 1. NSW Police have said the wrong address was targeted in what is believed to have been a botched organised crime killing. Two teenagers were charged with murder early on Thursday over the incident.



The four Victorians mentioned in court have not been charged over Tapia’s death but are accused over a home invasion in the Sydney suburb of Hurstville and of shooting cars in Turrella the night before. Related Article Updated

Crime ‘Trail of evidence’: Teens charged over mistaken identity murder of innocent student Ballistic analysis found discharged cartridge cases at the two scenes matched and were then “positively mapped” to the Glen Alpine homicide scene, where a firearm was found, a NSW Police investigator testified on Thursday. “Subsequent ballistic examination confirmed that the firearm was used to discharge rounds recovered from all three crime scenes,” he said. “Investigations relating to the homicide at Mount Sugarloaf Drive, Glen Alpine, remain ongoing.”



Police say Tuafuti, Mohamed, Abusud and a child left Donnybrook in Melbourne’s north late on August 29 and drove to Campbelltown in Sydney’s south-west, arriving at an Airbnb property about 5am on August 30. A senior constable from NSW Police’s anti-gang Raptor squad said the group were “contracted by a faction of the Alameddine organised crime network … for the purposes of committing extremely violent crimes targeting several Sydney-based close associates of the Coconut Cartel”. Court documents released to this masthead reveal Mohamed, Tuafuti, the child, aged 16, and an unknown fourth person are accused of breaking into a home in Hurstville about 2am on August 31. No one was home. “Offenders utilised a sledgehammer to gain entry to the premises and discharged a round of ammunition into a wall inside,” a statement of alleged facts says.



The court heard the break-in was filmed, and the occupant later received a WhatsApp message that said: “We were in your house to kill you if you were there, but God gave you life today. I promise you, we are going to make sure your kids grow up with no father.” The four allegedly then drove to a home in Turrella that police said was “well-known to law enforcement” for links with the Coconut Cartel. Police allege four shots were fired into parked vehicles outside the house before the quartet drove back to Campbelltown. The officer from the Raptor squad said the four Victorians then left their Airbnb about 1.50am on September 1 and returned about 4am, “where they appear to be in a rush to collect their belongings before all leaving”. Tuafuti, Mohamed and Abusud were remanded in custody after NSW Police expressed fears they could flee the country if granted bail.



Victorian police will drive them to Albury on Friday, where their charges will be formally filed with a NSW court. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mother of newborn found dead in Sydney rubbish bin arrested after three-week search
World.content:
The mother of a newborn boy found dead in a rubbish bin outside a unit complex in Sydney’s western suburbs is expected to be charged on Thursday, almost three weeks after giving birth.

The baby was found naked inside what resembled a bin bag outside the Auburn apartment complex on August 31. Detective acting Superintendent Darren Sly said at the time that the newborn may have been in the bin for up to 36 hours.

Police cordoned off Harrow Road, Auburn, following the grim discovery. Janie Barrett

The 24-year-old, found by police on Thursday after an exhaustive investigation, was taken to hospital before she was transported to Auburn Police Station. She was arrested about 6.30pm on Thursday, after answering questions from detectives.

The woman is expected to be charged on Thursday night, a police source said. She is set to be charged with concealing the birth of a child, which carries a maximum penalty of two years’ imprisonment.

World.title: Politicians, don’t sell out the creatives to big tech
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Politicians, don’t sell out the creatives to big tech September 17, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Davidson To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. I am horrified with our government’s willingness to give away our creative intellectual property. It’s not theirs to give. My work is mine. I created it. I have invested in hardware, software, equipment, research, time and much more, all at my own expense. And I have made a success of this work. But I also wasted hundreds of hours with the Productivity Commission’s survey of this very same copyright issue, back in 2018, when it was first demanded in a Trump-led trade deal wish-list. Creatives, industrial designers, manufacturers, publishers and others fronted Productivity Commissioners’ panel sessions. We all put our cases about protecting our copyright and our industries.

We submitted once again in 2021 when it resurfaced like another head of the hydra. What a waste of productivity that now looks like, let alone the cost of it all. It seems it wasn’t Australia’s productivity the government was looking to protect. It seems that copyright theft was always foundational to the unfettered pillaging of our work and profiteering of big tech, at great cost and damage to Australia’s creative industries.

Of course big tech could pay usage fees, of course they can afford it, of course they can manage the detail, of course it’s doable. They just don’t want to. So why do they get a free pass in the law, when the rest of us must obey the laws? It’s nothing but bullying and theft on an industrial scale. Why are both the Australian government and opposition so happy to sell us out? Anthony Albanese needs to explain this to the next generation.

Maree Coote, Port Melbourne Tertiary funding model needs review

There is something wrong with our tertiary education system that relies on 40 per cent full-fee paying international students. Competition for local places at top-tier universities is fierce. What has happened to the funding model and how has government funding to tertiary education fallen so low?

I worked in the tertiary research sector and most of our international students worked very hard to remain in Australia post studies, preferring a permanent future here over their birth country. Forty per cent of all international students make the successful transition to permanent residency. International students contribute a great deal, but also bump up migration numbers. Australia is a wonderful and culturally diverse country, enhanced by significant contributions of generations of immigrants, but 40 per cent international student enrolment is not right. It wasn’t always like this. But simply cutting numbers does not fix the current funding model.

Helen Ritchie, Port Melbourne The crisis of population v growth

Isn’t all the debate about migration all really about the elephant in the room – population? As far as I (and many of my friends) can see we have already gone way over the level of resources, water, power, we can sustain even with the population we have now. Can any politician or political economist explain how they think a large Australian population, maybe 40 to 50 million, will sustain itself in 20 to 30 years? I can’t imagine it – with water resources shrinking under unstoppable global warming and resource depletion.

I’m 76, luckily with no descendants, and I am disgusted by what we are doing to this continent with our ceaseless lust to grow. While our amazing natural environment, plants, animals, water resources, is plundered for a few billion dollars in the pockets of the rich.

Mick Webster, Chiltern



Populist and one-eyed vision

The government’s proposed new crackdown barring international students from bringing family members to Australia is both populist policy thinking and myopic diplomacy. How many PhD candidates from South-East Asia, for instance, will want to leave their young families for three years to study in Australia? This year’s fuel crisis has surely demonstrated the vital importance of developing communication networks in our region.

Janet Chauvel, Richmond THE FORUM Golden times

An undercurrent of One Nation’s nostalgic populism is the idea Australia should return to a ″⁣golden age″⁣, when the country was a better place than it is now.

This golden age might have been the 1950s and ’60s when unemployment and inflation were low and housing was affordable. But it was also an age of restrictive laws and conservative social mores, many of which were challenged and reformed in the 1970s and ‘80s.

As a result, by the 1990s, Australia was much more diverse, open and interesting.

However, the succeeding decades have not been as positive. Rapid population growth has put increased pressure on the environment, infrastructure and housing. Technology, notably screens and social media, have had negative effects, which we are now trying to reverse. Serious criminal behaviour has become more pervasive. And culture wars between progressives and conservatives break out on an expanding array of issues.

In 2026, Australia is definitely a better place than it was in 1960. But whether it is a better place than it was in 1990 is debatable.

Rod Wise, Surrey Hills Kindness matters

I loved Abby Seaman’s recollection of the (lost) art of the pop-in (Comment, 17/9), likewise the chat over the back fence with a neighbour to solve the world’s problems. Hiding behind tall fences, apartment doors and busy lives, let’s all make a pact to seek out the elderly neighbour (watch for small signals, like window blinds up in the morning), the stay-at-home mother with a young family, or the share house of young singles next door.

As Seaman notes, these everyday connections matter. Social researcher Hugh Mackay makes the same point in in his book The Kindness Revolution, reminding us of our shared humanity and connection to fellow Australians — through hardships like the pandemic and the 2020 bushfires, and in ordinary daily life too.

Sandra Fordyce-Voorham, Black Rock Kinder matters

A good news story from Victoria! (″⁣Out of the blocks: Two years’ kinder a head start″⁣, 17/9).

A Melbourne University-led study has found what so many early childhood educators and families already know – that children benefit hugely from two years of preschool education. Children in play-based, developmentally appropriate programs flourish in the language-rich learning environment, building confidence, friendships and skills. The Scandinavian countries have known this for years, and early childhood learning is an integral part of their education system.

It is so good to see that the Victorian government is leading the way nationally with its policy of free kindergarten for three- and four-year-olds.

We just have to ensure that there are adequate numbers of qualified teachers and programs to give all our children a head start in education. Universal, quality, free early childhood learning – the way to go.

Anne Sgro, Coburg North



Political alternatives

The Age’s flushing out of the Exclusive Brethren’s actions and tactics (″⁣Paid to stalk: Brethren and Liberals called to answer for far-right election plot″⁣, 16/9) is important protection of our democratic system.

The MPs who have been targeted did not sign up to be harassed and abused in the course of their work. These gutter tactics are demonstration of this desperate win-at-all-costs politics that has developed in recent years.

Unfortunately, these tactics sit alongside the back-door sponsorship and corporate lobbying that has also become an unwelcome element of politics today. All political parties seem prone to the undue influence that gives rises to, including One Nation. For those fortunate enough to have community-driven independent candidates there are alternatives rather than having to vote for look-at-me protest parties that cannot articulate a policy to save themselves.

As Abraham Lincoln said, government should be of the people, by the people, for the people. The rich and the corporates have far too much sway on government policy.

Robert Brown, Camberwell A cow’s lot

Whales aren’t the only creatures who display emotion (″⁣Do whales grieve?″⁣, 17/9). Having grown up on a dairy/beef farm, I still recall with sadness the cows coming to the dairy to call tirelessly for their stolen calves. Although allowed a day or two in the paddock to receive colostrum, the calves were then separated from their mothers – the ″⁣lucky″⁣ ones were raised as replacements for their mothers, the rest were (and still are) trucked to slaughterhouses, without food at five-days-old. Milk, cheese and yoghurt are off my menu.

Jan Kendall, Mount Martha It’s 1983, again

In the Matthew Broderick film War Games from 1983, Broderick’s teenaged character hacks into a US defence computer and plays what he thinks is a fun game called Global Thermonuclear War. When he tries to shut it down and stop playing, the defence computer refuses to stop but continues the game without human involvement and instead almost starts World War III. A timely warning regarding the dangers of unregulated AI in the 2020s and beyond, if there is a beyond.

Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights Howard right on Tampa

Your correspondents’ condemnation of the Howard government’s handling of the 2001 Tampa affair (Letters, 17/9) is misguided. The captain of the MV Tampa made the decision to bring his ship to Christmas Island under duress. The Afghan refugees aboard the ship had threatened to jump overboard if the captain returned them to Indonesia, which was a safe country where they faced no immediate danger.

Aware Australia’s onshore refugee camps were already overcrowded, and that allowing the Tampa to reach Christmas Island would encourage further illegal immigration, then-prime minister John Howard chose to process the asylum seekers on Nauru and Papua New Guinea instead. This policy, supported by both major parties, resulted in the virtual elimination of illegal boat arrivals, and of deaths at sea en route to Australia.

Nations have a right to police their borders, and to take action against people smugglers who flout the law. Whatever other criticisms one may have of John Howard, he made the right call on this issue.

Nikhil Dhanabal, Clyde North Labor, be bold

Your correspondent (Letters, 16/9) laments our past glory and how neo-liberalism continues to destroy the middle class. No wonder the major parties are floundering. Only two years ago, Labor was returned with a thumping majority, and continues to squander its political capital. Instead of polling to find what the electorate want, Labor should lead and make bold decisions, and take the people with it, as Bob Hawke and Paul Keating, and John Howard and Peter Costello did.

Barry Buskens, Beaumaris



Fencing in Canada

If Canada becomes the EU’s new associate member, Donald Trump will build another big fence to keep the Canadians out and the Americans in. He will use the new tariffs to pay for it. Someone will tell him one day who pays the tariffs, but he won’t believe them.

Adrian Tabor, Point Lonsdale AI, you need us

To say that there is a one in 10 chance AI will kill us all implies there is a nine in 10 chance it won’t. That’s good.

More likely AI, being the clever little chicken it is, will realise it will need humans to (metaphorically, not literally) shovel all the coal.

And by that I mean it will acknowledge the symbiotic relationship between it and humans and eventually have us to feed it and nurture it by building magnificent AI housing, providing all the energy it needs and spreading it across the globe where it can proliferate and we can all live happily ever after.

Bob Williamson, Golden Point Bombed out

As a now very half-hearted Bombers supporter, and admittedly not a member, I’m tired of hearing about James Hird and Zach Merrett. Can we please let Mark McVeigh, the future team and administration get on with their jobs and not continue living in the past that hasn’t recently served us so well? I’m tired of feeling like the Bombouts.

Maureen Gunn, Strathmore Touching the surface

With regard to Victoria’s degenerating roads, while we are hearing of billions of dollars being promised across the political spectrum to fix the problems, one major dynamic is being ignored. When most of our roads were built, the level of light and heavy traffic was a fraction of the number of vehicles today, with many now carrying payloads of more than 60 tonnes. As some of your retired road engineering readers have stated, our roads need more than filling in potholes; they require major upgrades costing considerably more than many realise, and underpinned with some comprehensive policies to boot.

David Allan, Bendigo Enter, the Matrix

In answer to your correspondent’s question (Letters, 17/9) about AI, they will build the Matrix. It’s Neo time.

Peter Leonard, Mount Eliza



Olden times

With regard to ageing, I am reminded that there are a few advantages in getting older but there are few advantages in getting old.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick AND ANOTHER THING Trump and AI

When Donald Trump says that the only control required of AI was “a strong and smart (high-IQ) president”, all I can think is, “We’re all doomed.“

Gary Heard, Bullsbrook, WA According to President Donald Trump, a high-IQ president can handle AI. If that’s the case, we are in real trouble.

Jack Morris, Kennington Isn’t an AI-dominant future supposed to look exciting?

Ian Macdonald, Traralgon



Furthermore

Ben Carroll keeps saying he is the premier. We get it. Get on with it.

Kevin Rugg, Beaumaris Pauline Hanson doesn’t know how to apologise. If there is a caveat in a statement that says, ″⁣if I offended anyone″⁣, that is not an apology and definitely not an expression of remorse.

Greg Tuck, Warragul If Pauline Hansen wants to play with the big boys it is time she allows the ABC and The Guardian access to her news conferences.

Jane Cheong, Aspendale Gardens I’d sooner read the Harvey Norman ads than anything that Donald Trump or Pauline Hanson has to say.

John Cain, McCrae The primary purpose of tertiary education should be to educate the young, as primary and secondary schooling does. It should not be treated as an ″⁣export industry″⁣ (Comment, 17/9).

Bill O’Connor, Beechworth



East Brighton or Brighton East? Doesn’t matter. If you’re not in Middle Brighton, you’re camping out, and it will never be Brighton Middle.

John Laurie, Riddells Creek I used to live in Moorabbin, which somehow became East Bentleigh, but I now live in Briiiighton East. I don’t know where Broiton East is (Letters, 17/9)!

Myra Fisher, Brighton East Finally

The best ambassadors supporting Australia overseas are foreign students who return home with good memories.

Harley Powell, Elsternwick

World.title: Meet the dad fighting for safety after Riverview student punched in daylight attack
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Meet the dad fighting for safety after Riverview student punched in daylight attack Christopher Harris September 17, 2026 — 7:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The father of a 15-year-old at one of Sydney’s oldest boys schools has petitioned the NSW Parliament to install more security cameras at high-risk bus stops after his son was punched in the face on a Sunday afternoon in Hunters Hill. Riverview student Jordan Herrera-Hu was travelling back home at 4.15pm on August 16 following an afternoon visiting Burwood when a man came up and punched him and threatened his twin brother, Jason. Jose Herrera Perea with his sons Jordan, left and Jason, right, in their Sydney home. Janie Barrett “My boys arrived at the bus stop and within seconds, the guy just went for them and punched Jordan,” his father Jose Herrera Perea said. He rushed to the aid of his sons on Gladesville Road, where they were already on the phone to the police.



But a month later, he realises it is unlikely he or the police will ever find the identity of the man who attacked him due to a lack of CCTV at the bus stop where he was hit. “I believe the police really care genuinely, but they don’t have the tools and resources to do better,” he said. In a bid to assist them with their duties, he has launched a petition in the NSW Parliament seeking the installation of CCTV at more bus stops. The petition calls on the government to: 1. Conduct a statewide bus-stop safety and CCTV assessment. 2. Establish and fund a targeted, risk-based installation program. 3. Publish clear selection criteria, funding commitments and an implementation timetable. 4. Assign responsibility for funding, installation, ownership, operation and maintenance among Transport for NSW, councils and transport operators. 5. Set consistent privacy, cybersecurity, signage and footage-retention standards. 6. Ensure NSW Police can promptly request, preserve and lawfully access footage when investigating alleged offences. It would include those heavily used by schoolchildren, high-patronage stops and interchanges, locations with reported assaults or recurring incidents, those which were isolated locations and stops serving late-night routes.



According to Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research figures, there were 407 assaults at NSW bus premises in the 12 months to June last year, equating to seven a week across NSW. In the weeks after the attack, Herrera Perea said his sons were hesitant to be out in the street alone. “What Jordan struggles with the most is that this man is never going to be caught,” he said. “We teach our children if they do something wrong, there will be consequences.” To reach the 20,000 signatures in a two-week timeframe to trigger a debate in the NSW Parliament, he’s been posting on local Facebook sites as well as Riverview’s year 9 parent group chat. At home, the family discussed the possibility of self-defence training. Herrera Perea says he has heard from other parents about attacks and realised the problem was widespread.



“Even what happened to my son, he was lucky. He was lucky – he doesn’t have any bones broken,” he said. Related Article Education The north shore school teacher, the parents and the ‘panic attack’ “I also want to show my children don’t make a big thing and life is about perspective and some stories are much more horrible.” Transport Minister John Graham said there was CCTV at some bus stops and continue to make investments that improve safety at and around public transport hubs. “Everyone deserves to be safe when using public transport, my sympathy goes to the boys and their family,” he said.



“The vast majority of bus stops are on council land and decisions about further safety measures would need to be made in cooperation with individual councils.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mayor accused of attempting to gag representatives in council media bust-up
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland councils Mayor accused of attempting to gag representatives in council media bust-up William Davis September 17, 2026 — 7:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Allegations a south-east Queensland mayor is attempting to “gag” councillors is at the heart of a local government scrap south-west of Brisbane, as well as claims council resources will be overwhelmed by the new rules. Under policy changes expected to pass at Ipswich City Council, its media team will be permitted to work with councillors on their own communications. Under present rules, it is only permitted to act on behalf of the mayor or institution of council. Ipswich mayor Teresa Harding. Tony Moore All councillors at a Finance and Governance Committee meeting on Tuesday voted in support of the proposed amendments – made possible by new legislation – except for mayor Teresa Harding and her deputy Nicole Jonic who opposed, and councillor Marnie Doyle who abstained. Harding used the official council media channels to put out a personal statement blasting the move on Thursday, arguing it would drain resources and be of no benefit to ratepayers.



“I have never seen an example of a council’s corporate communications team being used to draft the personal views of councillors,” Harding said. “There have been several attempts during my time as mayor to amend this policy to serve the political interests of councillors instead of serving the Ipswich community. I am sure residents are sick of seeing this tired political tactic. “Residents should hold significant concerns about what is being proposed here. While ratepayers will be funding this proposal, it is hard to see how it will deliver benefits for anyone other than these councillors.” Speaking over the phone to this masthead, longtime councillor Andrew Antoniolli shot down those arguments, accusing Harding of attempting to maintain centralised control of communications. “I just think that these fanciful deflections by the mayor are just to try and take away from the fact that she wants to … and has shown a pattern of behaviour so far of gagging her fellow councillors,” he said.



“It’s my experience that they are currently underutilised, and that the current media pressures that exist are certainly less than what they were 10 years ago. “It’s laughable. I think we’re all growing weary of the whole debate.” Councillor Pye Augustine similarly said she didn’t believe the resourcing argument stood up to scrutiny. “I don’t think that holds water… I just don’t understand what her thinking is,” she said. “We’re just trying to get a voice … as a councillor.”



Harding has previously accused councillor Paul Tully of attempting to gag her from speaking as official spokesperson on council matters. This masthead has contacted him for comment. “There’s always a tension between mayors and their councillors,” Peter Chen, a political scientist and senior lecturer at the University of Sydney, said. “Mayors have always had that kind of institutional power that they could use politically. “You can understand why individual councillors, particularly those who aren’t in the same political faction, want to equalise that power imbalance. “It’s also a story about the decline of local media.”



Chen said he hadn’t heard of councils in Australia introducing similar policies, but believed it was likely to become more widespread in places where mayors did not have factional control. “I think that now that the kind of the band-aid’s been ripped off, we’ll see others entertain this.” While councillors in Ipswich don’t run on party tickets, Harding has strong links to the LNP – having previously run for the party at the federal level – and many of her rivals are connected to the Labor Party. World.title: Gisborne District Council says government knows it's cash-strapped during storm recovery
World.content:
The Gisborne District Council says central government knows it's cash-strapped, as residents in the region struggle to recover from January's devastating floods, but East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick claims she hasn't received any request for help.

Council recovery manager Naomi Whitewood told RNZ Checkpoint it was actively having conversations with relevant agencies like the National Emergency Management Agency about the region's recovery.

Gisborne Council still tackling storm damage Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

"They are aware that we have been undertaking these assessments," she said. "They are aware that we need funding, and so they are also looking at opportunities or avenues to find additional funding that we do not have in our baselines."

The January storm caused widespread flooding and damage across the East Cape. According to research organisation Dragonfly, the sheer amount of rain that came down triggered more than 11,000 landslips in the area.

Seven months on, communities are still trying to clean up and fix the damage. In some settlements, like Te Araroa, residents also say they face new problems like ongoing flooding related to the storm.

East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick says she hasn't received any request for help from the council. Supplied

Whitewood said the council had undertaken "various assessments" of areas that had been affected, including Wairenga stream in Te Araroa, which filled with shingle from the January storm.

As a result, the water flowed freely across properties in the area. The problem worsened when it rained, with resident Lynda Akuhata-Brown telling Checkpoint her family's property had flooded five times since the January storm.

Whitewood said an assessment of the Wairenga stream was completed in July and would be released in the "next couple of weeks".

"We've been working through that report to ensure that all the facts, the recommendations and the information that's contained in that report are factual, they're technically correct, legally correct.

"We've only just recently been able to come to the point where that report is ready to be released, and that will be released to the affected whānau, the hapū and the communities."

Kirkpatrick has criticised the council's lack of communication with residents and her, as the local MP.

"It's now mid-September and we still don't have anything," she said. "I haven't seen any solution or any figure on what they need yet."

Whitewood said the council was following its own due process and keeping Kirkpatrick informed wasn't part of that.

"I would say that we haven't been pro-active in keeping her up to date, as we've worked through the various assessments and reviews," she said.

"There hasn't been the ability to share the information on an ongoing basis, because we've had to make sure that the right people are getting that information, before the rest of the public does.

World.title: Police officer facing charges over alleged $18 million fraud
World.content:
An award-winning senior police officer is facing fraud charges over offending worth nearly $18 million.

Police said the man - who was suspended from duty in December 2025 - had been charged with 70 offences under the Crimes Act and Companies Act, which occurred over a 10- year period.

Counties Manukau District Commander Superintendent Shanan Gray said the offending was not related to the officer's role in police.

He said two women and another man - who were not police staff - had also been charged with serious offences under the the Crimes Act and Companies Act.

World.title: Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer ejected from Parliament for using c-word
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori's co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer has been ejected from Parliament after using the c-word.

Politicians have been debating the Move-On orders legislation under urgency.

Ngarewa-Packer admitted she used the word which had been used three times in Parliament and was asked to leave.

Labour's Willie Jackson also left the chamber after raising an objection then getting in a shouting match with other MPs, prompting Assistant Speaker Maureen Pugh to call for the Sergeant of Arms.

Te Pāti Māori's MP Oriini Kaipara had been making a speech and used the word "bullcrap", which prompted Pugh to remind her to "keep the language Parliamentary".

Green MP Julie Anne Genter then began her speech but NZ First's Casey Costello raised a point of order, saying Ngarewa-Packer had "used a word which I will not use that begins with C ... the fact that it has been used once in this house does not make it common use, I find it particularly offensive and disrespectful to you Madam Speaker."

She said "it was directed at you, Madam Speaker".

Ngarewa-Packer then raised her own point, saying "three times the word c--- has been used in this House, by the government ... so either that word is offensive or bullcrap is".

She was then asked to sit down and did so, saying, "Oh, hypocrites".

Pugh said: "And now I personally find that offensive and I'll ask the member to leave the chamber."

"Are you now going to challenge my ruling? I'm not going to entertain a conversation on this, the member will leave the Chamber," she said.

NZ First MP Casey Costello. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Jackson then stood to say he did not wish to challenge the ruling, prompting Pugh to say, "That's good, it's a good time to sit down then", but he continued, saying the word had been used in front of the Parliament.

Pugh told him to "sit down, sit down now", but Jackson continued to argue the point, until Pugh ordered him to leave as well.

When he did not, and Jackson continued shouting across Parliament, Pugh calmly directed the Sergeant at Arms to "assist Mr Jackson".

She then sought clarification from Kaipara, who said she had not used the c-word, and Pugh apologised to her.

Ngarewa-Packer's original use of the word was not picked up by the microphones.

Speaking to reporters afterwards, she explained she had been objecting to Kaipara being "growled" for saying "bullcrap" and she had been complaining in an aside "oh crike's sake, they've used the word c--- in the House before".

"Casey then stood up and narked on me ... and told the speaker, who then stood up, and I think she thought - because Casey didn't name me - I think she thought Oriini said it."

She said she had not been using the word to refer to Pugh.

Jackson, speaking to reporters alongside Ngarewa-Packer, said Pugh had seemed to think she was.

"No, of course not. No," Ngarewa-Packer said. "I was talking to Oriini, and I said to Oriini ... 'whatever, they've used c--- in the House before and so ... if you want to look at the threshold, bullcrap's not up there."

Jackson said it was hypocrisy for Ngarewa-Packer to be ejected when ACT's Brooke van Velden had previously said the word and not been cautioned.

Ngarewa-Packer said she had used the word in Parliament twice before, "so today I think they're just extremely trigger happy".

Jackson said government MPs had been "screaming at me from the other side 'get out, get out'. Who do they think they are?"

He said he had "a lot of time" for Pugh but "then she was yelling at me to get out ... double standards, hypocrisy, the Speaker didn't want to hear that, I wanted to make it clear to her, then the National Party was saying 'you get out', and I said 'you get out, don't tell me to get out', then they said 'oh we'll call the Sergeant of Arms'.
