World.title: Five Karangahape Road venues lose their liquor licences after police intervention
World.content:
Five venues on Auckland's Karangahape Road have lost their liquor licences, following objections from the police and an alcohol licensing inspector.

Mavana Group Limited (MGL) operates Family Bar, Family Down Under, G.A.Y. Club, Las Vegas Nightclub (Empire), and Phoenix Venue, all on Karangahape Road.

Family Bar is particularly iconic, having been a popular LGBTTQIA+ bar for more than 20 years.

After taking over the venues, MGL applied for temporary authorities to sell alcohol earlier this year, with permission granted on 7 May.

The company was warned at the time, however, that "no further compliance failures would be tolerated".

MGL, which has Dalavou Niuhulu as its director and Justine Niuhulu as its sole shareholder, had been seeking another grant of temporary authorities to sell alcohol. Opposition from the police and an alcohol licensing inspector resulted in a hearing in Auckland on 28 August, where a myriad of concerns were raised about multiple incidents at the venues.

The decision to reject the venues' liquor licences as a result of that hearing has just been released.

Police told the hearing that MGL had failed to address concerns raised by Auckland's District Licensing Committee. Police felt MGL "had not demonstrated the level of control, oversight and compliance expected of a licensee in one of Auckland's highest-risk alcohol environments".

While large portions of what police told the hearing have been redacted from the decision, as the statements relate to active investigations, a number of incidents have been disclosed since the venues were given temporary permission to sell alcohol in May.

Sergeant Simon Dillon said unlicensed security staff had been used by MGL, which "demonstrated inadequate employment vetting and failures in compliance".

There was also allegedly an assault on police during a compliance check at Black Velvet - another MGL-owned venue - on 7 June, where the patron admitted to consuming a full box of alcoholic drinks.

He also noted a driver with alleged excess blood alcohol that crashed into a parked car claimed to have had his last drink at Family Bar.

G.A.Y. Auckland has lost its licence. GOOGLE MAPS

Another "disorder job" occurred outside Family Bar on 4 July. The matter was now before the court.

Auckland Council senior alcohol licensing inspector Ashley Wilson addressed compliance monitoring at MGL's businesses.

He said while some issues may appear to be minor administrative breaches, he believed they showed defective systems, staff and training, and reflected negatively on MGL's attitude toward adhering to the rules.

Drunkenness at the venues witnessed by various agencies "showed MGL's unsuitability directly contributed to alcohol harm", he said.

Jon Wiles represented MGL at the hearing. He said police and licensing inspectors' submissions mostly related to isolated incidents, many of which did not involve MGL serving alcohol to those involved.

Many did not occur within the licensed premises either, he said.

Administrative issues identified the licensing inspector were minor, and had been fixed promptly, he said.

Allegations relating to intoxication were largely subjective, he said, and while the company acknowledged some incidents had occurred, MGL believed prompt and decisive corrective action had been taken, "including the replacement of the previous security provider with Sila and Sons Security Group".

Niuhulu, MGL's sole shareholder, said she had made a substantial personal and financial investment in Karangahape Road's hospitality sector, and had made a long-term commitment to the area.

She said she wanted to operate safe, professionally managed venues that contributed positively to the local community and hospitality environment.

The District Licensing Committee labelled what it had heard from police "alarming" and "disturbing".

"MGL was given an opportunity to show that it could deliver on its vision for the premises and the Karangahape community," the committee said.

"It has failed.

"We do not consider MGL is suitable to continue to hold the temporary authorities.

"The applications are declined."

World.title: Pahiatua Medical Centre staff threaten resignations unless under-resourcing addressed
World.content:
Staff at a Tararua district health centre say they will resign en masse, if its owners don't address problems arising from under-resourcing.

Pahiatua Medical Centre nurse practitioner Victoria Perry told RNZ Checkpoint failure to replace departing staff had put preventative screenings for bowel, breast and prostate cancer a year behind schedule, while regular patients were waiting three months for appointments.

The clinic's owner, Tararua Health Group, declined to comment.

Perry said the clinic's 16 staff were also demanding the Primary Health Organisation (PHO) - which contracts the clinic for its services - intervenes before the end of next week.

Staff at medical centre threatening to resign due to shortages Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

She said she feared people would die, if the clinic could not provide even its most basic of services and follow-up tests for its 5000 patients.

"By the time they do see someone in our practice, that problem may be overwhelming and be unfixable," Perry said.

"We're not responding to those sorts of things in close to safe timeframes. It makes us feel sick to the stomach that we can't practice like we've been trained to do and like we're ethically obliged to do."

She said an external workflow review proposed by the PHO amounted to further "bureaucratic delay", and would not address the management failures behind the clinic's understaffing and delays.

"At the moment, what we can't do is even immunise children or give the flu vaccines," Perry said. "We've got 1.6 nurses where we used to have five.

"Although the Minister of Health is saying, 'please go get your vaccines', we don't actually have capacity to administer them."

The clinic's staff wanted the PHO to expand its proposed review to include investigation of the clinic's management and guarantee a timely process - including direct and confidential consultations between the reviewers and frontline staff.

Perry said, if the PHO did not instigate the broader review, the entire frontline team would submit their resignations by 16 October.

"Please, please can you listen? Please can we have more clinicians?

"Please can we have more nurses? Please can we have more administrators to support us?

"It's not working. We're at the bottom here, crying out for help."

PHO chief executive Tony Wai said all parties, including Health New Zealand, were working together to understand the practice's challenges, and support staff and patients.

He said the organisation was looking at a range of options to help maintain services, including workforce support, local clinical cover, telehealth and locum support where appropriate.

It was also keeping in close contact with partners across the region and monitoring general practice capacity.

World.title: FENZ Minister Brooke van Velden questions CEO over withheld information
World.content:
FENZ Minister Brooke van Velden says she no longer has confidence in the organisation's chief executive, following a "serious breach" of the 'no-surprises' clause.

"It is of a nature that is so significant that I no longer have confidence in the chief executive of Fire and Emergency or have confidence that the information I'm receiving is correct," said van Velden.

She said chief executive Kerry Gregory withheld information from her for a "full year" on a matter of a "seriously significant incident". The matter had now been referred to the Serious Fraud Office.

Van Velden said information had also potentially been withheld from the board.

She couldn't provide detail on the issue, but said she became aware in the last fortnight that significant information had been withheld by the chief executive, "even after he received external advice telling him that he needed to let me know".

"I immediately contacted the board chair, as well as the chief executive, to let him know that I have no longer any confidence in the chief executive.

"Having information of a significant nature withheld from me is not something I would expect of a senior official within the public service."

She added it was a "serious breach of trust".

Van Velden asked the board to meet "immediately to maintain or restore my confidence". The board will meet in the next few days.

A scathing select committee report into FENZ recommended the government look at changing the organisation's board and whether it should be allowed to buy its own firetrucks.

Van Velden said the report was disappointing reading, but also noted some of the recommendations were "things that I can't actually do as a minister".

"I'm surprised that those recommendations are in there, because they're of such an operational matter that it would actually be a breach of the Crown Entities Act for me to be that involved."

Van Velden emphasised the breach of confidence was a separate issue to the report.

A FENZ spokesperson clarified to RNZ that the original incident, not Gregory, had been referred to the Serious Fraud Office.

"The matter referred to is historical, from prior to 2021, and relates to Fire and Emergency's administration of the levy scheme.

World.title: NZ and Samoan nationals charged over alleged Vietnam murder
World.content:
A New Zealand national and a Samoan national have been charged by Samoa Police in relation to the alleged shooting murder of an Australian citizen and suspected gangleader in Vietnam in May.

In a joint statement, Samoa Police and the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said the two men, aged 31 and 33 years old, were charged with conspiracy to murder on 10 September. Under Samoa's Crimes Act, the offence carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

The two men appeared before a Samoan court on Wednesday and were granted conditional bail, the statement said.

Joseph Vaa, 27, admitted on Vietnamese television to gunning down suspected 'Coconut Cartel' ringleader Lorenzo Lemalu Tovia, outside a restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City on 21 May, while his associate, Steve Tofa, 23, then confessed to being his accomplice in the shooting.

"An investigation by international law enforcement authorities began following the death of an Australian citizen and serious injuries sustained by a second Australian citizen in a shooting in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, on 21 May, 2026," the joint police statement said.

"Vietnamese authorities arrested two Samoan nationals, aged 22 and 26, on 24 May, 2026, over their alleged roles in the shooting.

"On 27 May, 2026, Samoa Police first arrested and charged the 31-year-old in Samoa with misleading police and corruption offences as part of their investigation into the alleged murder. He was arrested while attempting to leave the country.

The statement said the AFP launched an investigation into the alleged murder to support international law enforcement authorities and identify any further individuals involved.

The AFP assisted the Samoa Police through the execution of a search warrant, financial inquiries, witness interviews and a forensic review of electronic material.

"These AFP activities, and further inquiries undertaken by Samoa Police, led to an additional charge of conspiracy to murder laid against the New Zealand man and 33-year-old Samoan national."

"Samoa Police will allege these men conspired with the Samoan men arrested in Vietnam to carry out the alleged murder in Vietnam," the joint statment said.

AFP acting commander Pacific Greg Davis said the charges reflected the strength of international law enforcement cooperation across the Pacific and broader region.

"Organised crime does not respect national boundaries, so law enforcement agencies must work together to combat them," he said.

"Criminal networks rely on international connections to facilitate serious offending, which is why regional partnerships are critical to disrupting and dismantling them.

World.title: Court battle looms for Socceroos star after drug test
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle with the Socceroos star's lawyer confirming he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

The 22-year-old returned a positive roadside reading for cocaine after he was pulled over by police on Sydney's Anzac Bridge on July 24.

He had been driving at 109 kilometres per hour in a 60km/h zone.

He later underwent independent testing at a private clinic, where it was claimed he returned a negative reading.

However, Volpato was then sent for a secondary oral fluid test by police, which again confirmed a positive result for cocaine.

He copped a $722 fine as a result of the second positive test, but on Thursday his lawyer Paul McGirr confirmed to AAP that he had elected to take the matter to court.

Volpato has maintained his innocence, insisting he never knowingly ingested the substance.

He also undertook a test when he returned to Italy, which was negative, his club side Sassuolo said.

The Sydney-born player was a late inclusion for the Socceroos' World Cup campaign after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia on the eve of the tournament.

In a statement provided to AAP, a Football Australia spokesperson confirmed the organisation was aware of reports concerning Volpato and a "traffic matter currently subject to a police process".

"As the matter is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for Football Australia to comment further at this time," the spokesperson said.

Regardless, the positive reading on Volpato's secondary police test could have major ramifications for his availability heading into January's Asian Cup.

Sources have previously told AAP that Volpato could be hauled before FA's disciplinary and ethics committee, where the sport's governing body has the power to suspend him from national team action.

The 22-year-old is currently playing in Serie A with Sassuolo but is sidelined with a right leg injury sustained against Bologna this month.

AAP

World.title: 'Cinema' expected as rival wingers go to battle one last time
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Toia will have a front-row seat to the last instalment of the battle between teammate Mark Nawaqanitawase and Ronaldo Mulitalo, and the Sydney Roosters centre is bracing himself for more box-office entertainment.

"Cinema, that's what I expect — [another chapter in] an ongoing battle and I think if we get the win that will top it off," Toia said.

Saturday's sudden-death semifinal could be Nawaqanitawase's last in the NRL, with the 26-year-old former Wallabies star switching back to the 15-man code with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights.

Few could have imagined the impact Nawaqanitawase would have had in rugby league when he crossed codes after the Paris Olympics.

There have been highlights in just about every game — be it his grubber ahead and tip toe down the sideline against Canterbury last season that was named try of the year, or last weekend's tap-ahead intercept before climbing off the deck and racing away to score against Penrith.

"It's pretty hard to stay alert because you don't know what's going to happen," Toia said.

"I didn't expect him to do what he's been doing, I think he has shocked everyone."

Nawaqanitawase's long-running on-field feud with the sledge-happy Mulitalo — the pair of wingers openly admire each other off it — has made Roosters-Sharks games fixtures to savour.

"There's a bit of competitiveness there but I think that is what makes the game so great — it's the best of the best going at it with each other," said Roosters forward Siua Wong.

Toia's opposite number KL Iro said of Mulitalo: "He can get personal at times but after the game he always makes sure he clears it up straight away and shakes his hand.

"He loves getting in the mix, he's a huge competitor."

Nawaqanitawase has made the switch to rugby league look easy, having won caps for the Kangaroos, played State of Origin for NSW and scored 41 tries in 44 games for the Roosters.

The Roosters and Sharks battle on Saturday night from the Sydney Football Stadium.

AAP

World.title: Canberra is the greatest mystery of the NRLW finals
World.content:
Of all the teams in the fight for the NRLW premiership, Canberra shapes as the ultimate wildcard.

Ahead of the first finals series in club history, the Raiders are a difficult puzzle to solve; for themselves and opponents alike.

Darrin Borthwick's side enter the finals in fifth place with a 6-5 record that belies a strange tendency that developed over the season: more than any other team in the league, they play to their opponent's level.

Can anyone stop the Roosters in the NRLW? After completing the most dominant regular season in NRLW history, the big question around the Sydney Roosters is simple: can anyone hope to stop them?

The Raiders have a winning record against fellow top six teams, highlighted by a 28-4 win over third-placed Broncos, comfortably the Brisbane team's biggest ever NRLW loss.

They even put the gloves up against powerhouses Gold Coast and Sydney Roosters, losing to the two competition heavyweights by a combined 10 points, finishing close enough in both games that they would fancy their chances in a rematch.

But as easily as the Raiders can be inspired by the challenge of taking on the big dogs, they can be complacent when facing teams they should handle easily.

Canberra dropped games to stragglers Parramatta, North Queensland and Cronulla throughout the season, costing them a home final.

As they prepare to head to Campbelltown to take on Wests Tigers in tomorrow night's sudden-death final, they are still trying to work themselves out as they head into the deep waters.

"I've found we've lifted for those bigger teams. We've spoken about that, that we need to believe we can win because if we get that down, our effort and our fight will come," said captain Zahara Temara.

"For some of the other teams who aren't as high on the ladder, we've matched them in terms of effort, and that's disappointing. But we know we can lift for the big teams."

It is an unorthodox way for Canberra to live, but now that only big teams are left, the Raiders' record against the top sides makes them perhaps the best candidate to break open the Roosters-Titans hegemony at the top.

Canberra will lean heavily on Zahara Temara's experience through the finals. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Temara's experience will be crucial for Canberra, with the clever halfback one of the few Raiders with an extensive finals pedigree, having won a premiership with the Roosters in 2022.

That was the 29-year-old's third grand final, and she admits she took the team's success for granted in the earlier years, something she is desperate to ensure does not happen to her Raiders teammates this time around.

"Something I wish someone told me in those early years at the Roosters was how hard it is to have regrets. I took it seriously, but not as seriously as I could have," said Temara.

"It's hard to make the finals. It's extremely hard to win a grand final, and with the position we're in now, I want them to have no regrets, to realise how we can make history."

That perspective was reinforced by former Roosters teammate and current Canberra co-captain Simaima Taufa, especially after their losing effort in the 2020 grand final.

The Raiders will be without gun lock forward Simaima Taufa tomorrow night. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The sight of the whole-hearted Taufa after the match has never left Temara, and inspires her to this day.

"She gave it her everything, and I didn't feel like I did," said Temara.

"We were all disappointed, but I tell her all the time now I couldn't look at her because I knew I hadn't done everything I could for her and the team.

"I still took it seriously. I just wish I took it as far as she did."

With Taufa sidelined due to suspension, there will be even more responsibility on Temara's shoulders tomorrow night.

The Tigers are polar opposites of the Raiders: they beat every side that missed the finals, but went 1-4 against the other play-off teams, with their sole success coming via a one-point win over Newcastle.

But there are similarities too. The joint venture is also playing in its first finals match, and given Raecene McGregor's form at halfback, the team will also lean heavily on an experienced playmaker to show the way.

Inside Tigers remarkable NRLW turnaround Few expected much from Wests Tigers in this year's NRLW competition, but after winning as many games this season as the rest of their history combined they've proved the doubters wrong ahead of a maiden finals push.

To add to the intrigue, this is a rematch only seven days in the making. The two sides met last Friday night at Leichhardt with the Raiders grinding out a 22-10 victory.

Winger Mackenzie Wiki and centre Leianne Tufuga, who was crowned the club's player of the year, both played blinders as Canberra's strike out wide carried the day.

It ensured the Tigers would enter the finals on the back of consecutive losses, but Temara understands how dangerous they still can be when the stakes are highest.

"Their fight stood out," said Temara

"They were down on the scoreboard, but their fight and hunger to keep coming at us was hard to manage. We got lucky with some errors and penalties that kept the momentum for us."

World.title: Croc-inhabited Fitzroy River gets green light for 2032 Olympic rowing
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

After months of fierce debate, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) has approved rowing and canoe sprint events on Rockhampton's Fitzroy River for the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games.

The central Queensland river will host the events despite concerns over its suitability, including its crocodile inhabitants.

Premier David Crisafulli said the doubters had been proven wrong with today's announcement.

"The IOC assessment for the site is complete," Mr Crisafulli said.

" The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours. It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered. "

International rowing bodies had questioned the location's suitability for competition. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

It comes after World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide also backed an independent technical assessment of the Rockhampton flatwater course.

The Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) and internationally renowned marine engineering experts WaterProof Marine Consultancy and Services B.V. (WaterProof) completed a comprehensive, independent technical assessment of the Fitzroy River.

The assessment included extensive on-water investigations and modelling to understand how the course would perform under a range of conditions, weather patterns, water levels and flood risk at both Games time and throughout the period leading into the event.

Loading...

Having reviewed the assessment, World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland and Paddle Worldwide president Thomas Konietzko endorsed the central Queensland waterway.

Mr Rolland said it could provide a safe, fair and consistent field of play suitable for Olympic and Paralympic rowing and canoe sprint competitions.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games, consistent with the requirements of Olympic and Paralympic rowing," he said.

A future Olympic dream is taking shape on the Fitzroy River, where young rowers could one day compete for their country on their hometown course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleije told state parliament "it's a win for regional Queensland".

"The experts have confirmed it. World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide have endorsed it," he said.

" Rockhampton is good for rowing and rowing is good for 2032 and beyond. "

Rowing Australia and Paddle Australia today acknowledged the completion of the independent technical assessment of the field of play for the Rockhampton flatwater course.

The assessment included detailed surveys of the riverbed and competition course. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

"This assessment forms part of the full project validation report," a Rowing Australia spokesperson said.

"Rowing Australia looks forward to the completion of this full report and will continue to support key stakeholders involved in the venue planning process for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games."

Brisbane 2032 president Andrew Liveris said "thorough and robust" assessments had been undertaken on the Fitzroy River before it was given the tick of approval.

Game on Rocky

Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams welcomed the confirmation of the Fitzroy River as the venue for rowing at the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Tony Williams has thanked the state government for its support of Olympic rowing in the city. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

"This endorsement proves what we've always known. That Rockhampton's Fitzroy River will be the perfect venue for rowing at the 2032 Games," he said.

"Rockhampton is ready for the world stage. Now it's time to get to work and secure the infrastructure and opportunities that will benefit our community long after the Games have ended."

Queensland senator and National Party leader Matt Canavan, who first championed the Fitzroy River as an Olympic venue, said it was a great day for central Queensland.

The Fitzroy River has faced intense scrutiny since it was selected as a venue for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

"The Fitzroy River is one of the most beautiful parts of our country. It's an iconic Australian river," he said.

" It's been a tough fight, and some people had not wanted rowing to be outside of south-east Queensland. "

But Tom Sharp, mayor of rival rowing location Scenic Rim, dismissed today's announcement, and said there was still a long way to go for Rockhampton as a host city.

"You've got the financial assessments, you've got the overlays for the visitors, spectators, you've got the accommodation assessments, you've got the rowers themselves," he said.

"We're only at the starting blocks and Rocky's only starting to catch up to Scenic Rim."

The Rockhampton rowing facility will host the Queensland Schools' Championship regatta this weekend. (Supplied: Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club)

The Queensland premier said GIICA would now proceed with the detailed planning, design and construction of the Rockhampton site.

He also told state parliament there would be no widening or dredging and that the Fitzroy Barrage was Rockhampton's "secret weapon".

While the river has passed an independent technical assessment, the region will require more accommodation to support an influx of athletes and visitors in 2032.

"Rockhampton knows how to host major events. It already hosts tens of thousands of people for Beef Week and Rockynats, and the Games will deliver extra accommodation for the future," Mr Crisafulli said.

The Fitzroy River has been used as a venue for Australian rowing team training camps over the years. (ABC Capricornia: Alice Roberts)

Rowing Queensland chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin also welcomed the outcome of the technical assessment, as the Rockhampton venue prepared to host more than 800 young rowers for the Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta this weekend.

"This is an important step to provide certainty to our athletes and community as we progress towards 2032," Ms O'Loughlin said.

"We note the references in the statement to legacy and investment in the sport and look forward to further information on this as it develops."

Sarah Black says the Olympics will bring a great legacy. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

President of the Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club, Sarah Black, was ecstatic when the ABC broke the news to her that Rockhampton had been given the final seal of approval from the IOC.

"We've known that the course here is fantastic, but to have that international endorsement for the technical assessment is just fantastic news for us here in Rockhampton," she said.

Capricorn Enterprise chief executive Mary Carroll said today's announcement was a major milestone for central Queensland and an opportunity to deliver lasting economic, tourism and community benefits for the region.

"Commercial in confidence discussions have been proceeding positively with major investors to this region who I strongly believe will be able to deliver new hotel accommodation, an athletes' village and legacy infrastructure including world-class rowing and canoeing facilities," she said.

World.title: Greene to leave Giants ahead of expected move to Cats
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The GWS Giants have confirmed Toby Greene will leave the club to potentially join Geelong ahead of the 2027 season.

The Giants released a brief statement on Thursday morning, announcing Greene's intention to return to his home state of Victoria.

Greene has told the Cats he wants to join the club from next season.

"The Giants have been advised by Toby Greene of his intention to move back to Victoria for family reasons with a view to joining the Geelong Football Club," the statement read.

Giants chief executive Dave Matthews told SEN radio Greene was leaving with the club's wishes.

"That's the decision he has made and we certainly respect that," Matthews said.

"He's been a celebrated figure at our club, a very important person and I know this has been a really tough decision, one he's largely made for family reasons."

Toby Greene (second from right) was a foundation player at the Giants. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Kolbe)

The 32-year-old has been offered a lucrative three-year deal to join Geelong.

Greene can join the Cats as an unrestricted free agent once the free agency period opens on October 2.

"We are really excited Toby wants to join the Geelong Football Club," Cats executive general manager of football, Andrew Mackie, said in a statement.

"We know this was a significant decision for Toby and his family, and we recognise what the Giants have meant to him and respect the contribution he has made to their club.

"We are looking forward to helping Toby write the next chapter of his career at the Cats."

Last week, Greene spoke about his talks with the Cats.

"With Geelong, I've had an open discussion," Greene said last week.

"Told them what I think about and what I wrestle with and they then explained what it would look like for me.

Zak Butters nominates Bulldogs as preferred club Port Adelaide's three-time best and fairest winner announces his desire to join the Victorian team.

"Geelong would be a lot less travel and more time for family. They discussed aspects of the role and how it would look in the team."

The news comes after Zak Butters chose the Western Bulldogs, instead of the Cats, as his preferred destination following his exit from Port Adelaide.

Greene was a foundation player at the Giants, spending 15 seasons at the club.

He debuted in 2012 and kicked 450 goals across 282 senior matches.

Greene won the club's best and fairest award twice and is a three-time All-Australian.

He was named Giants' co-captain in 2022 before becoming the sole skipper the following season.

World.title: Broncos NRLW stars credit 'Princey blow-up' for season turnaround
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane Broncos NRLW stars Romy Teitzel and Tamika Upton insist an emotive half-time address from coach Scott Prince was the catalyst for the team's return to form.

The defending premiers host Newcastle in an elimination final on Saturday at Brisbane's Langlands Park.

They enter the match on a three-match winning streak, which followed a mid-season slump.

The Broncos' last loss was a 28-20 defeat to the Gold Coast Titans on August 23.

Broncos, Titans record wins The Broncos thrash the Warriors to hit peak form before the finals, while the high-flying Titans beat the Knights in the concluding round of the minor premiership.

It was their third consecutive defeat.

Trailing 14-4 at half-time in that match, TV footage showed Prince laying down the law in no uncertain terms.

"We are a great team with great standards and we weren't living up to them," Teitzel said.

"We deserved every single word that he threw at us.

"The response comes from having a lot of respect for Princey and believing in his game plan.

"Everything is driven from that respect factor and believing in what he is trying to drive here at the Broncos."

Following the loss to the Titans, the Broncos beat Parramatta 44-10 and St George Illawarra 24-16, before thrashing the Warriors 52-18 at home last Sunday.

Tamika Upton says the players have deep respect for their coach, Scott Prince. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Broncos captain Upton said Prince, who coached the team to the premiership last year, told the players home truths they needed to hear.

"We had a few little things we had to fix, and we weren't doing it, hence the Princey blow-up," Upton said.

"To be honest, we are used to it. He is a very passionate coach. That's the thing, we are all competitors."

Upton said she and her teammates had enormous respect for Prince, who captained the Wests Tigers to the 2005 NRL premiership during his decorated playing career.

"I would rather him be yelling at us than not speaking to us," she said.

"Honestly, you feel that because he was a player.

"When he is talking like that, you feel the energy, and you respect that a lot because he has been there and done it before.

"He wouldn't do it if he didn't care. I respond to that."

AAP

World.title: WTA Finals hoped to become 'Super Bowl of women's sports'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The season-ending WTA Finals will be held in North Carolina for at least three years from 2027, as the tour seeks to take greater control of its flagship event amid financial concerns.

The finals, featuring the season's top-eight singles players and doubles ​teams, will be played in Charlotte at the venue which hosts the Hornets NBA team.

WTA chair Valerie Camillo said the tour wanted to build ‌the finals into the "Super Bowl of women's sports".

Camillo said the WTA would operate the event itself rather than rely on the type of outside-promoter arrangement previously used.

"The WTA will be taking greater ownership and control of the event and investing ⁠alongside our partners," Camillo said.

Financial details ​of Charlotte's package were not disclosed ‌ahead of a planned announcement by local partners.

Rybakina downs Sabalenka for US Open title Elena Rybakina already took Aryna Sabalenka's world number one ranking, now she takes her US Open title as well.

Camillo said it represented a "meaningful investment" that gave the WTA confidence to commit to the city.

The move follows the WTA's decision to relocate the November 2026 finals to Indian Wells, California, after ending an agreement under which Riyadh had hosted the event with the backing of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment ​Fund.

British newspaper The ‌Telegraph reported last week internal WTA projections showed the tour could run out of cash next year and move into debt by autumn 2027 if its spending pattern continued.

The report said the WTA expected operating ⁠losses of $US23 million ($32 million) in 2026 and cited the loss of ‌revenue associated with the Saudi finals deal ‌as a major contributor.

Camillo said 2026 was a transitional year and the tour was tightening spending while absorbing ‌the unexpected cost of moving the finals to Indian Wells.

The WTA has not yet set prize money for the 2027 finals.

Camillo said equal prize money remained an important goal, but added the tour was considering alternatives, including ⁠a profit-sharing model with players.

"We want this event to be built together with the players," she said.

"Why stop at equal prize money?"

The WTA also plans to establish a greater operational presence in Charlotte as it builds the event.

Reuters

World.title: Aussie F1 Grand Prix loses season-opening honour but gains sprint race
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Melbourne's Australian Grand Prix will not have the privilege of opening the 2027 Formula 1 season, but it will boast two races in its biggest weekend yet.

After landing the chance to open the F1 year in 2026 as it once traditionally did for two decades, the Albert Park event will be the third stop on next season's record-equalling 24-race program.

The main race will take place later than usual on April 4, with Bahrain replacing Melbourne as the season-opening venue on March 14.

Jeddah will host the Saudi Arabia Grand Prix a week after the Bahrain race.

Antonelli edges closer to historic title as teammate concedes the fight Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of becoming the youngest F1 champion in history, while his nearest rival says he is out of the fight.

But the key development will be the introduction of a sprint race in Melbourne on Saturday, on the eve of the grand prix itself.

Instead of two sessions of practice on the Friday before the grand prix, there will be just one with sprint race qualifying taking place in the afternoon.

On the Saturday, there will be the double attraction of a sprint race, followed later by qualifying for the main event.

Melbourne will be one of 10 circuits to stage a sprint race in 2027, four more than this year.

F1 bosses clearly believe the 30-minute shorter races on the Saturday are the way forward.

They claim data showed broadcast viewership of sprint weekends was 12 per cent higher than non-sprint weekends, with qualifying three times more popular with fans than free practice.

Portugal (June 20) and Türkiye (October 3) are additions to the program, with the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort and Barcelona having dropped off.

AAP

Tech.title: The streamers are fighting over Halloween
Tech.content:
The Toronto International Film Festival is a place to go to see the future of film, but this year it also provided a glimpse at what is coming very soon in the realm of streaming. Four different streamers — Peacock, Netflix, Amazon, and AMC — all premiered early looks at upcoming horror-adjacent series that are dropping very soon. And by doing it at TIFF, they showed just how important the month of October has become in the realm of streaming.

Perhaps the most high-profile is Carrie, which is coming to Prime Video. An adaptation of the classic Stephen King novel, which has already been turned into no fewer than three feature films, this version of Carrie is notable in particular because of who is helming it. Mike Flanagan has done a handful of King adaptations in the past — including Doctor Sleep and The Life of Chuck — but the director is perhaps best-known for his work on limited series for Netflix. That includes the likes of The Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass, and The Fall of the House of Usher. Those series came out on a near-annual basis between 2018 and 2023, making Flanagan’s particular blend of dramatic horror a staple of Netflix in October.

Then, in 2022, Amazon poached Flanagan to work on projects for Prime Video. The first of these is Carrie, which starts streaming on October 7th. It still tells largely the same story as its predecessors — a young girl’s destructive psychic powers awaken after getting bullied in high school — but it updates it in a few ways. For starters, the story has been thoroughly modernized, with much of the bullying happening in cyberspace. But since it’s a series instead of a movie, Carrie also stretches out the story, which gives it the space to explore the teen drama a little, and also adds plenty of opportunities for Flanagan’s trademark lengthy monologues. I’ve only seen the premiere episode so far, but early on it’s a combination of flavors that work really well together.

Netflix, meanwhile, has filled in the gap with a new series called Below, which premieres on October 8th, just a day after Carrie starts streaming. I saw the first two episodes earlier this week — there will be six in total — and while it’s a different kind of story compared to the likes of Hill House, it has a similarly dark and mysterious energy. Below is about what seems to be an ancient sea creature that begins terrorizing a small fishing village in Newfoundland, on the east coast of Canada. From what I’ve seen, the show does a great job of steadily building the terror of the creature’s reveal, while also mixing the scares with a healthy dose of family drama, led by Josh Hartnett as a struggling fisher who is struggling to keep his family together.

Then there’s Peacock, which is joining the fray with a prequel series. Fans of Friday the 13th will know that Jason’s mom plays a pivotal role in the very first film, and the new show Crystal Lake explores how she got to that point. It stars Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, a single mother who is thrown into a pit of despair and disbelief when her young son drowns to death.

I went into the show thinking that I didn’t really need to know much more about the backstory of Jason’s mother, but the first two episodes that premiered at TIFF — and Cardellini’s performance in particular — have me second-guessing that. Crystal Lake is surprisingly tense and dramatic, but, given its connection to Friday the 13th, it also has slasher-movie levels of gore and gross-out deaths, ones that are so brutal they approach comedy. If nothing else, it gets off to a very strong start. All episodes of Crystal Lake hit Peacock on October 15th.

Rounding out the list is Yaga, a supernatural detective series that’s coming to AMC Plus on October 23rd. Unfortunately I wasn’t able to catch the premiere screening for the show, but it does seem promising, with a cast that includes Carrie-Anne Moss and Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams, and a very intriguing trailer:

Tech.title: Snap is launching a new Specs AI tool, and it’s coming to iOS and Mac
Tech.content:
SPECS Intelligence builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose to connect. The service is designed to carry that personal context across devices and deepens its understanding over time, helping you move between work, personal responsibilities, and the things you care about.

SPECS Intelligence is designed to anticipate when help would be useful and surface relevant information and actions without waiting for a prompt. Before a meeting, it could highlight decisions to make, questions to ask, and things to remember. For an upcoming trip, it could bring together flight, hotel, and dinner plans while flagging a work deadline that falls during the visit.

Tech.title: I wore Snap’s $2,200 smart glasses
Tech.content:
My favorite part of wearing the Specs, Snap’s new augmented reality glasses, was playing dominoes. Sitting across the table from a Snap employee wearing the same pair of chunky glasses, I could select a virtual domino with a pinch and then move my hand to drop it in place, watching the tile snap down in front of us on a real table. It was unlike anything I’ve tried in other VR headsets or smart glasses — the ability to sit with another person and have a shared digital experience.

Snap really believes in AR glasses. The company has spent more than half a decade developing the technology, producing two generations of glasses that only ever shipped to a small number of developers. The company seems to want to untether itself from the limitations of being just one app in a big store and instead pioneer the next great platform.

Now, Snap is nearly ready to launch its first pair of AR glasses for consumers, the Specs, sometime this fall. That suggests Snap thinks these meet its vision well enough for regular people to enjoy using the $2,195 glasses. They’re certainly full of big ideas. But after an afternoon of testing at Snap’s offices this week, I’m skeptical of whether they’ll be fully ready for primetime.

Photo: Naohmi Monroe / The Verge

The Specs are big, black, bold glasses that come in two lens sizes, 47mm and 52mm. Part of why they’re so bold is almost certainly to make a statement — there’s no mistaking these for a regular pair of glasses, like you might with Meta’s Ray-Bans. (They’re a little too conspicuous for me personally; my glasses style is squarely “Elder Millennial Who Shops At Warby Parker.”) But they’re also so chunky because they house all the hardware necessary to let the Specs function as a standalone computer, meaning they don’t need to be tethered to a phone, compute puck, or external battery.

They may be chunky, but the Specs aren’t quite as heavy as they look. They’re heavier than my Warby Parker glasses, of course, which I can comfortably wear for most of the day. But the Specs didn’t drag on my face like a full-on VR headset. The Specs felt sturdy, too: I shook my head around and they didn’t fall off or even really slip. I wouldn’t suggest playing pickup basketball in these, but they’ll stay on your face while walking around. They made my ears sag just a little, though. And I wasn’t able to use the Specs enough to tell you if they’d start to feel uncomfortable over the course of a full four-hour battery cycle.

Actually using the Specs is kind of like using a hybrid of smart glasses and a VR headset. In front of your eyes, you can see menus, app windows, and elements of whatever app (“lens”) you’re using, like the digital dominoes. Those elements appear over whatever you’re looking at with your eyes through the lenses of the glasses, which have waveguide displays that can show “16 million colors” and “sharp, high-resolution visuals” (Snap hasn’t specified the exact resolution).

Thanks to hand-tracking tech in the Specs, you can pinch and drag to manipulate parts of the interface, such as resizing a window or moving a domino onto the game board, and Snap says you can even snap your fingers to take a picture in the Specs’ Snapchat app. Clever. You can also have windows follow along as you move your head, in case you want to keep a window in your vision no matter where you’re looking. You can access a home button, a Control Center-like menu, and status information like the time by holding up your palm in a setup that reminds me of the ill-fated Humane Pin.

In my limited testing, it was all rather finicky. I often had to pinch a few times or make sure my hand was placed in just the right spot to get something to work the way it should. I never quite nailed the two-part action of flipping my hand up and then using my other hand to press the home button. While standing in the sun, it was much harder to see the augmented reality graphics.

Snap has beaten competitors like Meta to shipping a pair of glasses with displays in both lenses, letting it deliver a true AR effect and not just another flat screen. But by putting the AR display dead center in your vision, the Specs’ 51-degree field of view becomes a major limitation. It meant that digital elements kept slipping out of sight during my demos, which ruined the illusion that they were actually in the real world. While watching Lanterns on HBO Max in a browser in a moving car, I had to shrink the window to make it easier to see in front of me. While playing dominoes, I had to keep physically turning my head to see my dominoes and the playing board and back again.

Because it’s 2026, the Specs also have a dedicated AI chatbot assistant, but in my limited experience it was slow and inconsistent. With a “Hey Specs” command, I asked it to show me funny cat videos on YouTube, as suggested by a Snap rep. I had to ask it twice because it didn’t pick up the command the first time. When the command worked, it then took about 15 seconds for the Specs to pull up a YouTube page with search results for funny cat videos.

Watching that video also revealed to me a bizarre social interaction that people will have to come to grips with if AR glasses gain any sort of traction. On that YouTube page, I picked some random cat video collection, and it played in the background while the Snap rep kept talking to me. Even though the Specs were playing audio through the onboard speakers, the Snap rep standing right next to me said they couldn’t hear anything.

That made me feel weird — these glasses theoretically let you watch and listen to a private video while staring somebody else straight in the eye. Even when I wasn’t watching the video, I found myself constantly distracted from the in-person conversations I was having during the demo because my eyes were caught up with what they were looking at while my hands were focused on arcane gestures for tasks that only I could see. I didn’t feel very present.

Like Meta glasses, which are currently grappling with a “pervert” glasses reputation, the Specs also let you take photos and record video. They too have a privacy indicator light, and it’s arguably more prominent than Meta’s take: Instead of a light that’s off to the side, the Specs’ light is right in the center of the glasses. But I don’t know if, given the growing pushback against Meta’s glasses, a blinking light is enough to deter concerns about potential unwanted recording.

That bar in the middle is the privacy indicator light.

In 2024, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel told The Verge that there is an opportunity for computers to evolve to “support the ways that humans have long interacted socially by looking at each other eye to eye with much more natural interaction.” Today, Snap has a simpler message: It says that its vision with Specs is to “make computing more human.” But even in my controlled demos, I found that Specs were actually more computer than other hardware; the glasses are unmissable on my head, and the digital content that only I could see was getting in the way of me interacting with the other people in the room.

Still, these headsets are coming. Meta is working on a pair, Google has a new glasses initiative, OpenAI has reportedly considered smart glasses, and Apple is apparently planning to announce Ray-Ban Meta-like smart glasses next year (and it’s worth noting that former Apple CEO Tim Cook has repeatedly praised AR in the past). It’s clear they all see the next frontier as glasses with tech like cameras and screens that sit on your head. Specs will be the first real test of what AR glasses can be. But even after Snap’s years of work, they still might be coming out too soon.

Tech.title: The 2.5-hour AI-generated Odyssey movie is 2.5 hours too long
Tech.content:
Christopher Nolan’s engrossing take on The Odyssey dominated at the box office and spurred a newfound interest in classic literature among filmgoers. But a new retelling of the story made entirely with AI is so bad that it might just make viewers hate the original tale altogether.

The new film, called Odysseus: The Fall, comes via AI firm Fountain 0 and is written and directed by company cofounder Ash Koosha, who also lent his likeness to the title character and created all of the music. (The film’s credits are very short.) The studio’s only previous work is an AI film called Dreams of Violets that made it into Tribeca earlier this year. The Fall is, on its face, a much more ambitious project, billed as “the first completely AI generated film produced at the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” In reality, it’s nothing close to “the level of a Hollywood blockbuster.” That may not necessarily be surprising, but after watching the entire 2.5-hour production I nonetheless found myself constantly surprised by just how much worse things could get. The Fall is the opposite of a glimpse at the future of AI filmmaking — it’ll make you wonder if there’s really any future in it at all.

The movie is available to rent now for $9.99 and, as far as I can tell, you can only watch it via a web browser. In order to view it on my living room TV I had to mirror the screen from my phone, which is not exactly IMAX in 70mm. Things didn’t get much better once I pressed play.

The Fall is plagued by two main issues. The first is consistency. The world of the film is constantly morphing, to the point that it’s incredibly distracting. The height of the cyclops that traps Odysseus and his men changes from shot to shot, waves move in the opposite direction of the wind, mouths don’t match the words spoken (and sometimes they move without producing a sound at all), and oars bend and twist as sailors row. In one scene a huge fleet of boats is racing through the ocean and one of them is inexplicably moving sideways. The AI-produced voice-overs can be incomprehensible, and at various points the names of both Odysseus and Zeus are pronounced wrong.

If it were just the odd hiccup it might be understandable, but there are so many faults in The Fall that it can be hard to focus on anything else. I watched the movie with my 13-year-old kid and it basically became a game of finding the weirdest mistakes. I noticed that a sword magically turned into a dagger, and then she one-upped me by spotting an alien carcass roasting over a spit. The Fall seems like a film designed to prove why script supervisors exist.

The thing is, while all of the AI-induced errors are distracting, they’re also the most entertaining part of the movie. There isn’t really much to distract from in The Fall because it is so dull. Because current AI models are really only capable of generating scenes that last a few seconds, the movie feels like a disjointed collection of moments from the odyssey that have been stitched together with little rhyme or reason. If you didn’t already know the story going into this, I don’t think you’d have any idea of what was going on, because the film explains very little. You don’t even learn about Penelope’s suitors until the movie is almost over.

I also can’t think of a single aspect of The Fall that feels improved because of AI. The “acting” is bafflingly bad, with characters pausing for seconds at a time for no apparent reason and bursts of laughter that jolt you out of nowhere. There’s no weight to the action, as if this takes place in a world where things like physics and gravity are suggestions rather than constants. Similarly, there aren’t any cool or impressive effects that wouldn’t be possible without the technology. The monsters look like shabby stop-motion creatures from the 1930s, which is all the weirder when they’re put beside the smooth, hyperreal human characters that AI spews out. It’s not just jarring, it’s boring and ugly.

Koosha claims that he adapted this story because he “always felt passionately about Homer’s epic tale since [he] originally read it years ago.” It seems much more likely that he’s trying to skate by on the hype and energy created by Nolan’s film, turning AI slop into a modern-day iteration of direct-to-video cash grabs. But this also puts the film at an incredible disadvantage from the very beginning, inviting comparisons to one of the most critically and commercially successful movies of the last few years, one that was especially beloved because of the director’s insistence on human craftsmanship. Nolan is someone who cares deeply about film, and his passion and enthusiasm is why stars want to work with him and viewers flock the theaters to see his movies.

The existence of The Fall, meanwhile, shows utter contempt for the medium, attempting to boil the work of hundreds of skilled workers into slop produced by a tiny team. It’s so terrible it’ll make you appreciate human-made art all the more.

Tech.title: The AI data center e-waste problem is huge — and getting bigger
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

E-waste from the AI boom has been vastly underestimated, a new report warns. By 2050, it could become enough trash to fill 23 million shipping containers — roughly enough 40-foot containers to circle the world six times if lined up in a row.

It’s a significantly higher estimate of AI’s e-waste than previous studies have found because the authors of the new report factor in all the infrastructure needed to support servers in data centers. The broader scope provides a clearer picture of junk AI leaves behind, according to the nonprofit Basel Action Network (BAN), which published the paper today.

”AI may feel weightless, but every model depends on an enormous amount of highly specialized, cutting edge hardware,” Jim Puckett, founder and chief of strategic direction at BAN, says in a press release. “If companies and governments do not begin planning for this new waste tsunami, today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”

“Today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”

Less than a quarter of the 68.3 million tons of e-waste created each year worldwide is formally collected and recycled. Most e-waste is ultimately dumped into shadowy “informal” waste collection where burning or burying equipment can expose workers and the local environment to toxic materials like lead and chromium.

BAN predicts e-waste generated globally will triple in amount to up to 211 million metric tons a year by 2050. It attributes about 15 to 20 percent of that garbage to AI. Unlike previous AI e-waste estimates that focused on servers and GPUs, BAN expands its count to include other categories of equipment: power supply and distribution, cooling systems, backup power, and networking equipment. Notably, BAN also counts what it calls “AI Waste Contagion” — a wide-ranging category that incorporates everything from telecommunications infrastructure to personal devices likely to become obsolete and replaced earlier as a result of advances in AI.

Counting it all up, BAN expects 70,000 metric tons of e-waste per gigawatt of data center capacity. It cites a McKinsey projection of total data center capacity reaching up to 219GW by 2030.

Considering AI-related electronic equipment retired between 2025 and 2050, BAN concludes that’ll add up to between 395 to 617 million metric tons of e-waste by the middle of the century. It breaks down to about 8.6 million to 13.1 million metric tons of equipment retired each year as a result of AI.

Previous estimates of AI’s e-waste have been more conservative. But by focusing on servers and accelerators, past studies miss about 87 percent of a data center’s electro-mechanical infrastructure, according to BAN.

A separate study published in 2024 predicted that e-waste from AI could reach between 1.2 million and 5 million tons by 2030. Another study published in February found that AI servers could create between 131,000 and 225,000 tons of e-waste annually by the end of the decade — an amount that’s still comparable to all the e-waste produced by a country the size of Denmark.

Tech.title: Resident Evil is a comedy first and a thrilling nightmare second
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

When Paul W.S. Anderson’s Resident Evil hit theaters in 2002, video game movies were largely seen as a niche. Films like Mortal Kombat and Tomb Raider had proven that big-screen game adaptations could be successful, but the commercial and critical failure of projects like the 1993 Super Mario Bros. still cast a long shadow. And while Anderson’s vision of Raccoon City might have captivated audiences on the whole, many hardcore fans of Capcom’s games were left disappointed by the way the original movies wildly deviated from the source material.

Weapons director Zach Cregger’s new take on Resident Evil is a return to the franchise’s fundamentals and a choice example of how video game movies have evolved. Its story is stripped down and its zombified monsters are terrifying. It’s also chiefly a movie that’s trying to make you laugh. Cregger uses humor to amplify his Resident Evil’s horror — his spin on the games’ infected ghouls are meant to be as funny as they are disturbing. The film feels like it could be the beginning of a fantastic new era for the franchise, but what’s most impressive is how well it can work as one and done.

Though this Resident Evil is peppered with nods to Capcom’s games, it focuses on Bryan (Austin Abrams), a medical courier character created for the movie. Like most people living in his mountain town, Bryan knows that a drive over to Raccoon City in the middle of winter can be hell, but a last-minute, high-paying delivery gig is enough to convince him to make the trip. Even with the treacherous weather and spotty cellphone reception, Bryan’s journey with his mysterious cargo is mostly uneventful as he first sets out. But he begins to understand what kind of danger he’s wandering into when he accidentally runs over a shambling woman (Andrea Miltnerová) who doesn’t seem to realize that she’s just been hit by an out-of-control car.

Resident Evil’s first big scare almost immediately establishes the sense of humor Cregger leans into throughout the film. You can feel the fear oozing out of Bryan as he trudges into the woods looking for the woman, but that tension momentarily evaporates as the film smash-cuts to him coaxing her into his car so that he can get her the medical help she clearly needs. The same dread rushes to the fore when Bryan witnesses how Resident Evil’s infected humans can mutate into creatures that feel like nods to Katamari Damacy and The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. But it’s hard not to laugh when Bryan muses about how interesting the zombies’ transformations are to see up close.

Cregger knows that while viewers might not be familiar with Resident Evil’s lore, we can all appreciate how horror movies need their characters to make poor decisions. Abrams plays Bryan with a wide-eyed guilelessness that’s charming, but what really makes the character work is the way each monster encounter forces him to evolve into someone with better survival instincts.

By building the film around a civilian instead of highly trained special agents, Cregger and co-writer Shay Hatten give themselves the ability to tell a story that leans into the survival aspect of survival horror. Because Bryan is a bit of a dolt who’s constantly screaming in terror and fumbling his bullets when he’s scared, it often feels like the movie is replicating the experience of playing (or watching someone else play) a Resident Evil game for the first time. Bryan finds a couple of guns and a very limited number of bullets, but they’re nowhere near enough to make him feel safe as he trudges toward Raccoon City making the occasional stop to search seemingly empty buildings in hopes of finding a way to call for help.

The movie’s indoor scenes where Bryan’s rifling through drawers and tiptoeing down dark hallways are its most suspenseful because Cregger establishes early on that danger is always lurking just around the corner. Those moments are when it really seems like Cregger is channeling the essence of Capcom’s games, but you can also feel the director winking at his audience whenever Bryan talks about video games teaching him how to navigate his situation.

Image: Columbia Pictures

There’s a general straightforwardness to Cregger’s Resident Evil that sets it apart from many other recent video game adaptations. The film isn’t as concerned with overall character development as The Last of Us and its set pieces aren’t as large as The Super Mario Galaxy Movie’s. But those qualities work in the movie’s favor because they help draw your attention to all of the imaginative ways Cregger interpolates classic elements of Resident Evil storytelling and gameplay.

Especially coming after Weapons, Resident Evil feels like Cregger putting his mark on a beloved gaming property while breathing new life into a film franchise that was always fun, but lost its way as it grew in scale. Cregger has found a way to make the world of Resident Evil seem primed for more cinematic exploration, and to show us how far video game movies have come.

Resident Evil also stars Zach Cherry, Will Merrick, Zoé Bellas, Chris Lew Kum Hoi, Griffin Newman, and Magdalena Sittovaas. The movie hits theaters on September 18th.

Tech.title: Walmart takes a bite off the cost of Metroid Ravenous physical preorders
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Metroid series is going back to its 2D roots again with Metroid Ravenous for the Nintendo Switch 2, the first side-scrolling game in the series since 2021’s Metroid Dread for the Nintendo Switch. If you’re already excited enough to consider preordering, you can save $10 on the physical version of the game when you buy it from Walmart. It’s $59.88 instead of $69.99, about the same as buying it digitally. The game launches on January 28th, 2027, but it’s not clear how long the preorder discount will last. If it’s anything like other Walmart preorders, it may occasionally disappear.

Nintendo first showed off the side-scrolling adventure game at its September 2026 Direct, with a frantic trailer cutting between cinematic sequences, Samus dashing and rolling across a variety of environments, and engaging a number of enemies and bosses in battle. Samus absorbs some powerful abilities at the conclusion of Dread, and Ravenous seem to be all about plowing through anyone stopping her from escaping the planet. Other details of the story, including unique new mechanics, are being kept under wraps for the time being.

If you haven’t played Metroid Dread, I recommend it, especially at its $41.99 discounted price at Amazon. It’s part of Nintendo’s “Customer Appreciation” sale happening through September 26th, and several other games and accessories are cheaper, too.

Tech.title: Apple might make servers again to cash in on the AI rush
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

According to The Information, Apple is planning to get back into the server game and might just pair up with Nvidia to make it happen. Apple retired its Xserve line in 2011 and has largely left enterprise machines to other manufacturers since. But the growing demand for compute power as the AI industry continues to expand has apparently led the company to believe there is an opening for its powerful but efficient ARM-based M processors. Its Mac Mini and Mac Studio have proven popular with AI developers, which has led to shortages.

The server product, whether it’s called Xserve or something else, likely won’t debut until 2029. Word is that it will run on two or four (depending on the model) M8 Ultra chips. Apple only just announced the M6 in August, so the M8 line is a ways out.

It’s also rumored that Apple’s servers could incorporate Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion tech, which connects multiple chips together so they can operate as one. While the two companies have historically had a frosty relationship behind the scenes, recently Apple turned to Nvidia chips to power its revamped Siri servers. Incorporating NVLink could lead to further collaboration between the two, but plans could still change.

Tech.title: Iceland-based Treble raises $18 million for its voice simulation platform
Tech.content:
Voice AI has emerged as one of the hottest sectors in AI, with investors pouring in billions of dollars to serve use cases ranging from automating customer support and sales calls to creating meeting notetakers and developing AI smart glasses that use voice as the primary interaction surface.

Meanwhile, AI labs are quickly releasing models, and hardware makers are trying to create the best experience for consumers to interact with devices.

All of this new technology needs testing and a feedback loop for improvement. An Iceland-based startup, Treble, is positioning itself to be at the center of the voice AI industry by creating a simulation platform that can cater to model makers, robotics companies, and consumer hardware makers.

The company, founded in 2020 by acoustic engineers Finnur Pind and Jesper Pedersen, has raised $18 million in an extension of its Series A funding led by Paladin Capital Group, with participation from existing investors KOMPAS VC, Frumtak Ventures, EIC, and Omega ehf. It received an investment of $12 million in 2024, bringing its total raise to date to over $40 million. The startup counts Amazon and Logitech as customers.

Treble co-founder Finnur Pind Image Credits: Treble Image Credits:Treble

Treble has a few verticals related to simulation and data. For voice AI companies, it has a synthetic data generation platform that could be used for speech enhancement, noise suppression, and model training. It also evaluates voice AI models in different conditions to provide feedback to labs. Earlier this year, it partnered with Hugging Face to launch a benchmark for speech recognition models across different realistic conditions.

“Audio AI is really a data challenge, and this is where the most opportunities to enable next-generation models and hardware lie. To date, pretty much all sound-related AI has been made from recordings and data scraped from the internet. We believe that accurate physics simulation can be an alternative way to create data for sound,” Pind told TechCrunch.

The startup also focuses on hardware design and testing from a voice perspective. For instance, it works with headphone and speaker companies for virtual prototyping to help them understand how their product might sound. It could also test how a smart speaker can understand commands based on the positioning of the speaker. Lately, Treble has ventured into providing simulation testing for smart glasses and AI devices.

Pind said that the company is excited to work on wearables that could enhance hearing for users.

“I’m really excited about the next generation of these devices like headphones and smart glasses that can enable [a feature like] superhuman hearing. That’s an area where you can really just hear better in challenging acoustic environments. Maybe you are in a restaurant, and you only want to hear people within two meters of range, or you are in a seminar, and want to mute people around you,” he said.

Treble aims to increase its focus in the physical AI space, including robotics, automotive, and drone companies, to enable sound-based functions for them through testing and simulation.

Francois Ruether, VP of Paladin Capital Group, told TechCrunch that Treble’s platform, which simulates different models and devices, stands out; the platform’s importance will increase as it gets involved in more areas.

“Our thesis is that, as more products depend on understanding sound, this infrastructure becomes increasingly valuable across voice AI, wearables, robotics, and physical AI. Customers retain ownership of their models, products, and development workflows, while benefiting from a shared foundation of a simulation-native acoustic infrastructure layer,” Ruether said.

Tech.title: Your startup’s next teammate might be an AI agent: Gusto, Insight Partners, and Leland explain what that changes at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026
Tech.content:
The first few hires at a startup can define the company. But increasingly, not every new capability requires a new employee.

AI agents are beginning to take on engineering, customer support, research, and operational work that would previously have been assigned to early team members. For founders, that creates a new question before they even open a job requisition: What should people own, and what should be delegated to AI?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Josh Reeves, CEO and co-founder of Gusto; Michelle Johnson, senior vice president at Insight Partners; and John Koelliker, CEO and co-founder of Leland, come together on the Builders Stage for an insightful session called “Hiring When AI Is a Co-Founder.”

This session will explore how early-stage companies are building teams where humans and AI agents work alongside each other — and how founders can do that without sacrificing speed, accountability, or culture.

Join them at Moscone West in San Francisco, October 13–15, alongside 10,000+ startups, investors, and tech decision-makers exploring what it takes to build and scale the next generation of companies. Register now and save up to $200 on your Disrupt pass before rates increase on September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT. Save up to 30% more when you register as a group.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

The first 10 people in a startup may no longer all be people

For an early-stage company, every hire is a trade-off between capability, cost, and speed. AI agents add another option.

Engineering tasks, customer support, and operational work can increasingly be delegated to systems capable of completing multistep tasks rather than simply helping an employee complete them. That gives founders an opportunity to rethink what their earliest teams should actually look like.

Instead of automatically asking, “Who do we hire next?,” the starting question can become: “What work needs to be done — and is a person the best way to do it?” That distinction matters.

Giving work to an AI agent can help a small team move faster, but it also introduces new questions around ownership. Who checks the work? Who makes the final decision? What happens when an agent gets something wrong? And which responsibilities are too important to delegate? Those are no longer theoretical questions for companies building AI-native startups.

All these questions, and more, will be answered on the Builders Stage at Disrupt. Grab your pass by September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT to save up to $200. Bring your community and save up to 30%.

Three perspectives on the AI-native team shared at Disrupt

Josh Reeves sees the shift across a particularly broad customer base. Gusto supports more than 500,000 companies across payroll, benefits, compliance, onboarding, HR, and retirement, while combining AI with more than a decade of experience serving small businesses. That puts Gusto close to the day-to-day realities of companies deciding how — and when — to grow their teams.

Image Credits:Chloe Ellingson/Bloomberg / Getty Images

Michelle Johnson brings the startup scaling perspective. At Insight Partners, she works with CEOs and CROs across North America and Europe on go-to-market strategy, revenue organizations, and AI implementation. Before joining Insight, she helped scale Flock Safety from less than $1 million to $90 million in ARR as an early sales and revenue operations leader.

Her perspective raises a different set of questions. If AI agents can research prospects, prepare outreach, analyze customer data, or manage parts of the sales process, what should the human members of a revenue team concentrate on? And how does that change the skills a startup should prioritize when hiring?

John Koelliker sits directly at the intersection of talent and AI. As CEO and co-founder of Leland, a career and talent platform for the AI era, he brings experience across product and growth roles at LinkedIn, Curated, and Uber, alongside building a company focused on how people develop and apply skills in a changing labor market.

Together, they bring three different views of the same challenge: How do you design a startup team when some of the work can be done by agents from day one? Register by September 25 at 11:59 p.m. PT to save up to $200 on your pass and hear this session live on the Builders Stage. Bring your team or community with you to save up to 30% on passes.

What should people still own vs. AI?

Some of the most important decisions inside a startup are difficult to reduce to a workflow.

Who understands what customers really need? Who challenges a bad strategy? Who takes responsibility when something fails? Who builds relationships, motivates a team, or decides when the data is pointing in the wrong direction? As AI agents become more capable, those questions could become more important, not less.

The role of an early employee may increasingly be defined by judgment, ownership, and the ability to direct both people and machines — rather than simply completing a larger volume of tasks. That has implications across the startup ecosystem.

Learn how to build the company, not just the technology, on the Builders Stage at Disrupt

Early-stage companies have always competed on their ability to do more with less. AI agents could take that principle much further.

But a company is more than the sum of the tasks it completes. Founders still need people who can make decisions, take responsibility, understand customers, and create the culture around which a business grows.

The challenge is deciding where those people create the greatest value — and where an agent might do the job instead. That’s the conversation Josh Reeves, Michelle Johnson, and John Koelliker will take on at Disrupt.

Join them on the Builders Stage, and explore what happens when AI doesn’t just help your startup — but also becomes part of the team. Then continue the conversation with 10,000+ founders, investors, and operators across Moscone West, the Expo Hall, Startup Battlefield 200, and countless networking opportunities.
