Tech.title: Snap tries to make the case again for its $2,200 smart glasses
Tech.content:
When Snap debuted its long-awaited smart glasses, Specs, earlier this year, the reveal was not only underwhelming but also a genuine disaster. The glasses — which cost a whopping $2,200 and are vaguely reminiscent of scuba gear — inspired jeers online and calls for the company’s CEO, Evan Spiegel, to resign. The company’s stock subsequently nosedived.

Since then, Snap has clearly been looking for an opportunity to explain why Specs — a heavy, expensive piece of hardware that most casual consumers will probably be unable to afford — deserves to exist.

This week, the company had its chance to make that argument. At an event in Los Angeles, Spiegel and other Snap executives unveiled a variety of new features and services connected to Specs. The new updates seem clearly designed to help integrate the glasses into a broader array of digital activities and, in doing so, give Specs a clearer sense of purpose.

Image Credits:Snap (screenshot)

During Wednesday’s event, Spiegel shared details about a number of the new features. After a trippy promotional video that vaguely brought to mind an ayahuasca hallucination, the CEO took the stage and began a series of live demos.

New entertainment options — Specs can now connect with HBO Max and Spotify — provide a baseline of interactive fun that smart glasses have largely lacked until now.

Yet perhaps the biggest announcement was the launch of Specs Intelligence, which the company calls a new “anticipatory AI” system designed to pair not only with the company’s glasses but also with user devices — including iPhones and Macs. Snap claims that this new system “builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose to connect, helping you focus on what matters now while making progress towards your longer-term goals.”

Image Credits:Snap (screenshot)

Spiegel called this system an “AI native operating system with intelligence designed around your projects” that helps users “connect the dots across Lenses,” Snap’s term for its AR camera effects, available on both phones and Specs, “so you can get things done while focusing on what matters to you.” In practice, it seems to function more like an AI productivity app that can be used with Snap’s glasses but doesn’t require them.

Snap has also announced a new program called Specs for Enterprise, which allows the device to be integrated into corporate workflows. On Wednesday, the company announced partnerships with a number of different tech companies — including Amazon, Salesforce, Nvidia, and other firms — in an effort to make the device useful to staff at those companies.

What is the real-world utility of this, and who is this service really for? Apparently, the answer is IT technicians. While the actual scenarios in which Specs can be used are a little vague, a demo video played at the event showed an IT technician repairing some hardware with the help of Snap’s new glasses.

“We’re building out mobile device management, security controls, and ways to deploy and manage stacks across teams with the world’s most trusted providers, bringing peace of mind to IT departments,” Spiegel said.

Other announced features were slightly more head-scratching. For instance, one of the new experiences is an app, developed through a partnership with the NBA and WNBA, that allows users to practice basketball and improve their shot via the glasses’ AR capabilities. But, realistically, who is really going to play basketball while wearing heavy goggles on their head?

Also announced Wednesday was a new connectivity package for anyone who wants to use Specs on the go, away from Wi-Fi — like outside the home or office. Sold separately, the package includes a charging case with built-in cellular connectivity. That connectivity, which is being made available via a partnership with Verizon, costs $10 a month for Verizon customers and $20 a month for non-Verizon customers.

Spiegel ultimately framed Specs as a new way to engage with computing in a more human-centric format. “I will say it’s an interesting time to be launching a new computer because things in tech are pretty weird right now,” Spiegel said. “We’re being told that AI will take our jobs, that virtual worlds will replace the real one. Well, no, thank you. We do not accept that future. Making people irrelevant is not progress, and computers should make us more important, not less.”

Snap has repeatedly justified the product’s cringe-inducing cost by characterizing the device as a computer — albeit one you wear on your face. Whether consumers will go for that or not remains to be seen. The company has announced that it is hosting a Specs pop-up in Los Angeles in October before the devices ultimately ship later this fall.

Tech.title: Musk’s long-time backer is giving SpaceX stock to its investors
Tech.content:
In Brief

VC firm Valor Equity Partners, founded by Antonio Gracias, a long-time Elon Musk backer and current SpaceX board member, has opted to simply give away a chunk of its SpaceX stock to its limited partner investors, according to an SEC filing spotted by Bloomberg.

Valor made a killing on SpaceX after investing in it over decades, with entities controlled by Gracias owning more than 500 million shares at the time of the IPO. This was second only to Musk (who owned over 6 billion shares at the time). But instead of cashing out and issuing returns to LPs, Valor handed over 8.5% of its holdings to them, worth about $8.5 billion, Bloomberg estimates. Valor will still own more than 460 million shares after the giveaway, the SEC disclosure form says.

Transferring ownership of the shares could give those Valor limited partners a tax advantage. More importantly, it avoids dumping a giant tranche of shares into the open market. Such a dump could cause a glut of available shares and a corresponding dip in price. SpaceX is already down about 10% since its blockbuster IPO day.

Tech.title: Al Gore says the real AI risk isn’t data centers
Tech.content:
Al Gore has spent more than two decades as one of the most recognizable voices in the climate movement, so when he talks about AI, it’s worth paying attention to what he considers truly scary. And it isn’t what has people protesting data centers in the streets.

In an interview with TechCrunch this week alongside Lila Preston, head of growth equity at their investment firm Generation Investment Management, Gore said emissions from AI data centers aren’t what should keep people up at night, despite the mounting opposition over their environmental impacts. What should concern people more, in his view, are the warnings coming from inside the AI industry itself, and he takes them seriously.

It’s not a new position for Gore. This past May, for example, he described AI data centers to another outlet as a “cause for deep concern, but not panic,” and in our conversation this week, his central point about emissions was about scale.

“If you look at the emissions of all of the AI data centers put together, it’s only a fraction of the emissions from uncovered landfills in the world,” he said, adding that a comparable build-out is tied to something that gets far less attention: air conditioning.

It’s a valid observation (and one the AI labs should be using in their discussions with cities and states if they aren’t already). The International Energy Agency estimates that global air conditioning already consumes more electricity annually than the entire European Union, and with ownership still under 15% across the hottest, fastest-growing parts of the world, that demand is expected to triple by 2050, putting far more pressure on the grid than AI data centers over the same period.

Gore isn’t dismissive of concerns about how these data centers are being powered. “It is a matter of deep concern that some of the hyperscalers are jumping into new methane turbines,” he said.

But what worries him about methane turbines isn’t the AI workload driving demand so much as the prospect that building new gas plants to meet that demand locks in decades more of fossil fuel generation.

“I much prefer those that are supplying their energy needs with renewables and batteries,” he continued, saying he expects more companies to move inexorably in that direction simply because renewables are increasingly the cheapest option available.

In fact, Gore thinks the public backlash at planning-commission meetings has less to do with carbon emissions than with anxiety over automation upending society in the not-too-distant future.

“I think that part of the reason for the growing bipartisan opposition to data centers in so many parts of the U.S. is being driven by the underlying concerns about job losses and some of the other threats that experts inside OpenAI and inside Anthropic have been trying to alert the public to,” he said.

We also pressed Gore on the wave of warnings from AI industry leaders that has dominated headlines over the last week. Though President Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared a laugh at their expense on Monday during a conference in Los Angeles (Trump suggested that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s public call to slow the pace of capability gains, quickly seconded by Sam Altman and Elon Musk, was a “hoax”), Gore said he takes the warnings at face value.

“I think we went through a phase where some cynically suspected that the apocalyptic warnings were some kind of bizarre marketing strategy. If that was ever the case, I don’t think it is now,” he said. “I do think that Dario Amodei is very sincere, and I think that Sam Altman and Elon Musk were sincere in seconding [Amodei’s] warning of a few days ago.”

Gore being Gore (he often reaches for literature, Scripture, and pop philosophy to make a point), he invoked Maya Angelou’s well-known line: “When someone tells you who they are, believe them the first time.”

Part of what’s changed his calculus, he said, is recent, concrete behavior from AI systems themselves — pointing to “the recent example of models escaping confinement, collaborating secretly, covering their tracks, engaging in deceptive behavior,” and noting that Anthropic has said it stopped instances of Claude being used to help develop biological weapons in different countries.

That said, Gore doesn’t treat AI risk and AI’s climate potential as being in opposition. He cited a recent study from economist Nicholas Stern of the London School of Economics projecting that AI applications aimed at efficiency and waste elimination could drive global emissions down by 6% to 9% per year starting next decade.

If Gore’s focus was risk, Preston’s was where capital is already moving in response. She pointed to several fronts where the AI build-out itself is generating investable opportunities, not just consuming energy.

Among these, the firm is focused on opportunities to decouple compute from energy intensity at every layer of the stack, from the power supply down to green cement and green steel used in construction, storage optimization software, and database design. The firm is also focused on grid resilience and flexibility, as the mix of power sources grows more complex. Here, Preston noted, Generation has invested in Volue, a European company helping utilities pull more renewables into the grid, and Gridware, which places sensors on utility poles to monitor and help protect the grid from wildfire risk.

Gore tied the AI moment to a broader argument made in Generation’s 10th annual Sustainability Trends Report: This year marks the second time in four years the world has been “brutally reminded” that fossil fuels are a volatile source of energy, first with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and now with the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.

But unlike past years, when Gore’s exasperation with the pace of the clean energy transition was obvious, he doesn’t see these events as a setback but instead as reasons for countries to embrace it at long last.

Indeed, Gore noted that globally, clean energy investment now runs at roughly twice the level of fossil fuel investment. Of all new electricity generation capacity added worldwide last year, 86% came from renewables, and in the U.S. specifically, that figure was even higher, at 91%, “in spite of Donald Trump’s best efforts to slow it down,” he said.

China, in particular, received high marks from Gore, who, among other things, applauded Beijing for wanting to be measured on emissions reductions rather than improvements in carbon intensity.

Asked what’s changed more than he expected a decade into publishing this report, Gore immediately pointed to solar power.

“For me personally, the scope and scale of the solar revolution is the breakout star of the sustainability transition,” he said. After observing that it’s at, or near, the cost floor for new electricity generation right now — roughly tied with wind and meaningfully cheaper than gas, coal, or nuclear — he closed with a line from a friend in Tennessee that had stuck with him:

“If God had intended us to have a limitless supply of cheap, clean energy, he — or she — would have put a fusion reactor in the sky,” Gore said with a chuckle. “The joke makes itself.”

Tech.title: US automakers could soon be forced to include AM radio for free
Tech.content:
It turns out that the one thing that can apparently bridge Washington’s partisan divide is AM radio. U.S. automakers may be forced to build AM radio into new vehicles within the next year.

The House of Representatives, in a rare instance of bipartisan support, overwhelmingly approved legislation on Wednesday that would require new cars, trucks, and SUVs to be built with AM radio at no additional charge to consumers. The AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act, which would direct the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to require automakers to include AM radio in new passenger vehicles as standard equipment, will now head to the Senate.

Until recently, proponents of AM radio have waged an unsuccessful lobbying effort for a mandate, arguing that it offers critical information during emergencies because its signal can travel long distances. But a groundswell of support from Democrats and Republicans, the broadcast industry, emergency responder organizations, and even former administrators of the Federal Emergency Management Agency is pushing this legislation closer to becoming law.

And there is reason to believe the Senate will follow the House’s lead on the bill, which was co-sponsored by Senators Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas). Earlier this year, the senators secured 60 co-sponsors for their version of the bill, a critical threshold to overcoming a filibuster.

Cruz, who chairs the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and Markey hailed the decision in a joint statement Wednesday.

“This vote sends a clear message to car manufacturers that AM Radio is a lifeline that must be protected in new vehicles. From emergency response to sports, entertainment, and news, AM radio is an essential communication tool for tens of millions of Americans. It is now time for the Senate to pass the AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act and for this legislation to become law so AM radio remains a trusted and essential resource for commuters and communities across the country.”

A growing number of automakers, including BMW, Rivian, Tesla, and Volvo, have moved away from the century-old broadcast band in favor of software-defined vehicles that offer streaming services like TuneIn and SiriusXM. Ford had also removed AM radio from some vehicles but has since reversed course.

Tesla couldn’t be reached for comment; Rivian declined to comment for this story.

EV makers have led the charge because the electromagnetic interference generated by electric motors can affect the frequencies used by AM radio. Automakers have argued that this interference degrades the AM signal and audio quality.

Tesla doesn’t have AM receivers in the base versions of its Model 3 and Model Y vehicles. Rivian’s new R2 SUV doesn’t have an FM or AM receiver; however, the vehicle model offers AM/FM radio through the digital radio platform iHeartRadio for free. The Rivian R1S and R1T models allow customers to access FM content digitally or via built‐in receiver.

Tech.title: Noise wants to help everyday people  become paid content creators
Tech.content:
Marketing platform Noise aims to connect brands with content creators at a much lower cost than hiring traditional influencers or running standard ad campaigns.

That’s because many creators on the Noise platform are everyday people — anyone can download the app, regardless of follower count — and Noise presents them with campaigns they can join and create content for on their platforms of choice (TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube). It then pays them per view rather than a flat fee. Brands, meanwhile, 

On Wednesday, Noise announced a $5.5 million seed led by Capital Midwest, M25, and Grishin Robotics, bringing its total raise to $7.2 million. Others in the round include Capitalize VC and operators from companies like DoorDash.

The startup is tapping into the ever-expanding influencer market, in which 57% of young people and just a little over 40% of U.S. adults overall now want to take part. It joins other content creator infrastructure companies like Billo and JoinBrands.

Diego Kafie, Stu Feldt, and Nic Weber launched Noise in 2025 after spending two years building a mobile game app called Playbite, and it now touts 1.5 million creators on the platform.

CEO Kafie said the company’s top creators make more than six figures a year, and the platform takes a fee from what brands pay creators once views are delivered.

“Our top brands work with several thousand creators on autopilot,” he said. Right now, many of its customers are mobile apps, those working with startup budgets that want to employ influencer marketers. The goal is to one day work with companies of all sizes.

“They are the most interested in reaching a really wide range of potential customers, making them the prime users for something like Noise, where they can easily recruit a small army of people to become their biggest users and advocates,” Kafie said. “This gives brands unprecedented level of content diversity and reach at a fraction of the cost of other traditional marketing playbooks.”

Kafie, Feldt, and Weber came to this idea from their experiences at Playbite. “We tried a bunch of different creative marketing strategies,” Kafie said of how they tried to scale Playbite. For example, they attempted to recruit their own gamers and teach them how to create social content that promoted the app. “We started with five, ten, 25, then 100 people,” he continued. “Before we knew it, our installs were skyrocketing as this small army of people went to places like TikTok and posted engaging content daily about mobile games and our app specifically.”

Most importantly, he noted, this happened “at a fraction of the cost of traditional marketing playbooks,” because they were teaching regular people how to be content creators from scratch. “Had we gone to established creators with big followings and clout, their rates would’ve been cost-prohibitive for our scrappy startup budget.”

That gave them the idea for Noise. The fresh capital will be used to expand product capabilities and to hire. Noise also just launched its Organic-to-Ads program, letting brands take the videos that Noise creators make and run them as paid ads on Meta and TikTok, in addition to the creators’ posts.

“The creators still post to platforms,” he said. “But in addition, the brands can now put paid ads spend behind those creatives to reach more people.”

He pushed back when asked if this was a way to pay creators less than they could make on their own if a brand approached them. He said that brands will name their rates and creators can decide whether to say yes or no. He also emphasized that the platform specializes in working with “everyday people and turning them into brand-new creators.”

It’s harder to become an influencer these days, so this, Kafie believes, could be a way for many people to get around the stress, time, and money it takes to make it big in content creation on their own.

He said when a user first joins the platform, they take Noise creator training modules that teach them how to create content for brands. Those early creators can access only certain campaigns, but as they do more training and get hired for more work, higher-paid opportunities can come to them, Kafie said.

“By democratizing ‘becoming a creator’ to literally anyone with a smartphone,” he said, “we’re bringing costs down for brands, but enabling millions of people to make their first dollar on the internet.”

Tech.title: Pulley, a Carta rival, is shutting down
Tech.content:
In Brief

Cap table management platform Pulley announced this week on its website that it was shutting down, and its final day of operations and services will be December 8. In a twist, it said it has partnered with its rival, Carta, to offload customers; it’s also redirecting prospective clients to Carta.

Yin Wu, a serial founder and ex-Microsoftie, started building Pulley in 2020 and went on to raise over $50 million from top investors, including General Catalyst, Stripe, and Founders Fund.

Pulley didn’t offer a reason for the shutdown (we’ve reached out to Wu for comment, but she didn’t immediately respond). However, a former employee speculated online that Pulley wasn’t so much competing with Carta as it was with spreadsheets. And these days, startups can easily use AI to keep, improve, and maintain their spreadsheets.

In a statement posted to LinkedIn, Wu thanked her team and backers, writing that “though this is the closing of one chapter, I, along with many of our strongest team members, have no intention of riding off quietly into the night.”

“There has never been a better time to solve big problems,” she continued. “Thank you again to everyone who supported us over the years.”

Tech.title: The EU Wants to Break Up Kids and Their Chatbots
Tech.content:
The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.

The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to 6% of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.

Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.

Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.

The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED: “it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only.” “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clamp downs on addictive design more widely.

In documents seen by WIRED the European Commission says it is worried that dependency on chatbots may negatively impact a child’s development and its relationships with other humans. It’s also concerned by chatbots giving minors dangerous advice, including on their mental health and personal development, which it said can shape and encourage risky behaviour.

“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with children’s mental health,” President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press conference on Thursday. Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey across France, Germany, Sweden and Ireland. Australia and the UK are both attempting to restrict minors’ access to chatbots through their social media bans.

It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes generated by chatbots, which von der Leyen nodded at in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech: “We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.” While the EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August, the rules currently only apply to deepfakes generated for commercial use.

The Commission also blames digital distraction for a decline in basic skills in young people. Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don’t, according to research spanning 91 countries by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling “expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools,” researchers from independent network EU Kids Online wrote in a report.

Tech.title: Hundreds of Election Deniers Will Be on the Ballot This November
Tech.content:
On November 3, when voters across the US go to the polls, almost 200 election deniers will be on the ballot. Many of them have repeatedly undermined the very process they are participating in, and they will be looking to win some of the most powerful elected positions in the country—positions that would help determine how voting goes in future elections.

Following the primaries, there will be 197 election deniers on the ballot for congressional and statewide races in the midterms across 43 states, according to new data shared exclusively with WIRED by States United Action, a nonpartisan nonprofit that supports state officials in protecting elections.

These numbers include a sitting US congressman who voted against certifying the 2020 election results; a former state representative who integrated QAnon conspiracy theories into election denialism; and local election officials who have actively sought to undermine election results by pushing baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizen voting.

But for election experts and officials, one of the biggest concerns ahead of the midterms is the possibility that these election deniers could obtain oversight of the 2028 presidential election process. The data shows there are already 27 election deniers in 20 states who hold a statewide office with election oversight, like secretary of state or attorney general—positions that allow the holder to set voting rules or prosecute those they believe are cheating at the ballots. In November, 33 election deniers will seek to secure similar positions in states across the country.

“All Americans should be concerned if people who are trying to undermine trust in elections and trying to interfere in the election process are taking positions of responsibility over elections,” Wendy Weiser, vice president for democracy at the nonprofit Brennan Center for Justice, tells WIRED. “We've seen in recent years an increasing number of election deniers taking some positions of public trust. As the numbers increase, it just increases the risk to our election system. This really is an attempt to corrode the system from within.”

Tech.title: The Trump Administration Sends a New Signal to Alien Disclosure Whistleblowers
Tech.content:
Just over a year ago, Dylan Borland—a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist—told a House Oversight task force that he'd watched a roughly 100-foot triangular craft lift silently off the flight line at Langley Air Force Base in 2012. But there were some questions he couldn’t answer.

Nearly half a dozen times during the hearing, he told members of Congress he could only answer their questions, such as whether a private company he worked for was reverse engineering nonhuman technology, inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF. He said he was concerned whether he was “legally even allowed to answer” some questions and at one point cited a fear of being charged under the Espionage Act.

A year later, on September 14, the Defense Department announced it had lowered that risk, though it falls short of what some in the unidentified anomalous phenomena research community say is needed to achieve broad transparency.

The Pentagon said on Monday that it had issued a "targeted legal waiver" allowing all current and former “service members, civilian personnel, and contractors" holding UAP-related national defense information to disclose it to the White House–directed effort that has been dumping UFO files on war.gov since May.

The waiver, which hasn’t been made public, "supersedes civil and administrative enforcement provisions" of NDAs and special access program agreements, "strictly for communications directed to the PURSUE team," a reference to the White House program. Basically, if you signed a secrecy agreement and know something about UFOs, you can now tell PURSUE without being sued or losing your clearance, though the same protections don’t extend to speaking with Congress, the press, or the public. The release announcing the waiver says nothing about criminal law, and only covers agreements "previously executed within the United States."

Tech.title: Flock Once Touted Its Cameras as ‘Made in the USA.’ Now It’s Not So Clear
Tech.content:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley has said the company made its first license plate cameras in his Atlanta home, permanently scratching his dining table with drill marks. A decade later, where the company assembles its signature—and fiercely debated—product has become more of a mystery.

For years, Flock touted publicly that its devices were produced in the United States. But more recent marketing materials from the company reviewed by WIRED no longer specify where its cameras come from. One US manufacturer that previously identified Flock as a customer quietly removed a mention of the company from its website earlier this year as public backlash against the company’s surveillance technology grew.

The startup has become the subject of a nationwide protest movement that has prompted dozens of local governments to abruptly stop using its cameras. Congress is also considering legislation that would cut federal funding to states that fail to limit use of Flock and other license plate readers. While police have argued the cameras are crucial tools for deterring and solving crime, activists have criticized Flock for enabling officers to track the cars of their exes, share footage with immigration authorities, and follow the movements of pedestrians.

But Flock’s manufacturing supply chain has received scant attention, even though where its hardware is produced could have implications for US national security. WIRED spoke with current and former Flock employees and supply chain analysts, reviewed data from US import records, and watched past marketing videos featuring Langley to piece together the first account of how its hardware pipeline has evolved.

These discounts stack. So if you sign up multiple friends with your referral code, you get multiple $10 discounts. Check out the HelloFresh meal kit referral program here.

Take Advantage of HelloFresh Come Back Offers

Some of these discounts are only available to new HelloFresh customers. But there’s a hack to getting discounts anyway. After you pause or cancel your subscription, check your inbox after the next few days or weeks. Often, you’ll get HelloFresh coupon codes for discounts.

Typical HelloFresh “come-back” offers after a canceled subscription include: $100 to $180 off (spread out over several meal boxes), free shipping on the first box (after re-subscribing), free items such as dessert, breakfast, or an extra protein per meal, or a free meal box is offered after a break. Typical retention offers, for when customers try to cancel, include: 40% off the next box, if you decide not to cancel, or 25% off the next two meal kits. None of this is failsafe, of course, offers vary for each customer. But as with magazine subscriptions, sometimes canceling, or trying to cancel, will lead to a good discount offer from a company eager to keep your business.

When to Save the Most on HelloFresh Subscriptions

HelloFresh almost always has some sort of deal going, whether to bring in new customers with an especially choice HelloFresh coupon, or bring back previous customers with HelloFresh discount codes and retention offers. But summer tends to be one of the times they offer the steepest discounts, including 10 free meals across several boxes, complimentary appetizers, free ready-made items, or free shipping on select boxes.

The other big times for HelloFresh coupon codes are around Black Friday and the end of the year. HelloFresh often launches limited-edition holiday meal boxes and themed meal kits, not to mention discounts for returning customers looking to cook more at home as part of New Year's resolutions.

Tech.title: I Tested New Keurig Milk Pods for Instant Frothy Lattes
Tech.content:
I’d wager most American coffee-drinkers have sampled a Keurig brew. If you don’t already own one of the single-serve coffee makers, perhaps your aunt shared a cup during the holidays, or there’s one in the office break room. Intuitive to use, easy to maintain and long-lasting, the appliance offers terrific practicality. Simply pop in a pre-bought coffee pod, hit a button and watch a cup pour out.

Courtesy of The Milk Pod, such easy extraction now extends to dairy, too. Compatible with Keurig brewers, these single-serve capsules produce rich-textured milk with a single push. Impressively, the pods are shelf-stable for 15 months and don’t even require refrigeration. Currently available in three classic coffee flavors — plain, vanilla and caramel—they’re made with milk powder and natural ingredients. Rather than just hot milk, the dairy’s composition turns out frothy, yielding a latte-like consistency. It’s an intriguing addition to Keurig’s already expansive pod selection.

Coffee and milk, all at the press of a button

Milk Pods load in just like normal pods. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Unlike a milk frother or steam wand, the pods require minimal instruction. They insert right into the K-Cup slot, no adjustment necessary. The Milk Pods entail no specialized setup; I was already sampling the dairy only minutes after opening the box.

As I brewed with Milk Pods one morning after the next, the initial ease continued. It’s recommended to brew the milk before the coffee, both to a six-ounce size, so the two liquids fit into a standard mug. As long as I didn’t accidentally press the wrong volume (my Keurig offers 6-, 8- and 10-ounce settings), I couldn’t make any mistakes.



Really, the only slight annoyance with the setup is the constant need to refill the water. My Keurig has a 30-ounce water tank, which means I need to top it up at half capacity. During only the second round of coffee, the brewer pinged me to take the reservoir to the sink, an upkeep that didn’t take much effort. Functionality-wise, the pods are remarkably easy. Pouring cold dairy out of the fridge is the easiest milk-integration technique. It’s hard to imagine a more consumer-friendly system.

Convenience is cool and all, but how do the pods taste?

Milk comes out hot and frothy, ready to be mixed with coffee. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

From dozens of seasonal K-Cups to various brand partnerships, Keurig capsules number in the hundreds. I sampled the Milk Pods with a generic brand of K-Cup from a local grocery store. Filled with dark-roasted coffee, the capsule brewed into a strong, lightly bitter-tasting brew – exactly the kind of flavor profile I’d dilute with milk. My chosen K-Cup wasn’t espresso-style, so the consistency resembled drip coffee.

Still, all three Milk Pods added a pleasant thickness to my Keurig coffee. The plain capsule lent the coffee a neutral creaminess, reminiscent of a latte, but nevertheless distinguishable from standard milk. The mouthfeel and taste reminded me of creamer, albeit with a more natural dairy character. Unlike the satisfying micro-bubbles in freshly steamed dairy, I picked up a smidge of powdery solids on my tongue. The cup wasn’t disappointing, but I still prefer the frothiness of fresh milk.

After you run a milk pod through the system, you simply load your coffee of choice. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

The bolder character of the flavored pods made the dehydrated downside less noticeable. I preferred the caramel of the two, which offered a complex nutty bitterness that paired well with my coffee. Sweet yet not saccharine, the pod reminded me of a well-made caramel candy. The vanilla capsule overpowered my coffee more, yielding a strong vanilla-syrup-like flavor. I could see this pod pairing better with other K-Cups, perhaps elevated even further in an iced latte. Overall, I found the Milk Pods pretty impressive for a shelf-stable product, but not quite cafe-quality.

In favor of shelf stability

Comparing the Milk Pods with fresh dairy reveals some differences, but you also have to consider convenience. The year-long durability, combined with no need for refrigeration, makes the pod worth stocking, even if it’s not a daily option.

Over several weeks of trialing the capsules, I left town and came back. The Milk Pods meant I didn’t need to worry about a carton left spoiling in the fridge. Plus, the morning after I returned, I didn’t need a bleary-eyed shopping run for my morning latte, either. I’d be happy to come across Milk Pods in a setting like an Airbnb or hotel. Given the self-contained ease of use, the pods align well with Keurig’s ecosystem. I could also see myself brewing the milk into a K-Cup of black tea or hot chocolate, making it a versatile Keurig option.

Milk Pods cost a dollar each, roughly the same as a coffee K-Cup. Nikita Ephanov/CNET

Thinking about cost

Consumed day to day, coffee costs add up. A hot latte from a cafe averages well over $5, and even home-brewing can dent the grocery budget. A K-Cup capsule and a Milk Pod cost $1 each, for an affordable $2 drink. Especially since you can buy a Keurig K-Mini machine for as little as $50, switching to this setup can save you money on coffee out in under a month. Plus, a Keurig requires minimal expertise, so you won’t need to learn how to make coffee.

Still, with a bit more effort, you can find better-priced coffee and milk options. On average, a gallon of milk retails for $4.30, with 21 six-ounce servings of dairy — that’s just over 20 cents per cup. You will need to steam the milk yourself. Handily, though, Keurig sells a $9.50 frother for the task. Fresh milk takes more effort — but to my taste, the flavor and texture are better. Not to mention, warming fresh dairy yourself lets you try out alternative milks as well as milks with varied fat compositions. Want a touch of sweetness in your cup? You can always grab a bottle of syrup and mix in a pump or two.

I wouldn’t switch to Keurig brewers specifically for this milk product, but Milk Pods are a convenient option and may be worth buying if you already use a Keurig. They’d also be handy to have on hand when you’ve run out of milk but are too bleary-eyed to make a morning run to the market.

Tech.title: Google Home Stuns by Announcing AI Support for Claude and OpenClaw
Tech.content:
Google told Google Home customers and developers on Wednesday that it would add smart home support for other AI agents beyond its own Gemini AI. The company’s announcement says that “any agent that supports calling [Model Context Protocol technology] tools can now interact with all of the devices and event history in the Google Home ecosystem.”

The announcement specifically names Anthropic’s Claude, the open-source AI agents OpenClaw and Hermes and the Google Antigravity coding platform as options that will soon work with Google Home.

Google previously released a version of its AI, called Gemini for Home, to act as a voice assistant and controller for all the smart devices that could connect to the Google Home app, including smart lights, smart heaters, home security cameras and smart thermostats.

Now, using Model Context Protocol technology that previously helped AI users add agents to Google Workspace. Google will begin rolling out support for other AIs in Google Home. This means you could use the voice mode in your Claude AI agent to control your thermostat, for example, or set up other automations and tap into data that Gemini for Home may not provide on its own.

Google says AIs will be able to perform more complex Google Home tasks, such as compiling security camera text summaries of what the cameras have seen, as well as use personalized dashboards for home control instead of the Google Home interface.

As of Wednesday, this ability has begun rolling out, but only to Google Home Premium Advanced users in the US, which means you’ll need a $20 subscription to access these capabilities. It’s early access, which means it could be buggy or have limitations. Google is encouraging users to report feedback to its smart home developers’ help channel.

A representative from Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.



Google has focused on Gemini and its own home speakers thus far. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

I’m interested in seeing whether Claude and the other agents will be more accurate and useful than Gemini for Home, which has its share of problems. I’ve found that Gemini for Home doesn’t always understand complex commands as intended, or fails to operate devices that are connected and ready. So there’s room for improvement, and opening the platform up to other AI agents could make that happen.

The versatility of AIs like OpenClaw could also allow users to set more advanced automations, like tying thermostat actions to very specific local weather reports, or – well, let’s just say I’m very curious what people will come up with.

However, I’m dubious of the benefits of creating your own customized dashboard and control center using AIs like Claude. I’ve seen and played with smart home dashboards like these before and haven’t been impressed. They’re still a bit clunky, get things wrong, don’t always do what they say and are difficult to troubleshoot thanks to the vibe coding involved. Google pays people lots of money to design a user-friendly interface with reliable settings and commands, which still tends to be the best option for the average user who doesn’t have very unique home interactions.

Google Home isn’t the first, but it is the biggest

Devices like the Homey Pro have offered third-party AI support for years. Homey

Google Home isn’t the only platform offering this AI support, although it’s the first of the big three — Apple Home, Amazon Alexa and Google Home — to offer anything like this.

For the past few years, the open-source platform Home Assistant has served as the premier gateway for users integrating advanced AI like OpenClaw and Claude into their living spaces. Backed by an extensive library of setup guides, the platform caters directly to privacy-minded and tech-savvy homeowners who prefer localized control over cloud-dependent alternatives.

While software forms the backbone of these setups, hardware ecosystems have quickly evolved to bridge the gap. Universal hubs like those from Homey streamline the integration process, offering plug-and-play compatibility for disparate devices. Device manufacturers like SwitchBot are actively building into this ecosystem by designing proprietary hubs that enable their smart hardware to communicate natively with OpenClaw.

But if you want to use Google Home and its existing smart device support and automations, this is the first time you can add an extra layer of control with a third-party AI.

Together, these shifting software and hardware landscapes reflect a broader consumer push toward highly customizable, AI-driven home automation.

Third-party AI in homes invites risks, too

I’d advise caution when integrating an AI such as Claude with your home system. Google’s MCP support includes safeguards that Google can implement when allowing AI systems to operate within its ecosystem. But expanding that access also introduces new variables, and it’s possible that new vulnerabilities could emerge as well.

One concern is prompt injection, sometimes referred to as smart home promptware. These attacks can hide malicious AI instructions in seemingly innocuous emails or calendar events, potentially allowing an attack to control home devices without the user’s knowledge. Google encountered similar issues in early versions of Gemini, though the vulnerabilities were swiftly patched. Adding additional AI systems into the mix could create more opportunities for vulnerabilities of this kind to emerge.

Tech.title: Tyrannosaurus Rex Was Warm-Blooded and Able to Live in the Arctic, Study Finds
Tech.content:
It was once widely believed that dinosaurs were all cold-blooded creatures, since they were classified as reptiles. But there is an increasing amount of evidence to the contrary, though scientists still don’t know the exact body temperatures of most dinosaurs. A domino in that discussion appears to have fallen, with a new study from researchers at UCLA that says the Tyrannosaurus rex had a similar body temperature to humans.

The research, published Wednesday in Science Advances, was done in cooperation with the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, which provided teeth from Thomas the T. rex, a 34-foot-tall, 66-million-year-old specimen found in Montana in 2003 and one of the most complete in the world.

Researchers from UCLA measured isotopic signatures on the tooth enamel to determine the giant predator’s body temperature.

According to Robert Eagle, co-author of the study and associate professor at UCLA’s Institute of the Environment and Sustainability, it’s possible to glean information from any bone in the body, but teeth are especially helpful because “tooth enamel has large crystalline structures that are extremely durable,” which helps them resist “chemical alteration” from being underground for eons.

Based on that process, the team determined that the T. rex’s body temperature was likely around 36.3 degrees Celsius (about 97 degrees Fahrenheit).

This puts the T. rex in the same general category as humans with our 98.6-degree bodies. It also puts them in the same neighborhood as Indian and African elephants, as well as large, flightless birds like ostriches and emus.

“This is the first thermodynamically and relatively direct measure of body temperature,” Eagle told CNET in an email.

UCLA created the process years ago and used it to determine that the megalodon was also a warm-blooded predator. However, the method destroys the samples, which led the National History Museum to deny UCLA the teeth until the process could be made more efficient, thereby sacrificing smaller parts of the teeth.

“Nobody hands you a T. rex tooth unless you can show them you only need a few milligrams,” Aradhna Tripati, climate scientist, co-author of the study, and director of the Center for Diverse Leadership in Science, said in an email to CNET. “The instrument and method that my lab did is what made the science possible. It was over a decade of work involving senior scientists, like Rob, and technical staff like the lead author of this study.”

What this tells us about the Tyrannosaurus rex

Thomas the T. rex, one of the most complete T. rex specimens in the world, on display at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles, donated parts of three teeth for UCLA’s research. Zissoudisctrucker/Wikimedia

This sounds like a simple little thing, but it actually has some rather large implications. A prior study from 2022 suggested that, while reptiles are cold-blooded, evidence supported the idea that meat-eating dinosaurs had avian metabolisms, which would make them warm-blooded, whereas others, like the plant-eating Stegosaurus, were possibly cold-blooded.

“It’s thought that many dinosaurs, but not necessarily all, were warm-blooded,” Eagle said. “However, even amongst warm-blooded (or endothermic) organisms there are questions of the degree — they can be warm-blooded like sloths or anteaters (low-level endothermy), modern large mammals, or avian endotherms, which typically have higher metabolic rates than mammals.”

At the time, researchers could only guess at the general temperature of many of these dinosaurs, so the study by UCLA not only backs up that the T. rex was warm-blooded, but it’s the first such study to produce precise measurements.

“For an animal this famous, it is remarkable how little we actually knew,” Tripati said. “We had constraints on T. rex metabolism, mainly from bone and biomechanics, some of which has been controversial. We did not have a direct body temperature determination.”

Figuring out the core body temperature of the T. rex can give scientists all sorts of data about how they behaved and where they lived, and help explain some things humans already knew. For example, Tripati says that T. rex fossils have been found all the way up in Alberta and Saskatchewan and all the way down to Texas. No reptile alive today has that kind of range since they are cold-blooded and need to stick to warmer climates.

“Thermal physiology drives behavior, range, energy budget and how a species responds to a changing climate,” Tripati said. “A warm-blooded T. rex could have gone almost anywhere on the continent, including the high Arctic. That is a very different animal from a sun-basking reptile.”

Eagle added that being warm-blooded means the T. rex likely had to hunt more often than originally thought to maintain its energy — and said it’s even possible that the T. rex migrated to find food, which may have led it into colder climates.

Tech.title: I Tried Snap Specs: Really Big, but Also Like Nothing Else Out There
Tech.content:
Out in a courtyard at Snap’s Santa Monica, California, headquarters, I’m kicking a soccer ball around. I’m terrible at sports. But a glowing arrow stretching across the ground points me to a flashing target I’m supposed to dribble the ball to. I get there and get pointed somewhere else. I’m playing a virtual soccer game, but the ball is real. And the big Spec glasses I’m wearing are making it happen.

When Snap announced its $2,195 augmented reality glasses back in June at the Augmented World Expo conference in Long Beach, California, everyone mocked them. Absurdly large, crazy expensive. I was waiting to try them first, and now I have, for about an hour. I don’t think they’re all-day glasses, and neither does Snap CEO Evan Spiegel, whom I spoke with after my demos. “I’d still think of them today as a computer, and it’s going to be more session-based,” he tells me. “Almost like a pair of reading glasses you put on to get something done. But I don’t think we’re far away from lighter, less expensive and far more capable versions.”

I don’t think I’d want to use them all the time in my everyday life. But damn, I want to go to a museum or theme park or theater experience that uses them.

While most of the smart glasses that exist right now either serve up just audio and cameras and maybe a basic head-up 2D display, Snap Specs are more like a portable mixed reality device, something like a very pared-down Meta Quest but with see-through lenses. It’s another evolution of AR headsets going all the way back to Magic Leap and Microsoft HoloLens, but unlike those, Snap’s got all the pieces to fit into one arguably reasonably sized set of glasses.

Snap Specs are big. But there’s no extra battery pack or processing puck. Jesse Orall/CNET

Are these doorways to smaller glasses? A toolkit for AI? A way for Snap to try to get ahead of Apple, Google, Samsung and Meta while it can? Yes, possibly, but they also feel like the best-functioning prototype of an AR glasses idea that still isn’t mainstream for anyone yet. Snap’s also announced a charging case that doubles as a cellular hotspot with Verizon service in the US, a way to try to make this work standalone without a phone, that costs an extra $200 in a bundle with the glasses.

In my time with Specs, I felt like I was back in familiar AR experiences… but in the best current glasses-like form possible, given where tech is at. Which ends up being a state of existence unlike everyday glasses at all.

Specs are big even on me, and their lenses have a hazy look with the lens inserts added in. Scott Stein/CNET

Big, chunky, fine to wear, not normal glasses

First, the fit: Are the Snap Specs uncomfortable? Weirdly, no, not for a half hour at least. The very thick arms sort of rested against my temples, with a bit of pressure that didn’t bother me. My ears bent down a bit, but not in a way I noticed (till I felt them). The 4.7- to 4.8-ounce (132- to 136-gram) frames (depending on the size you get) are much heavier than other smart glasses, but they balance the weight well on the side of my head, though I sometimes felt them slipping down my nose.

But these are clearly not normal glasses, in any sense. Not just the design, which pushes at the very edges of “big eyewear.” The lenses are rainbowed because of their waveguide layer that shows 3D projections in AR. Unlike Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays, which hide most of the waveguide, these have a notable sheen.

The -8 lens inserts on Specs, snapped into the pair I was wearing. Scott Stein/CNET

Also, they don’t use standard installed prescription lenses. Instead, there are lens inserts that, well, snap in. Honestly, I prefer this. That makes the glasses look even chunkier, but it also means that if Snap were to use these devices at a theme park, a museum or some public space, demoing them would be a lot easier. I use snap-in lenses for VR headsets all the time. And finally, Snap at least makes inserts that go up to -8, which is basically where my heavy nearsightedness is at.

Seen from the side, Snap Specs show off their rainbow-tinged waveguide lens sheen. Scott Stein/CNET

Displays that are fine, but not always great

Specs have a limited field of view, far more limited than that of VR headsets (or even Xreal’s upcoming Aura pair of tethered AR glasses). It’s better than Snap’s previous Spectacles, and kind of close to or better than my memories of Magic Leap 2. The portrait-style vertical viewing area is tall but not that wide.

It’s wide enough, at least, to watch YouTube video highlights of the Jets-Titans game in a browser, which I call up by saying “Hey Snap” and asking the onboard AI. The display is bright enough indoors, but semi-transparent and ghostly like all AR glasses, and it can get washed out in bright light. That’s why these glasses also have transition lenses that become sunglasses outdoors.

I tried them outside and found the experience usable. But the resolution and the clarity are steps below what sharper micro OLED displays in glasses and headsets can do.

Me kicking a ball around through a 3D game called Football Trainer (captured on Specs).

A familiar set of experiences (for me)

I tried Snap’s developer Spectacles a bunch of times in the past, which showed a whole augmented reality OS that works with hand tracking and launches “Lens” apps, some 2D, some full 3D, that can map into the real world. A lot of those were back here, because Specs supports all the independent lenses and creator stuff that Snap’s been building out for a while. But I only got to try a handful of the new Specs during my demo.

I browsed YouTube in a window I called up, resizing the floating window as big as I could and pushing it back and forth with a cursor I’d control with my hands outstretched and pinching to tap. Some apps let you “touch” things directly or pinch them, but most involve aiming your outstretched hand and controlling an air cursor like a Jedi. When windows got far away or small, it became a little hard to aim and tap at times, but looking at your open palm brings up a button dashboard for recentering things, bringing up the home screen, or turning AI on or off. Windows can follow you if you want, as you walk around.

What the app dashboard looks like inside Specs. I didn’t get my own capture of it, but it’s accurate. Snap

I even wore Specs in a car: One demo put me in an SUV circling the parking lot while I kept watching Jets-Titans plays, testing how the built-in travel mode handled stability in motion. Pretty well, actually. The display stayed pinned and didn’t drift, and I didn’t get carsick. I enjoyed my Jets win while I could.

I tried connected experiences, one of Snap’s more intriguing features, sitting across from a Snap team member wearing a pair. We looked at each other to begin a shared session, and launched a dominoes game that was apparently co-developed with one of Snap’s celebrity ambassadors, NBA star Jimmy Butler.

A capture from another pair of Specs showing the domino game we were both playing together. Snap

It was pretty basic: We laid virtual dominoes out one by one on the table in front of us, seeing the shared layout together. We could have just used real dominoes instead. But this idea, with other games I didn’t try – laser tag-like arena battles, virtual table tennis, or even larger group experiences that could support up to 30 people, according to Spiegel – could open some fascinating ideas. I like that these connect simply by looking at someone else wearing them.

Snap’s visualization of Navigation is exactly like what it felt like in-Specs when I tried. Snap

I tried a navigation app that hovered a 3D map in front of me, showing me how to walk to Santa Monica College. I shrank the layout down to a smaller directional arrow pointing the way.

And I tried working on Specs, launching Google Docs with a paired Bluetooth keyboard. That definitely wasn’t a great experience, mainly because of keyboard input lag in my session. But could you try to make this a portable work device? Snap is trying to prove it out.

Snap Specs have a set of quick-access buttons you can see when you look at your open hand. Scott Stein/CNET

I also tried live translation with a Snap employee who spoke Italian to me while I saw captions in English pop up in front of me – something I’ve done on other smart glasses, from Even Realities G2 to Meta Ray-Ban Displays to Google and Samsung’s upcoming glasses.

The most promising thing to me was kicking around a soccer ball outdoors using an app called Football Trainer. The training aspect wasn’t perfect, and I sometimes worried I’d try to finesse the ball to the virtual target and trip over myself in the process. But, I noticed that the glowing overlays had no occlusion, or a way of letting the ball or my legs look properly positioned over the graphics, something that exists on devices like Apple Vision Pro. Instead, the graphics overlapped the ball and my legs.

Snap Specs have thick arms that house the side projectors, but they feel solidly built. The arms don’t flex out, though. Scott Stein/CNET

But that real-world overlay showed me possibilities. I’ve tried Snap Specs with demos of overlaid virtual pets before, and tried theme park-like augmented reality experiences with other companies using hardware like the Quest 3 (DreamPark’s Mario Kart-like driving experience, where I rode a motorized unicorn along a virtual road). Snap Specs could do things like this if location-based experiences were built to support it. I saw an AR play in New York that used an older Magic Leap 2 to project virtual actors in front of a real audience. Snap Specs could do it better.

Snap promises its Intelligence AI agent will work across Mac, iPhone and Specs. Snap

AI ambitions with an agent called Snap Intelligence, too

Snap’s also betting hard on AI, to no one’s surprise. A newly announced agentic app called Snap Intelligence promises to work with Macs and iPhones and on Snap Specs glasses, tapping into your connected apps and information and providing recommendations and actions to help run your life.

The idea sounds like Meta’s recently launched AI agent Muse, which is likely to extend to Meta’s glasses hardware more expansively at next week’s Meta Connect conference. Snap’s getting ahead of that likely news here, but I wasn’t able to demo Snap Intelligence at all during my Specs briefing in Santa Monica. That’s all coming later this fall, per Snap, to time with the glasses launch.

“It actually installs on your Mac, so it can use your Mac for you,” Spiegel says to me about Snap Intelligence. “It can also log into services for you without accessing your credentials, because it can just use your keychain.” But he also promises the agent won’t act without your knowledge: “It just doesn’t do anything until you say it’s OK. It won’t change anything or send anything, or anything like that, until you say OK.”

Spiegel is bullish on lots of AI tools working in Specs beyond the company’s own Intelligence agent, from AI-infused AR experiences to running platforms like ChatGPT or agentic systems on the glasses. Snap’s also pushing promises of business partnerships for Specs with Amazon and Nvidia, among others, exploring how the chunky glasses could be worn in either offices or factory floors. Would they be safe and reliable enough to use? It’s unknown yet. But there aren’t any other current AR glasses with full world-tracking 3D and hand tracking in the size and form of Specs yet. Spiegel sees it as “get that big screen experience if you want it, but ultimately, hopefully, get the computer out of the way and just supervise agents who are getting things done on your behalf.”

The transitions lenses kicking in on Snap Specs. Would you know I was wearing smart glasses? Scott Stein/CNET

Privacy plans: Maybe being big and obvious is better?

Snap isn’t trying to hide what Specs are, something Spiegel seemed to celebrate as we chatted. Unlike Meta’s glasses, which can seem so normal that you wouldn’t notice the cameras in the corners, Specs are very much not standard-looking eyewear. Aas Spiegel said to me, you’d know if someone was wearing them. Will that help address growing privacy concerns on smart glasses that are increasing every month?

Recording photos and video clips, including captures that show your augmented-reality experiences overlaid, is done by pressing a side button on the glasses, which then lights up a big LED light. There’s also a clever new snapping gesture for taking photos, which is appropriately on-brand…and again a clearly visible gesture, although one people might not know was a photo-taking trigger.

Spiegel reflected on Snap’s own history of camera glasses, which extends way further back than Meta’s. He tried to make Snap’s Spectacles glasses look unique, even strange, to celebrate their distinct style…and also broadcast that they were different. It made me wonder if smart glasses should all be doing this, in the spirit of the at-the-time odd-looking, long-stemmed first-gen AirPods.

A cellular-enabled charging case for Specs could make these work away from phones. Scott Stein/CNET

Too ambitious, maybe, but these would be perfect for demos

Snap’s going for it all with these Specs, but I have concerns for sure. Battery life (promised as “up to four hours”), which I didn’t get to truly test during quick demos where I swapped pairs of Specs for different experiences. A not-perfect display. 3D experiences that sometimes looked good, sometimes a step below what a higher-powered VR headset could do. And would any of this really replace a phone at all? I doubt it.

But Snap is aiming to host demos for Specs at a new LA flagship store this fall, something I hope will expand to other locations. And installations and experiences. I’d gladly buy a ticket to a fun event where these Specs were used for a collective immersive experience, but I wouldn’t be compelled to buy a pair. Demos and experiences feel like the next step, and these Specs finally feel ready to be worn. Not all the time, but at least for a while.

Snap Specs (left) next to my own thick glasses (right) for comparison. Scott Stein/CNET

Specs seem like part of a new wave of odd VR/AR devices pushing beyond their previous categories, trying to be more or to connect to other systems and services: Valve’s Steam Frame, Xreal Aura and Snap Specs. Specs are the closest living relative to the Meta Orion AR prototype glasses I demoed two years ago, but they’re still full of question marks. And yet, they’re also likely to be a place to prototype AR and AI ideas in outdoor spaces.

I want to see what else they can do, but that’ll have to wait until a review later in the fall. In the meantime, I appreciate they’re trying something no other hardware is doing yet…but also, there’s a reason others haven’t succeeded yet. Size and compromises to get to AR glasses are still a big challenge, but Snap’s Specs are the closest I’ve seen to making it work. It’s far from perfect, but it’s a start.
